en: Now follow the Laugākṣi Gṛhyasūtras belonging to the Caraka recension of the Kaṭha school.
Accompanied by the commentary composed by Devapāla. First Section (Kaṇḍikā).
Homage to Narasiṃha, who is terrible with his fearsome fangs and claws.
He is intent upon the total eradication of the wicked and unsubdued Daityas who have obstructed the path of the righteous. || 1 ||
I offer this profound and expansive meditation,
which enables one to perceive the ultimate reality of the ocean of saṃsāra and serves as a wise helmsman for the attainment of the wealth of true human goals.
I bow with supreme devotion to Sarasvatī. || 2 ||
Having praised the feet of his father, Śrī Haripāla,
Devapāla will set forth the manual for the domestic ritual (gṛhya) concerning the sacrificial post (kaṭha) accompanied by its mantras.

The sacrificial rites (*vaitānika-karmāṇi*) have been expounded in thirty-nine chapters. Now, those rites to be accomplished by means of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) are being described. Although the sacrificial rites are preceded by the performance of domestic rites, nevertheless, because they are rooted in direct injunctions (*pratyakṣa-vidhi*), the author of the Sūtra has expounded them first. Thereafter, having prescribed the vows and other observances understood from those [injunctions]—since they are more proximate due to being statements of the injunction’s subject matter (*vidhyuddeśavākya*)—he will describe the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) as understood from the wording of the mantras (*mantravarṇa*).

In this regard, members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who have performed their marriage are entitled to the *gṛhya* (domestic) rites. Marriage, moreover, is for one who has studied the Veda, according to such Smṛti injunctions as: "Having studied the Veda and performed the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), one should take a wife. Study, in turn, is for the initiated student (*brahmacārin*). Regarding that, he will describe the initiation (*upanayana*) later. For now, he states the purificatory vows (*saṃskāravratas*).
From the time of the initiation ceremony (upanayana) onwards, he shall be a performer of the religious observances (vrata).

The word *vrata* denotes both *yama* (restraints) and *niyama* (observances). Among these, the *yamas* consist of prohibitions against specific inclinations, such as abstaining from eating meat and so forth. The *niyamas*, however, are those which fulfill the requirements of what has not yet been attained, concerning matters such as living by alms and the like.
"The *yamas* are non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness.
"The *niyamas* are purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord."

Thus have the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) been described by them; these too are determined here according to their applicability. From the initiation ceremony (upanayana) until the completion of the study of the Vedas, one should be habituated to the performance of vows. (1)
Dwelling on the path. || 2 ||

The word "syāt" (might be) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. This [supply] is to be applied to what follows as well. This is because the specific term "of the eṇa deer" will be stated later, whereas here it is referred to by the general term "mṛga. It "covers" (vaste), that is, it conceals; thus, "vāsaḥ" means a garment or covering. Since his garment is the skin of a deer, he would be "mārgavāsāḥ" (one whose clothing is the skin of a deer). || 2 ||
With hair tied together. || 3 ||

"Hanti" means one whose action is violence. "Samyak-kṣureṇa" means one from whom the hair has been removed by a razor and not by scissors or other such tools; the meaning is that his head is shaven. Some say that this would result in redundancy with the shaving that will be mentioned later. Alternatively, it refers to one whose hair is gathered together in a single mass.

This is what is meant: the author will later state, "shaven-headed, or with matted hair, or with a topknot. In that context, this statement of a restrictive rule is intended to preclude the optionality regarding time for a single member of the three castes who is a religious student (*brahmacārin*); namely, that the hair must be kept in one uniform manner by each individual—such that if he has matted hair, he cannot be shaven-headed or have a topknot. The same applies to the cases of being shaven-headed and so forth. || 3 ||
The livelihood consists of begging and the practice of a teacher. || 4 ||

The collection of alms is *bhaikṣa*. An *ācārya*, however, is defined by such characteristics as "he who, having initiated a disciple... and so forth. There is a rule that the body of a *brahmacārin* must be sustained by alms alone. His livelihood and maintenance—which consist of the nourishment of the body—must be dependent upon the *ācārya*. For the *ācārya* may direct him to give alms to certain people; thus, the *ācārya*'s role in providing his livelihood in the form of bodily nourishment is established, much like other activities. Alternatively, if alms are not obtained from elsewhere at some time, the *ācārya* himself provides food and the like. || 4 ||
A staff with bark attached. || 5 ||

Here, although the term "staff" (daṇḍa) is used in a general sense, it refers specifically to one made of *pālāśa* wood or others as will be described accordingly. The phrase "one whose staff is accompanied by bark" (*saśalkadaṇḍa*) means a staff that exists together with its bark; this is simply to be supplied [to the previous statement]. || 5 ||
He should wear a girdle made of seven strands of muñja grass. || 6 ||

One should wear that girdle (*mekhalā*) which consists of seven bird-feathers (*mayūravyañjika*) and serves for the cessation and recurrence [of seminal flow]. Here, they provide this etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) for the girdle: it is a "garland" (*mālā*) of the "aperture" (*kha*) connected to the organ of emission (*mehana*). It is said to be grammatically correct because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* class of compounds. [The root] *miha* means "to sprinkle"; the organ of emission (*mehana*) is so called because by it semen and other fluids are sprinkled; its "garland" is the aperture located above that [organ] in the lower part of the navel. 6.
One should not eat honey or meat.

The prohibition "one should not eat honey or meat" is a restriction on what would otherwise be practiced for the sake of satisfaction. Regarding the claim that honey (*madhu*)—which is also intoxicating liquor (*madya*)—is forbidden for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, this is merely one school's tradition (*ekīyam upākhyānam*). That is incorrect, because there is no such possibility [of their consuming it]; for if there were, then the prohibition "therefore a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya should not drink *surā*" would apply to all three castes alike. (7)
He should avoid alkaline substances and salt. || 8 ||

"Alkali" refers to saline earth (auṣara), sea salt (sāmudrika), and so forth; one who avoids these is "one whose habit is to avoid them. One should indeed consume rock salt (saindhava), black salt (sauvarcala), and the like. Some maintain that one should avoid all alkaline substances as well as salt. || 8 ||
He should not act contrary to the teacher. || 9 ||
The meaning is "favorable. || 9 ||
He is not independent in all his actions. ||10||
Let alone formal study and the like; the meaning is that one should not perform even a mere ritual action without the permission of the teacher. || 10 ||
Rising before [others] and retiring after [them]. || 11,12 ||

When the guru has taken recourse to his bed or other such resting place and wishes to rise, the student should be the first to rise; and while the teacher remains on his bed, the student should perform services such as massaging his feet before subsequently retiring to his own bed. The meaning of the term *jaghanya-saṃveśī* (one who lies down last) is this: when the teacher is on a couch (*khaṭṭā*), the student should occupy a seat lower than that couch, such as a mat, the ground, or a simple bed, and lie down there. In this manner, one should understand the injunctions regarding sitting on a lower level than the teacher when he is seated on his bed, and so forth. (11, 12)
Whatever he might approach, that he should give to him. || 13 ||
Whatever gold or other wealth should indeed come to him, that the religious student (brahmacārī) shall give to this teacher (ācārya). || 13 ||
By which [quality] he is joined with many. || 14 ||

Although a religious student (brahmacārī) may attend upon many teachers in due order and as appropriate for the sake of acquiring knowledge of the entire Veda along with its limbs (vedāṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas), nevertheless, whatever he receives while residing in the presence of a particular teacher, that he should give to him; the meaning is that he should not always distribute everything among all the teachers. || 14 ||
One should not lie down on his bed. || 15 ||

The meaning is that one should not occupy the bed upon which the teacher is situated—whether due to incapacity, out of compassion, or out of excessive affection—even if permitted by the teacher when he is no longer capable [of using it]. Thus, there is no tautology with the term *jaghanya-saṃveśin* (one who sleeps on the lower bed). || 15 ||
One should not mount a chariot. || 16 ||

The word "asya" (of this) is to be supplied [to the verb]. This, too, is a prohibition of what has been permitted. Others, however, explain that the mention of "bed" (*śayyā*) is intended to indicate by synecdoche the teacher’s seat, carriage, and so forth; they explain that the mention of "chariot" (*ratha*) is intended to indicate by synecdoche elephants, horses, and the like. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he should not mount," they connect it with the second negative particle (*nañ*)—either through ellipsis (*tatra*) or repetition (*āvṛtti*)—as follows: "He should not mount a chariot"; rather, when traveling to a village or elsewhere, if he is unable [to walk], [he may use a vehicle].
And he does not obtain another vehicle; therefore, even though it has been authorized and supervised by the preceptor, he may indeed mount an elephant or a horse—this is the meaning. ||16||
One should not wrap oneself [in it]. || 17 ||

One should not make one's garment identical to that of the teacher; one should not put on a garment already worn by the teacher; nor should one place one's own garment together with the teacher's garment in the same container, such as a chest or similar vessel. || 17 ||
One should avoid all tactile contacts with women. || 18 ||

One should avoid all actions that have physical contact as their cause—such as taking the hand or embracing—with all women whatsoever. This is an exception even to the traditional injunction, "One should behave toward his wife's sons and her [own] husband as toward one's own guru," for that rule concerns matters such as massaging the feet and the like. || 18 ||
One should not look at a woman who has been violated. || 19 ||
The meaning is that one should not look upon her as if she were robbed or naked. || 19 ||
One should not speak for the sake of dwelling. 20.

*Vihāraḥ* means play; one should not speak jests and the like for that purpose. Alternatively, since by the phrase "not independent in all actions" it is established that one must act only after receiving permission from the Ācārya regarding every activity, *vihāra* here refers to the voiding of urine and excrement; one should not speak for the sake of this *vihāra*, but rather for the sake of obtaining permission. 20.
One should not hold onto anything for the sake of pleasure. || 21 ||
Lust, attachment, pleasure, and delight—for their sake, one should not collect specific objects such as ornaments, games, and the like. || 21 ||
One should not bathe. || 22 ||
The phrase "having as its meaning delight" (rucy-artham) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. || 22 ||
Or he should go to water. || 23 ||

The meaning is this: bathing for the sake of pleasure is forbidden, but obligatory bathing must certainly be performed, as it is said: "Having bathed daily and being pure, one should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors."

Since this and other such rules are prescribed even for the religious student (*brahmacārin*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) therein: sometimes the bath consists of sprinkling with water consecrated by mantras, and sometimes it is immersion (*majjana*). Of these, the first has been described by the statement, "or he should enter the water. Regarding immersion, he says:
"If he should bathe, he should float in the waters like a staff" (24).

The word "yadi" (if), being restrictive and injunctive, requires a correlative restatement (*anuvāda*), as in: "If one should eat rice, then he should mix curd [with it]," or "If the Soma sacrifice should have the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu," and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is this: when the option of bathing consists of mere immersion, then the religious student (*brahmacārin*) should perform only a floating in the water with his staff; however, he should not exert himself to remove impurities or achieve beauty and the like. || 24 ||
He may be shaven-headed, wear matted hair, or have a topknot. || 25 ||
"Muṇḍaḥ" means one who is devoid of a topknot. || 25 ||
One should perform the twilight devotions (sandhyā) in the evening and in the morning. || 26 ||

The time characterized by the presence of the sun is the day; the time devoid of the sun is the night; and the time characterized by the sun half-risen and half-set is the juncture (*sandhi*). That which occurs at the juncture is the twilight (*sandhyā*). One should perform the worship of both of these every day. Worship (*upāsana*) means service. (26) To the question "How should one worship?", he says: "One should stand during the morning [twilight]. (27)

Having ceased his movement, he should remain during the forenoon portion; facing the east, he should stand reciting [the mantra] from the time when the stars are still visible until the light of the sun appears.
[She was] seated facing north. || 28 ||

Seated facing west during the latter part of the day, he should remain reciting [the mantra] starting from the time when the sun has set until the appearance of the light of the stars; because the period of the evening twilight is so very brief, such worship is thus desired. || 28 ||
Having uttered "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he recites the Sāvitrī verse, beginning with "tatsavitur," three times.

This is merely a brief indication. Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed the duties pertaining to the body—having performed either the primary or secondary ritual bath according to the Smṛti: "The body is exceedingly impure, endowed with nine apertures; it flows [with impurities] day and night; morning bathing is its purification"—one should proceed.

Based on the Smṛti rule, "Having sipped water three times, wiped [the mouth] twice, touched the sense organs, and purified himself with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one then becomes worthy of the syllable Om," he should perform three breath-restraints as prescribed in the Smṛtis, each measuring fifteen mātrās. Having performed these three breath-restraints delimited by the triple repetition of the Sāvitrī together with the Śiras and accompanied by the seven Vyāhṛtis joined with each Praṇava, he should mutter the Sāvitrī—"Tat savitur vareṇyam"—repeatedly, conjoined with the three Great Vyāhṛtis (Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ) and ending with the Sun-worship (sūryopasthāna), beginning with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn. In the phrase "he recites the Sāvitrī" (sāvitrīmanvāha), the word *anu* signifies repetition.

The phrase *tatsavitur* serves as the introductory designation (*pratīka*); although it has Savitṛ as its deity, it is intended to exclude other Sāvitrī verses such as "With the black path" (*ākṛṣṇena rajasā*). || 29 ||
Having gone out before sunset, one should fetch sacrificial fuel-sticks that are greenish-yellow, according to the Śruti: "One desiring spiritual luster [should do so]. (30)

Before the sun has set, one who desires the perfection characterized by the study of the Vedas and the performance of their prescribed duties should go out from the village and fetch eight green, fresh fuel-sticks for the purpose of kindling the fire; for this has been declared by Śruti, since Smṛti is rooted in Śruti. (30)
Emerging for the morning and evening twilight prayers, wandering for alms, and tending the sacred fire with fuel. || 31 ||

One must go outside the village for the purpose of performing the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) both morning and evening; and one must practice the wandering for alms (*bhaikṣācaraṇa*) both morning and evening. For eating at both times is prescribed by tradition: "Morning and evening is the meal ordained for humans by the gods.

Likewise, the kindling of the fire must be performed at both times. Four fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are to be offered in the morning and four in the evening. Thus, these three statements are intended to prescribe specific times other than [the general rule]. The former [time] is the morning period prior to midday, and the latter is the evening period. (31)
Some say that he should kindle the fire only in the evening.

"The kindling of the fire should take place only in the evening"—this is the opinion of some who are learned in the Vedas; and according to this view, four fuel-sticks (samidh) are to be brought. || 32 ||
There is a fault in failing to practice begging for alms and in failing to kindle the sacred fire;
if one has not performed these for seven nights, one should observe the vow of the *avakīrṇin*.

This is an illustrative indication. In the case of not practicing begging for alms, failing to kindle the fire, neglecting the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and so forth, there is a fault—a transgression—due to the violation of what has been prescribed. As it has been said:
"He who does not attend to the morning [prayer] and he who does not perform the evening [prayer] should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a *śūdra*."

Thus [it is said]. Now, for the destruction of whatever sin arises from the neglect of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), from not going out for alms, from not wandering for study, or from failing to kindle the sacred fire, one should perform the *avakīrṇi-vrata* as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). "Neglect" (*avakaraṇa*) means "neglected" (*avakīrṇa*), which is the emission [of semen] contrary to the rule; it is the intentional emission of semen by a student (*brahmacārin*). One who possesses such an emission is an *avakīrṇin*. For him, the following vow is prescribed: "He should go for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed."

"Living on alms obtained from them, he should eat only once a day; by bathing at the three sessions [of the day] for one year, he becomes purified. Regarding this, if one fails to perform the worship of the *saṃdhyā* and other such rites, one should perform the vow (*vrata*) for a student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*). Is it the complete initial rite? No, he says: "for seven nights. Others, however, explain that if one fails to perform the *saṃdhyā* worship and so forth for seven nights, one should perform the vow for a *avakīrṇin* in its entirety. Whether it is less than or more than seven nights, the failure is respectively deficient or excessive. Yājñavalkya says:

"Having neglected the duty of begging for alms for seven nights while not being ill, one should offer two oblations of clarified butter with the two mantras beginning with *kāmākīrṇaḥ*; then, he should perform the vow of the Nairṛta donkey for one year. Here too, the application is as before. (33)
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā). || 1 ||
Now begins the second section (kaṇḍikā).

We shall now explain the mantras used for the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*), beginning with *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. Regarding this, the Veda teaches the triad of deity, seer (*ṛṣi*), and meter (*chandas*) for all mantras by way of censuring ignorance and praising knowledge: "Whosoever, as a Brāhmaṇa, officiates at a sacrifice or teaches using a mantra whose seer, meter, and deity are not understood, he shall fall into a stump. *Note: The term *sthāṇu* refers to a felled tree standing upright, often used metaphorically for a person who has become paralyzed or rigid through error.*

In that regard, at the beginning of creation, there were sages such as Yājñavalkya and others, whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) had not fallen away, who performed meritorious deeds, who knew everything that is to be known, and who were like those awakened from sleep; and the Vedas are eternal through the lineage of Hiraṇyagarbha and others. Thus it is heard in scripture:
"From that very [source], Parameṣṭhin, the son of Prajāpati, perceived the sacrifice, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices," and so forth. The deities are those denoted by the mantras.

The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī are the seven classes of meters (chandas) of Jayadeva. Furthermore, by one who desires to correctly understand the meaning of the mantras, the rules of grammar such as "in Vedic usage (chandas), prefixes may be separated [from their roots] even when they follow" must be followed. Also, the *Nirukta* [rules], beginning with "the addition of phonemes" (*varṇāgama*), etc., should be consulted.

There is also a transposition of the seven births. Such details, if recited by name for every mantra, would result in excessive bulk of the text; therefore, only the meaning will be demonstrated. Om Bhūḥ, Om Bhuvaḥ, Om Khaḥ, Om Mahaḥ, Om Janaḥ, Om Tapaḥ, Om Satyam—these are the seven great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) together with the syllable Om, which are the names of the seven worlds. Among them, the first three are called "great utterances" because they denote a great object.

However, [the regions] beginning with Mahah are not qualified by the term "Mahat" (Great), because they denote specific parts of heaven. "Beneath all the worlds lies dense darkness, measuring eighty-five million one hundred thousand yojanas. Therein is the hell named Avīci, and above that [darkness] exists [heaven], extending from the Avīci hell up to the summit of Mount Meru."
The Earth has been described by all the great seers in the Purāṇas as consisting of seven islands; these, moreover,
have been enumerated by those learned in the Purāṇas.
"'Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, and likewise Śālmali, Gomeda, and Puṣkara— this is considered the group of the seven islands.
Their detailed division has been shown by us in the Vibhūtipāda of the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra.

Regarding the aphorism, "Knowledge of the lower worlds [is attained] through *saṃyama* on the sun": the world of space (*antarikṣaloka*) is variegated with stars and constellations; the world of the earth (*bhūloka*) extends from the peak of Mount Meru up to the Pole Star (*dhruva*). Beyond that is the heavenly world (*svargaloka*), which is of five kinds; thus, there are seven worlds. As for the fivefold nature of heaven: first is that of Mahendra, so called because Mahendra is its lord. Second is that of Prajāpati, whose name is *maha*. The world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) is threefold: *jana*, *tapa*, and *satya*.

The term "heaven" (svarga) is common to all five of these. Therefore, the worlds and deities that are the denotations of the vyāhṛti mantras are seen in the Taittirīya [Āraṇyaka] to have their application (*viniyoga*) in breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). This is also stated in the Smṛti.

"For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, in the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and in the three-footed *sāvitrī*, no fear exists anywhere. According to the Brāhmaṇa, the deities of the worlds beginning with the earth are the "vital powers" (*vīrya*); the seers (*ṛṣis*) of these [mantras] have been indicated.
First, Śaunaka says:
"The first seer of all the vyāhṛtis, whether taken individually or collectively, is Prajāpati; [their essence is] the syllable Om, which belongs to Brahman. Another [authority] also says:
Thus:
"Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, then Gautama, the sage Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa are [the seers] in due order.

Agni, Vāyu, Ravi (the Sun), Vākpati (Bṛhaspati), Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśvedevas are the deities of the *vyāhṛtis* in due order. Alternatively, Agni, Soma, Sūrya, Vākpati, Varuṇa, Indra, and Āditya are the deities of the *vyāhṛtis* in due order."

Another said: "By Prajāpati, whose resolve is true, desiring to create the seven worlds for the enjoyment of the inhabitants of the world, it was thus uttered: 'The seven worlds shall come into being.
Therefore, Prajāpati himself is their seer (ṛṣi), and they possess the nature of vyāhṛtis. Thus also says the Purāṇa:"
"Having himself created this fourteen-fold creation, he uttered these [syllables];
therefore, the seven worlds are known as the *vyāhṛtis*. And it is logical that many observers may exist in one place, either at different times or simultaneously."
Oṃ. We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects. Oṃ.

The meter is Gāyatrī, Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi), Savitṛ is the deity, and its application is for muttering, the initiation ceremony (upanayana), oblations (homa), and so forth. Thus says Dvaipāyana:
"Viśvāmitra is the seer, the meter is Gāyatrī, and likewise Savitṛ is the deity; its application is for the initiation, for muttering, and likewise for the oblation."

Thus, "Sarvamitra" (the friend of all) refers to Viśvāmitra, who is intended here as Prajāpati himself. Furthermore, because he is the subject denoted by the term, the Sun possesses the nature of a deity [in this context]. Although the meaning is difficult to deny because it is also perceived in the case of *japa* mantras, even though a *japa* mantra is perceived, the reciter meditates upon its meaning with that mantra. This is logically consistent, since the roots *jalpati* and *japati* function in the sense of distinct speech.

This very state of being manifest (*vyaktatva*) consists in the capacity for conveying meaning; conversely, the state of being unmanifest (*avyaktatva*) belongs to the cries of cocks and the like when they lack such capacity. No one is able to assert that what is actually perceived does not become denotable simply because it is not intended to be expressed. For water and other objects perceived by the eyes and other senses do not cease to be objects of those senses merely because one does not seek them. Furthermore, there is no cause for non-intention [to speak] regarding the Sun, since he, when propitiated through meditation accompanied by the recitation of his mantras, is the cause for the attainment of both the higher and lower goals of human life.

For even in the case of the *japa-mantras*, it is required that one who recites them be "one who knows thus" (*ya evaṃ vidvān*). Furthermore, in all the Upaniṣads, the nature of Brahman is declared, as well as the fact that both the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava are the self of all beings. Thus it is read in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this, whatever exists here; the Gāyatrī is speech, for speech is all this being; she is called Gāyatrī because she sings (*gāyati*) and protects (*trāyate*). She is indeed this earth, for upon her all this is established."

And so forth. Although the word *gāyatrī* has a general meaning, here it refers specifically to the *sāvitrī* under discussion. For this very reason, the etymological derivation found in various places is "she who protects (*trāyate*) the one who sings (*gāyantam*). And "protection" (*trāṇa*) consists of guarding, warding off calamities, and bestowing benefit.

And for one who recites this at the junctions of the day (sandhyā) and so forth, when there occurs the dispersal of the afflictions of the individual soul, the senses, and other faculties—which have been overwhelmed by the pollution of the impressions of beginningless ignorance—there comes about the attainment of liberation characterized as the Supreme Brahman, whose nature consists of consciousness and bliss, devoid of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca). For those possessed of desire, there is the attainment of heaven and the like, as well as the destruction of accumulated sins. Furthermore, the utterance of the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and end [of Vedic recitation] is intended to demonstrate that even the phenomenal world remains established within Brahman, which is of the nature of the *oṃkāra*, at both its commencement and conclusion.

"One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*; what is not preceded by the *oṃkāra* flows away, and what is not followed by it falls apart. Likewise, in the *Smṛti*:
"The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*."
Thus it has been said. And in the Yogaśāstra: "The Praṇava is its designator; its repetition and meditation upon its meaning."

"Or from devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). This refers to what was just mentioned. Furthermore, "Lord" (īśvara) has synonyms such as Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, and so forth. The Gāyatrī is essentially identical with Brahman, established through the teaching that it is the self of all beings. This is also heard in the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa: "Earth, atmosphere, and heaven—these are eight syllables. Indeed, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables. He who knows this foot of hers thus, conquers as much as there is in these worlds. (1)

"The Rig-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants"—these consist of eight syllables. Indeed, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; this is truly its [the Gāyatrī's] foot. As much as this threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā) extends, so much does he conquer who knows this foot of hers in this manner. || 2 ||

"Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, vyāna"—these are eight syllables. Now, one foot of the Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables; this is that very foot of hers. Whoever knows this foot of hers in this way wins as much as there is of this living world. || 3 ||

Now, this very fourth state has been shown as "the one beyond the dust, who shines yonder. That which is the fourth is indeed the *turīya*; it is called "the shown state" (*darśitaṃ padam*) because he, as it were, appears to be seen. It is called "beyond the dust" (*parorajā*) because he shines higher and higher above all the dust (*rajas*). In this very way, he who knows this state of his shines with splendor and fame. || 4 ||

This very Gāyatrī is established upon that fourth quarter which has been revealed, the one beyond the dust of the atmosphere; it is indeed established upon Truth. The eye is Truth, for the eye is indeed Truth. Therefore, if two people should come disputing, one saying "I saw it" and the other "I heard it," we place our faith in him alone who says "I saw it. That Truth is established upon Strength. Vital breath (prāṇa) is Strength; it is established upon the vital breath. Therefore, they say: "Strength!"

This Gāyatrī, known as the "Satyādohīyā," is thus established with reference to the self (adhyātma). She indeed protected the *gāyās*; the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are the *gāyās*, and she protected them; therefore, her name is Gāyatrī. That which he recites is this very same one; for whomever he recites it, he protects that person's vital breaths. || 5 ||

Regarding this, some recite the Sāvitrī as an Anuṣṭubh verse, saying, "The Anuṣṭubh is speech; thus we are repeating speech. One should not know it so; one should recite the Sāvitrī as a Gāyatrī verse. For even if one who knows this accepts a gift as large as a mountain, it does not equal even a single foot of the Gāyatrī.

If someone were to receive these three worlds full, he would obtain only this first foot of her; and if one were to receive as much as this triple knowledge (the three Vedas) exists, he would obtain this second foot of her; and if one were to receive as many living beings as exist here, he would obtain this third foot of her. But this fourth foot of hers, which is shown as "that which shines beyond the dust of the earth," cannot be obtained by anyone at all—how then could one receive even that much?

The worship of that [Gāyatrī] is as follows: "O Gāyatrī, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed; you are footless, for you cannot be reached. Homage to your fourth, revealed foot, which is beyond the dust of the world! O Sāvitrī, may my desire not be fulfilled—[saying this] regarding someone whom he hates, 'May this desire not be fulfilled for him,' or 'I have attained that [desire]'—for whomever he thus worships, that desire is either not fulfilled or it is fulfilled. (8)

Janaka of Videha said this to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: "O Gāyatrī-knower, if you are indeed such an expert, then why do you carry [the sacrificial fire] having become an elephant? He replied, "O Emperor, I did not know its mouth. "Fire itself is its mouth," he said. "For even if one who possesses fuel throws anything into it, it completely consumes it all; even so [is the Gāyatrī]."

"Even if one commits sin, having fully comprehended all this, one becomes pure, cleansed, ageless, and immortal. This is the purport of the passage in this Upaniṣad beginning with "Earth, atmosphere, heaven—these are eight syllables": the three worlds are either an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) or a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Gāyatrī, whose essence is Brahman; therefore, because she possesses manifold powers, she is endowed with the powers of earth and the other elements.

Although the triad of the Vedas—beginning with "The Ṛks, Yajus, and Sāmans"—possesses the quality of illuminating objects not previously known through other means of valid cognition, that which is consciousness itself within the Gāyatrī, whose essence is Brahman, is what has expanded, evolved, or become manifest. Likewise, [the passage] beginning with "Prāṇa, Apāna, Udāna, and Vyāna" refers to that which is called the "Thread of the World" (jagatsūtra), which exists within the three worlds and has entered into the relationship of signifier and signified as expounded in the immediately following quarter-verse.

The movement that is observed in the wind, which is of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), is the very power of the Gāyatrī of Savitṛ known as Brahman; it is solely by virtue of that [power] that such a transformation or manifestation occurs.

By the passage beginning with "This very fourth state has been shown," the knower of the Veda establishes that the culmination of the three quarters resides in the Sun—which is the form existing in proximity to the Supreme Brahman, which resembles an ocean whose waves have all subsided and which is free from agitation—having attained the dustless state after surveying the entire world. For in this context, whatever meaning is understood immediately following the word is indeed the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

Therefore, it appears appropriate here that the deity Savitṛ alone should be the object of expression. What is meant is this: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), in the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*), there exists no reality apart from the reality expressed by the words *brahman*, *praṇava*, and *gāyatrī*. However, through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the linguistic convention of the signified and the signifier is completed within a single entity. In that regard, the status of being the signifier belongs to its imagined form consisting of three feet, while the status of being the signified belongs to its nature as Savitṛ.

Even the figurative application of the term "fourth foot" (*turīya-pāda*) to the sun is made, by way of metaphor, as if it had three feet, solely for the purpose of teaching the one ultimate reality. Enough with this restlessness born of an over-zealous desire to plunge into the dense forest of the Vedānta garden—a garden vast with the power of experiencing the joy of savoring the secret essence [of Brahman] spread forth through the force of an overwrought intellect. At this juncture, this remains established: even when this *ṛc* is employed for recitation (*japa*), its deity is Savitṛ.
And this is the meaning of the word: "yat-tat" (that-which) is a general term, and that which is general—pervading all particularities—is the true nature of Brahman. As it has been said:
"Om, Tat, Sat—this is remembered as the threefold designation of Brahman."

Thus [it is said]. For even this is merely a general statement, employed for the purpose of establishing what has not yet been critically examined. Indeed, the word *om* is employed in reference to that which is accepted without critical examination; and such unexamined establishment is possible regarding an object free from doubt. Furthermore, doubt arises because one clings to alternative positions (*koṭi*) based on difference. Therefore, it is only in the non-dual Brahman that unexamined establishment is logically possible. Consequently, the words *yat* and *tat* are the two terms to be predicated of Brahman. As for the word *yaḥ*, there is a change of gender.

The word *dhī* is recited among the names for action; therefore, by that word *dhī*, actions as well as cognitions are expressed. "We" refers to all the worlds and ourselves. In the case of pronouns such as *tyad* and so forth, the subsequent [form] remains.

"Of them"—that is, of us who are devoted to them. Regarding the word *dhīmahi*: the root *dhyai* means "to think"; there is a Vedic *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization), and the *liṅ* (optative) is used in the sense of the *laṭ* (present indicative) by way of grammatical substitution. Thus, the meaning is "we reflect upon," "we contemplate," or "we meditate upon. The same applies to the phrase *pracodayāt*. Alternatively, *pracodayāt* is used in the sense of a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) with the *liṅ*. The term *bharga* denotes radiance; it is synonymous with *bhāsana* (shining), *prakāśa* (light), and so forth.

The term *bharga* is derived from the root *bhā* (in the sense of "shining") with an *uṇādi* suffix, along with Vedic phonetic augmentations and modifications. It is called *bharga* because it shines, glows, and radiates as the nature of eternal bliss and consciousness (*nityānanda-caitanya*). Alternatively, it is *bharga* from the root *bhrāj* (in the sense of "shining"), meaning that which shines (*bhrājate*). Or again, it is *bharga* from the root *bhrasj* (in the sense of "cooking"), meaning that which cooks or ripens medicinal herbs and the like. For indeed, Brahman, in the form of the sun, cooks and brings to fruition all things such as grain. Even water and wind are of the nature of the sun. And so says the author of the *Nirukta*:

"Parjanya, Vāyu, and Āditya ripen the herbs by means of cold, heat, and rain. Likewise, in the Araṇyaka section, it was stated by Dhaumya to Yudhiṣṭhira at the time of his propitiation of the Sun: "Just as during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), the Sun, having drawn up the essences from the earth with its rays, produces food, herbs, and the six tastes."

It has been stated that during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), having drawn up the heat of the day with the splendors of the moon, [the sun] produces food and other things through water; thus it is said: "In this way, food consisting of light indeed sustains the life-force of the worlds. Furthermore, from the root *bhṛñ* meaning "to sustain" or "to nourish," it is called *bharga* because it sustains, maintains, or nourishes the worlds.

Alternatively, from the verbal roots *galbh* (to be bold) and *dhṛṣ* (to dare), through the modification and reversal of their syllables, *bhargaḥ* refers to power (*sāmarthya*), meaning that which is capable and assumes audacity in the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and illumination of the universe. Or, from the root *vṛj* (to avoid), *bhargaḥ* is that which avoids the suffering of the manifold world of duality caused by ignorance. By this, the form of Savitṛ as the inner self (*adhyātma*) or as the divine principle (*adhidaivata*) has been described. Thus says the Śruti:
"He who shines yonder is indeed this Savitṛ."

Thus: the root *vṛñ* (to choose) takes the Vedic suffix *-enya*. "Vareṇya" means worthy of being chosen; that is to say, it is desirable as the object of meditation and as the goal to be attained in the form of liberation (*mukti*). "Deva": he plays (*divyati*) and sports through the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world; he desires victory (*vijigīṣate*), transacts, praises through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and moves in the form of phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*)—namely, in the form of evolution and reabsorption (*saṃvarta*); thus he is "deva. "Savitṛ": he brings forth crops and so on; thus he is "savitṛ. This is the meaning of the words as stated.

Alternatively, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: "We meditate upon that most excellent splendor (*bharga*) belonging to the divine Savitṛ. For that indeed—which is that form consisting of Brahman whose nature is universal—excellently impels, sets in motion, or may be expected to set in motion, according to suitability, the actions and knowledges of the world. This is one way of construing the passage. Or else, the word *tat* is the genitive case ending elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39]; and the word *yat* is taken exactly as it is heard in the text.
We meditate upon that excellent splendor of that god Savitṛ. Of which Savitṛ? Of him who is the Savitṛ who impels our actions and our cognitions with excellence.
O Waters, you are indeed the sources of bliss; grant us strength so that we may behold great joy.
The metre is Gāyatrī. The deity of the hymn is the Waters. Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son, Ambarīṣa, or Sindhudvīpa, saw it. Its application is for cleansing and other such rites.

*Mayas* is a name for happiness; *ūrmi* is a name for food. By this, everything that is to be enjoyed is indicated here. O Waters (*āpaḥ*), since you are *mayobhuvaḥ*—that is, because you are the bringers of happiness (*sukhasya bhāvayitryaḥ*)—therefore, you who possess such qualities, being the objects of the action, sustain (*dadhātana*) us, the agents. The substitution of *tan* for *dhā* is according to the rule "taptanaptanathanāśca. For what purpose do you sustain us? For *ūrje*, that is, for the enjoyment of food.

Having thus petitioned for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga*), he now petitions for the sake of liberation (*apavarga*): "For great delight, for seeing. For "great" (*maha*) means vast. The greatness of anything other than the Supreme Brahman is relative; however, the Supreme Brahman alone possesses the absolute, ultimate greatness. Therefore, Brahman itself is denoted by the word "Great" (*mahat*). The verb "bestow" (*dadhātana*) is to be supplied. Of what sort is this Great One? For "delight" (*raṇa*), meaning that which is delightful, whose nature is eternal bliss and consciousness; and likewise for "seeing" (*cakṣas*), meaning that which is worthy of being seen, the object of direct perception through the meditation and recitation of yogis.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is: "O Great Brahman, who are worthy of being seen, whose nature is eternal bliss and consciousness, sustain us for the sake of attaining Brahman."
Whatever most auspicious flavor you possess, grant us a share of it here, like longing mothers.

There exist essences (*rasa*) of water that are *śiva*, *śivatara*, and *śivatama*, distinguished by their respective substrates. Alternatively, the essence of water, being of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, is considered *śivatama*—the most auspicious and the most blissful. It is prayed for by the members of the three twice-born classes as follows: "O Waters, grant us a share, feed us with, or lead us to, that essence of yours which is the most blissful. Here, the genitive case (*naḥ*) is used in place of the dative (*asmākam*), or it implies a requirement for a portion. The meaning is: "Establish us as partakers of a portion of that most auspicious essence, in relation to the whole [of water]."

Those seeking enjoyment pray for the attainment of the essence of milk and other such things, while those seeking liberation pray for the realization of the nature of the Supreme Brahman. To what is it like that they cause [the gods] to enjoy? He says: "Like longing mothers. [The root] *vaś* means "to desire. Just as mothers, desiring the growth of their young children, feed their offspring the most auspicious essence of milk and so forth by giving them the suckling of the breast out of an excess of maternal affection, even so [do the devotees].
Therefore, we come to you for refuge, O Waters, for whose dwelling you quicken us; do you give birth to us.

The word *yasya* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) by means of a grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*). O Waters (*āpaḥ*), that essence (*rasam*) which you quicken (*jinvatha*) within living beings—[the root] *ji* meaning "to conquer"; the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is used by transposition as *bhū*; then the *śap* affix is added; and by way of irregularity (*bāhulaka*), the absence of the intermediate suffix (*vikaraṇa*) occurs, followed by the *yaṇ* substitution according to the rule *hnu-voḥ sārvadhātuke*. Roots have multiple meanings; therefore, the sense here is: "you conquer" or "you augment. For what purpose? "For destruction" (*kṣayāya*).

The root *kṣi* means "dwelling" and "going. For the dwelling, the staying, and the going of living beings—for the sake of activity consisting in the enjoyment of various forms and actions, and for the sake of knowledge—to that [Rasa], we go toward you. The dative case is used here according to the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi*. We would go quickly and sufficiently, or amply, toward that Rasa which belongs to you, in order to obtain it for the sake of life; thus, attachment to enjoyment is being prayed for.

O Waters, with the intention of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), you have provided a chariot for the journey; for that Supreme Self (*paramātman*) whose abode you are—you who strive and exert yourselves toward His realization by means of eternal bliss—may we, through your grace, reach, know, and attain that very supreme nature of yours, making it full and sufficient for us. We pray: "May there be the attainment of liberation for us. O Waters, bring us forth as well.

Since we hope thus through your grace alone, therefore, please cause us to become fit for the attainment of liberation; that is, bring it about. Because of their great majesty (*mahānubhāvatva*), it is heard in scripture that there is but one deity everywhere, whether in the form of Brahman or in the form of the Sun. Regarding the word *gamāma*, although it is an optative in the sense of a benediction (*āśīrliṅ*) and thus, by the rule "the optative [is used] in benediction" (*aliṅāśiṣi*), it possesses the status of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, nevertheless, because of the rule "in Vedic [usage], both ways," it also possesses the status of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; hence, the suffix *śap* is attached. Furthermore, because of the principle "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaśchandasi vikalpyante*), the substitution of *cha* does not occur. This should be understood in other instances as well.
May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity.
This verse is addressed to the Waters (Abdaivatyā), composed in the Gāyatrī meter, and attributed to Sindhudvīpa Āmbarīṣa.

May the divine Waters, endowed with qualities such as generosity, be auspicious (*śam*) for us. *Śam* is a name for happiness; thus, may they be of the nature of happiness or the bestowers of happiness. Alternatively, it should be understood as being for the sake of that: "may they be for our happiness. Furthermore, may they be auspicious for our desired goal (*abhiṣṭaye*). That which is desired is *iṣṭi*; directed toward results such as heaven, it is *abhīṣṭi*. The phonetic modification of the suffix is Vedic; although *abhīṣṭiḥ* would be the expected form, *abhiṣṭaye* occurs here. May the Waters be for us so that we may obtain the food and other things we desire.
Water indeed transforms into the form of food and so forth; and thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Water and earth are food," and "Forests consist of these."

And thus: "May they be for drinking"—where "drinking" (*pāna*) is an indicative term meaning "may they bring about the pleasant digestion of what has been eaten and drunk. Alternatively, *abhiyajana* means sacrifice, and *pīti* means the drinking of Soma; the meaning is: "May the waters be for us for sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and for the drinking of Soma. The presiding deity is thus invoked: "May they flow toward us for the sake of health (*śam-yoḥ*). [In the root] *yu*, the sense is "to mix"; that which mixes or becomes blended is *yuḥ*, namely disease, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), fever, and so forth.

By the term *śam*, he indicates here the absence of suffering through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "May the waters flow toward us" means "may they bring about. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "May the waters bring about for us that absence of suffering which pertains to *yu* (disease). Alternatively, the word *yu* refers to the Self (*ātman*), because it "unites" (*yauti*) with the body and so forth. "May the waters flow toward us" means "may they manifest that *śam*—the eternal bliss—which belongs to *yu*, the Self.

[May] the waters [be] auspicious for us; may the waters of the desert be auspicious, may the waters of the marshes be auspicious for us; may the waters of the ocean be auspicious for us, and may the waters of the wells be auspicious for us. [This verse] has the Waters as its deity (*abdaivatyā*), is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and belongs to Adhvaryu, the son of Soma. "Waters of the desert" (*dhanvanyāḥ*) refers to those existing in the desert, the wasteland, or the jungle. Likewise, "waters of the marshes" (*anūpyāḥ*) refers to those existing in a watery region. Similarly, "waters of the ocean" (*samudriyāḥ*) refers to those in the sea, and "waters of the wells" (*kūpyāḥ*) refers to those in wells.

"Likewise, may they be for drinking"—here, "drinking" (*pāna*) is an indicative term meaning that they may bring about the pleasant digestion of what has been eaten and drunk. Alternatively, *abhiyajana* means sacrifice, and *pīti* means the drinking of Soma; thus, the meaning is: "May the waters be for us for sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and for the drinking of Soma. In this way, the presiding deity is invoked: "May they flow toward us for health and for joy. Regarding the word *yu*: from the root *yu* (in the sense of "mixing"), that which mixes or becomes blended is *yu*; it refers to disease, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), fever, and so forth.

By the term *śam*, through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he refers here to the absence of suffering. "May the waters flow toward us" means "may they bring about. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "May the waters bring about for us that absence of suffering which pertains to *yu* [the self]. Alternatively, the word *yu* refers to the Self, because it "unites" (*yauti*)—that is, it becomes mixed—with the body and so forth. "May the waters flow toward us" means "may they manifest that *śam*—the eternal happiness—which belongs to *yu*, the Self."

May the waters of the desert be auspicious to us; may the waters of the marshes be auspicious to us. May the waters of the ocean be auspicious to us; may the waters of the wells be auspicious to us. [This verse] has the Waters as its deity (Abdaivatyā) and is in the Anuṣṭubh meter. "Dhanvanyāḥ" refers to those waters existing in the desert (*maru*) or arid land (*jaṅgala*), which is the domain of the sacrifice (*adhvara*) belonging to Soma’s son. Likewise, "anūpyāḥ" are those existing in a marshy region (*anūpa*) where water flows. Similarly, "samudriyāḥ" are those existing in the ocean, and "kūpyāḥ" are those existing in wells. The meaning is: "May all of them be for our happiness.
In the phrase "śamu naḥ," the syllable *o* is a particle (*nipāta*) used for the purpose of completing the metrical foot.

May the Waters, our mothers, purify us; may those who cleanse with ghee purify me with ghee. For the goddesses carry away every impurity; from them, I emerge bright and purified. (Triṣṭubh meter. The seer is the one mentioned immediately above; the deity is the same. The Waters are the mothers, the creators of the worlds. "Asmān" (us) is used in the accusative case with the sense of the genitive; [thus it means] "our. May they purify—that is, destroy—our *ripra*, which is sin, by means of *ghṛta*, the essence.

"May they purify me—that is, cleanse me—by means of the destruction of sin through clarified butter; may they destroy our evil. How wonderful is this, since they carry away—that is, flow forth and are able to remove—all sin, even that which pervades the entire universe within the three worlds! For these are goddesses (*devīs*), endowed with qualities such as generosity (*dāna*) and radiance (*dyotana*). [The mantra continues: "Id, from them I emerge pure and purified. *Id* is a particle (*nipāta*) used for filling out the meter; it is connected with the word *emi* ("I go").
Purified and sanctified by these waters, I indeed rise up as pure; that is to say, I come forth, attaining both heaven and liberation.
O waters, carry away whatever evil is in me—whether it be that I have committed an offense, or that I have been negligent, or even that I have spoken falsehood.

The seer is as before; the metre is Anuṣṭubh. O Waters, whatever evil—whatever ill-performed act of a sinful nature—I have committed, carry that away, drive it off. Or, whatever I have maligned, whatever I have harmed, and whatever falsehood or lie I have uttered without cause, whatever I have reviled—all that, carry away. Although "evil" (durita) is used as a general term, the specific mention of malice and false accusation is for the sake of emphasis.

May the Waters purify me from mental sin; may they release me, as one released from wooden fetters (drupada), as one distressed is freed from impurity, and as clarified butter is purified by a strainer. [Anuṣṭubh meter. The seer is Kokilarājaputra. May the Waters purify (*śundhantu*) and liberate me from mental sin (*enasaḥ*), making me fit for a good rebirth. Who is released from what so that he becomes one who moves about at will? [One is released] "as one released from wooden fetters" (*drupadādivenmumucānaḥ*). Wooden fetters (*drupada*) are wooden sandals; thus says a Vedic mantra: "Like two new wooden sandals placed upon the feet."* *Note: The citation refers to Ṛgveda 10.75.6.*

Alternatively, *drupada* refers to a place where the path is slippery (*druta*) because it is a region overrun by robbers (*dasyu*), or *drupada* refers to a wooden footstool (*drumayam padam*), meaning a binding post. The particle *yat* is used here for metrical completion. [The root] *muc* (in the sense of "releasing") takes the suffix *kānac* with the *liṭ* ending used in the sense of the *laṭ* by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). Just as a man being released from a *drupada*—characterized here as a sandal, a seat, a region, or a binding post—becomes one who moves at his own will, like one who has bathed away his fatigue, dirt, and so forth; "fatigued" (*khinna*) means possessed of exhaustion, as in the heat of summer and the like.

The word *snātvī* is derived as a nipāta (irregular formation) according to the rule "snālyādayaśca. The meaning is: "Just as one whose limbs are covered with sweat becomes purified of impurity and attains relief after bathing, or just as clarified butter purified by a strainer of *darbha* grass becomes stainless like flour through a sieve, so may the waters make me stainless and free from sin."

We appease your wrath, O Varuṇa, with prostrations; we entreat you with sacrifices and oblations. O wise Asura, O King, grant us a dwelling and loosen the sins we have committed. *Triṣṭubh*. The seer is Śunaḥśepa, or [alternatively] the gods and asuras. Varuṇa is the deity. *Ava* is a prefix that connects with the verb *īmahe*, according to the traditional rule: "And those not separated [by other words]. O Varuṇa, we appease (*ava-īmahe*)—that is, we remove—your *helaḥ*, your anger. By what means? [By prostrations, sacrifices, and oblations.]

[We worship you] with salutations and hymns, with sacrifices such as the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña), and with oblations such as the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). Therefore, having cast aside your anger and being of a gracious mind, grant us a dwelling or food. Likewise, loosen—that is, destroy—those sins which we have committed through the practice of forbidden acts and so forth. "O Asura," "O Pracetā," and "O Rājan"—these three forms of address are epithets of Varuṇa.

*Asu* is the vital breath, a specific power; one who possesses that is an *asura*. O powerful one (*balavan*)! One whose mind, consciousness, or intellect is preeminent—addressing him as *he pracetaḥ* (O wise one)! O King (*rājan*), you who shine!

Loosen the highest bond of Varuṇa from us, loosen the lowest, and loosen the middle one. Then, O Āditya, in your service, may we be sinless before Aditi. The understanding of the meter and the deity follows immediately [from the previous verse]. It is the same in what follows as well. Śunaḥśepa, bound with three bonds at the base, middle, and top sections of the sacrificial post, offered praise to Varuṇa for his release. The prefix *ud* is connected with the verb *śrathāya*. "O Varuṇa, the highest... [the rest of the verse follows].

"Loosen the noose from our side"—that is, loosen it upward; having loosened it, "draw it upward," meaning remove the noose from the upper end. "Loosen the lower part"—that is, loosen the noose situated at the base by drawing it downward; meaning remove the noose from the root.

"Loosen the middle one"—having loosened the middle loop situated in the middle region in various ways, that is, having made it slack, you should release the middle loop from the sacrificial post by means of the root or the end; this is the meaning. Now, after the release of the three loops, O Āditya, son of Aditi, may we, abiding in your *vrata* (rite or vow), be sinless, free from evil. For what purpose? For the sake of Aditi, because wretchedness (*dainya*) is rooted in sin.
I approach the principles, praising them with sacred prayer; the sacrificer, with oblations, seeks this from you. O Varuṇa, being mindful here, grant wide renown; do not steal away our life.

O Varuṇa, whatever the sacrificer hopes for through oblations such as the *puroḍāśa* and *soma*, that I entreat from you; I beg of you. Doing what? Praising with the *brahman*—that is, with the Veda in the form of mantras. Be mindful of this entreaty and praise here; take note of it. Being "ahelamānaḥ"—the root *heḍ* meaning "to disregard"—do not show disregard. O "uruśaṃsa"—one whose praise (*śaṃsa*) is wide or manifold—addressing you thus, O you who are praised by many:
do not steal away our life; do not cause the destruction of our lifespan.
Untie for us the highest bond, loosen the middle one, and release the lowest so that we may live.

Vāruṇī; Gāyatrī meter; the seer is Śunaḥśepa himself. Having prayed for release from the bonds, he now prays for freedom from old age and death. The prefix *ud-* is connected with the verb *mumugdhi*. "Unloose our highest bond—release it upward; loosen the middle bond; loosen the lower fetters, releasing and removing them from the lower part. For what purpose?

"O Jīva, live!"—the meaning is: having released the bonds for the sake of living (*jīvana*), grant us much longevity; or alternatively, "living" here refers to *kaivalya* (liberation). By releasing the bonds—the debts to the gods, sages, and ancestors, categorized respectively as high, low, and middling—liberation is prayed for. As it has been said: "Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation."

Golden-hued, pure, and purifying—those waters in whom Kaśyapa was born and in whom Indra [was born], those who, assuming various forms, have held Agni as their embryo; may those waters be auspicious and gracious to us. [This verse] has the Waters as its deity; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. "Golden-hued" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*) means those whose color is as pure and stainless as gold. "Pure" (*śucayaḥ*) means having become sanctified. For this very reason, they are "purifying" (*pāvakāḥ*), that is, the bringers of purification. In whom sages such as Kaśyapa were born, and gods such as Indra; what need is there to mention others? And so says Manu:
"In the beginning, he created the waters; upon them he cast his seed.

That became a golden egg, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns," and so forth. And those waters, existing in various forms within the sky, the ocean, and other realms, bore Agni as their embryo—whether in the form of lightning or the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha). Thus says the Vedic mantra:
"When the great waters came encompassing the universe, bearing the embryo and generating Agni."
Thus: may those waters be most auspicious and most pleasant for us.

Those whom the gods make their food in heaven, those who exist manifoldly in the intermediate space, those of diverse forms who have taken Agni as their embryo—may those waters be auspicious and gracious to us.

The gods, beginning with the ancestors (pitṛs), partake in those waters offered by the three social classes (traivarṇikas) in heaven, in the celestial realm; it is understood that once consumed, they serve the gods even when transformed into the form of sacrificial oblations (haviṣya). Thus says the Śruti: "From that, the gods subsist upon procreation.

This means that they subsist from humans alone, and do not themselves take [the water] directly from clouds and such, even though it exists there. Furthermore, those waters which exist in the intermediate space (antarikṣa) in various forms, such as frost, hail, and drinking water—the rest has been explained.
In whose midst King Varuṇa moves, beholding the truth and falsehood of men; those waters of diverse forms who have borne Agni as their embryo—may they be auspicious and gracious to us.
In the midst of which waters Varuṇa moves resplendent, observing the truth and falsehood, the dharma and adharma of human beings.

Behold me with an auspicious eye; touch my skin with your auspicious body. May those waters, which drip with sweetness, pure and purifying, be auspicious, gracious, and beneficial to us. [The meaning is already explained.]

Golden-hued, pure, and purifying, the waters have moved forth, leaving behind all that is blameworthy. A hundred filters are spread out for them; with these may the divine Savitṛ purify me. Golden-hued, pure because of their purity, and bringing about purification, the waters—having abandoned the sin that is fit to be cut away by its parts—have moved forth in various ways and reached the earth. The mention of "a hundred" is indicative of a great abundance. The word *pavitrāḥ* (filters) is used here with a change of gender (masculine for feminine).
Since these [waters] possess forms that are exceedingly vast and purifying, therefore may Savitṛ, their lord, purify us with them.

These verses have been declared as "Golden-Colored" (*hiraṇyavarṇā*). From here onwards, six verses shall be declared as *pāvamānī*. Their seer is Pavamāna; Soma is the deity, acting as the presiding authority based upon half [of each verse]; and the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. He who studies the *pāvamānī* verses—the essence collected by the seers—eats everything purified and made savory by Mātariśvan.

Whoever studies the *pāvamānī* verses, which are the purifiers of the waters—for him Sarasvatī milks forth milk, clarified butter, honey, and water. Since the *pāvamānī* verses are the verbal expressions that purify the waters, they are indeed the *ṛc*s. Whoever recites those *pāvamānī* verses—which possess the nature of the essence gathered and offered here by the seers (*ṛṣis*), the knowers—eats and enjoys every supreme essence of food and so forth; it is an essence made savory, purified, and sanctified by the naturally pure wind.

In this way, Sarasvatī as speech yields—that is, she milks out and fulfills—milk, which, by metaphorical extension due to its purity, signifies *dharma*; clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), due to the common quality of being unctuous, signifies *kāma* such as heaven and the like; honey (*madhu*), because it consists of the single sweet flavor, signifies *apavarga*, whose nature is eternal bliss; and water (*udaka*), meaning that milk and the rest originate from water. Some others, however, say that by the word "water," the absence of suffering, which consists in the state of continuity, is indicated.

"The *pāvamānī* verses are indeed auspicious, yielding well, and dripping with clarity; they are the essence collected by the seers, for that is the nectar within the *brāhmaṇas*. The *pāvamānīs* are those that purify. They are "auspicious" (*svastyayanīḥ*), meaning they bring about well-being (*svasti*)—that is, non-destruction—and thus bestow long life. They are "well-yielding" (*sudughāḥ*), meaning easy to milk. They are "dripping with clarity" (*ghṛtaśrutaḥ*), meaning they flow with clarified butter."

This essence has indeed been gathered and concentrated here by the seers who know the core of the mantras—namely, these *pāvamānya* verses. For among the Brāhmaṇas, that is the nectar; the meaning is that this essence brings about immortality and bestows long life, while for those attached to worldly enjoyments, it grants liberation, and for those seeking release, it bestows liberation.
The Pāvamānī verses bring about well-being; by means of them, one goes to the Nandana grove. One partakes of meritorious foods and attains immortality.

Likewise, there are the *pāvamānya* hymns and those that ensure well-being (*svastyayanya*); by the study of which a man goes to and attains the Nandana grove, the celestial garden of the gods, and likewise enjoys edible fruits consisting of merit such as heaven and the like, and attains immortality characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*).
May the purifying verses (pāvamānīs) point out this world to us as well as that world; may the goddesses, brought together with the gods, fulfill our desires.

Thus may these Pavamāna verses grant us—may they reveal—this earthly world and that heavenly world; and may they fully increase for us all our desired objects and longed-for goals, being as they are gathered together and unified by the gods, the sacrificial sites, and the seers.
By that purifying filter with which the gods always cleanse themselves, by that thousand-streamed one, may the Pāvamānī hymns purify us.
May the Pāvamānī verses purify us with that very stream of infinite flow, by means of which purification—consisting of a special water—the gods purify themselves.
May the waters release me from the curse, and also from that which pertains to Varuṇa;

and also from the fetter of Yama, and from every sin against the gods. [This is] the seer’s [verse] of the Atharvan physician. It is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; the waters are addressed by the seer. [The meaning is: from the curse—that is, from what originates in a curse—from the fetter, that is, from the noose, and from sin; likewise from that which pertains to Varuṇa, caused by the noose of Varuṇa, from that sin by which Varuṇa binds with his nooses, and from the fetter caused thereby. The word "and" (*uta*) is used as a conjunction. Likewise, may the waters release me from the fetter and the sin belonging to Yama.

That sin by which Yama prevails—that is the noose of Yama. Furthermore, regarding "from every offense against the gods": that which must necessarily be performed, such as sacrifices and oblations for the gods—the sin that arises from the non-performance of those is what is meant by "offense against the gods"; from all such sin, may the Waters release me.

Whatever sin I have committed while awake, may the Waters release me from all that evil. [The Gāyatrī]: The Waters are said to be [the purifiers]. Whatever sin I have committed while awake—having done it intentionally—and whatever [sin] while asleep, as if in a state of sleep due to ignorance; from all that evil, may the Waters release me, meaning they shall set me free. The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye fixed in the sky.
We pray that we may attain the supreme state of Viṣṇu, the all-pervading one, which is the very form of Brahman and characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*).

The method of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) has been explained here. Following the cleansing, one should mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn beginning with "Ṛtaṃ ca satyam," while meditating upon Prajāpati, the subject of the hymn, who is the agent of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. Furthermore, it is established in various places throughout the Upaniṣads that creation, maintenance, and dissolution—which are denoted by this hymn—are dependent upon Prajāpati.

For Prajāpati, indeed, being inlaid with manifold powers, creates the three worlds from his own body by mere volition alone; and at the time of dissolution, he withdraws them back into himself once again in the form of power. And thus says the Śruti:
"Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning."
"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, indeed, the existent was born. That made itself by itself.
Thus [says the scripture]. Also, the Brāhmaṇa says:
"I, seeking liberation, take refuge in that God who illumines the self-intellect, who in the beginning fashioned Brahmā and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him."
"From this [Brahman] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs;
as well as space, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe. This refers to Prajāpati, who has assumed the role of the creator of the world.
They explain the Śaka hymn.

From the heat of the kindled austerity (*tapas*), *ṛta* and *satya* were born. From that, night was born; from that, the billowing ocean. From the billowing ocean, the year was born, ordaining days and nights, the controller of all that blinks. Dhātṛ fashioned the sun and the moon according to the ancient order, as well as heaven, earth, the intermediate space, and the sky. The seer is Aghamarṣaṇa; the meter is Anuṣṭubh.

Prajāpati is the deity who, as the creator of the universe, is to be meditated upon at the time of reciting this hymn. *Tapas* means knowledge, according to the Vedic scripture: "Austerity consists of right knowledge. From that which was kindled (*abhīddhāt*)—meaning from that which was shining forth toward the objects to be created—*Ṛta* and *Satya* were born. *Prāṇa*, which serves as the thread of the universe, is *Satya*, according to the scripture: "Prāṇa is indeed *Satya*. *Ṛta* likewise has the very nature of Prāṇa because it possesses motion; for *Ṛta* is a form derived from the root *ar*, which signifies motion.

The mind (*manas*) also consists of *ṛta* and *satya*, because it possesses the nature of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*) and moves with the speed of a flash of lightning. The meaning is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), accompanied by the mind, was created by Prajāpati through mere resolve alone. Thereafter, following the origin of the vital breath, from that very same resolve of Prajāpati, night (*rātri*) was born. The word "night" is applied to the ether (*ākāśa*) due to its similarity in color to a mass of collyrium. After the origin of the vital breath, there are scriptural accounts in the Upaniṣads regarding the origin of the ether in various places.

Then, immediately after the arising of space, the ocean—the watery expanse—came into being; the meaning is that water, possessing movement and surging, was produced. The mention of the "ocean" indicates the arising of the other three elements as well. Thus says the Śruti: "From space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth."

Showing the lack of fixed order in various places, the Seer declares the non-ultimate reality of temporal sequence within non-duality—since the manifestation of difference is constructed by ignorance—by stating: "From the ocean, the sovereign year. Here, the word *samudrāt* takes the ablative case (*pañcamī*) by grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*), although the locative (*saptamī*) would have been expected according to the rule *adhir īśvare* ("*adhi* [is used] in the sense of lordship") and *yasmād adhikam* ("from which something is superior"). The mention of the "ocean" (*samudra*) is an elliptical expression for the five elements (*bhūtapañcaka*). Thus, the meaning is: among the elements, the Sovereign (*samrāṭ*) was born; that is, the Lord of beings was born as a being.

Doing what was the Sovereign born? He was born creating day and night, and establishing the sun and moon as their delimiters. If it is asked how the Virāj creates and appoints the sun and other elements for the remaining tasks, the text answers: because he is the *dhātā*, the creator, of the entire universe (*viśvasya*)—that is, of all that blinks, possessing both closing and opening of the eyes—he therefore ordains them; and being their master (*vaśī*), he assigns them according to their respective fitness. How does he ordain them?

The meaning is that this process of creation and dissolution is beginningless, occurring as before without transgressing the sequence of previous kalpas. Alternatively, "as before" means according to previous karma; thus, he does not endow liberated beings with bodies and so forth. Or else, "as before" means in due order; he did not fashion all beings as equals—lest there be the undesirable consequence of a lack of diverse experience—but rather fashioned them as high and low.

Alternatively, the connection is that he fashioned the three worlds—earth, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and heaven (*sva*) as *svarga*—in their respective order. Above the earth is the intermediate space, the world of the stars and so forth; beyond that is the fivefold heaven previously described. If one asks what the purpose of his creation of the universe was, it is said: "Heaven" (*divam*). [The root] *div* means "to play"; thus, the meaning is "for the sake of sport."

Thus, based on the *Kāṭhaka* Śruti passage, "One should repeat [the hymn] joined with this [verse]: 'The dust that arose after the sweeping, both the true and the false,'" the recitation (*japa*) of the *Aghamarṣaṇa* Sūkta must be performed. Following that, there is the restraint of breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*). Accordingly, Yājñavalkya has enjoined the restraint of breath even at a time subsequent to the sprinkling (*mārjana*), stating: "Sprinkling and the restraint of breath. Furthermore, it is also useful for bathing and other such acts. Thus, Vasiṣṭha has stated its purpose as expiation (*prāyaścitta*), describing it as a cause for the destruction of sin.

One who is constantly disciplined should repeatedly perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) again and again, practicing unsurpassed austerity from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails. One should maintain the three types of breath-restraints according to the scriptures without sloth; the sin committed during a day and night perishes at that very moment.
Thus it is said:

"And whatever living beings a twice-born man kills unintentionally during a day and night, he should bathe for the sake of purification and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). In the Yoga-śāstras and the Upaniṣads, it is primarily taught that once mastery over the vital air (pavana) is attained through breath-restraints alone, there follows mastery over the elements and the senses. Therefore, its definition must be stated with great effort; and that has been explained in exactly that manner by Yājñavalkya and others.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Praṇava; this is the threefold restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama).
Thus [it is said]: "Vasiṣṭha says:

'One who has restrained the breath should recite the Gāyatrī, joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, together with its head (śiras), three times; that is called prāṇāyāma. In this regard, for the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana), atonement (prāyaścitta), and so forth, they desire the restraint of the functions of prāṇa and apāna by means of kumbhaka alone; whereas in samādhi, it is by means of both kumbhaka and recaka. Kumbhaka occurs when, during the inhalation of external air, the belly is filled like a jar; recaka, however, results from the expulsion of internal air, thereby producing emptiness in the belly. In this matter, the sequence is as follows: *oṃ bhūḥ*...
Oṃ khaḥ oṃ oṃ bhuvaḥ.

*Mahas*. Some, however, recite the word *mahat* ending in the letter *t*, as in "Oṃ mahat. Thus it is said in the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*: "The world of Brahmā consists of three levels; beyond that is the Great (*Mahān*) world of Prajāpati; and the world of Indra is called *Svar*. In heaven are the stars, and on earth are the creatures. Oṃ *janaḥ*; Oṃ *tapaḥ*; Oṃ *satyam*. Oṃ, we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects. Oṃ, water, light, essence, immortality, Brahman, *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*, Oṃ.

Prāṇāyāma is the restraint of the vital breath for as long a time as it takes to recite this [formula] three times; that is what should be practiced. They also desire this prāṇāyāma at the commencement of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana). However, there is this distinction:
"Three prāṇāyāmas consist of a measure of fifteen mātrās."

Thus, this [method] taught by Gautama is to be performed first; afterwards, this other [method] follows, as there is an entitlement to it here beyond that of Gautama’s rule. As it has been said: "Purified by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one then becomes worthy of the syllable Om. In the same way, our tradition from the elders is as follows: at the very commencement of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), during the time of initiation (upanayana) itself, we were diligently made to practice both types of breath-restraint by our venerable fathers, who were the most excellent knowers of the meaning of the Vedas.

In this regard, the meaning of the *vyāhṛtis* and the *sāvitrī*, which is the nature of Brahman, has already been explained. Indeed, even the seven worlds have been stated to be the form of Brahman, as expressed by the *praṇava* (*oṃkāra*) and the *sāvitrī*. Furthermore, because the mantra "āpo jyotiḥ" stands above all its limbs and is preeminent, its denotation—expressed by the word "head"—is likewise the very form of Brahman, due to its possession of the word "Brahman" itself. This constitutes the subject matter of the *jñānakāṇḍa* regarding non-duality (*advaita*), and the subject matter of the *karmakāṇḍa* regarding duality (*dvaita*). In that context, "Brahman" is the substantive term (*viśeṣyapada*).
