The four qualifying terms beginning with "āpaḥ" (waters) are as follows: from the root *āp* in the sense of "pervasion," "āpaḥ" means the pervader; thus, because it is connected to all effects, the pervasiveness of Brahman alone is expressed. By "jyotiḥ" (light), its nature as the illuminator of knowledge is expressed. By "rasaḥ" (essence), its quality of being the core or quintessence is expressed. By "amṛtam" (immortal), its nature as eternal bliss and its supreme indestructibility are expressed. By "bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ," its nature as consisting of the three worlds is expressed. Furthermore, the power of this head is also described.

"The Brahman consisting of sixteen syllables is remembered as the head of the Gāyatrī; by constantly repeating it, a learned brahmin is swiftly liberated from saṃsāra. There is no meter for the Head because it belongs to the Yajurveda. Its seer (ṛṣi) is Prajāpati. Its deities (devatās), however, are Agni, Brahmā, Vāyu, and Sūrya. And so says Pārāśarya:

"The head of the Gāyatrī is said to be *āpo jyotī raso'mṛtam*. In that regard, the seer is Prajāpati; it is remembered as a Yajus devoid of meter (*chandas*). Brahmā, Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya are proclaimed to be its deities. After breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) accompanied by mantras. As Śaṅkha says:

"Having thus performed the sprinkling (*saṃmārjana*) and the breath controls, the knower of Dharma should thereafter sip water at the two twilights with this mantra: 'O Waters, you move within all beings, in the secret cave, in all forms...'"

"You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call; you are the waters, light, essence, and immortality. Thus, Brahman is spoken of, and the waters are praised as having that form. You alone move within all beings. For indeed, you are the waters themselves. You alone are in the cave—the meaning is that you are the mind (*manas*) within the space of the heart; this is also an indication for all the sense organs. Furthermore, those individual souls (*jīvātman*) who reside in all embodied forms are also you alone. You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call; the meaning is that you alone are the form of both the goal to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment. You are light, you are essence, you are immortality—and you are those very waters.

Thus [it is said]. The second mention of "water" (*ap*) is for the purpose of concluding with the form of Brahman within the water being sipped. Gautama also says: "May the horse and the sun purify me" at evening; "May the night and the moon purify me" in the morning. The word "one should sip" (*ācamed*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Following the breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*), there is the "worship" (*upasthāna*) of the Sun...
This is because of such scriptural evidence,
and because of the statement: "Reciting the two verses, 'udutyaṃ jātavedasam' and 'citram devānām,' a twice-born man should duly offer a handful of water to the Sun."

"Regarding the verse *ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam*, the seer (ṛṣi) is said to be Praskaṇva; the meter (chanda) is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity (devatā) is said to be Sūrya. Regarding *citraṃ devānām*, Trita or Kutsa is celebrated as the seer; the meter is Triṣṭubh, and Sūrya is proclaimed as its deity. According to the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*), "In the Atirātra sacrifice, during the recitation for the Aśvins, there is an application of this [verse], as well as in silent prayer (*japa*)," one should worship the Āditya with these two verses, *ud u tyam* and *citraṃ devānām*, while holding a handful of water.
His rays bear aloft that god Sūrya, the Jātavedas, so that everyone may behold him.

The word *tyad* is a pronoun (*sarvanāma*). The word *u* is a particle (*nipāta*) used for the purpose of filling the meter. It is connected with the verb *vahanti* (they carry) following the prefix *ud*. "They carry" that *jātavedas*—one whose wisdom is born, or whose wealth is born—the god endowed with qualities such as generosity, the sun full of splendor; his rays or horses carry him. For what purpose do they carry him? For the sake of seeing (*dṛśe*). Whose? For "all" (*viśvāya*), where the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive, meaning for the sake of the entire threefold world.

The brilliant array of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni. Sūrya has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space; he is the soul of all that moves and stands. Āditya is Brahman. And here, he who exists in both transcendent (para) and immanent (apara) forms is praised. Regarding his immanent form, the praise begins from the time of his rising: "Citra" is an adverbial modifier [meaning "brilliantly"].

He who has risen—has ascended—having dispelled the darkness of night (*śārvara*) and having taken away the splendor of the night; having taken up the host, the multitude, or the face of the shining rays of the gods. Who? The Sun. Of what nature? The eye of the moving world (*jagat*). Or rather, it is said generally: he is the leader even of Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others. And he who has filled (*āprā*), that is, completely pervaded, both Heaven and Earth, as well as the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

He praises [the Self] by means of another form: "The Self of the world—of that which moves (jaṅgama) and that which stands still (tasthuṣaḥ). By this, the non-duality of the Sun is expressed; Brahman is to be meditated upon in the form of Āditya. And so says the Śruti: "Those who know that Puruṣa who is Āditya—he is Indra, he is Prajāpati, he is Brahmā."

Based on the statement, "The twice-born should worship the Sun with mantras having that deity," it is explained that other mantras as well— those addressed to the Sun— are to be employed for the purpose of praising the Sun.

The Haṃsa dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the intermediate space, the Hotṛ priest dwelling at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house, the one dwelling among men, the one dwelling in the waters, the one dwelling in the rays of light, the one born from the lotus, born from the cow, born from Truth, born from the mountain—the Great Truth. The meter is Jagatī; the seer is Vāmadeva; the deity is Sūrya, who is praised as the Supreme Self. He is called *Haṃsa* because he destroys darkness (*han*) and moves along the path (*sā*), or because he destroys ignorance in his aspect as the presiding deity.
Thus it has been said: "Haṃsa is declared to be Nārāyaṇa; Haṃsa is determined to be the Self. That Self is the Blessed Viṣṇu; that is Brahman, all-pervading."

Thus: the *śucayaḥ* are the pure, radiant rays; or, heaven (*svarga*) is pure (*śuci*); or, eternal knowledge and bliss are pure there, and he dwells therein—thus he is *śuciṣat*. Likewise, he causes the world to dwell (*vasayati*) by means of rain and so forth, through the processes of manifestation (*vivarta*) and transformation (*pariṇati*), and in his internal form (*adhyātmarūpa*); thus he is *vasu*, the Sun. He dwells in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) in the form of wind and so forth, thus he is *antarikṣasat*; or, in his internal form as the inner self (*antaryāmin*) of all individual souls (*jīvātman*) dwelling in the intermediate space of the heart-cavity (*hṛdayākāśa*), he dwells—thus he is *antarikṣasat*. *Hotā*: this is the form of the word *he*.

The meaning is that he "challenges" (āhvayati), "contends with" (spardhate), or "offers oblations to" (juhoti) living beings who are asleep at night, by bringing them face-to-face with the accomplishment of their activities, or by taking away [their vitality]—either in the form of the presiding deity (adhideva) or in the form of the inner self (adhyātma)—thus censuring ignorance. He is "sitting on the altar" (vediṣat) because he sits on the altar in the form of fire; and in the form of the inner self as well, he is "sitting on the altar" (vediṣat) because he sits on the "altar" (vedyām)—meaning in that which consists of eternal knowledge—as one who knows (from the root *vid* "to know"). Being a guest, he sits in the "dwelling" (duroṇe)—that is, in the house, in the abode of the individual soul (jīvātman), or in the entire body.

Alternatively, he is the "guest in the house" (*duroṇasat*) because he dwells in the *droṇakalaśa*—the vessel for the Soma juice—as the essence of deities such as Agni. Furthermore, he is a guest because of his impermanence within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and within all bodies; for a guest is impermanent, since he moves from one house to another. He is "dwelling among men" (*nṛṣat*) because he resides among human beings as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and in the form of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The mention of "men" is intended to indicate sentient beings in general.

It is called *nṛṣat* because it dwells (*sīdati*) among men and all sentient beings in the sphere of the deities (*adhidaiva*), by way of being the illuminator and as an auxiliary to the eye. It is called *varasat* because it dwells in the excellent place of heaven (*dyusthāna*) in its aspect as the deity (*adhidaivātman*). And so says the Brāhmaṇa:

"Or rather, this is a *varasat* [excellent seat], for he sits and shines within it. Alternatively, in the sense of *vara*, he sits (*sīdati*) and sports in excellent, superior places such as the Nandana grove, Mahāloka, and so forth, by assuming the state of Indra and other deities; thus, he is *varasat*. In the *adhyātma* (inner/self-referential) perspective, he abides in *ṛta*—that is, in the eternal consciousness which is the nature of truth; thus, he is *ṛtasat*. Or, in the *adhidaiva* (divine/cosmic) perspective, he sits as a deity within *ṛta*—the sacrifice consisting of solar rites and the like; thus, he is *ṛtasat*. He sits in the *vyoman*—the intermediate space or the space of the heart; thus, he is *vyomasat*. There is no fault in tautology when it occurs in praise (*stuti*). As it has been said:

"A speaker whose mind is distracted by joy, fear, and the like, while praising or censuring, may utter a word more than once; that repetition is not a fault. Here too, the Speaker is the Self of the Vedas (Vedātman). Thus says the Śruti: "He whom all the Vedas do not know, of whom all the Vedas are the body—he is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the Immortal.

Alternatively, by the repetition of the utterance, he makes this known: that the entire collection of words is of such a nature as to denote Brahman alone. [The term] *abjāḥ* means "born in the waters."

According to the Mānava-śāstra beginning with "In the beginning he created the waters alone...", the Sun is born from the waters (abjāḥ). Alternatively, he is born from the waters in the sense of being seen from the shore of the ocean. Thus says the Śruti:
"Verily, this one rises in the morning as the waters; he enters the waters in the evening."

Thus: He is "born from the waters" (*abjāḥ*), for the nature of the Sun consists of the fire of lightning and the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*). He is "born of the cow" (*gojāḥ*), for he is born in the sky (*go*)—in the form of Indra and others—or in the intermediate space as the nature of light, or on earth in the form of food, fuel, and so forth. He is "born of Truth" (*ṛtajāḥ*), for he is born and abides within Truth-knowledge (*ṛta*). And thus says the Śruti: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

Thus, they are called *adrijāḥ* (born of the mountain) because they are born and perceived on Mount Meru at the time of sunrise. Or rather, what need is there for much speaking? *Ṛtam* is the Sun himself; *ṛtam* is that which is all-pervading, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman—he is the Sun. The sentence should be completed as: "May we attain that Supreme Brahman. *Bṛhat* means pervasive.
Rising up from out of the darkness, beholding the higher light, we have gone to the Sun, the god among gods, the supreme light.

The meter is *anuṣṭubh*; the deity is Sūrya. The prefix *ud-* is connected with the word *aganma*. "We have gone up" (*udaganma*) refers to the supreme light characterized as Brahman. The form *udaganma* is used in the sense of the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*) by way of grammatical substitution; the meaning is that we pray, "May we go upward. What are we doing? Beholding—that is, meditating upon—the Sun, who is the light superior to, more excellent than, or situated above other lights such as lamps; the meaning is "by means of this meditation on the Sun."

Furthermore, what kind [of being] do they behold? He who exists "from out of darkness" (*tamasas pari*), that is, above darkness; the meaning is that he is the destroyer of darkness, both in the sense of physical gloom and in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, what kind? A "god" (*deva*), one endowed with qualities such as generosity (*dāna*) or one who shines (*dyotamāna*). Likewise, "among the gods" (*devatrā*), because of his protection (*trāṇa*) of the gods—namely, the thirty [deities] and the Brāhmaṇas. [The root] *traiṅ* means "to protect"; [the suffix] *ka* is added by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*; the vowel *ā* is an augment (*varṇāgama*); and the accusative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

But it is not the case that the secondary derivative suffix *trā* in the word *devatrā* means "protecting from gods, men, and humans," because its meaning is already conveyed by the word *devam* itself.
The fame of the god Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is winning; his splendor possesses most wonderful renown.

Gāyatrī. Mitra impels men as he speaks; Mitra has supported both the earth and the sky. Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; let us offer an oblation rich in ghee to Mitra. This [verse] is in the Triṣṭubh meter. The two deities for both [verses] are Mitra and Āditya. The commentary on these follows in order: "I meditate upon the *śravaḥ*—the glory or majesty—of Mitra, the son of Aditi, who is smooth of aspect. The word *śravaḥ* (glory) is so called because it is heard (*śrūyate*); the meaning is that it is the form of the Supreme Brahman well-known from the Upaniṣads. Of what nature is this *śravaḥ*?

*Dyumnam* means shining. Likewise, *sānasi* means exalted. It is *citraśravastama*, meaning most wonderful, most marvelous, and most renowned, because it is perceived by all individual souls as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*) in the form of the presiding deity (*adhidaiva*). For everyone thinks: "I am impelled by someone to perform this action. As it has been said: "This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it goes either to hell or even to heaven."

Thus [it is said]. Of what kind [is he]? "The supporter of the people" (*carṣaṇīdhṛt*): the "people" (*carṣaṇayaḥ*) are human beings; he supports them by means of rain and so forth in his form as the presiding deity (*adhidaiva*), and in his form as the inner self (*adhyātma*), by means of being the nature of the manifestation and transformation of consciousness (*caitanya*).

Now follows the verse, "Mitra, who brings people together" (*athottarā mitro janānīti*). The change of gender in *janānīti* is significant; *janāḥ* means those who are born, and he "brings them together" (*ātayati*) means he extends them or impels them toward their activities. What does he do? He does not merely cause actions to be performed by making others visible; rather, even while speaking in the form of the Vedas and so forth, he ordains both injunctions and prohibitions. As Mitra, he supports (*dādhāra*)—the *liṭ* suffix here being used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*) for the present tense—the earth and the sky, sustaining them through the medium of rain and other such means.

Likewise, Mitra alone gazes upon the *kṛṣṭīs*, that is, human beings, with unblinking eyes—meaning he looks toward them without closing his eyes. Who among them performs good deeds or evil deeds? As we have stated in our hymn to Viṣṇu: "The Sun is also the witness of all actions," and so forth. Furthermore, we meditate upon Mitra as our supreme friend; for unto this Mitra, who is the Sun and possesses the form of Agni, we offer oblations (*havyam*)—that is, the sacrificial food mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—every day at evening and at dawn. This is the meaning.

From this point forward, the water-libation (udakatarpaṇa) prescribed by the Ṛṣis must necessarily be performed. That is now demonstrated according to different traditions. Regarding this, Baudhāyana first says: "Immediately after this, he satiates the deities: 'I satiate Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Serpents—these eastern doors together with the deities, the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas; and I satiate the Vasus.'"

I satiate Tapan, Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni—these southern doors together with their deities, their constellations, their planets, their days and nights, and their muhūrtas; and I satiate the Rudras.

I satiate Mitra, Indra, Nirṛti, Pūṣan, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these western doors together with their deities, their constellations, their planets, their days and nights, and their muhūrtas; and I satiate the Ādityas.

I satiate the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja-ekapāt, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama; these, together with their deities, their constellations, their Saṃgrahas, their days and nights, and their Muhūrtas, as well as the Sādhyas, I satiate.

I satisfy Brahmā; I satisfy Prajāpati, the four-faced one; I satisfy Parameṣṭhin; I satisfy the attendants of Brahmā; and I satisfy the female attendants of Brahmā. Oṃ Bhūḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa; Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa; Oṃ Svaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa; Oṃ Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa. Oṃ Bhūḥ, I satisfy [the worlds]; Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Svaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Mahaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Janaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Tapaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ Satyam, I satisfy.

Oṃ, obeisance to the god Bhava; Oṃ, obeisance to the god Śarva; Oṃ, obeisance to the god Īśāna; Oṃ, obeisance to the god Paśupati; Oṃ, obeisance to the god Rudra; Oṃ, obeisance to the god Ugra; Oṃ, obeisance to the god Bhīma; Oṃ, obeisance to the god Mahādeva.

Oṃ, [I worship] the wife of the god Bhava; Oṃ, the wife of the god Śarva; Oṃ, the wife of the god Īśāna; Oṃ, the wife of the god Paśupati; Oṃ, the wife of the god Rudra; Oṃ, the wife of the god Ugra; Oṃ, the wife of the god Bhīma; Oṃ, the wife of Mahādeva.

Oṃ, [I offer] the son of the god Bhava; Oṃ, the son of the god Śarva; Oṃ, the son of the god Īśāna; Oṃ, the son of the god Paśupati; Oṃ, the son of the god Rudra; Oṃ, the son of the god Ugra; Oṃ, the son of the god Bhīma; Oṃ, the son of the god Mahādeva; Oṃ, [I offer] the attendants of Rudra and the female attendants of Rudra.

Oṃ, I satiate Skanda, Sanatkumāra, Ṣaṣṭhī, Viśākha, the attendants of Skanda, and the female attendants of Skanda. I satiate the obstacles (Vighnas), Vīra, Śīla, Vīradanta, Hastimukha, the attendants of Vighna, and the female attendants of Vighna. I satiate Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the goddess Śrī, Sarasvatī, Puṣṭi, the attendants of Viṣṇu, and the female attendants of Viṣṇu.

Yama, Kāla, Vaivasvata, Citragupta, the male attendants of Vaivasvata, and the female attendants of Vaivasvata; Bharadvāja, Vidyā, Dhanvantari, the male attendants of Dhanvantari, and the female attendants of Dhanvantari.

Then the seers: "I satiate the seers; I satiate the great seers; I satiate the supreme seers; I satiate the divine seers; I satiate the Vedic seers; I satiate the ascetic seers; I satiate the seven seers; I satiate the Kaṇva seers; I satiate the female seers; I satiate the wives of the seers; I satiate the sons of the seers; [I satiate] Kāṇva, Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtras, Satyāṣāḍha, Hiraṇyakeśin, Vyāsa, the Praṇava, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, the meters, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and all the collections of Vedas—I satiate all living beings.
Thus.
From the *Yājñavalkīya-yoga-śāstra*:
"Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana; Kapila, Āri, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha—these seven sons of Brahmā are proclaimed as human beings. And Kātyāyana:
"Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada."

Now, the Purāṇa states: "Having first performed the libation (tarpaṇa) for the deities and then for the sages (ṛṣis), one always becomes authorized for the libation for the ancestors (pitṛs). Thus, at the time of bathing, the libation for the deities must necessarily be performed. Now, that which was stated by Āśvalāyana:

"May the deities be satisfied; may Agni be satisfied; may Vāyu be satisfied; may Sūrya, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the Vedas, the Ṛṣis, the syllable Oṃ, the syllable Vaṣaṭ, the Vyāhṛtis, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, and the Sacrifices be satisfied. May Heaven and Earth be satisfied. May the intermediate space, the stars, the Sāṃkhyas, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the rivers, the mountains, the fields, the herbs, the trees, the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, the Brahmins, the birds, the cows, the Yakṣas, the Rakṣasas, and all beings ending with these, be satisfied."

Now, may the seers be satisfied: the Śatarcins, the Mādhyamas, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, the Pragāthas, the Pāvamānyas, the authors of the short hymns, and the authors of the long hymns. May Vaiśampāyana, Paila, the Sūtrakāras, the Bhāṣyakāras, the teachers of the Mahābhārata, and the teachers of Dharma be satisfied. May Jānaki, Vāhavi, Gārgya, Gālava, Gautama, Śaunaka, Śāṇḍilya, Vābhravya, and Māṇḍūkeya be satisfied. May Gārgī Vācaknavī be satisfied.

May Vaḍavā, Prātitheyī, Sulabhā, and Maitreyī be satisfied. I satiate Kahoḍa Kauṣītaka, Mahākauṣītaka, Āśvalāyana, Aitareya, Mahaitareya, Paijaya, Vāṣkala, Ajātaśatru Audavāhi, Mahaudavāhi, Saujāmi, and Śaunaka. May all other teachers likewise be satisfied; having satiated them, may they drink [the water] for each individual person.

Now follows this ancient legend: "Salutations to Brahmā; salutations to Viṣṇu; salutations to Maheśvara; salutations to Vahni, Sūrya, Soma, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, Kubera, Indra, Pṛthivī, Apas, Tejas, Vāyu, Ākāśa, Agni, Āditya, Varuṇa, Candramas, Kumāra, Bhauma, Viṣṇu, Budha, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Sarasvatī, Śukra, Prajāpati, Śanaiścara, Gaṇapati, Rāhu, Rudra, Ketu, Brahmā, and Dhruva."

To Ananta, Agastya, Dhruva, Kāla, Viśvakarman; to the Prajāpatis, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, the Ṛṣis, the Devarṣis, the Brahmarṣis, the Rājarṣis, the Siddhas, the Vidyādharas, the Gandharvas, the Nāgas, the Vainateyas, the Apsarases, the oceans, the mountains, the lunar mansions, the deities of the lunar mansions, the mothers of the gods, and the wives of the gods.

"Salutation to the daughters of the gods, to the Vedas, to the Vedāṅgas, to the limbs of sacrifice, to Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa, to the seven authors, to sentient beings, to the cardinal directions, to the intermediate directions, to the lords of the directions, to the sacred fords, to the rivers, to the seven worlds, to the seven netherworlds, to all the gods, to Śrī, to Sarasvatī, to the spirits that roam by day—salutation! To the spirits that roam by night—salutation! Thus says Baudhāyana.

"Sitting on *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, and facing the east, one should repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times. One should also mutter the *Gāyatrī* joined with the *Praṇava* and the *Vyāhṛtis*. Then, taking up a thread, one should count the recitation by means of that very thread.

A wise person should perform the recitation (*japa*) in a low voice, especially that of the *Sāvitrī*. A human being who conquers the *Sāvitrī* goes to heaven. For the purpose of pacification (*śānti*), the recitation should be mental; for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it should be whispered (*upāṃśu*). But for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), it should be done aloud, facing north, east, or south. One should meditate on the mantra mentally, without moving the tongue or lips. One should not shake the head or neck, nor should one show the teeth. Having withdrawn the collection of senses into a single point and fixing the mind upon the meaning of the mantra, one should recite.

One should perform the recitation of the *japa* purely with respect to its vowels, syllables, words, and sentences. The *Gāyatrī* destroys the impurity arising from ten births with ten repetitions, that committed in a previous life with a hundred, and that originating from three ages (*yugas*) with a thousand. [This applies even] to food eaten without *darbha* grass, or a gift given without water, provided it is done with effort.

But all that sacrifice which is performed without [proper] counting becomes fruitless. Recitation performed with golden teeth and jewels becomes a hundredfold; with *indrākṣa* beads it becomes a thousandfold; with *rudrākṣa* beads it becomes ten thousandfold; and with lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*) it becomes a hundred thousand or a millionfold—of this there is no doubt. There is no limit to the number of recitations performed with *putrajīvaka* seeds.

He who knows this, being a son of Brahman, a Brāhmaṇa who follows the sacred teaching, attains the world of Brahman by worshipping this very [fire] day after day at the junctions of the day and night.
May He—the beginning of the world, stainless and imperishable—be for your eternal welfare, whom they constantly meditate upon as the conscious Self preceded by silent recitation.
Thus ends the second section. 1.
The Third Section (Kāṇḍikā).
Regarding the vow of studentship (brahmacarya), he states the limit by means of the procedure for honoring the teacher:
"Having understood the meanings of the Veda, one who is about to bathe (snātaka) should cause a cow to be given and should honor the teacher. (1)

In the *chandasa*, that is, the Veda characterized by the *ṛg*, *yajus*, and *sāman*—which consists of the divisions of *mantra*, *brāhmaṇa*, *arthavāda*, and names—one should understand those established meanings which are to be determined in the twelve chapters (*adhyāyas*). Because of his fitness for this, one who is about to bathe (*snāsyan*)—desiring to take a wife and wishing to undertake the duties of a *snātaka*—should cause a cow to be prepared for the teacher for the sake of the *madhuparka* offering; having given his own wealth, he should honor him. That cow, being intended for use in the *madhuparka*, shall be given to the guru.

Some maintain that the teacher gives the *madhuparka* to the student who desires to undergo initiation, while the student gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher. Others, however, explain that the word "cow" is intended to signify the *madhuparka* produced from a cow; thus, the meaning is that after having studied under the teacher, one should cause the *madhuparka* to be prepared with the request, "Let the *madhuparka* be given to me. And having accepted the *madhuparka*, the religious student (*brahmacārī*) should honor the teacher according to his ability with a sacrificial fee and other offerings.

Others, however, explain [the text] according to a division of the Sūtras: "Having understood the meanings of the Vedas, one who is about to bathe (perform the *samāvartana*) should cause a cow to be given" is the first [sūtra]; "one should honor the teacher" is the second. The meaning of the first is: "At the beginning of his studies, one should cause a cow and the *madhuparka* to be given for oneself by the teacher. And the student, having been honored by the teacher and having received the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), should subsequently honor the teacher with the giving of fees and so forth. For it is the teacher who first honors the student once he has properly studied and understood the Veda.
Thus says the Smṛti: "Him, who is renowned for his own duty and who has inherited the Veda as a legacy from his father..."

"One should first honor with a cow that student who is wearing a garland, seated upon a couch. This means: the teacher should honor with a cow that student—who is known for his own duty, namely the duty of a disciple; who has come before him; who brings the Veda to the teacher and inherits the father's legacy; who wears a garland (sragvin); and who is seated (āsīna) upon a couch (talpa). Therefore, having acquired knowledge and being permitted by the teacher, he should perform the ceremonial bath (snāna); and having bathed, he should take a wife. But if he does not discharge [his semen], he returns [to his studies] after having emitted it. And so says the Śruti:
"Indra indeed lived as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with Prajāpati; having left it unfinished, he returned after casting away his vigor."
Thus it is said:
"The teacher is Prajāpati to the religious student.
And so forth. || 1 ||

There are two types of *brahmacārins*: the *upakurvāṇa*, who, having practiced the life of a student, resorts to ritual bathing, taking a wife, and so forth; and the *naiṣṭhika*, who reaches his final goal through the lifelong practice of celibacy. Among these, the life of studentship for the *upakurvāṇa* is limited by a specific duration; with reference to him, it is said, "the meanings in the Veda," and so on. However, with reference to the *naiṣṭhika*, this is stated: "a *śrotriya* is one other than a mere reciter of the Vedas. (2)

Another is the lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*). A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda; the word *śrotriya* is established as denoting a Vedic scholar in the sense that "one who studies the *śruti* (Veda) is a *śrotriya*. The repetition of the term "Vedic scholar" is for the sake of emphasis, meaning that he alone does not perform the ritual bath (*snāna*) and other such duties; the meaning is that his vow of celibacy lasts until death. || 2 ||
For this very reason, he says for the sake of clarity:
"For him there is no ritual bathing. (3)
The meaning is that for that lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) just mentioned, there is no ritual bathing (snāna). || 3 ||
Regarding that student (*upakurvāṇaka*) for whom bathing and other such rites exist, [the text] now states the duty of bathing:

"Then, having caused him to put on a garment for traveling (*vrajaparihita*), and having removed his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails, he should bathe with the three verses beginning 'āpo hi ṣṭhā,' with the two verses beginning 'hiraṇyavarṇāḥ,' and with the two verses beginning 'śaṃ naḥ. (4)

A *vraja* is a herd of cattle; having brought [the student] to—that is, having caused him to enter—a place occupied by such a herd, this is the instruction for the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), namely the teacher. According to what is possible—either the shaving of matted locks (*jaṭā*) in the case of the *jaṭila* option, or the shaving of hair in the case of the *śikhin* option—he should cause him to bathe, that is, he should cause him to immerse himself, while performing the ritual sprinkling (*saṃmārjana*) with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," after having removed the matted locks and so forth and having caused them to be shaved.

One should perform the second bath with the two verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and the third with the two verses beginning "śaṃ na āpaḥ. Here, by the mention of "beard" (śmaśru), the hair situated above the lips is also included; by the mention of "body hair" (loma), the hair in the private parts is included, but not that on the arms and so forth, as that would contradict common usage among the noble ones (ārya). || 4 ||

Then, having bathed three times and become purified, it is said that he should perform this and that; with the mantra "The sky is your back," he should hold an umbrella. (5) With the mantra "This [is for you], O Agni," [he should hold] gold. (6) With the mantra "You two are supports, O divine ones; do not harm me," he puts on shoes made of boar-skin. (7) From this point forward he should wear two garments; therefore, beautiful clothing should be worn—so says the Śruti. (8) He should always carry a bamboo staff. (9) He should carry an umbrella. (10) He should not yield the path to others. (11) Taking what is not given is forbidden. (12)

13. Exiting through a side door; 14. Conversing with a woman in her menses; 15. Sleeping on the same bed with a woman in her menses; 16. Speaking harsh words to one's teacher; 17. Smiling at an inappropriate time; 18. Running; 19. Singing; 20. Dancing; 21. And looking at such [dancing].

In this collection of sūtras, because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more authoritative than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), one must arrange the specific order of the mentioned and unmentioned items according to the force of their meaning. For instance, for one who has bathed three times and emerged from a body of water with food and other items, the washing of the feet and so forth—which were not explicitly stated—and the wearing of clean garments and so forth—which were stated—should be understood according to their proper sequence.

One should hold up the parasol with the mantra beginning "dyauste pṛṣṭham," and according to one's means, [wear] gold ornaments such as bracelets and earrings with the mantra beginning "imam agne. With the mantra beginning "pratiṣṭhe sthaḥ," one puts on or dons sandals made of boar-skin; the word *varāha* here refers to the skin of a boar.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "made from" (in this case, *varāhacarmaṇā nirvṛttaḥ*). Then, by the rule *aṇiñoḥ anārṣayor gurūpottamayoḥ ṣyaṅ gotre*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied. By the rule *yaṅaś cāp*, the feminine suffix *cāp* is added. Thus, they are *vārāhy-upānahau* (boar-skin sandals). A *varāha* is a boar. Furthermore, the existence of boar-sandals is understood from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like in the context of the *Rājasūya* sacrifice. Others, however, explain that the word *vārāhya* denotes a pair of sandals characterized by a specific shape, just as in the case of the term *catuṣkaccha*.

Others describe them as being merely the size of a hide, for no teacher is ever seen wearing sandals made of boar-hide. However, some read the text as *vārāhupānahau*; in that case, there are two words: *vārāhī* and *upānahau*. According to the rule "Sūtras are like Vedic meters," the dual ending of the first word is elided or replaced by the *pūrvasavarṇa* substitute, in accordance with the rule *supāṃ suluk pūrvasavarṇa* and so forth.

"Two-clothed from then on": beyond this stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), he is two-clothed. As a student, he wore a single garment, for he wore a deer-skin over it, and the word "garment" (*vastra*) is not used in common parlance for that. Therefore, two garments should be worn according to one's means, and they should be excellent; thus says the Śruti: "Therefore, a beautiful garment should be worn. And he is one who habitually carries a staff made of bamboo; such is the meaning of "one who carries a bamboo staff" (*vaiṇavadaṇḍadhārī*).

"Constantly" means not only at certain times for the purpose of supporting [the king] and so forth. Likewise, he is a "parasol-bearer. He is one who does not give way to another—that is, he should not yield the path to anyone other than for a visible purpose. However, the reading "apathadāyī" (one who does not give way) is more appropriate; for since Gautama and others have stated that "the king must yield the path to a *śrotriya*," how could this person, being a distinguished *śrotriya*, yield the path to any mere living being?

Taking for oneself is forbidden: one should not take property belonging to another that has not been given by that other, because it is prohibited by such scriptural injunctions as "one should not seize the wealth of another. "By another door" refers to exiting; the word "forbidden" is to be supplied as a grammatical adjunct until the end of the section. As for the well-known and unobjectionable door, exiting and entering by any other door—namely, an unknown one intended for secret entry and exit from the inner apartments and so forth—is forbidden.

One who wears soiled clothes refers to a dog-cooker (śvapaca) and others; conversing with such a person is forbidden. Likewise, lying down with one wearing menstrual blood—namely, a woman in her courses, also known as *udakyā*—is forbidden. This is stated because bathing marks the commencement of marriage; for, apart from marriage, there is no occasion for bathing as part of such a ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*). [The same applies to] a guru, that is, one worthy of honor.

"Wealth, kinship, age, action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect, each subsequent one being weightier than the preceding. With reference to such [teachings], the speaking of wicked or harsh words is prohibited. Laughing or smiling out of place—that is, in the presence of elders, women, and others—is prohibited. Likewise, wandering or moving about out of place, specifically in secret or in the presence of elders, is prohibited.

Thus, singing, chanting, and dancing are prohibited when performed at an inappropriate time or place; however, they are not forbidden for one who is among those of similar character during festivals and the like, or in a private setting. Accordingly, the performance of singing, instrumental music, and dancing is prescribed in the *Mahāvrata* sacrifice. It is heard in the scriptures: "The *Udgātṛ*, having caused him [the sacrificer] to recite, hands it to the *Prastotṛ*; the *Prastotṛ* to the *Adhvaryu*; and the *Adhvaryu* to another Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, the playing of the lute (*vīṇā*) is mentioned in such passages. And Yājñavalkya says:

"One who knows the principles of playing the lute, is proficient in the musical scales (*śruti*) and modes (*jāti*), and understands rhythm (*tāla*), attains the path of yoga without effort. Furthermore,
the observation of such things as dance and song at an improper time is forbidden, but not during festivals and similar occasions.

The verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" have already been explained. As for the verse beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," because it belongs to another recension (śākhā), the author of the Sūtra has cited it in its entirety.
Heaven is your back, the earth your seat, the atmosphere your self, and the ocean your womb. Having surveyed with your eye, do you trample upon those who attack us.

The *bṛhatī* [meter] is employed in the praise of the horse; here, it is likewise used in the praise of the umbrella (*chattra*). Your sky, the heavenly world, is the back—that is, the upper surface. The earth is the common place (*sadhastha*), the shared location. The atmosphere is the self (*ātman*); this is a praise of the greatness of the umbrella as a whole. The ocean is the water, the source or cause, because of the traditional praise that "the horse is born from the waters"; since the horse is the source of all things originating from water, even the umbrella is likewise so, as are the net, the garment, and other such items.

If you are thus of such great power, then, having made them known by sight and having gazed upon them, stand firm; overcome them at will! Whom? Those who desire an army (*pṛtanā*); those who seek it are *pṛtanyantaḥ*, those [you should overcome] are the *pṛtanyataḥ*.
Grant these [gifts] for long life and splendor; O Varuṇa, sharpen our keen vigor. Like a mother, O Aditi, grant us protection, so that all the gods may see us reach old age.

Make this golden ornament for long life and for the radiance of splendor; perform it. O Varuṇa, you too, provide perfectly sharp and intense vigor and strength. O Aditi, Mother of the Gods, grant and bestow happiness and comfort upon this graduate, like a mother, a progenitress. O Viśve Devās, all you dwellers of heaven, act in such a way that there may be the attainment of old age—that is, act so that we may become possessed of bodies worn by old age.
You two deities are the supports; do not harm me.
"O divine sandals, you two are well-established; may you be of auspicious departure! Do not harm me—do not cause me injury!
This is the third section (kāṇḍikā). 3.
Now begins the fourth section (kāṇḍikā). Now, therefore, follows that which is measured by forty-eight [verses].

The word "we shall explain" is to be supplied as an ellipsis. And by the context, it is understood that this refers to a *vrata* (vow). We shall explain that substitute for the vow prescribed in the four Vedas—which is measured and delimited by forty-eight years—that is to be accomplished in one year. This must be performed by one who has studied the four Vedas but whose vow, as ordained according to the time [of study], was not fulfilled. For this very reason, this is called the *traividyaka-vrata* (the vow of the three-fold knowledge).

Furthermore, the purpose for mentioning this immediately after the bath is that even one who has become a *snātaka* (graduate) must perform this before marriage. Others, however, explain that although he may have fulfilled the vows prescribed for his specific time of life, this annual vow is enjoined by this rule as something to be performed for the sake of attaining excellence in austerity (*tapas*). The word "atha" (now/then) serves to complete the vow, as it has been said: "The word *atha* is used in the sense of auspiciousness, completion, cause, immediate sequence, and introduction."

"This word *atha* (now/then) is recorded as having six meanings, including that which refers to what has been previously introduced. Other meanings may also be applied as appropriate. The word *ataḥ* (therefore) signifies a reason (*hetu*). Since it is possible that for some person there might be a failure to fulfill the prescribed vows at the time of study, for this reason we shall describe another vow that serves as a substitute. || 1 ||
In that regard, there is a specific rule: || 2 ||
The word "it is said" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 2 ||
In the observances, one should have the teacher as the primary authority.

One should perform the observances (niyamas) to be described hereafter, such as standing and sitting, under the guidance of a teacher; for it is through the preeminence of the teacher that the mastery of the Veda and the practice of its meaning are maintained. || 3 ||
One seeking shelter should not enter a house occupied by a young man. || 4 ||

Fearing cold and heat and seeking shelter, he should not enter a hut, hall, or any specific type of dwelling made of leaves and the like, which is constructed from young bamboo, reeds, grass stalks, and so forth. || 4 ||
He should be homeless. || 5 ||
The meaning is that not only should one not enter a specially constructed dwelling provided by others, but one should not even build a mere shelter for oneself. || 5 ||
Anticipating the objection that "if this were so, the body might perish due to disturbances such as wind, fire, or predatory animals," he says:
"except for a tree or an anthill. (6)
The meaning is that one should take refuge in trees and so forth; "valmīka" refers to anthills, the ground of anthills, and the like. || 6 ||
Some say it is free from the state of youth.

Some say that "tantu" (thread) means bamboo; when struck by cold or other factors, it enters another substratum distinct from its bamboo-made form. Others say "tantu" means rope; that which is produced from ropes and the like, such as a tent or a hall, is "tāntava" (woven). || 7 ||
As it has been stated: "But there shall be only one garment, either made of hemp or of wool. (8)

That which was previously stated regarding the single garment applies here as well. This, however, is the distinction: here it is either a *śāṇī* or a *kutapa*. A *śāṇī* is a coarse hempen cloth, not the well-known linen (*kṣaumī*), though others say it is made of moistened and pounded *darbha* grass. A *kutapa* is made from the hair of goats. (8) He states the dimensions of this garment:
"Measured" means reaching up to the chest and extending above the knees. (9)

Starting from the chest up to the upper part of the knees, this garment should be made of such a measurement; this alone is prescribed for one who has mastered the three Vedas (*traividya*). However, at the time of study, there should be a cloth (*paṭolikā*) on the lower part and a skin (*carma*) on the upper part; and it is stated that such a [double-layered] garment is not called simply "cloth" (*vāsa*) in common worldly usage. || 9 ||
He eats and drinks at the fourth mealtime. || 10 ||

"Twice a day—in the evening and in the morning—is the mealtime ordained by the gods for human beings. This refers to the time for eating. Regarding this, some maintain that one should avoid the two periods characterized as "evening and morning" of the first day, as well as the morning of the second day, and instead perform eating and drinking during the fourth period on the evening of the second day; the meaning is that one should eat at a single session with a single day's interval.

Others, however, say: *pāna* means that which is drunk, such as milk, buttermilk, and so forth; he whose food (*bhakṣa*) consists of that at the fourth period, namely the last watch of the day, is [a *caturthabhaktika*]. The word *bhakṣa* is seen used for liquid drinks such as milk, as in the expression "one who subsists on water" (*abbhakṣa*) or "one who subsists on air" (*vāyubhakṣa*).
One who possesses no accumulation. || 11 ||
The meaning is that one should not accumulate gold and other such things. || 11 ||
Or he may eat almsfood day after day.

*Bhaikṣa* is a collection of alms. Although by the preceding [rule] the accumulation of even alms was prohibited, this [verse] provides an exception to that. One should eat alms every day. However, if the body is weak, one may sometimes eat even a single alms; or, if unable to wander for alms, one may eat flour-grains and the like. The word *vā* (or) is used with the intention that one should accumulate only that much. || 12 ||
He should stand during the day and remain seated at night.

When there is continuous connection (atyantasaṃyoga) with time or distance, the second case ending is used after the word *ahar*. "He should remain standing during the day" means he should remain in an upright position. "At night he should sit"—that is, he should remain seated. If he is extremely fatigued, he may occasionally sleep for a brief moment in between. Because there is no continuous connection [in this latter case], the second case ending is absent. || 13 ||
One who observes the vow of a sage should practice both.
One should maintain restraint of speech for both day and night; this is the vow of the sages. 14.
"One should not converse with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who act with impetuosity, or those who are menstruating," so said Cyavana Bhṛgu. || 15 ||

Cyavana, however, the descendant of Bhṛgu, maintains that one should not converse with those [who are outcasted] by reason of their [impure] appearance and so forth, but not with everyone. The causative suffix *ṇic* in the word *saṃbhāṣayet* is used in its own sense (without changing the meaning), as in the expression "Rāma caused the kingdom to be ruled" (*rāmo rājyam akārayat*). This includes even those of the three higher castes who have fallen [from their status]. The *rabhasas* are those who speak without being asked, such as jesters, panegyrists, and the like. The *rajasvalās*, however, are those who smear their bodies with blood and cause others to provide them with food and other necessities. || 15 ||
Or for twelve nights on both sides of the new moon and the full moon. || 16 ||

This refers to those who are incapable [of performing the full year-long vow]. One should perform this practice—consisting of standing, sitting, silence, and so forth—for twelve nights at both ends of the year, characterized by the commencement and the conclusion, namely on the full moon (paurṇamāsī) and the new moon (amāvāsyā). By that means, there are forty-eight days within the middle of the year. Thus, including the two sets of twelve nights for the beginning and the end, there are twelve full moons and twelve new moons. || 16 ||
The fuel-sticks are always made of *pālāśa* wood, or else from the trees prescribed for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

Those fuel sticks that are constant for the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) are here made of *palāśa* wood. In the absence of *palāśa*, there is a substitute; and regarding the substitute, one should take those belonging to the trees used for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). The trees for the enclosing sticks—and likewise those for the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*)—are the *bilva*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, *rohītaka*, *udumbara*, *badhira*, and so forth. Thus says both the Brāhmaṇa and the Śruti.

"Whether it be of *vailva*, or *khadira*, or *pālāśa*, or *rauhītaka* wood, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for the Soma-sacrifice should be made; however, the sacrificial post is [here] made of *audumbara* wood. "He binds [the animal] to a *khadira* post, he binds it to a *pālāśa* post, he binds it to a *rauhītaka* post. Indeed, all trees used for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are fit for sacrifice; for a Brāhmaṇa passage on this subject is heard.

"Indra brought the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) from sacrificial trees for him. Since the use of *palāśa* wood is already established by the very fact that they are enclosing-sticks made of sacrificial trees, their separate mention here is for the purpose of making them obligatory; thus, there is an explicit mention of their necessity in this context. [Objection: Why was this not stated directly in the primary archetype (*prakṛti*) itself? [Reply: You have spoken well; however, it will serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For instance, it is stated in the *Sādyaska* sacrifice that "the work of the sacrificial post (*yūpakarma*) takes place when the middle pressing has been completed," whereas in the primary archetype it is stated that "the work of the sacrificial post takes place during the *upasad* offerings."

In that regard, since there is an expectation regarding the time [of performance], the teacher has formulated the sūtra in this way to make it understood that even a modification (*vikṛti*) takes up the archetype (*prakṛti*), because there is no contradiction. This same principle should be applied elsewhere as well, since the logic is identical. Therefore, even when the *samid-dāna* (offering of fuel-sticks) is performed with the *aṃhomug* verses, one should understand it exactly thus:
"Indra brought forth the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) from the trees fit for sacrifice.
Having given way with his hand while reciting "May wisdom be mine," he shall perform the ritual touching of water at the three periods of the day and night for one full day and night.

The word "should perform" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having performed a cleansing consisting of rubbing upwards from the navel to the Brahma-door with the two mantras beginning with "medhāṃ mahyam aṅgirasaḥ," he wipes upwards with his hand only above the navel.

According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), one should perform the touching of water (*udakopasparśana*) in this manner during all three pressings—the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the midday pressing (*madhyandinasavana*), and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*)—that is, throughout the three divisions of the night as well. Here, *upasparśana* means bathing. For the word *upasparśana* is seen to be used for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), touching, and bathing—as in the passage, "Having touched [water], there is auspiciousness" (*svastyayana*)—referring to *ācamana*, and not to that which is established by good custom (*sadācāra*) as a penance (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by passing between sacred streams and the like.

In the case of "having touched water, they should touch Soma," it refers to touching; in "having touched [Soma], they should touch water," it refers merely to sipping water; and in "one should touch water on a road, etc.," it refers to bathing. In each instance, the specific application is determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*), just as the word *saindhava* can refer to a horse, salt, or a person from Sindhu.

Water is always pure by virtue of its contact with the sun and wind during the day, with the stars and wind at night, and with fire and wind during the two twilights. Regarding this, they say that one should establish the fire there and place gold nearby. Just as the *vasatīvarī* waters are taken after sunset, because of the non-difference [of the mantra] from "O Waters, Speech," speech itself must be uttered even in the absence of fire; in this same manner, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) and other rites at night as well. 18.

Having bathed in this manner, at each of the three daily libations (anusavana), he should satisfy these very deities with water, saying: "Homage to Hama and Mohama; to Agni Vaiśvānara, Tapas, Tāpasa, Tapantā, Vindu, Vinda, Vasuvinda, and Sarvavinda; homage to Pāra, Supāra, Pārayantā, and Śānta; homage to Ūrmya and Sūrmya; homage to Cyavana and Bhārgava. || 19 ||

The connection is as follows: while satiating these very deities with water, one should perform the ritual sipping (upasparśana) with four mantras delimited by the word "namaḥ. Here, the Sun (Āditya) himself, as delimited by various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is intended to be the form of multiple deities. Thus, in this context, Āditya is praised as the "goer" (gantṛ). The form "hama" is derived from the root *hamm* in the sense of "to go" (*gamane*), according to the rule *dramahammamīmṛgatau*.

The form *mīṃ* [in *mohamāya*] is a Vedic formation derived from the root *mīñ* in the sense of "to injure," with the suffix *tva*. *Mohamāya* means "to one who dispels darkness. *Tapaḥ* is that which heats (*tapati*). A *tāpasa* is one who practices heat (*tapaścacāra*); thus, Āditya himself is praised in the form of Prajāpati. *Tapaḥ* is also the creation of the cosmic egg and so forth; he extends (*tanoti*) or produces that, hence *tapantaḥ*. The elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*) occurs according to the rule: "All rules are optional in the Veda."

He finds and perceives, thus he is *Vindu*; he is found and perceived, thus he is *Vinda*—Prajāpati, whose form is both the object of perception (*cetya*) and the perceiver (*cetayitr*). Salutation to him! He finds wealth (*vasu*), thus he is *Vasuvinda*; likewise, he finds everything, thus he is *Sarvavinda*. This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) of those two. The root *pṛ* (in *pāra*) signifies the completion of an action; he carries one across, thus he is *Pāra*. He extends that which carries one across, thus he is *Pārayantaḥ*. He moves through the waves—the rays and ripples—thus he is *Ūrbhyaḥ*. Thus he is the Sun (*Sūrya*). He causes things to fall away, thus he is *Cyavanaḥ*. He roasts and ripens beings, thus he is *Bhṛgu*; his offspring is *Bhārgava*—here, it is the Light itself (*bhānu*). || 19 ||
Having practiced this for a year, he becomes stainless and free from evil. || 20 ||

This person, whether a student or one who has completed his studies, having observed the prescribed vow for a year, becomes stainless—devoid of the impurities of passion and the like—and free from sin. || 20 ||

By demonstrating the absence of sin, he shows that this one-year vow serves as the expiation for the failure to perform the vows prescribed for the time of Vedic study, which are auxiliary to that study: "If one who has completed his student life (brahmacarya) for all the Vedas does nothing else... (21).

If he does not reach the end [of his studies] at the time of Vedic study, then, when that year-long vow—which serves as its substitute—is performed, he becomes one who has completed his student discipline (*brahmacarya*) for all four Vedas that were to be studied; the meaning is that his study of the four Vedas becomes complete through the fulfillment of the vow.

However, those who describe this year-long vow as independent, intended for the sake of an excellence of austerity for one who has mastered the three Vedas, explain it thus: it forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding [text], meaning that by performing this year-long vow, having fulfilled the vows of all the Vedas, he becomes pure and free from sin, provided he does not commit any other prohibited act during that interval. || 21 ||
Indeed, having practiced the holy life, he purifies ten descendants and ten ancestors—himself being the twenty-first.
The word *tu* (but) is used for the conjunction of another result; *khalu* is used for emphasis. To illuminate the well-known status of this as a Vedic rite, he states another result:
"And as far as one can see the row [of guests] in which he sits. (23)

The word "purifies" (*punāti*) is to be supplied [to the preceding]. By the power of his asceticism (*tapas*), he makes those whom he sees—even if they are not purifiers of the assembly (*apaṅktipāvana*)—into purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*); and even those whom he does not see sitting together at a single meal, he likewise purifies. When this [rite] is completed, he offers an oblation of food for these very deities. A cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

When this vow is completed, one offers food—either rice characterized by *taṇḍula* or a cooked sacrificial oblation (*sthālīpāka*)—to the aforementioned deities. The word "chandovatsūtrāṇi" involves a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*). For the word *anna* is seen used both for what is unprepared and for what is cooked: it is used in the sense of the unprepared in the statement, "One should perform the *nidhana* with *heṣibhi* for one desiring food," and in the sense of the cooked in such passages as, "He mixes food, ghee, honey, and rice," and "One should eat food. All three types—unhusked grain, husked rice, and the cooked oblation—are to be performed in turn according to the specific requirements.

May the Aṅgirasas grant me intelligence; may the Seven Seers grant me intelligence. May Agni and Vāyu grant me intelligence; may Dhātṛ grant me intelligence. (1) May King Varuṇa grant me intelligence; may Agni grant me intelligence. May Indra and Sūrya grant me intelligence; may the goddess Sarasvatī grant me intelligence. (2) That intelligence which is among the Apsarases and that mind which is among the Gandharvas—the divine intelligence that is in humanity—may it enter into me here. (3)
May my body be discerning; may speech yield sweetness for me. May I perceive what has been perceived; may what has been heard abide within me. May that which has been recited by me find delight;
may I be capable of what I repeat. May we be dear to sacred learning; may we be endowed with wisdom. Homage to *hamā* and to *mohamā*.

This consists of five verses with sacrificial formulas (*yajus*). May the Aṅgirasas and the gods bestow wisdom (*medhā*) and intellect upon me; may they perform it for my sake or grant it to me. May Kaśyapa and the other Seven Sages also bestow wisdom. Likewise, may Agni, Vāyu, Dhātṛ, and Prajāpati bestow wisdom upon me. Similarly, may King Varuṇa, Agni, Indra, and Sūrya bestow wisdom upon me, as well as the goddess Sarasvatī.

Likewise, let that intelligence which resides in the *apsarases* and that mind which resides in the *gandharvas*—let both of these enter into me while I exist in this very human body. And let that divine, superhuman intelligence which exists in the distinguished among men also enter me. Furthermore, may my body be discerning, wise, and proficient in all the arts. May Sarasvatī, in the form of the triple Veda (*trayī*), milk for me the honeyed fruit—the sweet ripening result consisting of heaven, liberation, and so forth.

And that which was heard by me, born [in my mind], observed, and understood by me—that I observe, I would observe; the meaning is: "May there be the power of memory for me therein. And that which was spoken to me by the teacher, uttered by him—

May that [Veda], which has a hundred branches, delight us; may it spread forth through disciples, grand-disciples, and others, culminating in its fruit. And that which I desire to declare, may I be able to recite. Likewise, may we be dear to what has been heard (the Veda); may the Veda be supremely gracious in bestowing its fruit upon us; and may we be endowed with, that is, connected to, wisdom. The Yajus has been explained. 24.
Thus ends the fourth section. 4.

Now begins the fifth section (kāṇḍikā). Regarding one who has studied [the Veda] but has not performed the prescribed vows, nor the annual vow, for him [the author] prescribes another independent expiation or another form of austerity, such as the kṛcchra and so forth, as before.
Now we shall explain the procedure for the Kṛcchra penance. ||1||

*Kṛcchra* (hardship) is so called because it consumes (*kṛcchati*) the unwholesome action (*akṛśala-karma*) characterized by the performance of what is prescribed and the practice of what is forbidden. Thus, he will state immediately thereafter: "for the liberation from all unwholesomeness. Gautama says: "Now, having performed these three *kṛcchras*, one becomes purified in all the Vedas; one becomes purified at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."

Thus [it is said]. "Three" refers to the *kṛcchra*, *mahākṛcchra*, and *taptakṛcchra* penances. Alternatively, the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) of *kṛcchra* is "the crushing (*cchradana*) of committed sin (*kṛta-pāpa*). The elision of the vowel [in *kṛta-cchradana*] is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatva*). Accordingly, the *Cārāyaṇi-sūtra* states: "In the case of *puru* and *kṛta* before *chacchrayaḥ*. Here, the words *puru* and *kṛta* are elided respectively when followed by *cha* and *che*. Thus, the crushing of the tail (*puru*) is *puccha*; and the crushing (*cchradana*), that is, the destruction, of what has been committed (*kṛta*) is *kṛcchra*.

"Difficult to cross," "dense," "arduous," "painful," and even "difficult to perform"—the meaning of this [term *kṛcchra*] is understood through its synonyms well-known in the world, as well as through its etymological derivation (*lipi*). "The rule for *kṛcchra*" means the procedure, the power, and the method of performance regarding *kṛcchra*; the statement "we shall explain that" is intended to focus the minds of the disciples. This same principle should be followed elsewhere as well. (1)
For the sake of praise and for his own benefit, he states an explanatory narrative from a former age regarding this vow:
"Just as the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Aṅgirases practiced it in the past. (2)

In this vow, the usage *devādīnām* follows the archaic Vedic style (*ārṣa*). The intended meaning is that this is praiseworthy because it was practiced by the gods and others for the sake of liberation from sin. The word *devāsaḥ* means "the gods" [formed from *devāḥ* with the substitution of *asuk* for the nominative plural ending]. The syntactical connection is: "We shall describe the manner in which the gods and others observed it. || 2 ||
One should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra. || 3 ||
While performing the Kṛcchra penance, one should not converse with a mere woman or a mere Śūdra. || 3 ||
Accompanied by the commentary composed by Devapāla:
"He should remain seated at night, having taken refuge [in the practice]. (4)

Relying merely on a support such as a wall or a piece of wood, he should remain—that is, sit—during the night in order to dispel excessive fatigue; however, he should not sleep. For in this way, his austerity becomes superior. If he is extremely exhausted, he may take a brief nap while remaining seated from time to time, since the collapse of the body must inevitably be avoided, but he should never resort to a bed. || 4 ||
He should remain standing throughout all the days.
During all these days, he should remain standing and must not sit down. || 5 ||
A celibate student. || 6 ||
"One whose nature is the practice of celibacy. By this, he shows that even a householder has the qualification [for this practice]. || 6 ||
One who sleeps at night. || 7 ||

If, in order to dispel excessive fatigue, one should take a slight nap, then it must be during the night while sitting with support against a wall or similar object; by no means during the day, nor upon a bed. ||7||
One should avoid honey, meat, salt, and funeral feasts (śrāddha) without hesitation.
As it is seen in the Vājasaneyaka and other texts: "Honey offered unintentionally does not become tainted," and likewise, "Salt from the Sindhu region is not tainted";
and: "Having given [meat] to the gods and Brahmins, one does not incur fault by eating meat."

Without even considering such scriptural injunctions as, "One should diligently feed one's daughter's son at a śrāddha ceremony even if he is observing a vow," one should avoid honey and other such items during this vow with special care. || 8 ||
A garment made of cow-hide, hemp, bark, or goat-skin is prescribed as clothing. || 9 ||
*Gavājina* is cow-hide; *śāṇīcīra* is a garment made of hemp; *mārga* is the hide of a deer; *kutapa* has already been explained. || 9 ||
Even the Maruts acted in that same way for the sake of liberation from all unwholesome states.

When this vow is properly performed, it serves for the liberation—that is, the destruction—of all unwholesome and sinful karma committed in this life as well as in previous births, including that which was done at other times than the period of study and that which resulted from defects during study.
Furthermore, even the Maruts and others practiced it for that very purpose; thus, since they were not subject to delusion, this is established by firm evidence. || 10 ||
For three days he should eat in the evening, for three days in the morning, and for three days he should eat what is unasked for;
for three days, however, he should not eat at all. This is the vow practiced by the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.

It should be understood that this is performed with the Maruts. One should eat only in the evening for three days after the time of the fire-oblation; for three days one should eat only in the morning; for three days one should eat only what is obtained unasked; and for three days there is fasting. Thus, in this sequence, the vow lasts for twelve days. This Kṛcchra is explained. Its name is Prājāpatya. Other penances of this kind, which are accomplished through hardship—such as the Kūrca, Sāntapana, and so forth—are also designated by the term "Kṛcchra. || 11 ||
Extending this very same method to the *atikṛcchra*, he says:
"This very rule for the *atikṛcchra* is prescribed in this manner. (12)

The very same rule that was stated for the *kṛcchra*—consisting of [specific] postures, sleeping arrangements, celibacy, and so forth—is indeed the procedure for the *atikṛcchra*. If this were the case, there would be no distinction at all; therefore, one might ask: "What scope is there here for an extended application (*atideśa*), since their subject matter is different? Anticipating this, he says: "In this way it is prescribed," the word "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) being understood as the ellipsis. || 12 ||
And so it has been said:
"On these very occasions, one should consume each single morsel. (13)

The meaning is that there is a specific rule regarding the food. Thus, while performing the Atikṛcchra penance, one should eat only a single morsel at each of these aforementioned meal-times, beginning with the morning. As for the measure of the morsel, it remains unchanged: it is the amount that fits in the mouth or fills the hand when eating. || 13 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter (kāṇḍikā). 5.
Now begins the sixth section. He describes the *taptakṛcchra*:

"We shall explain the *taptakṛcchra*: for three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot milk; for three days one should drink hot clarified butter; and for the final three days, one should subsist on air alone. (1)

In times of hardship, such as at evening and so forth, one should drink warm water and the like; *payas* means milk; *sarpis* means clarified butter; *ayācita* means obtained without asking; and *vāyubhakṣaḥ* means that for the sake of purification and the maintenance of the body, one should subsist on air alone and eat or drink nothing else—this is the prescription for three severe fasts. ||1||
This very same procedure is prescribed for the *kūrca* of Bṛhaspati. || 2 ||

"Bṛhaspateḥ" refers to the seer (ṛṣi). The term "kūrca" is a designation for the purpose of providing encouragement. Whatever method of standing, sitting, and so forth has been prescribed for the *kṛcchra* penance, that same method applies to the *kūrca* as well. The word "tu" (but/and) has the sense of "also" (*apy-arthe*) and its position in the verse is displaced. ||2||
He states the specific details as before:
"Barley gruel, barley meal, vegetables, milk, clarified butter, and water infused with kusha grass."
For three days at a time he should eat, and for the final three days he should subsist on air alone.

*Yavāgū* is well known as a drink consisting mostly of gruel made from barley whose husks have been removed; *yāvaka* is similar to that, but it is solid and consists mostly of boiled rice. *Śāka*, however, must be sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), specifically fresh. This should be understood to apply to eating as well, beginning with the evening meal during penances such as the *kṛcchra*. Regarding "water of *kuśa* grass" (*kuśodaka*), because it is expressed as a collective compound (*samāhāra*), they are to be used together. Thus, there are seven three-day periods.
Thus ends the sixth section. 6.
Now begins the seventh section:
Now follows the Sāntapana [fast].

"We shall explain the procedure for the *kṛcchra* penance"—this is the completion of the sentence. The word "atha" (now/then) indicates that this constitutes a separate section from the preceding ones. || 1 ||
The oblation for the Maruts shall satisfy the Maruts. || 2 ||

In this case, the seership belongs to the Maruts alone; therefore, the oblation is offered to them alone. One should satisfy them alone by means of the *codaka* (the water-offering). This [rite] also takes place after the ritual bath (*snāna*). || 2 ||
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water infused with kuśa grass,
and fasting for one night.
This is known as the Kṛcchra-sāntapana penance. || 3 ||

That which consists of both *kṛcchra* and *sāntapana* is the *kṛcchrasāntapana*. [It consists of] drinking *kuśa*-water on one day, [drinking] cow-urine and so forth on each successive day, and fasting for one night; thus it lasts for seven nights. || 3 ||
This very same [practice], when repeated three times,
is known as the Mahāsāntapana.

This very *sāntapana* penance, when practiced three times according to its proper place by way of consuming cow urine and so forth, or performed in the manner of a "repeated staff" (*daṇḍakalitaka*), becomes the *mahāsāntapana*. By this method, seven fasts result for the *sāntapana*, and twenty-one for the *mahāsāntapana*; thus, this is a truly great austerity.

As for the fact that in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* the *sāntapana* penance is understood to last one day and the *mahāsāntapana* seven days, even that is postulated as an alternative for other individuals, depending on their specific capacity, since all the *smṛtis* possess authority. However, one should not experience the hardship of interpreting [the texts] with such restrictive limitations everywhere. In that regard, the statement of Yājñavalkya is: "The *pañcagavya*, however, consists of cow's milk, curd, urine, and dung."

"Having consumed [the substances], one should fast on the following day while performing the *sāntapana* penance. By this, the simultaneous use of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth on one day and fasting on the second day is prescribed; for he describes the *mahāsāntapana* as follows: "With the separate substances of the *sāntapana*, [one performs it] for six days along with a fast;
this seven-day penance is known as the *mahāsāntapana*. Here, because of the separate use of the *pañcagavya* and other items, there are six days, and fasting occurs on the seventh day. || 4 ||
Thus ends the seventh section (kaṇḍikā). 7.
Now begins the eighth section (kāṇḍikā).

Since all *kṛcchra* vows exceed twelve days in duration, while the twelve-day period itself is secondary (*gauṇa*), the author states a specific detail regarding its qualities with the intention that the very properties belonging to that [twelve-day vow] should be applied here as subordinate attributes (*guṇa*).
Now follows the undertaking of the vow in this rite. || 1 ||

Among all these hardships, regarding that which was previously mentioned as the vow (*vrata*) and the observances (*niyama*), its *upāyana*—meaning the means of undertaking, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and the duration—is stated to be "twelve days" (*dvādaśāha*); it should be understood that the means of relinquishing (*tyāga-upāya*) follows from that very same source. || 1 ||

Having undertaken the vow with the words, "The Vasus are lords of vows, the Rudras are lords of vows, the Ādityas are lords of vows, the Maruts and Aṅgirases are lords of vows," he should satiate the Vasus with water on the first night, the Rudras on the second, the Ādityas on the third, and the Maruts and Aṅgirases on the fourth.

On the first day of the first three-night period, having bathed near the fire, one should undertake the vow (*vrata*) with the mantras beginning with "O Vasus, lords of vows" (*vasavo vratapatayaḥ*). For, from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras such as "O Vasus, lords of vows, I take up the vow; I declare this to you; may I be able to do so; may I prosper through it," it is understood that there is an entreaty to the deities for the sake of obtaining permission to undertake the vow until its successful completion.

Likewise, at the conclusion of the vow, the renunciation of the vow must be performed with the mantras beginning: "O Vasus, lords of the host, we have observed the vow; we were able to do that which we have declared to you; protect us. Having thus undertaken the vow with these four mantras, one should satisfy the Vasus with water every day during the first three nights, the Rudras during the second, and the Ādityas during the third. During the fourth three-night period, one should satisfy the Maruts and the Aṅgirasas with water. || 2 ||
With the two verses beginning "ā me gṛhāḥ," he offers oblations of the cooked rice (sthālīpāka) to the Vasus.

On the first three days, every day, an oblation of *caru* for the Vasus should be performed with two mantras; this may be done by a student (*brahmacārin*) or a graduate (*snātaka*) in a common fire (*laukika*), or by a householder (*gṛhastha*) in either the *āhavanīya* or the domestic (*gṛhya*) fire.
"Incalculable" refers to the ten Rudras. ||4||
The Homa sacrifice should be performed on the second third-day period.
With the five verses beginning with "kadācana starīrasi," [he offers] to the Ādityas.
This refers to the subject matter of the third three-day period.
With the six [verses] beginning with "The Sāntapanas," [he worships] the hosts of Maruts; with "O Agni, you whom the Aṅgirases... and "Vāyu, who goes before... ||6||
On the fourth day, during the three-day period, the meaning is that the oblation (homa) must be performed daily with these mantras, as appropriate, for the Marudgaṇas and the Aṅgirases. || 6 ||
"Regarding 'havyavāham' [it refers to] the Sviṣṭakṛt.
(7) One should offer the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation with the mantra beginning "havyavāham," without distinction, in all three-day rites. (7)
O Vasus, lords of vows, I undertake this vow; I declare this to you; may I be able to do it, and through it may I prosper.

O Vasus, you who are the dwellers [of all], since you are the lords of vows (*vratapati*), the protectors of the vow (*vrata*), therefore I declare unto you: in this unassailable state, I undertake the vow. Therefore, through your grace, may I be able—may I have the power—to fulfill it; and by means of that vow being accomplished, may I attain prosperity (*ṛdhyāsam*), consisting of the excellence of its fruit.
O Rudras, lords of vows, I undertake this vow; I declare it unto you; may I be able to do it, and through it may I prosper.

The meaning is already established by the previous explanation. However, the Rudras are distinguished by their specific request; likewise, in the subsequent [sections], the Ādityas and the Maruts along with the Aṅgirases are distinguished. The remainder is the same.

O Ādityas, lords of vows, I undertake this vow; I declare it to you. May I be able to do it; may I prosper thereby. O Maruts and Aṅgirases, lords of vows, I undertake this vow; I declare it to you. May I be able to do it; may I prosper thereby. May houses be mine, may progeny be mine; may the heroic sacrifice enter me. May the divine, sacrificial waters enter me.
May the abundance of a thousand not forsake me—svāhā!
May my houses be here; may the Puroruc and the Stotra-Śastra enter me from both sides together;
may the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus be my fellow-sitters in the assembly.

May I not be among a thousand; may [the enemy] not mock me. *Svāhā!* The meter is *triṣṭubh*. The seer is Mudgala Bhānyaśva. May my house and my wife be mine; may my offspring and sons be mine. May the powerful sacrifice enter me. Likewise, may the divine waters, worthy of sacrifice and the means for accomplishing the sacrifice, enter me and grant me their assistance. *Svāhā!*

The word *sahasra* is intended as an indication of extreme abundance; the word *bhūman* refers to abundant wealth. May that great wealth of many things not abandon me—may it not leave me. *Svāhā*: may there be a well-offered oblation. Likewise, may my "houses"—namely, the *upāṃśu* [graha] and the others—be present for me. And may the *puroruk* (the introductory mantra recited before the taking of the sacrificial offering) belong to those very houses; and may the *stotra* and *śastra* enter me, being *samīcī*, meaning well-directed or facing toward me.
May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus be my members of the assembly (*sadasya*) in this assembly; the words beginning with "sahasra" have already been explained.
Those thousands of Rudras who are upon the earth—for them we unstring our bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas. || 1 ||

In the section concerning Agni, six sections (anuvākas) designated as Rudra are recited, beginning with "Obeisance to your wrath, O Rudra" (*namas te rudra manyave*). Among those, these ten mantras [are included]. In all those sections, there is the mention of the gods; and thus it is heard in the Śruti:

"The gods indeed excluded Rudra from the sacrifice. He turned back against the gods with an army that was drawn out and long. Those gods, being afraid, saw this Śatarudriya; with it they appeased him. When one offers the Śatarudriya, by that he appeases this Rudra—him whose bow is drawn, whose wrath is concentrated, and who has mighty arms."
