Thus: those Rudras who dwell established as lords upon the earth—that is, within the world—numbering countless thousands (the *ś* is elided by the rule *śerluka chandasi bahulam*, meaning there are immeasurable Rudras); of them, when they are enraged, having strung their bows and being intent on slaying, we unstring their bows—we unstring them, making the strings slack through the pacification brought about by our hymns—at a distance of a thousand leagues. (*Mas* ends in *-d* according to the rule *idanto masi*.)

Standing at a great distance, [we stretch] the bows of those who are upon this vast ocean, the atmosphere; we stretch their bows across a thousand yojanas. 2. (Note: The grammatical notes provided in the source—"ūdhaso'naṅ" and "dhanuṣaśca"—indicate that the suffix *anaṅ* is applied to the words *ūdhas* and *dhanus*.)

Those who are here in this perceptible atmosphere, in the intermediate space, in the ocean—the sky, for they say it is joined with a subtle ocean because one observes the falling of water in the form of dew and so forth at the beginning of night—or rather, those who exist as sovereign lords (*adhipati*) over the great ocean and the intermediate space; we shall, from afar, unstring their bows, as before.

Those Rudras who have blue necks and white throats, who have taken refuge in heaven—may we unstring their bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas. Those Rudras who have blue necks and non-white throats, who have taken refuge in heaven, the celestial realm—the rest is as before.

Those Śarvas who have blue necks and dark throats and roam upon the earth below—their bows we unstring at a distance of a thousand yojanas. Those Śarvas who are Rudras roaming upon the earth below, wandering in the netherworld (Pātāla), those in the forests who are green with young grass, blue-necked and deep red—their bows we unstring at a distance of a thousand yojanas.

Those who dwell in the forests, amidst the thickets of trees, shrubs, spreading creepers, and grasses—those who are tawny like young grass or straw, as well as those with blue necks and those who are deep red.

I consider their bows to be at a distance of a thousand *yojanas* from those arrows with which they pierce people drinking from vessels—those who, remaining hidden within food being eaten or milk and other drinks being drunk, strike, wound, and afflict the eaters and drinkers.

Those who are the lords of beings, who are shaven-headed or wear their hair in braided tufts—may we unstring our bows a thousand yojanas away from them. [Note: Those who are the lords (adhipatayaḥ), that is, the protectors, of beings (bhūtānām)—such as the earth and other elements—or of specific classes of deities; who are "viśikhāsaḥ," meaning shaven-headed (muṇḍāḥ); and "kapardinaḥ," meaning those with matted locks (jaṭilāḥ).

Those who are the guardians of the paths, who soften the food-offerings (*aiḍamṛdaḥ*), and who mingle in battle (*yavyudhaḥ*)—we extend their bows even unto a thousand leagues. [Commentary: Those who are the guardians of the paths (*pathīnām pathirakṣayaḥ*) are those who, being travelers themselves, are protectors; the meaning is that they are of the nature of the Ādityas. *Aiḍa* refers to food (*iḍā*); *aiḍamṛdaḥ* means those who soften (*mṛganti*) that collection of food. *Yavyudhaḥ* means those who join together (*yu*) in battle (*yudhi*); the meaning is "warriors."

Those who wander among sacred fords, armed with spears and bearing quivers—*their bows we unstring at a distance of a thousand yojanas*. Those who wander among sacred fords for the sake of attaining perfection through supreme austerity are "armed with spears," meaning they possess superior intelligence; they are "quivered," meaning they carry swords and are equipped with them.

Those Rudras, whether they are this many or even more, who have spread themselves throughout the quarters—of them we unbend the bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas. Those Rudras, whether determined to be this many by measure, or more numerous than that and thus not determined by measure, who have spread themselves through the quarters—that is, who stand variously in the directions.
O Indra, you are never one who neglects the donor;
indeed, O Maghavan, your gift as a god is ever more abundantly bestowed. 1.

*aindrī* (addressed to Indra). *bṛhatī* (meter). The word *upa* is for filling the verse (*pādapūraṇa*), according to Pāṇini’s rule: "The particles *pra*, *sam*, *upa*, and *apa* are used for filling the verse. The root *stṛ* means "to injure" (*hiṃsā*). O Indra, you are never—at no time at all—an injurer (*starī*) of the sacrificer; on the contrary, you favor (*saścasi*) the donor (*dāśuṣe*). The root *saś* denotes the act of favoring. The form *dāśuṣe* is a dative used in place of the accusative by metrical license (*vyatyaya*). You favor the donor, the sacrificer, and endow him with the fruit [of his action].

The first word *nu* signifies speed; the second has the sense of certainty (*niścaya*). The first word *iti* serves for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), whereas in the phrase *upehi*, it serves to complete the meter (*pādapūraṇa*). One who possesses food (*ghasman*) and wealth (*dhana*) is called *Maghavā*. O *Maghavan*, O Lord of Wealth, the gift belonging to you—the God endowed with qualities such as generosity—being given, its fruit, such as heaven and so forth, is joined (*upapṛcyate*) more abundantly and very swiftly. [The root] *pṛcī* means "to join. By what? [By the merit of the giver.]

By implication, this refers to the donor, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The word *dāśvān* is a Vedic formation derived from the root *dā* (in the sense of "giving"), as established by the rule: "The forms *dāśvān*, *sāhvān*, and *mīḍhvān* are [irregularly] prescribed."

"Never indeed do you neglect; you protect both births. O Āditya, the fourth libation (*savana*) is your power (*indriya*); established in heaven, it is your immortality. (2) The word *indra* is derived from the root *idi*, meaning "supreme sovereignty. That [term] was also applied to the Āditya in the preceding mantra, because of its application to the *sthālīpāka* offering for the Ādityas. Here, the Āditya is Indra, Brahmā, and Prajāpati, because he alone possesses the glory of manifestation. The root *yuccha* means "to be negligent."
O Indra, being duly honored, you never fail or become negligent toward the sacrifice by way of defects in its fruit and so forth; for you thoroughly protect both the divine and human births.

O Turīya, you who are the fourth, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman consisting of the fourth foot of the Gāyatrī; O Āditya, your *savana*—the ritual act being performed, so called because "by this [act] the fruit is produced"—that *savarna*, the sense-organ (*indriya*) perceived by Indra, has established itself in heaven, the celestial abode, as the immortal, characterized by immortality; the meaning is that it causes the sacrificer to abide there.

Or rather: May the sacrifice attain the favor of the gods; O Ādityas, be gracious! May your benevolent thought turn upward toward us; may it be the best finder of wide space even from out of distress. (3) [Triṣṭubh meter; having the Ādityas as its deity. "Ādityās" means the Ādityas themselves, [formed] by the rule "ājaserasuk. "Bhavatā" is a substitution for the nominative case ending.

In place of the triplet beginning with *mṛḍayantaḥ*, there is the present participle *śatṛ*. O Ādityas, since you are *mṛḍayitāraḥ*—that is, bestowers of happiness (*mṛḍa* means "to give happiness"—for that reason, this sacrifice dedicated to you approaches the *sumnam*, the happiness, of the gods who are the sacrificers; it goes toward happiness, meaning it accomplishes happiness.

Furthermore, may your auspicious wisdom (*sumati*), belonging to you, turn hither—turning toward us; that is to say, let your auspicious intellect repeatedly be directed toward us. Of what nature is this wisdom? It is that which "is even more a finder of wealth than from distress" (*aṃhościdyā varivovittarāsad*). The particle *cit* has the sense of "even. *Asat* means "it becomes. *Varivaḥ* means "wealth. It is that which is a greater obtainer of wealth (*varivovittarā*) even for one who is most distressed (*aṃhaḥ*) or most sinful.
"O Vivasvat, O Āditya, this is your Soma-drink; rejoice in it! With that divine rain, I mix you.

He is called *vivasvān* because he causes darkness to disperse (*vi-vāsayati*). O *vivasvan*, O Āditya, offspring of Aditi, this is your *somapītha*—the drinking of Soma. Because of its application in the Soma-graha rites, the *somapītha* in the Jyotiṣṭoma is the Soma-juice; but here, by means of modification (*ūha*) or metaphorical usage, the *somapītha* is the cooked rice-offering (*sthālīpāka*). Rejoice in that cooked rice-offering; partake of satisfaction therein. By this very performance of the ritual...
By that divine rain, I mix you—that is, I blend you or unite you with the rain through the medium of clouds and so forth—this is the meaning.
O Savitṛ, with your undeceivable and auspicious protections, guard our household today. O golden-tongued one, for the sake of new prosperity, protect our home;

let no malevolent person have power over us. (5) O Savitṛ, on this day, protect—that is, preserve—our *gaya*, our home. With what? With your rays, which are characterized by protection (*pāyu*), or by drinking (*pāna*), and which are *adabdha*, meaning unassailable. Since you are golden-tongued, a speaker of truth, therefore, for the sake of *suvitāya*, the production of fruit, that is, for the sacrifice, protect our *gaya*, our home, for the sake of something new (*navyase*).
Furthermore, let no one whatsoever—a "ghaśaṃsa," meaning a most wicked person who utters evil against us—prevail over us or have power over us.
O Maruts, you who destroy the enemy, may you graciously accept this offering, the *sāntapanā* oblation; it is yours. 1.

O Maruts, this oblation is yours; therefore, enjoy it, take pleasure in it, and partake of it. And with your aid, grant us protection. They are called *sāntapana* because they thoroughly scorch (*sam-tap*) the obstructors, such as the *rakṣas* demons and others. For they are *riśādasaḥ*: the root *riś* means "to injure," and *adas* [is related to] the root *adas*, meaning "to destroy"; thus, they are those who cause the destruction of those who inflict injury.
O Maruts, O Vasus, if some mortal of evil intent, with a hostile mind, should seek to strike us down, may you release upon him the snare of malice; slay him with your most scorching heat!

O Maruts, that mortal—meaning a human subject to death—who, desiring evil, wrath, or harm toward us, stands nearby in concealment or with a hidden form, or who, being "tiraścittaḥ" (one whose mind is turned away or whose mind is unclear), seeks to strike you, or whoever seeks to strike even you—O Vasus, you who provide dwellings—and furthermore, such a mortal who is by nature a "duhaḥ" (an injurer)—cast him down thoroughly against him.

Release him, O leaders! Do not strike, do not harm him! By what means? By the most intense heat—that is, by an excessive degree of ascetic fervor (*tapas*). Of what sort is he? "With his bond" (*sapāśam*); a "bond" (*pāśa*) refers to one's own circle, such as children, wife, and so forth; thus, "with his bond" means together with his family and kinsmen (*sapaśubāndhavam*).
O Maruts, destroyers of enemies, who dwell with the household, do not abandon us; deliver us from distress.
Gāyatrī meter. O Maruts, be Gṛhamedhas for us—those who "meditate upon the house" (gṛhaṃ medhayanti) are Gṛhamedhas. Being of what nature? Riśādasaḥ: destroyers of those who cause harm; [protect] us.
Delivering us from distress and evil, may the virtuous ones not overcome us; let them not cause us defeat.
By your noble guidance, your great powers surge forth;
O you who are worthy of sacrifice, extend your names. Bring this domestic portion, endowed with splendor.

O Maruts, enjoy this domestic sacrifice (gṛhamedhīya). [Triṣṭubh] O Maruts, enjoy—that is, partake of—this portion characterized by the oblation, the *sthālīpāka*. It is "domestic" (*gṛhamedhīya*), meaning it is fit for the household deities and is devoid of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. By means of this portion, being worthy of worship (*prayajyavaḥ*) and being worshipped, grant us what is worthy of taming (*dayam*)—that is, new elephants, horses, and so forth—and grant it together with prosperity (*saśriyam*), endowed with the splendor of gold, gems, strings of pearls, and the like.

And you must counteract their greatnesses, splendors, and names—such as "sacrificers," "righteous ones," and "virtuous sons"—because people dwelling on the earth, through their understanding, direct themselves toward you; that is to say, they approach you, for their success depends upon you.
Sing forth, O Kaṇvas, to the sporting host of Maruts, the irresistible, who shine upon their chariots. 5.
O destroyers of the malicious, you who bring about the end of violence, releasing us from distress and sin—do not be overcome; do not let them prevail over us.
Forward your splendors go by your own will; O you who are worthy of worship, extend your names. Bring this domestic portion, endowed with glory.

O Maruts, enjoy this domestic sacrifice (gṛhamedhīya). [Triṣṭubh] O Maruts, enjoy—that is, partake of—this portion characterized by the oblation, the cooked rice-offering (sthālīpāka). It is "domestic" (gṛhamedhīya), meaning it is fit for the household deities and is devoid of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. Being those who are worthy of sacrifice (*prayajyavaḥ*) through this portion, while being worshipped, grant us what is worthy of taming (*dayam*)—that is, new elephants, horses, and so forth—and grant us that which is accompanied by prosperity (*saśriyam*), endowed with the splendor of gold, gems, strings of pearls, and the like.

And you must counteract their greatnesses, splendors, and names—such as "sacrificers," "righteous ones," and "virtuous sons"—because people existing on the earthly plane (bhūmi-loka) approach you with their intellect; that is to say, they depend upon you for their success.
Sing forth, O Kaṇvas, to the playful host of Maruts, the irresistible, resplendent upon their chariots! 5.

O Maruts, let your natural host (*śardhaḥ*), your strength, playfully sport with us. *Kaṇ* is a verb meaning "to sound"; those who sound are the *kaṇvas*, the winds. You yourselves, O Maruts, should sing forth—that is, celebrate—the host belonging to the Maruts (*mārutaṃ śardhaḥ*). Of what kind is that host? It is *ratheśubham*: favorable for the movement of chariots, celestial vehicles, and so forth; likewise, *anavīṇam*—here there is a change of gender (from feminine to masculine)—meaning "unassailable" or "irrepressible."

The Maruts, who are like swift chargers, moving with their own will, have adorned themselves like youths visible to the seer; they stand upon their chariots like brilliant children, like playful calves, dispensing milk.

Triṣṭubh meter. *Antatyā* means horses. The word *na* is used everywhere in the sense of comparison (*upamārthīya*). Those Maruts who are like horses, swift-moving (*svañcaḥ*) with beautiful gaits; and those who, like *yakṣas*—that is, sacrificers (*yajvānaḥ*)—shine forth (*śubhayantaḥ*), desiring splendor (*śubha*) and performing perfect observation; and those who are like mortals (*maryāḥ*, i.e., mortal beings)—may they be *harmyeṣṭhāḥ*, meaning may they be situated in the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*) and sport there. They are like children (*śiśavaḥ*), brilliant (*śubhrāḥ*), endowed with an irrepressible beauty.

The calves are so called because they are by nature fond of playing; for this very reason, they are playful. Those who drink milk are "milk-drinkers" (*payodhāḥ*), meaning they are young; for indeed, both calves and infants are by nature fond of playing.

The Aṅgirases found you, who were hidden in secret, dwelling in every wood. You are born when being churned with great force; they call you, O Aṅgiras, the son of strength. O Aṅgiras, the Aṅgirases found you, who were hidden in secret—concealed within the embers—and they obtained you as you dwelt in every wood, taking refuge in the forests of those trees and other plants. Being churned with great force—that is, with mighty power—you are born.

Since you are such as this, therefore the seers call you the son of *sahas* (force). O Aṅgiras, you were born from the embers. Vāyu, who goes first, the lover of sacrifice, comes to the sacrifice together with the mind, auspicious with his auspicious teams of horses.

Since Vāyu alone goes at the head of all the deities, therefore he alone is the first *yajñaprīḥ*; he is pleased and satisfied in the sacrifice. From this indicative mark—that when the oblation is being offered to the Aṅgirases, the oblation is also given therein to Vāyu—Vāyu’s status as a deity is understood, since Vāyu alone goes to the sacrifice together with the mind (*manas*). He is auspicious and peaceful.

They are "niyuta" because they are yoked by their form as assistants to the sacrifice; he goes having made himself equal to those horses. We invoke Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—the bearer of oblations, the overcomer of enemies, the slayer of Rakṣasas, the victor in battles, the luminous, the giver, the fulfiller of desires.

We invoke Agni; we call upon him who carries the oblation (*havyavāha*), he who conveys the offering to both the gods and the ancestors. He is the *abhimātiṣāh*: *abhimā* is the enemy (one who thinks against), and he who overcomes or subdues that enemy is *abhimātiṣāh*. [We invoke him] the slayer of the *rakṣases*, who is victorious in battles (*pṛtanāsu*) against the armies of others, who is full of light (*jyotiṣmantam*), formidable with his flames, and intensely radiant (*dīdyutam*). [We invoke] the *purandhi*: he who holds or consumes the assembly (*puram*) or multitude.
[We invoke] the *sviṣṭakṛt*: he who makes the sacrifice well-offered, who renders the desired offering auspicious.
I satiate the Vastus; I satiate the Rudras; I satiate the Ādityas; I satiate the Maruts and Aṅgiras.
O Vasus, lords of vows, I have performed this vow; I was able to do it. We declare this to you; protect us.

O Rudras, lords of the host, we have performed the vow; we have accomplished it; we declare this to you; protect us! O Ādityas, lords of the host, we have performed the vow; we have accomplished it; we declare this to you; protect us!
O Maruts, lords of hosts, we have performed this vow; we were able to do it, and we declare it unto you: protect us.

O Vasus, you who are the dwellers [of all] and the lords of vows, the protectors of the vow; through your grace, I have performed the vow—the vow has been carried out and accomplished by me. Through your grace, I was able—I had the power to complete that vow; this is the meaning. Therefore, we say to you: "Protect" (gopāyata)—that is, guard—this vow belonging to us. By this, the other three mantras are also explained.
Thus ends the eighth section. 8.
Now begins the ninth section:
In the rainy season, he performs the opening ceremony of the Vedic studies under the asterism Śravaṇā.

In this context, the phrase "desiring the union of his pupils," which is to be mentioned later, should be connected [to the present]. Whatever is traditionally recorded as being ancillary to study and teaching must indeed be stated here; and the *upākaraṇa* (initiation) is an ancillary to both study and teaching. Thus, from the statement "desiring the union of his pupils," the connection of the result with the student is understood.

From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "For such-and-such a desire, for life, thee," it is understood that the fruit [of the rite] accrues without distinction to both the disciple and the preceptor when the rite is performed by the preceptor who initiates them (*upākarty*). In that context, the vows (*vrata*) consisting of Vedic study have been prescribed for the purpose of achieving the status of one learned in the three Vedas (*traividyaka*). Furthermore, even for a disciple who has completed his Vedic studies, residence with the teacher is required for the sake of mastering the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and sub-auxiliaries (*upāṅga*), as well as for training in crafts and the like.
Thus says the *Smṛti*: "Even one who has mastered a craft should reside in the teacher’s house for some time as a resident pupil (*antevāsī*)."

And so forth. In this regard, the teacher, desiring to establish a connection—that is, the bond of *yoga*—with his pupils, should perform the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) of the Vedas. *Upākaraṇa* means making [the teaching] one's own; it is the mental resolve: "I shall expound these specific sections and so forth to this disciple. For even while living with the teacher for the sake of thoroughly understanding the primary and secondary branches of the arts (*śilpa*), a pupil learns even the specific sections and so forth from the teacher; therefore, the teacher, while instructing him, must perform the *upākaraṇa*.

If a student teaches someone else, then that person must also perform [the duties] toward him; for he too is the teacher of the student. Nor should it be argued that because the student’s conduct is that of a teacher (*ācāryavṛtti*), there can be no [corresponding] conduct toward a teacher who is not a fellow-student (*anācāryabrahmacārin*), on the grounds that he lacks the capacity to provide food, bedding, and so forth. This is because even those who subsist on alms (*bhaikṣavṛtti*) are included among "those who are not teachers" (*anām*). Furthermore, it is possible for even a student of the three Vedas (*traividyaka-brahmacārin*) to possess the capacity to support his own students through the acquisition of specific wealth or through knowledge and other means.

Therefore, he too must perform the *upākaraṇa* (commencement of Vedic study) as far as possible. The months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada constitute the rainy season (*varṣā*). Therein, the *upākaraṇa* should be performed at the very first appearance of the asterism Śravaṇā, because there is no reason to abandon the first instance; according to the principle that "the first [instance] should be fixed, for deviation would require a specific cause. While doing what?

The explanation according to the result is as follows: for those residing with a teacher in order to receive training in the primary and secondary branches of knowledge (*sāṅgopāṅga*), who desire the connection characterized by the relationship of teacher and student; and for the students (*antevāsins*), who desire the connection characterized by the excellence of wisdom. || 1 ||

He offers [the oblation], saying: "Thou art named Apā; may I attain thy state of being a lover [of sacrifice]. I have indeed surpassed the wisdom of the wise; I have grasped the wisdom of the Eternal; I have been born like Sūrya, Svāhā! The three subsequent [oblations] are: "Thou art named Ranti," "Thou art named Yukti," and "Thou art named Yoga. In each case, he appends the phrase "of thee" (*tasyāste*).

He offers oblations while performing the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) with the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) beginning with "Apanā nāmāsi" and so forth; there are three others as well. In these *yajus*, the phrase "tasyāste" from the first formula is attached [to the subsequent ones] because of the necessity of completing the sentence, according to the principle: "The attachment [of a word] occurs for the completion of the sentence, since it applies equally to all. Thus, there arise three sentences: "Rantirnāmāsi tasyāste," and so on. The recitation of them all together is due to their belonging to another Vedic branch (*śākhā*). || 2 ||
"Yuje svāhā! Udyuje svāhā! Yuktyai svāhā! Yogāya svāhā!"—one who desires the application of yoga for his pupils [should offer these oblations].
"Desiring the spiritual union of his disciples"—this is to be connected with each [disciple] individually. || 3 ||

Having consumed curd three times with the verse "O Dadhikrāvan," holding darbha grass in his hand, he recites the Sāvitrī three times and the first three Anuvākas, as well as [the hymn] beginning with "Who yokes you? (Kaḥ tvā yunakti).

The mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo... is recited once. The consumption of curds (dadhibhakṣa) is repeated three times. The Sāvitrī is that which has Savitṛ as its deity, beginning with "Tat savitur vareṇyam," because of its great power; no other [verse] such as "Ā kṛṣṇena rajasā" is meant. Regarding the three Anuvākas at the beginning: the first begins with "Iṣe tvā," the second with "Devasya tvā," and the third with "Vasoḥ pavitram asi. The verse "Kaḥ tvā yunakti" is employed in the Aśvamedha sacrifice for the fastening of the enclosing sticks (paridhi). The phrase "he recites after" (anvāha) is to be supplied in both cases. || 4 ||
For him, there is no suspension of study. || 5 ||
For that teacher and for that student, it is declared to be a time unfit for study.
It does not flash when it thunders. || 6 ||

Because this is stated in the present tense, this suspension of study is for that specific moment: when lightning is flashing—that is, when the fiery energy of lightning is manifest—and when it thunders, that is, when the cloud is roaring.
There was a sudden, tumultuous divine storm, with lightning, clouds, and meteors. ||7||

"Ākālika" is said to mean "simultaneous. If that which is the beginning is itself the end, the word *ākālika* is prescribed by the rule "ākālikaḍādyantavacane"; the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of forming the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Thus, *ākālikī* refers to lightning; the meaning is that the very time of its commencement is the same as the time of its destruction.

Similarly here as well, the time at which the tumult of the gods and so forth arises during the first half-watch and so on is its "initial time" (*ādikāla*); that very same moment becomes the "concluding time" (*antakāla*) on the second day. This is what is expressed by the term *ākālika*. What is meant is this: for as long a duration as the tumult of the gods and so forth arises, for that very same duration on the second day there is fitness for study; however, in the interval between, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*).

However, those who connect the word *ākālika* with the preceding [rule], interpreting it as "when it is not lightning nor thundering, it is *ākālika*," and explain that the suspension of study lasts only for as long as the tumult of the gods and so forth is heard—for them, the suspension of study for a day and night (*ahorātrika*) must be applied [to the subsequent cases] based on the word itself, and the restatement of what was already obtained through the present-tense indication would be redundant. In this context, *devatumula* refers to the sound of singing and instrumental music in the atmosphere produced by Gandharvas and others.

By "lightning" (*vidyut*), a lightning strike is intended here during the occasion of study, such as day or night; by the word "bow" (*dhanus*), the rainbow is meant when it occurs outside the rainy season. During the rains, its occurrence at that specific time is established by traditional custom (*sadācāra*). By "meteor" (*ulkā*) as well, the fall of a large meteor is intended; for the term "meteor" is indeed used even when only a single star falls. (7)
Others [are established] by conduct.

Other causes for the suspension of Vedic study mentioned in the Ācārādhyāya are also to be followed, such as earthquakes, eclipses of the moon or sun, the death of a king or a great personage, and so forth. || 8 ||
For example, words that transcend the syllables and the continuous flow of fleeting moments. 9.

"Excessive syllables" refers to sounds that transcend the normal syllabic measure, such as thunderclaps, the utterance of "huṃ," or the slapping of palms. A "continuous leak" refers to the dripping of a roof-thatch; it is not merely a single drop, because such occurrences happen frequently. These two constitute grounds for the suspension of Vedic study throughout the duration of the event. || 9 ||

Having studied for four and a half months, or five and a half months, he dismisses [the Veda], saying: "We dismiss the lessons; may the *Chandas* (Vedic meters) trust us again," and also, "Who releases you? (RV 10.75.5).

Those for whom there are four and a half months are "ardhapañcamāḥ" (four and a half); likewise, those for whom there are five and a half are "ardhaṣaṣṭhāḥ. Having studied for these months according to the prescribed rule—having completed the study by performing the activities that facilitate the purpose of learning, which is to say, having finished the teaching—they "utsṛjate" (dismiss) the chapters; the meaning is that they perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of dismissal. However, there is no abandonment of the Vedic study itself; rather, even regarding the dismissal from specific periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*), he states the connection with his own age in the words "utsṛjāmahe" and so forth. || 10 ||
For him, there is no study on the new moon day; he does not recite for two days and the intervening night.

This is another occasion when study is prohibited: on both sides of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), namely the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) and the first day (*pratipad*). Although it is stated in the *Ācārādhyāya* that "there are two full moons and two new moons," thus referring to the full and new moon days as being accompanied by the fourteenth day, nevertheless, this repetition is for the purpose of prescribing the first day (*pratipad*) as well. As it has been said: "A repetition [of a rule] is for the sake of additional qualities (*guṇa*). (11)
Beyond this, there are no [clouds] in the higher regions. || 12 ||
Therefore, after this general rule, one must not study even when merely a cloud is seen; what need is there to mention cases such as lightning flashes and the like?

Thy name is *Apanā*. May I go to thy place of delight (*joṣṭrīya*) as one who has attained the sacrifice. I have grasped the wisdom (*medhā*) of the Eternal Truth (*ṛta*); I have been born like the Sun. *Svāhā!* Thy name is *Ranti*, thy name is *Yukti*, thy name is *Yoga*. To the Union, *svāhā*; to the Rising Union, *svāhā*; to the Application, *svāhā*; to the Yoga, *svāhā*. The deity is Brāhmī Vidyā. *Pavā* refers to that which flows away from its own nature; thus it is unstable (*adhruvā*). By the negation of that, *Apavā* is the stable (*dhruvā*) knowledge. Some read *apve* instead; even there, the meaning is the same.

"Your name is Nityānandā; may I attain—that is, reach—that blazing form (*iddha-rūpa*) which belongs to you. The repetition of 'blazing, blazing' (*iddham edha*) is for the purpose of proclaiming its beginninglessness. Of what nature is this blazing? It is *joṣṭrīya*, meaning it is to be served with exceeding devotion."

The wise ones have grasped the intelligence (*medhā*) of this immortal, deathless Brahman, which consists of knowledge and is the very form of wisdom; the meaning is that the intelligent ones have attained Brahman, whose nature is knowledge. Alternatively, the wise ones have grasped the intelligence of the Truth (*ṛta*), which is Brahman. Therefore, I too have been born like the sun; like the sun, may I become possessed of supreme light and be near to the form of Brahman.

This is the meaning. *Svāhā*: may there be a well-offered oblation. *Ranti* is that which delights or sports through the manifestation of the world and so forth; it is the knowledge consisting of Brahman (*brahmamayī vidyā*). *Yukti* is that which is joined in the world with the powers of manifestation (*vivarta*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*). In this manner, *yoga*, *yuk*, *udyug*, and so forth, are to be explained. The repetition is for the sake of praise. "I have performed [the hymn] for Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited horse. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives. [This is in] the *anuṣṭubh* meter. And the name of this *ṛc* is "Surabhimatī" (Possessing Fragrance). Thus says the Śruti:

"The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) recite the *surabhimatī* verse; they purify speech itself. Elsewhere, this request—occurring after the consecration of the horse and at the time of the priests' and sacrificer's consumption of curd—is to be applied here as well, according to what is appropriate. He who strides is *kāva*. One whose nature is to conquer is *jiṣṇu*. From the root *aś*, meaning "to pervade," comes *aśva*; one who possesses speed (*vāja*) is *vājī*. Elsewhere this refers to a horse, but here it refers to Prajāpati.

At the time of preparing the swift, victorious, prize-winning horse of Kaṇva, I have purified its mouths—which had become impure through the utterance of vulgar speech—by means of curd; the singular number is used by way of grammatical substitution (vyatyaya), as the plural is seen later on, thus [the sense is] "we have purified them."

May Prajāpati—who is the self of all—or the Veda, whose self is the Veda, by means of his ignorance, mispronunciation, or through states such as childhood, purify our mouths that have become impure; [here *mukhāni* becomes *mukhā* due to the rule *śeś chandasi bahulam*, which allows for the elision of the case-ending *naḥ*]. May he make them fragrant (*surabhi*), that is, pure; [the form *karat* is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*), derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *leṭ*; the *i* of *ti* is elided by the rule *itaś ca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*; and the augment *aṭ* is added by the rule *leṭo 'ḍāṭau*]; thus, let him make them so. Furthermore, may the horse—or Prajāpati—prolong (*pratāriṣat*) our lifespans; [this is the aorist optative of the root *tṛ*]. Let him extend them.

From the roots *tṛp* and *lavanataraṇa*, as before, the fifth lakāra (the optative) and so forth; *sip* [is the suffix]; by the rule "there is frequently *iṭ* in the *leṭ*," there is *iṭ*; there is *guṇa*; and by the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), the vowel becomes *ā*.
For sap, thee; for strength, thee. O Vāyu, you are the refreshing draughts. May the divine Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent rite.

Swell with food, you who are the portion of the gods; may you be rich in offspring, free from disease, and free from consumption. Let not the thief nor the ill-wisher master you; may the missile of Rudra pass you by. May you remain firm under this lord of cattle; guard the many cattle of the sacrificer, for you are the guardian of the sacrificer’s cattle. 1.

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee up. Thou art the seat of cattle. The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemy is burnt away. This prayer has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass, prepared by Manu and fashioned by Svadhā.
Go through the wide atmosphere; you are the portion set aside for Indra. Do not strike me down, nor strike me above; may he who cuts you across prosper, and may he who cuts you not be harmed.

O divine sacrificial grass, grow with a hundred shoots; may we grow with a thousand shoots. You are the night of Aditi, the girdle of Indrāṇī; let Pūṣan tie your knot; may it not loosen for you. With the two arms of Indra, I lift you up; with the head of Bṛhaspati, I carry you; you are one that goes to the gods.

Therefore the sages bring it forward: "The sacred grass, beloved by the gods, for them to sit upon here. "You are the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of the Vasus, with a thousand streams. Free from disease, I unite you with offspring and with the abundance of riches, so that you may become numerous. Swelling with honey and ghee, living and full of life, may we dwell near you."

Thou art the nature of Mātariśvan; thou art the sky; thou art the earth; thou art the all-sustainer. By the highest abode thou art offered; do not falter! Thou art the life of all, thou art the all-encompassing, thou art the all-sustainer. The drop is offered, the spark is offered to the great Ākāśa, Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth!
Unite, O immortal ones, with your wave, you who are most rich in sweetness; you are pleasant, for the winning of wealth.
I have extended you, Indra’s portion, with Soma; you are the lowest [layer]. For Viṣṇu! Protect the oblation for Viṣṇu! O Waters, be watchful! 3.

The mantras beginning with "iṣe tvā" are employed in the cutting of the branch and other rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) by means of direct Vedic statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth. Among these, the seer (ṛṣi) is Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati; the branch and other objects are the deities (devatā). Some maintain that there is no metre (chandas) for the Yajus formulas, while others assert a specific metre as recited by Piṅgala, such as "daivī ekā" and so on. In that regard, the term "pāda" is used to denote the total number [of syllables], because of the governing rule [of the Piṅgala-sūtra]. "iṣe tvā."

The verse beginning with *daivī* is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, consists of three syllables, and is employed for the cutting of the branch, as stated in the rule: "They cut [the branch] with the mantra *iṣe tvā*. In the word *iṣe*: the root *iṣ* (meaning "to desire") takes the *kvip* suffix; the fourth case (*dative*) is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). By the rule *sāvekācastṛtīyādirvibhaktiḥ*, the word *iṣe* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable). Alternatively, *iṣaḥ* refers to that which is desired, such as food and so forth (*iṣyamāṇa-annādi*), where *akāra* is the suffix. The seventh case (*locative*) is used because of its connection with the object (*nimittāt karmasaṃyoge*). By the rules *ā guṇaḥ* and *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, the resulting single substitute vowel is also oxytone.

The word *vā* is the object (*karman*) and the substitute for the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*). And the object [is defined] in relation to an action (*kriyā*). Since no action is explicitly heard there, the verb *chinanti* ("they cut") is supplied by the force of the injunction. Thus, the collective meaning is: "They cut you for the sake of obtaining food and so forth. Furthermore, its status as the cause of food and such occurs through the indirect sequence described in scriptural passages such as: "From fire smoke is born; from smoke mist; from mist rain."
For vigor, thee!

The root *ūrj*, meaning "to strengthen" or "to give life," is known as a *kvip*-derived noun denoting both food and strength. This two-footed mantra, consisting of a divine *anuṣṭubh* with two syllables, is employed for the bending of the branches and for wiping them clean. The words "we wipe" (*parimārjima*) and "I bend" (*sannamayāmi*) are to be supplied in turn. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "For the sake of strength, I wipe you and I bend you."
O you who abide in the wind, O you who abide in the means!

[The meter is] Anuṣṭubh; [the deity is] the calves. While touching the calves belonging to four cows with a branch, he leads them from place to place once they have begun to flow. "O calves, you are like the winds (vāyavaḥ); having begun to flow, depart with speed while I am drawing the milk. You are near the fodder (upāyavas); go to the vicinity of the mother, follow her—meaning, so that you may drink the milk again."

"May the god Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent rite. Dhṛti is the metre, the cows are the deity; with this [verse], he causes the milch-cows to go eastward. O cows, may the god Savitṛ—whose qualities consist of giving and so forth, the authorizer of action or the impeller of its fruit—impel you: may he deliver you into connection with another body, or cause you to reach another region, for I am not merely a human being. For what purpose? Toward the most excellent rite, for the sake of sacrifice; for the Śruti declares, 'Sacrifice is indeed the most excellent rite.'"

The *yajus* beginning with "āpyāyadhvam" [is as follows]: O other [cows], who are not to be slain (*ahantavyāḥ*), or rather, those who slay the sin (*agha*)—swell (*āpyāyadhvam*), meaning increase, that portion characterized by the *sānnāyya* offering which is to be partaken of, belonging to the god Indra. (The root *pyāyī* means "to grow.")

Since you are rich in offspring—possessing children and grandchildren—and are free from *āmīvā* (the word *āmīvā* being derived from the root *am*, meaning "to be ill"), thus devoid of specific diseases; and since you are free from *yakṣma* (a specific disease known as consumption or pulmonary tuberculosis), or alternatively, *ayakṣmāḥ* means those for whom there is no *kṣmā* (earthly affliction) in their movement (*ayanamayaḥ*); [may it be said: "May the thief not master you"—may the thief or robber have no power over you. "May the evil-plotter (*aghaśaṃsaḥ*)—one who proclaims sin—such as a *cāṇḍāla* or similar person, not master you."

"May the weapon of Rudra avoid you!"—let it avoid, let it spare you. "May you be firm in this lord of cattle; may you be many!"—be steadfast in this sacrificer; and may you become numerous in him. "Protect the cattle of the sacrificer; you are the protector of the sacrificer's cattle. With this [formula], he establishes the branch: O branch, since you by your very nature are the protector of the sacrificer's cattle, therefore protect the cattle of the sacrificer. The First Anuvāka. 1.
I take you at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan.

With this [verse] he places the oblation. *Saṃkṛti* is the metre. O grain and other materials, being in the impulse—the permission—of the god Savitṛ, the Sun, because he impels one toward ritual acts through that medium of light, I take you with the arms belonging to the Aśvins and with the hands of Pūṣan, but not with my own [hands], which are made of skin and so forth. Its application is also found in receiving [gifts] and similar contexts. "Thou art the earth's station."
He says that *barhirlavaṇī* refers to horses and cattle; because cows sit upon it, it is called *goṣad*, and thus it is said that cows exist in *barhirlavaṇī*.

"Scorched is the *rakṣas*, scorched is the enemy (*arāti*)," [with these words] he addresses the fire while heating the sacrificial animals. The root *uṣ* means "to burn. The term *rakṣas* is an elliptical designation for Rākṣasas; may the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and so forth, be utterly consumed. That in which there is no *rāti*—wealth—is *arāti*; this is a synonym for the absence of fortune, misfortune (*alakṣmī*), and so on, or it refers to non-giving, stinginess, or an enemy (*śatru*). May that *arāti* be burnt away.
Rising to strew the sacrificial grass, he says: "The prize has gone toward the sacrificial grass, prepared by Manu and fashioned with the power of the ancestral offering."

This *dhiṣaṇā*—my intellect—has set out toward the *barhis*, which serves as the locus of action. According to the rule "acchābheḥ śākapūṇiḥ," the word *accha* denotes the sense of *abhi*, namely, directionality or facing toward. Of what nature is this *dhiṣaṇā*? It was fashioned by Manu, the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*), and likewise sharpened by *svadhā*, that is, by food.
He goes to the place of the sacrificial grass; enter the wide mid-air.
O you whose pair of feet are wide-spreading, traverse the vast expanse of the sky and go!
He traces around the bunch of darbha grass three times [with the formula]: "Thou art the chosen portion of Indra."
O cluster of darbha grass, you were born purified for the sake of Indra.
He joins the cooked [portion] with the middle [portion].
Do not look down upon me, nor look up at me with contempt.

O clump of darbha grass, let your joint—the part below and the part above—not be damaged; the meaning is that it should remain like the edge of an axe. May the one who cuts you with prosperity not be harmed.

The root *ṛṣ* (from which *riṣa* is derived) has the meaning of "to injure. The sense is: "May that which cuts off or lops away your prosperity (*ṛddhi*)—that is, may it not injure your power to accomplish the sacrifice—not harm you. The word *ṛddhyā* is used in the instrumental case by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
He touches the remaining roots of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that are still attached to the ground and capable of sprouting again:

"O divine *barhis*, grow with a hundred shoots; may we grow with a thousand shoots. O divine *barhis*, having been produced, grow—expand—with a hundred shoots, meaning a hundred branches; and by your grace, may we also grow—may we expand—with a thousand shoots, meaning a thousand branches.
He makes a cord for the purpose of binding: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi."
You are the ruler, the cord of the Aditi-like earth. He binds the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

May Pūṣan untie for you the knot of Indrāṇī’s binding; may it not remain [tied] for you. Since you are the binding, the fastening of Indrāṇī, therefore may Pūṣan, who is Indra, untie the knot of your *barhis*—the meaning is that Indra shall bind you. And that knot, once loosened, must not remain for you long; the meaning is that it should be used for the sacrifice as soon as it is released from you.
He raises the sacrificial grass;
with his own two arms, he raises it for Indra.
"I lift you up with the two arms belonging to Indra, and not with my own arms made of skin and so forth."
That which has been extracted with encouragement, he places upon his head; "By the head of Bṛhaspati, I take you."
"I take you up, O Bṛhaspati, with my head—my crest—and I bear you."
As before, he says outside: "Thou art the path leading to the gods."
You are the sacrificial grass that goes to the gods; the meaning is that your leading [of the sacrifice] is for the sake of the gods.
"It is not only we who lead you for the sake of the gods; this has been practiced by those of old as well," he says: "The wise ones bring that forward."
The poets, who possess far-reaching vision and have correctly understood and practiced the entire meaning of the Vedas, brought it forth exactly in this manner; such is the intended sense.
He places it upon the altar: "O Barhis, come here to sit, acceptable to the gods."

"This sacrificial grass (barhis) is pleasing to the gods"—thinking thus, "I place it here upon the altar" (vedi). This is the second section (anuvāka). He prepares a purifier (pavitra) of darbha grass for the purpose of drinking the milk.

"You are the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of the Vasus, with a thousand streams. O purifier, you are the means of purification—that is, the cleanser—of *vasu*, meaning wealth or milk. The mention of "a hundred" and "a thousand" is intended to indicate limitlessness; because it possesses innumerable pores, the meaning is that it has countless streams. Regarding the term "of the Vasus": let this small amount of milk prepared by a single sacrificer suffice; rather, you are the purifier of all the milk prepared by other sacrificers throughout the entire world.
Alternatively, those who are called the Vasus here are the Maruts acting in assistance to Indra; for they are called "Vasus" because they "clothe" (vasate) or cover. And thus says the Brāhmaṇa:
"This is indeed the portion of the Vasus."
Thus [it is said].
He consecrates the cows being gathered by their calves with the mantra:
"I unite you with offspring free from disease; becoming abundant, may you be rich in the increase of wealth."

"I unite you with offspring—[offspring] that are free from disease, devoid of specific ailments, or invincible and wealthy. May you become abundant, with bodies increased through the nourishment of riches consisting of various kinds of food, or rather, may you become numerous and plentiful along with the increase of wealth. While they are being milked, he murmurs [this prayer].

"Flowing with honey, like clarified butter, may we, living and full of life, sit near you. O cows, we pray that we may sit near you without ceasing. Of what sort are you? Living, meaning long-lived; "jīvāḥ," meaning endowed with breath, that is to say, vigorous. What are you doing? Flowing—that is, pouring forth—milk that is rich in honey (sweet-tasting) and like clarified butter (extremely unctuous). He separates a heap of embers from the *gārhapatya* fire: "Thou art the cauldron (*gharma*) of Mātariśvan."
O heap of coals, you are the *dharma*—the heat—of Mātariśvan, the wind. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa:
"The intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is indeed the *dharma* of Mātariśvan.
Here, the word *antarikṣa* refers, by virtue of its location (*tātsthyāt*), to the solar light situated within the intermediate space.

When the heap of coals has been removed, he places the cooking-pot over it [with the words]: "Thou art heaven; thou art earth; thou art the all-sustainer; by the highest support thou art invoked; do not be afraid."

The Śruti says: "In this way, she is indeed spread out. When she is prepared with water fallen from heaven, she is praised as "Heaven" (dyauḥ); and because she is fashioned from a portion of the earth, she is called "Earth" (pṛthivī). She is the "All-Sustainer" (viśvadhā), for she supports everything; by means of her supreme, most excellent *dhāman*—her splendor, her essence—you are *atā*, meaning not crooked (*akuṭilā*), since the root *tan* here signifies "crookedness. And because you are not crooked, therefore, while engaged in the supporting of substances, do not become crooked.
When three cows have been milked, upon the question, "Which one have you milked?", and the milker having replied, "That one," [the response is:
"She is the sacrifice; she is all-life; she is all-pervading; she is the sustainer of all."

That which was milked first is *viśvāyuḥ*, the sustainer of all life (*sarvasya āyuṣaḥ dhātrī*) by means of its milk and other products; thus says the Śruti: "Clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*). That which was milked from the second place is *viśvavyacāḥ*; [the root] *vyac* means "to contain," for the universe (*viśvam*) originates from it by way of sacrifice. That which was milked from the third place is *viśvadhāyāḥ*; she is called *viśvadhāyāḥ* because she nourishes the universe (*viśvaṃ dhāpayati*), meaning she brings satisfaction to all through her milk. He consecrates the individual drops of milk as they fall apart.
The drop that was taken away, the drop unoffered, [is for] Agni, for the great firmament, Svāhā! For Heaven and Earth.

Whatever small drop and whatever large globule has fallen upon the ground—may all of that, though unoffered, be as if offered. To whom? To Agni, the vast and great; likewise to Nāka, so called because there is no *aka* (suffering) therein, that is, to heaven; and to Heaven and Earth—*svāhā*, may it be well offered!

"O Heaven and Atmosphere!"—having thus performed the milking into the vessel, when milk has been poured into the *ukhā* (cooking-pot), whatever remains clinging to the milking-vessels, that he washes with water and pours into the pot, [reciting]:
"Be united, O you who are rich in nectar, most honey-sweet with your wave; you are pleasant, for the winning of wealth."

O Waters, be united with the milk and with the vessel that stands upon the fire-altar! You who are possessors of cosmic order (*ṛtāvarīḥ*), possessors of truth (*satyavatyaḥ*), and possessors of sacrifice (*yajñavatyaḥ*) because you are the means of accomplishing it—with what? With your waves (*ūrmiṇā*), your surging billows. You who are most rich in honey (*madhumattamāḥ*), endowed with the sweetest essence; who are *mandrāḥ*—the root *mad* meaning "to rejoice," thus those who cause delight—and who are the *sātayaḥ*, the bestowers or achievers of wealth. He pours curds into the milk: "I mix you, the portion of Indra, with Soma."
I contract you with milk and Soma; "tanacmi" has the sense of contracting. What kind of you? Your portion, that which is to be enjoyed by Indra.
Near the *gārhapatya* fire, he places the milk with the formula: "Thou art unharmed; [I offer] thee for Viṣṇu."

The root *das* means "to perish"; thus, O milk, you are "adasta," meaning not perished. Since you are for Viṣṇu—that is, for the sake of Viṣṇu, meaning for use in sacrifice—the Śruti states: "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice."
He consecrates the oblation with the mantra:
"O Viṣṇu, protect the offering!"
O Viṣṇu, protect this oblation which is to be offered.
With a wooden vessel containing water, he covers the cooking pot, saying:
"O Waters, be watchful!"
O Waters, be watchful; remain vigilant for the sake of protection. The third Anuvāka. 3.
Who yokes you? Let the warrior yoke you; let Viṣṇu yoke you for this sacrifice.

The ritual action under discussion, such as sacrifice and the like, is described thus: "Who is Prajāpati? O Action, he joins you—that is, he accomplishes you or unites you with the fruit. The word "he" (*saḥ*) is also a reference to Prajāpati himself in an indirect form. They consider that repetition conveys greater significance, as in the expression: "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful! Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and he is indeed Prajāpati. May the sacrifice join you—may it cause you to prosper with the fruit. For what purpose?
For the success—that is, for the magnificence—of this commenced rite such as sacrifice and the like, its recitation is like that of the Sāvitrī-anuvāka.
For this desire, for life, for out-breath, for diffused breath, for in-breath, for dawning, for wealth, for prosperity, for nourishment, for sound, for non-sound, or for falling away—[I take] you.

In this context, the phrase "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*) should be supplied and applied to each instance. "For such-and-such a desire (*kāma*), I satiate you, O Prajāpati. When "such-and-such" (*asau*) is uttered, one should understand it to refer to a name. Therefore, from the word "for such-and-such" (*amuṣmai*), the names of specific desired fruits—such as cattle, sons, and so forth—are to be understood. "For life" (*āyuṣe*): I satiate you for the sake of long life. In all cases, the dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).

I satisfy you, Prajāpati, for the sake of *vyuṣṭi*—the burning away (*uṣ* means "to burn") of the afflictions characterized by ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live; for the sake of *rayi*, which is wealth; for the sake of *rādhas*, which is food; for the sake of *poṣas*, which is the nourishment of the knowledge of reality; and for the sake of the supreme transcendence (*prakarṣeṇa cyutiḥ*) from saṃsāra. I satisfy you for that purpose.

Salutations again and again to Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Brahmā, Indra, Prajāpati, Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Īśvara, Viṣṇu, Bṛhaspati, the Yajurveda, the meters, the seers, the Vedas, the Brāhmaṇas, the Somas, the drinkers of Soma, and the teachers.
Thus ends the libation with water as described in the Ācārādhyāya; this same procedure also applies to the opening ceremony (upākaraṇa) of the study of the Veda.
Thus ends the ninth section (kāṇḍikā). 9.
Now begins the tenth section (kaṇḍikā).
Now, those who are worthy of the Upaniṣads [are described]. || 1 ||

The word "disciples" (śiṣyāḥ) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the verb]. Following the commencement of the term for study, those who are worthy of the Upaniṣad—the secret scripture—on account of their application to Vedic study, are called "disciples worthy of the Upaniṣads" (upaniṣadarhāḥ), such as the lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins) and others. || 1 ||

The celibate student, the one of good conduct, the wise man, the performer of rites, the giver of wealth, the beloved, and he who seeks knowledge through learning—these are the sacred sites (tīrthas) of Brahman. || 2 ||

A *brahmacārī* is one endowed with lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*). A *sucaritī* is one who possesses good conduct; this includes even householders and others who follow right behavior. A *medhāvī* is one endowed with the capacity for grasping and retaining knowledge. A *karmakṛt* is one devoted to the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), as well as one who performs service and attendance upon the teacher. A *dhanada* is one capable of giving abundant wealth; [this applies] at the conclusion of the period of study (*grahaṇānta*), that is, at the end of the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*), but not before, because it has been prohibited previously:
"One who knows the Dharma should not provide anything to the teacher beforehand."

Thus [it is said]. A "dear one" refers to a son or similar relative who follows good conduct (*sadācāra*). Furthermore, he who desires to acquire another branch of knowledge through his current learning—these are the "sacred sites" (*tīrthāni*) of Brahman; that is to say, they are the points of descent for the Vedas in their secret form when it comes to giving, and the means for receiving them. For a sacred site is traditionally known as a watering place (*nipāna*). As it is said: "The wise desire three things to be designated as 'sacred sites': the scripture, the watering place, and the water frequented by the seers. (2)
Thus ends the tenth Kaṇḍikā. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh section (kāṇḍikā).

Having selected a new site for the final settlement that is level and has even drainage— or where water flows out toward the northeast or the northwest— one should have a shelter constructed with its door facing either east or south.

The author will later describe the one who has established the sacred fires (*adhyāhitāgni*). This [present passage], being connected to that, is stated by way of anticipation (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*). Desiring to marry his lawful wife (*sahadharmacāriṇī*), he should have a dwelling (*śaraṇa*) constructed in a specific location by architects (*sthapati*) and others, even prior to the wedding itself. What kind of dwelling?

[It should have] an eastern gate or a southern gate. Likewise, it should be new, constructed from wood and other materials not previously used. "New site" (*navāvasāna*) means a site that is new; that is to say, a new location. It should be level, meaning neither depressed nor elevated. "With its roots" (*samūla*) means endowed with the roots of auspicious play-flowers and the like. "Evenly draining" (*samavasrāva*) means where the drainage is even; that is, where water poured down flows away evenly and spreads out—that is, not slanting excessively. The connection is: "on that ground-circle which is evenly draining. Having drained evenly...

Or, from which [side] the waters might flow out toward the northeast, or be carried away toward the northwest; or else, one should cause a shelter to be built even on a transverse side where the waters flow toward the west or the north. || 1 ||
Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward for the maker of the middle [post], he places the pillar upon them.
I fix you, the firm one, the consort of immortality; abide in security, pouring forth clarity. As such, O Pillar, may we dwell here with all our heroes, with goodly heroes, and with unharmed heroes.
Right here, O Pillar, grow with immortality; rich in horses, rich in cattle, rich in immortality, rich in truth, full of vigor, and full of milk—O Pillar, turn toward us with milk!
May the young boy come to you, may the calf come with the moving world; may the jar of flowing liquor come to you, and this [cup] with vessels of curd. Thus. 2.

Having strewn upon the pit—the hollow dug for the post belonging to the middle pillar—blades of *darbha* grass arranged in the form of a *svastika*, with their tips pointing either eastward or northward, he places or inserts the middle pillar into those very *darbha* blades serving as the substrate.
Regarding the insertion [of the pillar], he recites these three mantras beginning with *dhruvām* and so forth:

"Having fixed it, I bind [it]—that is, I insert it—into the pit. For you are the wife (*patnī*), the protector, of immortality (*amṛta*), which has the nature of being deathless. Therefore, stand firm; stand for the sake of security (*kṣema*). What are you doing? Pouring out—that is, bestowing—clarified butter (*ghṛta*); the mention of clarified butter is intended as an illustration of all forms of prosperity. Since you are such, O Pillar (*sthūṇā*), we pray that we may enter into you."

And having entered this house which is dependent upon you, may we, all these heroes, become possessed of many sons, excellent heroes with excellent sons, and heroes who meet no harm with sons who are never harmed.

O Pillar (Sthūṇā), being characterized here in this very place by the imperishable form that is immortality (amṛta), do thou grow, do thou take root. Being what? Endowed with horses (aśvāvatī); likewise, endowed with cattle (gomatī); and being endowed with immortals—that is, with the human inhabitants of the house—and with *sūnṛta*, which is truth and Vedic ritual such as sacrifice; and being full of vigor (*ūrjasvatī*)—the meaning of "ūrj" being "to give strength" or "to sustain"—that is, sustaining life or being powerful; and being full of milk (*payasvatī*). The meaning is: "Make our house possessed of all prosperity."

Therefore, it says: "O Stūṇā, envelop us with milk. O Stūṇā, cause us to turn toward [prosperity] by means of milk and other such substances that are directed toward us. Furthermore, let the youth, the child, enter you who are the object of the action; and let the calf also enter. The singular number is used by way of substitution for the plural. Let the jar of milk, surrounded—that is, encompassed—by the moving world, such as the state of dwelling in the womb, enter you, along with these pitchers of curds. 2.

He erects the bamboo pole facing eastward with the verse: "Mount the pillar by means of Truth; O formidable bamboo pole, shining forth, drive away our enemies; then may we spread out, possessing all heroic sons and wealth."

He states the measure: "With truth, O beam, as a pillar... This is the *virāj* [meter]. O beam, with *ṛta*—that is, with truth, with an imperishable form—ascend the pillar; that is, stand upon the column. Of what nature? Being *ugra*—unconquerable—and shining pre-eminently. Furthermore: "Drive away, destroy the enemies"—those who are one's own obstacles to stability, and those who are ours. It is the deity presiding over the pillar who is thus addressed. Thus...

"Having overcome our enemies and those who hate us, while you remain at home free from anxiety, thereafter we—all the heroes among you, endowed with many sons—shall possess *rayi* (wealth) every day through the offering of oblations; for by this very act, we shall become your own. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra. Since the application of the mantra is prescribed for the middle pillar and the central beam (*vaṃśa*), the mounting of the other pillars and beams is recommended to be done silently, without mantras.
The resolution is in the north-eastern direction. || 4 ||

It has been stated: "He erects the beam facing eastward," and "One should have the shelter constructed with a door facing either east or south. In that regard, since the beam must be placed with its tip pointing eastward under the view that the door faces east, this sūtra is intended for that purpose. "Samādhāna" means proper placement; it refers to the fixing of the beam upon the tops of the walls.
Thus ends the eleventh section (kāṇḍikā). 11.
Now follows the twelfth section:
having performed the sacrifice of the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Vāstoṣpati with the four verses beginning "O Vāstoṣpati, carry these [oblations] away," he should then enter the dwelling-place.

Now, when the marriage has been performed and the nuptial fire (*vaivāhanāgni*) has been brought inside, he who has established the sacred fires (*adhyāhitāgnika*) should enter the dwelling (*vāstu*). "Dwelling" (*vāstu*) is that in which they dwell; it means the house. Having done what should he enter? Having sacrificed with the *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Vāstoṣpati. Vāstoṣpati is the presiding deity of the dwelling, i.e., the house. The elision of the case-ending (*supo'luṅ*) is due to the inclusion [of this term] in the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class of compounds.

That which has Vāstoṣpati as its deity is *vāstoṣpatīya*, according to the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*. The genitive case is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), or because of the relationship between part and whole (*avayavāvayavisambandha*) with the *sthālīpāka*; for it is not the entire [sacrificial substance] that is offered, since there is the preservation of what is to be consumed. [Objection: But was it not said that "he should enter as the *iṣṭṛ*"? Is that not improper, since one performs the sacrifice after having entered? [Reply: True; however, it is by virtue of the priority of the mental resolve (*adhyavasāya-paurvakālyena*), just as in expressions such as "he closes his eyes and laughs" (*netre sammīlya hasati*).

Alternatively, the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in "having caused [them] to sacrifice" (*yājayitvā*) should be applied here. Since the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is intended to be without a measuring vessel, he recites the four verses beginning with "These are the carriers" (*amī vahāḥ*) and ending with "with the four" (*catasṛbhiḥ*) for the benefit of the disciples, and then offers them.
O Vāstoṣpati, these [people] of yours have entered all forms; be a most gracious friend to us. 1.

O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us; be a gracious refuge for us and free from disease. Whatever we implore of you, grant that to us; be a source of well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds. O Lord of the Dwelling, be our protector and prosperer of our household with cattle and horses, O Indu. May we remain unaging in your friendship; as a father his sons, so do you favor us. 3.

O Lord of the Dwelling, may we dwell with you in a gracious assembly, one that is golden and provides a path to prosperity. Protect us in peace and in exertion; O our patron, protect us always with your blessings. 4.

The first verse is in the *gāyatrī* meter; the others are in the *triṣṭubh* meter. Vāstoṣpati is Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), or else he is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). O Vāstoṣpati, Lord of the Dwelling, you who enter and preside over the forms—the very natures—of all our dependents, bring these dependents here; first, cause them alone to enter the house. The sense is: first grant permission for the dependents to enter the house, and afterwards for us.
Acting in this very manner, be a friend and a companion to us, one who is easy for us to enter.

O Vāstoṣpati, recognize us; being our supreme lord of the house (*gṛhapati*), accept us as your subordinate masters as well—this is the meaning. Be easy of access and provide us with a pleasant entrance. Likewise, be free from malady, devoid of disease for us. Furthermore, accept and enjoy some oblation and other offerings belonging to us. Thus, be a source of happiness (*śam*) for our two-footed beings in human form, and for our four-footed beings such as cows and horses.

O Vāstoṣpati, be for us our deliverer—be one who enables us to cross over the afflictions of the ocean of saṃsāra with ease. [The verb *edhi* is derived from the root *as* ‘to be’ in the imperative (loṭ), with the substitution of *sip* for *hi*, the change to *dhi* by the rule *hujhalbhyo hedhiḥ*, and the replacement of *dh* by *e* with the elision of the reduplication by the rule *dhvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca*. O Indu, Supreme Lord, being prosperous in our home (*gaya*), flourishing in our dwelling, and accompanied by cattle and horses, may we remain free from decay (*ajarāsaḥ*) while abiding in your friendship.
And you, favor us; delight us. Like what? Like a father his sons.

O Vāstoṣpati, may we be joined with that same abundance which attends and serves you—[the root *ṣac* meaning "to join" or "to associate"]. Of what nature is it? It is *śagmayā*, consisting of happiness; *hiraṇyayā*, delightful or endowed with gold; and *gātumatyā*, possessed of fame in the form of song or accompanied by the chanting of the Udgātṛ. And whatever excellence of ours has been bestowed by your grace, protect—that is, preserve—all of that. What while doing so?

Abiding in *yoga*, which consists in the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained, and in *kṣema*, which consists in the preservation of what has already been attained—the word *uta* being used in the sense of "and"—or rather, why specifically should Vāstoṣpati alone be entreated? O deities of the house, may you all likewise protect us at all times with blessings (*svasti*), that is, with non-destruction. || 1 ||
One should feed Brāhmaṇas who are capable of tracing their lineage. ||2||
In that house, one should feed the Brahmins; and this rite is named "the looking up at the lineage" (vaṃśodvīkṣaṇika), for they eat while looking up at the lineage. || 3 ||
Thus ends the twelfth section (kāṇḍikā). 12.
Now begins the thirteenth section (kāṇḍikā). Now, the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas). || 1 ||

The entry into the household together with one’s lawful wife is followed immediately by the performance of the *pākayajñas*, because the opportunity for their practice has now been obtained. The *pākayajñas* are sacrifices (*yajñas*) performed by means of cooking (*pāka*); here, they are merely introduced, while they will be explained in detail later.
The *pākayajña* sacrifice is of four kinds: the *huta*, the *ahuta*, the *prahuta*, and the *prāśita*. || 2 ||

The use of the singular number here for those [sacrifices] introduced with a plural refers to their commonality as "sacrifice" (*yajña*); it is intended to demonstrate that even a single sacrifice has four varieties, just as perception (*pratyakṣa*) is divided into visual and other types. There are six intermediate subdivisions of these very four, which Gautama stated: "The *Aṣṭakās*, the *Pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the *Śrāvaṇī*, *Āgrahāyaṇī*, *Caitrī*, and *Āśvayujī*; and the six forms of *pākayajña*. Among these, the *huta* is that which is accomplished by offering into the fire, such as the *Vaiśvadeva* and others; the *ahuta*, however, is that which is accomplished without offering into the fire, such as the presentation of oblations (*bali-upahāra*). That sacrifice, moreover, at whose commencement there is an offering into the fire...

The *prahuta* consists of the *anvaṣṭakā* and other such rites. That which is accomplished by means of excellent food, such as the feeding of guests and Brahmins, is the *prāśita*. All of this is indeed a sacrifice (*yāga*), because it involves the mental dedication (*saṃkalpa*) of a substance for the sake of a deity.
He is the offered among those who have offered. || 3 ||

The word "prakṛti" (archetype) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is that for those offerings belonging to this world, the Vedic *homa* is the archetype (*prakṛti*). That from which the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is derived is the archetype; that which derives [its procedure] is the modification (*vikṛti*). Thus, in the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, the archetypal actions—such as sweeping the ground, sprinkling water around the fire, strewing grass, uttering the *svāhā* call, and casting the food into the fire—are performed. || 3 ||
The offering of what has not been sacrificed. || 4 ||

The Vedic offering is the archetype for all offerings performed here. The procedure is as follows: having spread the sacrificial grass (barhis) upon which the deities are seated, having performed the invocation (āvāhana), having presented garlands and perfumes, and having offered incense, one prepares the sacrificial food-oblation (bali). Thus is the ritual procedure. 4.
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña belongs to the Prahutas.

The Vedic Piṇḍapitṛyajña is the archetype (prakṛti) for the Prahuta offerings performed here. Since it serves as the disposal (pratipatti) of the Piṇḍas remaining from the Vaiśvadeva, its Piṇḍa-mantras, the giving of morsels of food, and other such rites become applicable by extension (atideśa).
The honey-mixture and the Brahman-rice are for those who have eaten. ||5||

The *prāśita* (consumed) offerings are of two kinds: those consisting of the feeding of guests and those consisting of the distribution of meals to Brahmins. Among these, regarding the feeding of guests, the Vedic *madhuparka* offered during hospitality (*ātithya*) serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*). In that context, the concluding ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) includes such elements as the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful oblation (*arghya*), and the *madhuparka*, followed by a meal primarily consisting of meat, and so forth, for those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).

However, when a meal is given to Brahmins with a specific deity in mind, the *brahmaudana* prescribed for the *ādhāna* rite serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*). In that case as well, the procedure consists of seating them on seats arranged outside, offering the *arghya* water and so forth, dedicating food mixed with ghee to the deity, and then eating after first obtaining permission with the words, "May you partake," and so on—such is the manner of performance. ||5||
The *pākayajñas* have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices as their archetype.

This is an extension of common *itikartavyatā* (procedural details). However, the specific *itikartavyatā*s have already been demonstrated previously. Since the procedure pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*) is obtained without distinction, he states an exception in certain cases: "But among those [acts], the performance is silent. (Sūtra 7)

*Āvṛt* refers to the ritual action; *upacāra* refers to the performance. The meaning is that the silent performance of actions such as pouring out the oblation (*nirvāpa*) and threshing (*avaghāta*) is done without mantras.
Not deprived of its purpose. || 8 ||

Whatever purpose is rendered useless—even if it was observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—should not be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*), even if it lacks a mantra. For example, the grinding of grain and the placing of the potsherds are useless in the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice. Likewise, because the *sāmidhenī* verses have been omitted, the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) need not be performed as its purpose has been lost; and because of the absence of the *prayāja* offerings, the *upabhṛt* ladle is likewise unnecessary. The omission of the *sāmidhenī*s and other such elements follows from the enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*) that will be stated hereafter.

It should not be argued that the *pākayajñas* possess an entirely independent status (*apūrvatva*)—like the *darvihoma* or the *gṛhamedhīya*—merely by virtue of this much; for it must be stated that they have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype (*prakṛti*), because they depend upon the ritual details (*dharma*) such as the *juhū* ladle and the *homa* oblation.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter (kāṇḍikā). 13.
Now begins the fourteenth section:
One should take a wife during the northern course of the sun.

"One should approach one's wife after bathing"—this indicates that the time for seeking a wife is immediately following the ritual bath. She is called *bhāryā* because she is worthy of being supported (*bharaṇam arhati*); the suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule "the gerundive suffixes and *tṛc* are used in the sense of being worthy. "One should find" (*vindeta*) means one should obtain or see her. "During the northern course of the sun" (*udagayane*) means when the sun moves from the southern direction toward the northern direction; that is, during the summer solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*). || 1 ||
He speaks of the lunar mansions:
one should choose [the bride] under Kṛttikā, Svāti, and the [three] Pūrvas.

One should cause someone else to choose [the bride] under the asterisms of Kṛttikā, Svāti, and the three Pūrvas; one should employ another, but not choose her oneself—thus the causative suffix (ṇic) indicates what is appropriate. || 2 ||
One who possesses the defining characteristics should examine those characteristics. ||3||

One who knows the characteristics of the hands and other limbs should examine those marks that indicate auspiciousness. Since the order of meaning is more powerful than the order of the text, the sequence should be understood according to the sense—that is, the choosing [of the bride] must be preceded by the examination of her characteristics. || 3 ||
Regarding the examination when the [auspicious] characteristics have not been obtained, he states another means of examination:
"Or one should examine [the site] by means of heaps of clods of earth. (4)

The word *api* indicates the acceptance of other means; the word *vā* indicates an alternative. The meaning is that if the previously mentioned [means] do not yield results, one should examine fortunes by means of *piṇḍas* (almanacs) to bring about favorability toward the husband.

From the heart of the Vedic altar, from the cow-pen, from the gaming-ground, from the fire-hearth, from the crossroads, and from the barren wasteland—one should collect nine portions. Truth alone is the Supreme Lord; nothing whatsoever transcends Truth. Upon Truth this earth rests; may all this, and that yonder world, become [Truth]. (5)

The *vedi* is well known as the sacrificial altar. *Sītā* is the furrowed earth. A *hrada* is an unfathomable reservoir of water containing lotuses and other such features. A *goṣṭha* is a cow-pen or a place where cattle reside. An *ādevana* is a gambling ground where people play for stakes. An *ādahana* is a cremation ground, so called because bodies are burned therein. A *catuṣpatha* is a crossroads where two paths meet in the shape of a swastika. An *iriṇa* is...

A saline tract. From each of these, one should take a lump. And the ninth is "to be collected" (*saṃbhārya*); the meaning is that one should make the ninth by collecting small portions of earth from the altar-ground (*vedi*) and so forth.

He states the mantra for the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the lumps (*piṇḍas*) extracted from the altar (*vedi*) and other locations: "Ṛtam eva... (Only Truth...). The word *iti* serves to indicate all the preceding parts [of the mantra]. Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin does not transcend or go beyond Truth (*ṛta*); therefore, having become present here, may he illuminate Truth. This earth, consisting of the altar and so forth, is also supported by Truth. When "that" (*asau*) is said, one might understand it to refer to a name; thus, "that girl" refers to one named Śobhāvatī and so on, because she exists as a perceptible reality. This [mantra] further concerns Truth and its manifestation. (5)

Having uttered the name of the girl, he should take all the balls marked with signs in his hand and present them to the maiden, saying, "Take one of these. He should marry her if she takes one of the first four.

If one should take any [girl] extracted from the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), the heart, the cow-pen (*goṣṭha*), or the lake (*hrada*), he may marry her; however, he should avoid one taken from elsewhere. For, "In the case of a girl from the sacrificial altar, she brings assistance in the performance of Vedic rites; in the case of a girl from the cow-pen, she brings offspring; in the case of a girl from the lake, she is fit for ornaments of flowers grown in water, she bestows satisfaction, she is the cause of shrines (*caitya*), and she ensures the longevity of her husband.
