A girl from a cremation ground will certainly become a widow; one from a gambling ground is fond of strife; one from barren soil is constantly distressed; and one from a crossroads is unchaste. Some say that even such a girl may be married. (7)
The word "they think" (*manyante*) is to be supplied; "he should marry her who [is] taking [the hand]" (*gṛhṇatīm upayacchet*) is to be connected [to the preceding]. || 7 ||
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Śraviṣṭhā, and the Uttarās [are auspicious] for marriage. || 8 ||
*Upayama* means acceptance; the meaning is that these very asterisms are favorable for that [acceptance].
Or rather, as stated by Puṇya: || 9 ||
The meaning is that one should follow what has been stated by the virtuous and what is declared in the treatises on astrology (jyotiḥśāstra) according to their applicability.
Thus ends the fourteenth section (kāṇḍikā). 14.
Now begins the fifteenth section.
Next, we shall describe the procedure for the giving away of a girl to be given as a Brāhma gift. 1.

That which is given according to the Brāhma rite is called *brāhmadeyā* (given by the Brāhma rite). We shall now describe the rule—the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—for the excellent giving of her. The word "now" (*atha*) serves to introduce the subject. There are eight forms of marriage: the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca. Among these, the regulations for the six forms excluding the Brāhma and Āsura are well-known and do not require mention here; therefore, the procedure is stated only for the Brāhma and Āsura rites.

For instance, the *rākṣasa* marriage consists of abduction by force; in that case, what is the use of specifying a particular form? Likewise, the *paiśāca* marriage consists of approaching a woman while she is unconscious; because it is an extreme transgression, it is also unworthy of being designated as a specific type. The *gāndharva* marriage is the union of one who desires her with her who desires him; even there, there is a unique procedure (*itikartavyatā*). The *prājāpatya* rule is well-known: "Let there be the practice of dharma together, let offspring be procreated together, and you must not deviate from dharma, wealth, and pleasure."

Having adorned her, the girl is given to the officiating priest within the inner altar; thus the Daiva marriage is described by the authors of the Smṛtis. "One should give a pair of cattle to the one who receives the girl"—this is the injunction for the Ārṣa marriage. ||1||

On an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, or on a festival day, having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing northward, they both sit upon it: the recipient facing east together with his attendants, and the giver facing west.

On an auspicious day belonging to the bright fortnight, purified according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥ-śāstra*), or on a festival day such as the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), having spread out *darbha* grass with its tips pointing toward the north for the sake of purification, the recipient—being accompanied by his attendants—should sit upon them facing east. Who? The recipient. Of what sort? Accompanied by his retinue (*sāmātya*). The donor, moreover, should sit facing west, likewise spreading out *darbha* grass with its tips pointing toward the east, together with his attendants. (2)

Having spread darbha grass with the tips pointing eastward in the middle, having placed water upon them, and having scattered rice and barley grains, the officiating priest (ṛtvij), seated to the south facing north, should cause the support (upayamana) to be prepared.

Seated facing north in the southern direction between those two—the giver and the receiver—the specific officiating priest, the *ācārya*, should cause the *upayamana* (the formal connection) between the giver and the receiver to take place. Having done what? Having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward between the giver and the receiver, and having placed water in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātrī*) upon those *darbha* blades, he should perform the sowing of rice and barley grains into that water.

Now, as for the question "How is the bronze vessel (kaṃsa) obtained from the general statement 'having placed water'?"—it is obtained from the observation [of another text] stating, "having poured gold into the bronze vessel. ||3||
When they have assembled, he announces three times, "I give," and [the recipient] announces three times, "I accept."

When the assembly has gathered and the givers, receivers, and relatives have come together, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should speak: he should say to the giver, "Let this girl be given to him," and to the receiver, "Let the girl be accepted from him. Then, he should instruct the giver to utter three times, "I give to you, I give to you, I give to you. The giver should do exactly so. Likewise, having been informed by the priest, the receiver should say, "I accept. For there is a Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "The gods are indeed true to their word thrice."

"Because that which is stated thrice does not become erroneous," it is for this reason that the threefold recitation is desired; thus it is said, "he speaks when they have assembled. This is so that he will not be able to seize back or abandon what has been given and received in the presence of a great multitude of people. || 4 ||
Having said, "This is the truth for you," he mutters the two verses, "May your minds be equal" and "May your thoughts be united," while looking at both the officiating priests.

With the worldly formula, "May this act of giving and receiving be true and unfailing for you," the officiating priest recites the two verses beginning with "samānā" while looking at both the giver and the recipient.

Equal are your intentions, equal are your hearts; may your mind be one, so that you may be well-disposed toward one another. I have brought your minds together, your vows together, and your thoughts together; those who stand apart with divergent purposes, them we cause to bend together. (These two verses are in the Anuṣṭubh meter.)

"May your intentions—the purposes and desires belonging to you, both giver and receiver—be equal, similar, and of one form; let there be no evil intention in anyone, such as the desire to abduct a maiden. Thus, "may the mind be common [to us]"; and I, by means of this recitation (*japa*), act for you in such a way that there may be a perfect state of union (*susaha*) among you. That is to say, I have made the minds common and I bring the vows into harmony. In the same way, it should be applied to the phrase "I have made the consciousnesses (*cittāni*) common."

And those among you who are wavering and of contrary conduct—whom some call "you" and others point out directly as "these"—to them he points out their misconduct by means of facial expressions and so forth, saying: "Stay [as you are]; we do not bend them down. (The addition of the syllable *na* is for emphasis; the meaning is: "We indeed bend them down (*sannayāmaḥ*), that is, we make them properly bowed (*sannatān*), we bring them to a state of right conduct. || 5 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth section (kāṇḍikā). || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter;
it describes the procedure for the Āsura form of marriage.
Now, concerning the girl who is to be given for a bride-price. || 1 ||
The phrase "the rule for giving is stated" is the ellipsis. She who is given for a *śulka*—that is, for a price—is called *śulkadeyā*. || 1 ||
They exchange gold. || 2 ||

When two people, intending to acquire gold, give it to one another, both the giver and the receiver are Asuras because they are primarily characterized as robbers and conquerors; thus, their mutual exchange is performed with a Rajasic nature and is not praised. However, when the two—the giver and the receiver—act together to determine and exchange gold that serves as the price for a maiden, both meanings [of giving and receiving] are understood simultaneously through the single act. || 2 ||
With the words, "For the subjects, thee," he hands it over.

The bridegroom gives that aforementioned gold to the father of the girl with the mantra, "For the sake of offspring, O gold, I give you"; [the meaning is: "O gold, I give you for the purpose of progeny. || 3 ||
He receives it with the words, "For the increase of wealth, thee! ||4||
The father of the maiden: "I accept you for the increase of wealth. 4.
Having poured gold into a bronze vessel, they touch it together with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. || 5 ||

Having accepted the gold that serves as the bride-price and placed it in a bronze vessel filled with water, they touch it together—meaning they sip it—for the purification of terrible sins, reciting the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. The use of the plural number refers to all the kinsmen, intended to show that all share in the responsibility for the sin. These verses, beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," have already been explained in the section on cleansing. "I give you to offspring; I accept you for the increase of wealth."

Some employ only these two mantras, as they constitute the completion of the sentence, like [the formulas] "For food, thee," and so forth; however, according to another view, the supplement for the first mantra is "May the subjects breathe after you, and may you breathe after the subjects," while the supplement for the second is "I accept you for the sake of good offspring and for the sake of vigor."
Thus ends the sixteenth section. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth section (kāṇḍikā). Next, he describes the marriage ceremony.

Having adorned the girl with Gaudānika mantras, while she sits facing east upon a four-legged auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), four women who are not widows, her mother, her father, and the preceptor as the seventh, having bathed her with a filter (pavitra) of a thousand holes and covered her with a new garment, offer oblations from the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, saying: "Svāhā to Indra, to Indrāṇī, to Kāma, to Bhaga, to Hrī, to Śrī, to Lakṣmī, to Puṣṭi, and to Viśvāvasu, the king of the Gandharvas. || 1 ||

Since the sequence of meaning is more powerful than the sequence of recitation, the explanation must be made according to that [meaning], just as one says, "He offers what has been born with the *janman* [verse]," and "He breathes upon what has been born," so too, "He offers with the *agnihotra* [verse]" and "He places the gruel on the fire. Therefore, this is the meaning: for her who is seated facing east upon a beautiful seat—a *bhadrapīṭha* consisting of four parts—there are four non-widowed women in the four directions; on her left side is the mother, and on her right side is the father.

The performer of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is the preceptor (*guru*), who is the seventh [in the lineage]. When they are seated according to their respective positions, at the Godāna ceremony, the preceptor—having adorned the girl with bracelets, armlets, and so forth, according to his means, using those very *gaudānika* mantras for the sake of obtaining good offspring, and having covered her with a new garment that has not yet been worn, with a purifying cloth (*pavitra*) consisting of a special cloth provided with a thousand holes—he offers the oblation (*sthālīpāka*) with those same *gaudānika* mantras.

Here, four women who are not widows hold up four sprouts of cloth for the purification. The parents sprinkle water [over the child]. The preceptor recites the mantras. In the bathing and the decoration, the preceptor alone is the instigating agent; therefore, there is a common agency with the *homa* offering. Those, however, who explain "decoration" (*alaṃkaraṇa*) by way of indirect indication (*viparīta-lakṣaṇā*) as meaning "shaving the hair," are inauspicious.

In the phrase "of the *sthālīpāka*," the singular number is intended to be significant because it qualifies the object being taken up, just like the singularity of the animal in a sacrifice (*paśu*). The singular verb "he offers" (*juhoti*) indicates, by the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), that there is only one oblation even though there are nine offerings; thus, he enumerates the offerings accordingly. [The first offering is] to Viśvāvasu, the king of the Gandharvas; thus there are nine. Indra is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Indrāṇī is Śacī. Kāma is the desirable. Bhaga is the one to be honored. Hrī is modesty. Śrī is the one worthy of taking refuge in. Lakṣmī is the one to be characterized. Poṣa is nourishment. Svāhā means "may there be a well-offered oblation. || 1 ||

Having smeared with scented water the flute, the tūṇava drum, the mṛdaṅga drum, the paṇava drum, and all musical instruments, the maiden plays them, saying: "Sound forth, O Dundubhi drum! O Gomukha, for the sake of noble offspring! Let the maidens, joyful in mind and having performed the auspicious rites, sport together with Indrāṇī. Thus [it is said]. (2)

Having smeared all the musical instruments, such as the *nāḍī* and others, with fragrant scented water, a maiden first plays them. While they are being played, she recites the Guru-mantra. In this context, *nāḍī* refers to a flute; *tūṇava* and *gomukha* are specific types of wind instruments. As for the meaning of the mantra: "O drum (*dundubhi*), O kettle-drum (*paṭaha*), speak the sound, that is, the wind; cause the sound to resound. For what purpose? For the sake of good progeny (*suprajastvāya*), meaning for the sake of virtuous offspring. Likewise, "O *gomukha*, speak the sound," and so forth, as before.

Let the maidens, having become friends with the girl whose marriage has commenced, sport together with her. For they too ought indeed to be maidens, since friendship among those of similar character exists through mutual intimacy. Of what sort are the maidens? *Sumanasyamānāḥ*, meaning well-disposed, cheerful, or joyful. It is hoped that Indrāṇī also descends here to sport at this festival along with [the bride]. They are *sumaṅgalāḥ*, making the sound of songs primarily concerned with auspiciousness. Now, the mantras for the *gaudānika* (hair-cutting) rite are explained.

The waters that have come into being with milk—those of heaven, those of the intermediate space, and those of the earth—with the luster of all of them, I sprinkle you with splendor. I have sprinkled you with splendor, together with sacrifice and milk; so that you may be a multiplier of friends, even so may Savitṛ make you. Svāhā to Indra!

The first [verse] is Virāj; the second is Anuṣṭubh. Those waters which are divine, existing in heaven; those which are atmospheric, existing in the intermediate space; and those which are earthly, belonging to the earth—those which have come into being with milk, that is, they have been produced with the milk used for sacrifice—with the splendor (*ruc*), the radiance, and the essence of all of them, O maiden, I sprinkle you; I, indeed, sprinkle you. The meaning is: "Together with the sacrifice, the milk, and the radiance, I make you fit for the sacrifice and other such rites. [This is] of Mitra.

Just as Savitṛ, the Sun, has made this [offering] an increaser of wealth, heaven, cattle, sons, and so forth, as well as of sacrifices and the like, so may he do for you, O maiden! May it be well-offered to Indra. Thus ends the seventeenth section (kāṇḍikā). 17.
Now begins the eighteenth section (kāṇḍikā).

Having covered with a single thread of wool a branch of a sacrificial tree that extends toward the east and has been cut in one stroke, he gives it to the girl with a verse addressed to Savitṛ: "Whatever misfortune (*alakṣmī*) is yours—whether derived from your mother, derived from your father, inherited, or even innate—that I banish and drive away along with the deity Tiṣya; let it go to your enemy. Homage, homage to Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati! (1)

The term *yajñiya* means "fit for sacrifice," according to the rule *yajñavigbhyāṃ ghakhanau*. He gives the girl a branch belonging to one of the trees suitable for sacrifice, such as the *vaṭa* (Ficus indica) and others—a branch that has been cut once, extended and spread out toward the eastern direction, severed with a single stroke, and covered with a single-strand thread of uniform strength—reciting the mantra beginning with *devasya tvā* and ending with the words *tāṃ prayacchāmi*.
The teacher consecrates the girl who has grasped the branch with the mantra beginning with "yā te," and so forth.

O girl, whatever misfortune (*alakṣmī*) you may have—whether it consists of inauspicious marks inherited from your mother or your father, transmitted from your mother or father due to defects in the seed and so forth, or transmitted from some other source—that I drive away from you with this mantra; I render it excluded from you. Is it alone? No, he says: it is performed together with the deity Tiṣya. Thus I push it out completely, I expel it. And having been expelled, let it go to your hater, your enemy.

"May there be salutation to Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati for the removal of obstacles for me who am intent upon the removal of non-characteristics (alakṣaṇa). Others, however, having extracted this portion of the Yajus mantra, "Salutations again and again to Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati," employ it even at the conclusion of a Vedic recitation (śākhotsarga).
Its disposal [should be] in stagnant water, or in pure water, or in a temple of the deities. || 2 ||

"Stable water" refers to ponds and the like. In such a place, the disposal—that is, the ritual of final dedication—of that branch should take place in a pure temple. Since a temple might be considered impure due to offerings of liquor, blood, and so forth, the word "pure" is used for that purpose.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter (kāṇḍikā). 18.
Now begins the nineteenth section:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the sacrificial oblation (haviṣya).
The term "haviṣyakalpa" is a technical designation for a specific type of ritual action. || 1 ||
For maidens, the period of celibacy is ten years, or twelve years.
After ten years, a maiden must not be kept by her father; or, at the very least, twelve years must not be exceeded. || 2 ||

At the conclusion of the period of studentship, having kindled two fires either in the presence of a Gandharva or in a divine assembly hall, he dedicates two animals: the southern one to Aryaman and the northern one to Prajāpati.

At the conclusion of the period of celibacy, prior to the marriage, in a place where water flows spontaneously from no visible cause, or in a temple of the gods, one should kindle two ordinary fires and prepare two goats for the consecration of the bride according to the ritual for animal sacrifice (*paśukalpa*): one for Aryaman in the fire situated on the southern side, and the second for Prajāpati in the fire situated on the northern side. We shall explain the procedure, along with the explanations of the mantras, in the *paśukalpa* itself.
But in the event of impossibility, there is only one animal.

In the absence of an abundance [of animals], only a single animal dedicated to two deities should be immolated. Furthermore, the portions (avadānas) must be taken twice each from the twelve parts beginning with the heart and ending with the fat. There is also a modification of the formula: "Svāhā to Aryaman and Prajāpati. And there is only a single offering (yoga), because the property of being a single location belongs to the two combined. For this very reason, some do not desire double portions from the heart and the other organs. || 4 ||
Or one may perform it with rice grains. || 5 ||
If there is poverty of wealth, or when observing the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), one may perform [the rite] with rice grains; the mention of "rice grains" is intended to include flour as well. 5.
Just as the animal is according to its place, so too are the portions for sacrifice and the oblation according to their respective places.

In the very same place where the primary animal sacrifice was performed with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, there the flour-animal (*piṣṭakapaśu*) is offered; likewise, the portions (*avadāna*) are taken from the heart and other organs. For these, the cooking and the offering are always performed according to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of other sacrifices, including the binding with the rope, the fastening to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the immolation, and so forth. With the exception of those elements whose purpose has been lost, the oblation is a cooked mess (*sthālīpāka*) in place of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), which is also placed in its proper position according to the sequence of the animal-cake ritual; however, in place of the offering of the omentum (*vapāhoma*), there is an offering of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*).

One should worship Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Skanda, Rudra, Vātsīputra, Bhaga, the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) of Bhaga, Kālī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Bhadrakālī, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Mahiṣikā with offerings of fragrant substances.

The oblations consisting of fragrant substances such as sandalwood and camphor mixed with clarified butter (ājya) are called *gandhāhutis*. With these, one should worship the seventeen deities beginning with Āmya. Since the deity is to be understood solely through sound (*śabda*), the name of the deity is "Vātsīputra. By changing the case endings, the deities beginning with Āmya are to be sacrificed to by means of words ending in the dative case accompanied by the utterance *svāhā*, such as "To Agni, svāhā," and so forth.
Thus ends the nineteenth section. 19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Now, therefore, follows the auspicious day for sacrificial food (*haviṣya-puṇyāha*).

This too is a technical designation (*pāribhāṣikī saṃjñā*). Its basis for application (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*) is the performance on an auspicious day using sacrificial materials such as *vrīhi* rice and the like. (1)

Having gone to the edge of water, or having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (oblation of rice) in milk as the occasion permits, he bathes her together with her head using all kinds of perfumes and the best fruits; then, having covered her with a new garment, he offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka* to Indraṇī, Varuṇānī, Gandharvāṇī, the Waters, Agni Jīvaputra, Prajāpati Mahārāja, Skanda, Aryaman, Bhaga, and Prajānaka.

Having gone near water—if the village is very far from a pond or similar body of water—then, wherever it may be convenient, one should prepare a *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) in milk and bathe the girl with water containing all medicinal herbs and fragrant substances, along with auspicious fruits such as bilva, akṣoṭa, and others, and with *āmalaka* fruits. By the phrase "including her head," he indicates that on other occasions, bathing for women may even be performed without including the head.

The *sthālīpāka* oblation is performed with the intervals of bathing, offering new garments, and clothing [the child]. It is intended that the sequence is such that the *sthālīpāka* occurs prior to the bathing. As before, the fourth case ending is used for the substitution of the deity’s name, and the utterance of *svāhā* is likewise as previously described. "Agni whose son is living" (*jīvaputra*) is a single deity; it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose son—namely, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the wind (*vāyu*)—is a protector," and since the *agnisannidhāna* (proximity of Agni) is appropriate and primary, Agni himself is the referent of the compound.

Regarding the term *mahārāja*, the prohibition [of the suffix *ṭac*] by the rule "not after a word of worship" (*na pūjanāt*) does not apply here, because of the reliance on a specific restriction based on the statement: "In the sense of worship, the inclusion of *su* and *ati* must be made. Otherwise, the prohibition of *ṭac* would also apply in cases such as *paramarāja*. Those who read the form *mahārājāḥ* with a long final vowel (*ākārānta*) do not heed the restriction regarding *su* and *ati*.
Thus ends the twentieth Kaṇḍikā. || 20 ||
Now begins the twenty-first section (kāṇḍikā).

On the very second night when one intends to marry a girl, at the end of that night, having fetched a new pot and cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) in milk, having bathed her including her head with all kinds of perfumes followed by fruits, and having covered her with a new garment, he offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka* to Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Uda, Bhaga, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and King Prajāpati.

The day and night of the wedding and the preceding night constitute [the period]. Of these, the first is the second night—that night during which the father, intending to give away his daughter in marriage, is possessed by the resolve, "I shall marry her," or rather, that second night which precedes the future night with reference to which the father intends to marry the girl; having commenced the ritual procedures in reliance upon that [second] night, he should perform the sacrifice with the *sthālīpāka* as before, during that very night, after the middle two watches have passed, at the time called *mahāniśā*, for the deities beginning with Guru, Agni, and the others. || 1 ||
One should worship these very deities, as well as Vaiśravaṇa and Īśāna, for a male [child]. || 2 ||

For a man as well, on that night, for the sake of the consecration, he should sacrifice to these same deities with this very procedure, including the three Kumbhāya offerings. And this is the only difference:
twelve oblations for a woman, and fifteen for a man. || 2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter (kāṇḍikā). || 21 ||
Now begins the twenty-second section (kāṇḍikā).

Four or eight widows, having fed Brāhmaṇas with balls of vegetables and food, should sing together with lute-players; or alternatively, four [widows] should perform a dance [to the verse]: "Sing forth, O Kaṇvas, to your playful host of Maruts, the irresistible, resplendent on their chariots! (RV 1.165.1). 1.

"Non-widows" means those whose husbands are still living. "Vegetable-piṇḍas" (śākapiṇḍyaḥ) means piṇḍas mixed with vegetables; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "mixing with something edible. The words "four" and "eight" are in apposition with the feminine nominative nouns [referring to the widows]. There is an option between four or eight as circumstances permit. This is intended to establish a rule regarding the number being equal [to the number of recipients]. However, some maintain that it is intended to establish a rule regarding the specific numbers four and eight.

Thus, the syntactical connection is as follows: not fewer than four widows, equal in number, excluding those who have six [sons], having fed the Brāhmaṇas with vegetable-piṇḍīs and other available special foods, and having become associated with those whose habit it is to sing while a lute is being played, they should sing auspicious songs together with them.

What is intended here is the occasion for auspicious singing immediately after the feeding of the Brahmins; however, there is no particular insistence on the requirement of a common agent (i.e., that the same person must perform both). Therefore, whether those [same] Brahmins should feed them or others should do so, in any case, the auspicious singing must be performed after the feeding of the Brahmins. Alternatively, one skilled in dancing—meaning one who is proficient in the art of dance—should perform a dance, provided he is endowed with virtues such as good character (*sauśīlya*); but in the opposite case, one should not dance with women. It is with this intention that the word *apivā* ("alternatively") is used.

Regarding the performance as it is observed in Āryāvarta, we shall describe it as follows: after the mother and seven others—or four, if widows are excluded—of the bride have been fed according to one's means, and the Brahmins together with those non-widowed women and lute-playing singers, they sing and dance with great enthusiasm.

Accordingly, this is the meaning: four or eight women, acting as the agents of the rite, should feed the Brahmins with vegetable balls (*śākapiṇḍī*) and other kinds of food, and then sing together with unmarried women who play the lute. Who [should sing]? By implication, the girl’s mother and the others. The word *api* is used in a conjunctive sense. That entire group of women, being clever and full of enthusiasm, should perform a dance.
He consecrates [the water] with this Gāyatrī verse, "krīḍaṃ vaḥ," which has already been explained in the section on Kṛcchra penances. || 1 ||

One should sacrifice unhusked barley-meal (akṣata-saktu) to Agni, the Lord of Prosperity (Puṣṭipati), and Prajāpati [with the mantras]: "Through Agni may he obtain wealth and nourishment day by day, glorious and most abounding in heroes"; and also, "O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you. || 2 ||

One should worship Agni, the Lord of Prosperity, with the flour of unhusked, unthreshed barley grains, using the verse beginning with "By Agni [I obtain] wealth. Likewise, one should worship Prajāpati with the mantra beginning with "O Prajāpati. These two offerings are to be performed at the conclusion of the Ājyabhāga (butter-portion) rites.
In all marriage rites where no specific deity has been prescribed, one should worship Agni as the Lord of Prosperity and Prajāpati.

In the marriage section of the ritual, wherever a deity is indicated by name or by the syllables of a mantra, there one should sacrifice to Agni Puṣṭipati and Prajāpati with unhusked barley-meal (*akṣatasaktu*), because they are the subject under discussion. This should be understood to apply to the rites to be performed later, such as those at the time of departure (*prāsthānika*) and so forth; however, in the previously mentioned rites, the deity is recognized in all cases—sometimes by name and sometimes from the syllables of the mantra.

By means of Agni being worshipped with oblations, may I attain *rayi*, wealth—[the root] *aś* meaning "to pervade," thus may I pervade it—and having pervaded and obtained it, may I follow after its nourishment and growth day by day. What kind of wealth? That which brings glory (*yaśasam*), that which makes one glorious; that which is most rich in heroes (*vīravattamam*), endowed with heroic men, or pre-eminently possessed of heroic sons. [The verse beginning] "O Prajāpati, not indeed... will be explained in the context of the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). || 3 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second section. 22.
Now begins the twenty-third section:
next, the ritual for departure.

The meaning is that the rite pertaining to departure (*prāsthānika*), which has departure as its occasion, will be described immediately hereafter. And "departure" refers to the groom's journey to his father-in-law's house in order to perform the marriage ceremony. || 1 ||
Having kindled the fire in that place as prescribed and having offered oblations with the Jaya and other formulas, the sister thereafter takes hold of the garment while holding a weapon.

Having performed the rites pertaining to departure as prescribed, the preparation of the fire—which must first be performed—is defined as follows: for the fire that has been dug up and sprinkled with water, one performs the sweeping, the sprinkling around, and the strewing of grass, followed by the consecration with five oblations of clarified butter and eleven *santani* offerings; therein, one should perform the oblation with the mantras beginning with the *jaya* verses, or perform the oblations known as *jayas*, namely: "Ākūtaṃ cākūtiśca," "Bṛhaspatipurohitāḥ," and "Ṛtāṣāḍ."

The meaning is that one should perform oblations (*juhuyāt*) with these and other such mantras. For these mantras, or the oblations accomplished by them, are well known as being performed through the use of terms such as *jayāḥ*, *ābhyātānāḥ*, *rāṣṭrabhṛtaḥ*, and *ājyabhāgāḥ*. Some maintain that at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should sacrifice to Agni Puṣṭipati and Prajāpati, on the authority of such sūtra statements as: "In all marriage rites where no specific deity is prescribed [the same applies].

Others, however, say that precisely because of the authority of the Sūtrakāra, the term *jaya* here serves as a technical designation (*paribhāṣyate*) for the two oblations to the deities Agni and Prajāpati, and that the rite of kindling the fire (*upasamādhāna*) concludes with the *ājyabhāga* offerings.

Someone says: because it is enjoined intermittently within the section on marriage (*vivāhaprakaraṇa*), one should perform the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings and then offer oblations of unhusked rice and parched barley (*akṣatasaktu*) to Agni Puṣṭipati for the sake of prosperity; otherwise, since the deity is understood everywhere either by name or from the wording of the mantras, there would be no rite among the marriage ceremonies for which a deity is not already prescribed, and thus there would be a lack of comprehension regarding the meaning of the Sūtra.

Thus, when the *jaya-homas* have been performed, at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the bride’s sister—standing behind the groom, being either the eldest or the most honored—silently takes hold of one of the specific weapons, such as a sword or a razor, according to what is available. She silently grasps the hem (*sic*) of the upper garment belonging to her brother; that is to say, she touches the fringe of the lower garment with her hand. This is for the purpose of ensuring the fulfillment of the injunctions of the author of the *Aṃcala-sūtra*.

The taking up of a weapon is also for the purpose of purifying what has been seen; likewise, it is observed in Āryāvarta that generally that very same weapon is kept near the bed and other places even at a later time for the sake of protection. || 2 ||
Saying "Pūṣan is mine," they go where there is water. ||3||
The meaning is that they proceed facing the water, reciting the mantra beginning with "May Pūṣan protect me on the path. || 3 ||
Having touched water with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," they proceed toward the directions according to their respective quarters with the mantra "prācī dik. || 4 ||

Having reached the edge of the water, they perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) by sprinkling water on their heads; then, with the mantra beginning "The eastern direction has Agni as its deity," and so forth, they address each direction according to its characteristic mark using the respective mantra for that direction which is to be traversed, and the bridegroom and the others depart. In this matter, the officiant (*guru*) who performs the marriage ceremony is the one who recites the mantra for the bridegroom, whether he be the father or another.
May Pūṣan protect me on the path; may Pūṣan, the guardian of cattle, protect me; may Pūṣan, the sovereign lord, protect me.

He nourishes and causes to increase, thus he is Pūṣan—the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky. Accordingly, the Brāhmaṇa states: "This [earth] indeed is Pūṣan on the path; the intermediate space is the herdsman; the sky is the overlord. For this shows that the word *pūṣan*, used here with the direct demonstrative "this" (*iyam*), has the earth as its referent in the mantra. Furthermore, by the mantra "the intermediate space is Pūṣan," which refers to that which is situated in the middle, it shows that the word *pūṣan* also functions with respect to the intermediate space.

Just as the earth is called *Pūṣan* because it nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) all beings, so too the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is *Pūṣan*, since it protects (*pāti*) and nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) cattle by providing them with room. Likewise, the sky (*dyu*) is also *Pūṣan*, for it is the sovereign of all worlds and thus nourishes all worlds through rain and other means. Therefore, this is the meaning of the mantra: may *Pūṣan*, who is the earth, protect me on the "prapatha"—the path or way set out upon for traveling; and likewise, may that *Pūṣan* characterized as the intermediate space, who is the protector of cattle (*paśupā*), also protect and guard me.
Likewise, may Pūṣan, who is the sovereign lord characterized by the sky, also protect me as I travel on the path. The mantras beginning with "śanno devīḥ" have already been explained. || 4 ||

The eastern direction has Agni as its deity; may he reach Agni who seeks to harm me from this direction. The southern direction has Indra as its deity; may he reach Indra who seeks to harm me from this direction. The western direction has Soma as its deity; may he reach Soma who seeks to harm me from this direction. The northern direction has Mitra and Varuṇa as its deities; may he reach Mitra and Varuṇa who seek to harm me from this direction. The upward direction has Bṛhaspati as its deity; may he reach Bṛhaspati who seeks to harm me from this direction. This downward direction has Aditi as its deity; may he reach Aditi who seeks to harm me from this direction.

The eastern direction has Agni as its deity. Therefore, whoever—related to that very direction—who seeks to harm me (the root *das* meaning "to destroy"), desiring to bring about my destruction, may he encounter Agni; may he run toward Agni; taking Agni as his target, may he experience the dissolution of his senses; the meaning is that Agni shall exercise restraint over his eyes and other faculties. This same application is identical everywhere.

Since there is ascending and descending mountains, as well as movement upward and downward, it is also appropriate for the mantra to be directed toward those [directions]. Some say that only that portion of the mantra which has "going toward" (*yad-abhimukham gamanam*) as its indicative mark should be employed; however, this is incorrect because this mantra is for the purpose of warding off calamities. For one who has set out to go toward any particular direction, a disaster is possible from all directions—from serpents, thunderbolts, and so forth, both below and above.
The same applies to those originating from the sides and so forth; this procedure is to be understood as applicable in all systems.
Thus ends the twenty-third section (kāṇḍikā). 23.
Now begins the twenty-fourth section.

There are six persons worthy of the *arghya* offering: the teacher (*ācārya*), the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the king, one with whom one has entered into a marriage alliance, a dear friend, and a graduate (*snātaka*).

Even before the marriage, the bridegroom must be honored by the father-in-law with water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). The rule for this mode of worship applies equally to all six; thus, these are the six persons designated. They are called *arhyas* because they are worthy of honor (*arghya*) and worship. The *ācārya* is both the initiator (*upanetṛ*) and the teacher (*adhyāpayitṛ*) of the pupil. The *ṛtvij* is the officiating priest for the sacrificer, and he too is to be honored prior to the performance of the ritual. The *rājā* is the Kṣatriya, though he is not honored merely by virtue of his consecration (*abhiṣeka*), but as the ruler of the realm.

One who is worthy of marriage (*vivāhya*) is so called because he "deserves marriage" (*vivahana-marhati*); the suffix *ṇyat* is used here according to the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*. Such a person is worthy of the *arghya* offering from the father of the bride. Likewise, whoever is dear to someone due to the excellence of his qualities is worthy of the *arghya* at the time of giving [the bride] and other such occasions. However, a *snātaka* who has just bathed is [worthy of it] from his teacher. || 1 ||
Then they honor him. || 2 ||

The word *atha* (now/then) signifies the acceptance of the method that is about to be described, since indeclinables possess multiple meanings. They honor, revere, and respect this person—one among the teachers and others—in the manner that is about to be described. || 2 ||
And at the beginning of the action. || 3 ||

Some authorities maintain that since honoring is prescribed for the period following the marriage, the offering of the *madhuparka* and other honors must be performed only after the wedding, according to the principle of "following the sequence as enjoined. For this very reason, they explain this [verse] by extracting it from its context to apply specifically to the time after the marriage. To refute that view, [the author states]: "The worship must be performed at the very beginning of the rite," because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more authoritative than the sequence of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

For this *saṃskāra* has the purpose of imparting a specific fitness for ritual action to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others by way of generating enthusiasm and so forth; if it were performed after the sacrifice, marriage, or other rites had already been completed, it would be entirely fruitless. Furthermore, this *saṃskāra* is prescribed by the *Smṛtis*, and in those *Smṛtis* it is enjoined prior to the performance of the rite itself.

Furthermore, the suffix *kṛtya* is used in the sense of "one who ought to" (*arha*) or "that which is necessary" (*āvaśyaka*). Thus, "one who ought to marry" (*vivāhya*) means either that he is worthy of marrying, or that he necessarily marries a maiden. This is according to the traditional grammatical rule (*smṛti*): "The *kṛtya* and *tṛc* suffixes are used in the sense of being worthy (*arha*)," "The suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) and debt (*adhamarṇya*)," and "The *kṛtya* suffixes [are also used in these senses]. Moreover, one does not become worthy of marriage after having already married. || 3 ||
He states the characteristics of the *arghya*:
"The *arghya* consists of water, medicinal herbs, and *darbha* grass. (4)
Water, either rice or barley, and *darbha* grass—these three constitute the *arghya*. || 4 ||
He states the manner of performing the reception of the guest, which follows the definition of the *madhuparka* and is not explicitly taught [elsewhere]:

"Having poured curd and honey into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, having covered it with a larger [lid], and having grasped it with two mats, they first proceed with the water for the feet (*pādya*). (5)

In this context, the term "those who perform the worship" is understood by implication. Curd and honey are poured into either a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) or a wooden cup (*camasa*), which is a specific type of wooden vessel. This [mixture] is called *madhuparka*.

Having covered and concealed that *madhuparka* vessel with a large bowl (*bṛhatpātra*), and having grasped it with two bundles of grass (*viṣṭara*), the worshippers themselves undertake the worship—without even requiring further instruction—even regarding those items beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*), namely the water for the feet, the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the *madhuparka*, according to their respective suitability, above, below, and in the middle. || 5 ||
"May there be milking for me; may there be milking for Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj from the foot"—with these words he recites the mantra over it as it is being brought.

When the giver of the girl has approached the one to be married, the officiating priest (ṛtvij) brings the water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings near the giver of the girl. At that time, the one to be married consecrates the items as they are being brought with this mantra. If the one to be married is ignorant of the mantras, then the officiating priest himself teaches him. This should be understood to apply everywhere in the same manner.

This is the meaning of the mantra: *duh* (to milk) means "filling"; thus, *doha* is that which fills or nourishes. *Virāj* refers to Prajāpati in heaven and other realms; the term *pādyādi* (water for washing the feet, etc. is used. O *pādyādi*, you who are the filling or nourishing *doha* for me—that is, for my sake—be such a *doha* as to fulfill the needs of Virāj Prajāpati, since water and other things were appointed by Prajāpati from heaven. Therefore, become available for my reception (*pratipatti*). And may I partake of this *doha* consisting of water for the feet and so forth, which belongs to Virāj Prajāpati.
"I shall pervade" means "I shall see"; the seeing is for the purpose of consecrating the water for the feet (pādya). || 6 ||
Having spread out the seat with the formula, "Thou art a seat; may he sit upon thee, O mother," he sits down upon it. || 7 ||

Having spread a layer of *darbha* grass upon another seat with the mantra beginning "viṣṭo'si" (You are entered), he sits down silently after having performed the marriage ceremony. [The meaning of the mantra: O *viṣṭara*, you are a *viṣṭara*; you are a seat. Therefore, cover the other seat; for the sake of covering it, sit—that is, remain—upon the mother, the other seat. || 7 ||
To him who is seated on a seat, he recites each [verse] three times.

To the bridegroom who is seated—that is, sitting upon a special seat covered with *darbha* grass—the giver of the girl recites each of the items, beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*), three times: "The water for the feet," "The respectful offering (*arghya*)," "The honey-mixture (*madhuparka*)," and "The water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). The use of the dative case in the word *āsīnāya* (to the seated one) signifies the locative sense; thus, the meaning is: "to the bridegroom who is seated upon the *viṣṭara*."
He did not say "Bhoḥ," nor did he say "Mārṣa. || 9 ||

He prohibits that which has been obtained as a respectful address—namely, the invocation "Bho" used to bring one worthy of honor face-to-face, as well as the invocation by name such as "O noble Brahmadatta," and so forth. || 9 ||

Having consecrated the water with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," he washes [the guest's] feet with the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), saying: "Wash the right foot; here I bestow spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon this family. Wash the left foot; here I bestow upon myself splendor, vigor, food, progeny, cattle, and spiritual luster."

Having consecrated water with the mantras beginning with *śanno devīḥ*, as previously explained, the giver of the girl washes the feet of the bridegroom—who is worthy of honor—with special water for the feet (*pādya*) that is capable of cleansing them. For the washing of the feet, there are two mantras according to their respective gendered signs: "the right one," etc., and "the left one," etc.

By the word "this" (*idam*), he shows the immediate fruit: the giving away of the girl and that which is accomplished through the subsequent marriage, taking the form of the connection to the performance of rites and so forth from that very moment. Of this bridegroom, I wash—purify—the left foot, which is endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). "I give this splendor, virility, food, progeny, cattle, and spiritual luster to the bridegroom and others who are worthy of the *arghya* offering.
The meaning is: "May that splendor and so forth which has reached me remain within me alone for a long time. (10)

Having taken up the arghya water with the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, he takes the madhuparka with the Sāvitra formula. Having drawn out the seat-grass (*viṣṭara*) with the words "Thou art the seat; settle upon the atmosphere," and having pushed it aside with "Wide for thee," and having looked at it with "That eye," and having placed it on the seat-grass with "Of the earth for thee," he stirs it clockwise with his index finger while reciting the three verses beginning with "Honey the winds pour for the righteous one. (11)

He accepts [the guest] with the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, whose meaning has already been explained. He accepts the *madhuparka* with the mantra addressed to the deity Savitṛ, beginning with *devasya tvā* and supplemented by the insertion of the words "I accept the *madhuparka*. With the mantra *viṣṭaro 'si*, he removes the upper seat-cushion (*viṣṭara*). Having removed it and cast it aside, he moves it away with the mantra *uru tvā*.

Having gazed at the *madhuparka* with the mantra beginning "That eye," he places the *madhuparka* vessel upon the lower seat with the mantra beginning "Of the earth. With the three verses beginning "Honey for the one who follows the Truth," he mixes the curd and honey while circling them clockwise using the finger known as the *pradeśinī*, which is situated near the thumb; *pradeśinī* refers to the index finger (*tarjanī*) because it has the habit of pointing out or threatening (*pradiśati tarjayati*).
At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I accept the honey-mixture (madhuparka).

At the impulse (permission) of the divine Savitṛ, who possesses the qualities of giving, illuminating, and so forth, I accept this honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) with the arms of the Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, and with the hands of Pūṣan—not with my own [hands], which are made of leather. You are a seat (*viṣṭara*); rest upon the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
You are a mere seat, a false concealer; therefore, move away from this lower seat and take refuge in the intermediate space, the sky.
To the broad wind.
O Viṣṭara, I cast you upon the earth; therefore, go far away. For what purpose? For the sake of the wind, that is, for the purpose of the air.
That eye, beneficial to the gods, rises pure in the east;
may we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns.

This very eye is praised, which, being beneficial to the gods, rises in the east; that same eye, having performed its function, serves as the means for the sake of the gods in the acts of gazing at the oblation and so forth, sacrifice, giving, and offering—this is the meaning. Of what nature is it? It is *śukram*, i.e., bright. Therefore, we pray: may we see the means of sacrifice and other rites for a hundred years, and for that very purpose, may we live for a hundred years.
I accomplish this upon the navel of the earth.

O Madhuparka, although you are present within this vessel, I do not prepare you upon the lower layer of Darbha grass. Grains and sacrificial offerings are prepared upon a layer of Veda grass; for herbs are the essence of the earth, and among those, Darbha is the essence—thus, you are indeed the very soul of the Darbha layer.

Honeyed are the winds for the one who follows the cosmic order; honey do the rivers flow. May the plants be sweet for us. (1) Honeyed be the night and the dawn; honeyed be the earthly realm. Honeyed be the sky, our father. (2)
May the lord of the forest be full of sweetness; may the sun be full of sweetness;
may our cows be sweet for us. 3.

May the winds—the blowing airs—be honey; may they result in sweet essence. For whom? For the one who desires *ṛta*—truth or sacrifice—for him. May the rivers—the flowing streams—flow with honey; may they pour forth and stream. Likewise, may the plants—those ending with the ripening of their fruit, such as rice and others—be full of honey for us. May the night—the first part of the night—be honey-sweet for us, and moreover, together with the dawn—the latter part of the night.

May the earthly dust be honey-sweet; "dust" (*rajas*) refers to the world of earth (*bhūloka*), or simply to soil. May the sky (*dyauḥ*), the celestial world (*dyuloka*), be honey-sweet, pouring forth sweet flavor by way of rain and other means. Of what nature is the sky? It is the Father, the protector. May the fruit-bearing tree be honey-sweet for us. Likewise, may the sun be honey-sweet for us. By this rite, may our cows also be honey-sweet—sweet-flavored through the giving of milk and other products. (11)

"May the Vasus, whose king is Agni, consume you; may the Pitṛs, whose king is Yama, consume you; may the Rudras, whose king is Soma, consume you; may the Ādityas, whose king is Varuṇa, consume you; may the Viśvedevas, whose king is Bṛhaspati, consume you"—with these mantras, he wipes away the remnants of the smearings at the edges of the vessel, moving clockwise from direction to direction. || 12 ||

Beginning from the east and proceeding clockwise, one wipes away the finger-prints on the rim of the madhuparka vessel with the final mantras. Because of the instruction that "for each direction, there is a separate mantra," it follows that with the fifth mantra, the wiping occurs in the previously mentioned intermediate direction (southeast). As for the meaning of the mantras: "O smear, may the Vasus—the specific deities residing in the eastern direction—consume you; let the Vasus be satisfied by you. Of what nature are the Vasus?

"Agni-rājānaḥ" means those for whom Agni is the king (*rājā*). For in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, a suffix at the end of the compound would [otherwise] apply. This method of interpretation is the same for all [the following] mantras. || 12 ||

"Since you are the honey of honey, the supreme form of the supreme food, through that may I become the supreme eater of honey, the honeyed one, of the honey of honey, the supreme food, the supreme eater of the supreme food. You are the glory of the threefold knowledge; you are the glory of prosperity; you are the glory for glory; you are the radiance of Brahman; you are the true prosperity, the glory, the fortune. May fortune rest upon me; may fortune rest upon me. With these words, he consumes four mouthfuls of the *madhuparka*, using the little finger first, then the ring finger, the middle finger, and finally the index finger, with the thumb accompanying each.
He then gives what remains to a friend. || 13 ||

With the mantra beginning with "yanmadhunaḥ," he takes portions of the *madhuparka* with each finger together with the thumb and eats them four times: first with the little finger (kaniṣṭhā) together with the thumb, then with the ring finger (anāmikā), the middle finger (madhyamā), and the forefinger (pradeśinī), each time together with the thumb. When four such portions have been taken, whatever remains he gives to a close friend or a younger brother and so forth.

The meaning of the mantra is as follows: the elements, beginning with earth, are like honey—that is, like nectar; "madhavyam" means the essence of honey, the essence of nectar, the essence of essences—meaning that which belongs to honey, to nectar, is the essence of essences, namely the earth.

Because the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* establishes that "this earth is honey for all beings" and so forth, by presenting the earth as the essence of all elements (*bhūta-sāra*), [the text continues: through that which is the supreme, most excellent form—characterized by food and the like—of that very essence of essences characterized by the earth, [I am] the consumer of that which is to be eaten, which consists of food and drink, which is to be experienced through perfect awareness, and which is the supreme *ātman* itself, existing in identity with the supreme *madhu* (honey)—that is, the immortal nectar (*amṛta*) consisting of eternal bliss, which is the essence of all immortality.

The supreme eater of food is the very nature of the Supreme Self; because of dissolution therein, may I become more abundant—that is to say, may I attain the state of Brahman. Furthermore, O Madhuparka, you are the glory—the manifestation—of the triple knowledge, that is, of the three Vedas; likewise, you are the glory—the manifestation—of prosperity. Therefore, for the sake of glory, I consume you.

Furthermore, you are the radiance and light of Brahman, the Supreme Self; you are the prosperity of Truth, the meaning of the Vedas, and the prosperity of fame. Therefore, let Śrī, the Goddess of Prosperity, take refuge in me—meaning, let Śrī abide in me again and again. || 13 ||
He sips water with the formula: "Thou art the underlayer for the nectar. ||14||
With this mantra he sips water: "O water for sipping, you are the underlayer, the covering, of the nectar-like *madhuparka*. (14)
Therefore, with sword in hand, he spoke to the cow. || 15 ||

Having honored him and offered the madhuparka, he, with sword in hand, says to that worthy guest who has consumed the madhuparka, "I shall prepare the cow," thus requesting permission for another purpose; this is the meaning. And the preparation of the cow is a *nipātana* (an irregular formation). 15.
He instructs her. || 16 ||
He instructs that cow, "Oṃ, perform [the task]"; the meaning is that the one worthy of honor gives this permission. (16) The one who honors her recites this mantra:
"Destroy the evil of both myself and such-and-such; my evil is destroyed; destroy my evil. (17)

"O cow! And [you], O Agniśarman, and that venerable Viṣṇuśarman—whatever sin I, being subject to the authority of Vedic injunctions, commit by performing this which ought not to be done, destroy that, meaning 'annihilate it. Or rather, the meaning is: 'My sin is destroyed; therefore, because this act is impelled by sacred law (vidhi), there is no sin for me. O immolators, destroy my sin, annihilate it. || 17 ||
Oṃ, do it! || 18 ||
The meaning is that he gives permission, saying, "O slaughterers, let the cow be prepared. || 18 ||
One should feed four Brahmins of different lineages; this is the first method. || 19 ||

First, one should feed four Brahmins of various lineages (*gotra*) and various ancestral clans (*pravara*), and afterwards, those who are worthy of honor along with their kinsmen. This means that this method for a Brahmin—the procedure beginning with the *gokaraṇa*—has been taught; therefore, no doubt should be entertained regarding this matter. || 19 ||

If she should let it loose, he should mutter: "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality—may I declare this to the discerning people: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi! May she be blessed with good pasture; and may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you wander. (20)

Even when a matter is already certain, the word "if" (yadi) is observed, as in the example: "If the Vedas are authoritative. Having performed the prescribed procedure, one should release the cow; the meaning is that one should not kill it. Furthermore, one should recite the verse beginning with "mātā rudrāṇām," and so forth.

This cow is the mother and nourisher of the Rudras—those specific deities who roam the intermediate space; she is the source of milk and, through the medium of oblations and subsequently rain and so forth, the daughter and sustainer of the Vasus—the dwellers—and of the herbs born from the earth. She is the sister and offspring of Aditi, belonging to the Ādityas. Therefore, having made this certain, I shall proclaim it for the sake of the discerning person; the word *nu* indicates certainty. I speak with resolve for the discerning person, one possessed of superior consciousness. What do I say?

O you who are the slaughterers, do not kill the cow! Of what sort? One that is *anāgāḥ*—sinless, unblemished, or free from wretchedness. Why? Because she reaches (*ati*) excellent fodder (*sūyavasa*), thus she is *sūyavasāt*. Furthermore, O Cow, may you become *bhagavatī*—possessing wealth (*bhaga*) in the form of milk and fame—and likewise, through your grace, may we also be *bhagavantaḥ*, endowed with wealth and renowned. Eat the grass without causing injury; consume it.
Since you are at all times the giver of everything through the medium of milk, drink pure water while moving and wandering about on all sides. 20.
Having said, "O, release her; let her eat grass," he releases that cow or the animal.
"It is traditionally known that the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should not be without meat. || 22 ||
Or rather, it may even be simply rice cooked with ghee.

Having honored [the guest] and made it established without further deliberation by saying "Om," [the host says: "O slaughterers, release the cow! Once released, let her eat grass at her own will. Having said this and seeing that cow released, one should substitute a goat as the sacrificial animal, or a piece of meat from the limbs of a sacrificial animal. For it is known from the Śruti—where the word *ha* indicates traditional history—that there should be no *madhuparka* devoid of meat (*amāṃsa*).
Alternatively, for one who dislikes meat, or for those [who are similarly inclined], a meal mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be prepared. 21, 22, 23.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section (kāṇḍikā). || 24 ||
Now begins the twenty-fifth section:

"May the paths be thornless and straight by which our friends go to choose a bride; may Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; may the lordship over the wife be well-governed, O Gods!"—with these words he sends forth the messenger.

With the mantra beginning with *anṛkṣarāḥ*, he sends forth the water-bearer—the one who fetches the vessel of water—meaning he dispatches a man to bring water suitable for the girl’s bath and other rites. As for the meaning of the *ṛc*: it is the seership of Brahmā or of Sūrya; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. The word "path" (*panthāḥ*) is in the singular by grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*). "Thorny" (*ṛkṣarāḥ*) refers to harsh things such as thorns or specific types of grass; may those paths be "without thorns" (*anṛkṣarāḥ*), meaning free from them, and also "straight" (*ṛjavaḥ*), meaning not crooked.

By means of those [helpers] who go to the desirable place for fetching water, such as the Gaṅgā and other sites, which belong to us—here "sakhāyaḥ" (friends) is used in the plural by way of grammatical substitution—and furthermore, may Aryaman, the Āditya, and Bhaga lead our friend properly to the place of water.

O gods, beginning with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the Ādityas, by your grace may *jāspatya*—the union of husband and wife—be perfectly well-governed, well-restrained, more stable, and complete. The word *jāspatya* is a Vedic formation (nipātita) according to the rule: "In the Veda, [the forms] *jāyā* and *patya* may optionally [be used]. || 1 ||
Having covered it with a branch of the Śamī tree together with its leaves, he should fetch it. || 2 ||
He should respond by bringing water after having covered and concealed a water-pot with a branch of the Śamī tree that has leaves. || 2 ||
One should perform the functions of water with these very waters. ||3||

Taking portions again and again from these very waters that have been brought, one should perform the purposes accomplished by water—such as the bathing of the bride, the rinsing of gold, and the sprinkling around the fire—and not with any other water.

"May the waters of the desert be auspicious for us; may the waters of the marshes be auspicious for us; may the waters of the ocean be auspicious for us; may the waters of the wells be auspicious for us. With these verses, he causes her—who has bathed with pure water—to put on an unwashed garment, reciting: "Those who cut [the wool], those who carded it, those who spun it, and you divine goddesses who wove the ends all around—may those goddesses clothe you with old age; O long-lived one, put on this garment. Having caused her to put on the unwashed garment, he girds her from within with a girdle made of muñja grass or darbha grass, reciting: "Aśāsānā... (VS 14.20). 4.

With the mantra beginning with *śann āpaḥ*, he should bathe the girl with water that is not alone, but mixed with fragrant substances such as various herbs and accompanied by specific fruits. Then, with the mantra beginning with *yā akṛntan*, he should cause her to put on a new garment—one that has never been worn before, is exceedingly fresh, and is unwashed (*ahata*). Thereafter, with the mantra beginning with *āśāsānā*, he should perform the girding of the girl by tying a cord made of *muñja* grass or *darbha* grass around her waist in such a way that she is concealed within and cannot be seen.

The *anuṣṭubh* verse beginning with "śanna āpaḥ" has already been explained. Regarding those waters which have been brought here by means of fetching, the specific point is: "may they be *śam*, i.e., happiness, for us."

The verse beginning with "yā akṛntan" is a Jagatī. O long-lived maiden, put on this garment—wear it! And may all those goddesses clothe you with old age; may they envelop you with old age. May the deities make you one who is worn out by age, yet possessed of a husband; the meaning is that they shall grant you a long life. Who are those goddesses?

Those who cut this garment—those presiding deities by whom the cloth was produced through cutting; those who wove it—those by whom the garment was completed; those who spun it—those by whom the thread was stretched out lengthwise; and those goddesses who extended the ends on both sides—the meaning being that they stretched out the fringes at both ends of the root and the leaf; and those deities are mentioned by their own names in another mantra: "The Revatīs have spun you."
Desiring goodwill, offspring, prosperity, and wealth, being devoted to Agni, sit down for the sake of well-performed deeds.

Anuṣṭubh; the seer is Pṛthivī. I bind on this garment. For what purpose? For the sake of well-performed action—that is, for the sake of rites such as marriage, sacrifice, giving, and oblation; the meaning is "for the sake of desire. Just as in the phrase "What for the eye is first cast off," there is the perception of a desire for the eye, so here in "for well-performed action, what [is cast off]," there is the perception of a desire for well-performed action. Being of what nature is she (the garment) for the sake of winning (*sannaye*)?

Desiring a cheerful mind, clarity of spirit, as well as good fortune, favor from her husband, and wealth—meaning riches—and likewise being devoted to Agni, meaning one whose nature is to attend upon the Āhavanīya and other sacred fires, she remains [in this state] at the time of the Sannāyya offering. || 4 ||

"May Pūṣan release me from here; well-bound, may he lead me away from there. O bountiful Indra, so that she may become possessed of good sons and good fortune. "May Pūṣan lead you from here by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot. Go to the house so that you may be mistress of the household; may you speak with authority in the assembly. "May those highwaymen who lie in wait not find the couple. Having crossed over the difficult path by easy ways, let the enemies flee away. Having thus led her out, the ritual concerning the garment is performed.

The meaning is that with the three verses beginning with *preto muñcātu*, having lifted [the girl] from the place where she was led forth (*udānīya*) and placed her upon his lap, the father or the eldest brother should perform the rite over the upper part of the garment—that is, as one does for the lower covering—with the mantra beginning with *yā akṛntan*, just as prescribed. These are the ṛṣis of the Sun; the first and third are *anuṣṭubh* meters, and the second is *triṣṭubh*. "O maiden, may he release you from this place"—that is, I release you and lead you away.

The forms "muñcatu" and "iti" involve a transposition of the verb and a transposition of the person (puruṣavyatyaya), for in another Vedic branch the mantra is recited as "preto muñcāmi. Regarding this girl, who is pure and virtuous in both her father’s family and her husband’s family—let no one cause her departure from that father’s family or from that husband’s family; the meaning is: let no one whatsoever effect her separation from these two families.

O Indra, Supreme Lord, O bountiful bestower, act so that this maiden may possess excellent sons and be fortunate. O maiden, from this place, may Pūṣan and Indra lead you forth; grasping your hand with their hands, may the Aśvins carry you away in their chariot to your desired destination. Thus, in due order, go to the home of your husband.

And in that regard, may you be as a mistress who protects the household; may you be self-controlled, having brought under your influence the servants and other members of the family. And at the *vidatha*, which is the sacrifice, do not speak what is contrary to the sacrifice; do not speak anything opposed to your husband—meaning, be one who is favorable toward the entire collection of Vedic rites.

May those who are waylayers on the path—enemies such as thieves and the like—who approach the husband and wife with evil intent and lie in wait for them, not find you; may they not see you. May you pass beyond all difficult paths by means of fair ways, which are excellent for traveling.

Furthermore, let the enemies—the stingy ones, meaning those devoid of charity and characterized by poverty—flee; being terrified and turning their backs, let them run away and obtain a contemptible state of stumbling gait. This is the meaning.
The rules of conduct. 6.

At this juncture, one should cause the customary rites—those derived from traditional conduct and well-known through the customs of country, caste, and family—to be performed; that is to say, such acts as stating the purpose of the arrival, mentioning the maiden's name, worshipping the family deity, and striking her with *sumanā* flowers and creepers, and so forth. || 6 ||

Having silently produced fire by friction from the hearth, or having established the *sāntapana* fire which is already burning outside, he sweeps around it, sprinkles water around it, pours water around it, and spreads sacrificial grass around it. Having prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*) by melting and purifying it, and having offered the oblations from the *āghāra* up to the *ājyabhāga* portions, he parks either a chariot or a cart to the west of the fire. With the verse "At every yoking," he yokes the right [ox] with one [verse] and the other, the left, with the other.

"He is either the *aupasada* fire or the *vaivāhana* fire," as he will state [later] with the words, "in it [are performed] the *pākayajñas*. Here, four alternative primary forms (*prakṛtis*) of the *vaivāhana* fire are mentioned. That which is produced by friction from two kindling-sticks (*araṇis*) on the same day is conventionally designated by the term *nirmanthya*. Since the act of churning is common to it, the mantra would have applied from the other instances of churning; however, it is stated that it is done "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*). This is the first. The second is from the hearth (*bhrāṣṭra*). The third is the *sāntapana* fire.

That fire which is produced by force from a portion of fire that has been removed after it has been heated—by means of contact with cotton, cow-dung powder, and the like—or that which is produced by heating a stone or a bronze gem (*kaṃsamaṇi*) and placing it facing the sun, or by placing a sun-crystal (*sūryakāntamaṇi*) facing the sun, is intended here. Regarding the fourth type, which blazes [spontaneously], although there is no specific mention here, it should be understood that one must exclude fires taken from a *tretā* (three-fire) hearth, a dwelling, a cremation ground, or those belonging to a woman in childbirth or an outcaste (*patita*).

The term *upasamādhāya* (having placed near) is to be connected with each [action]; the meaning is: having placed [the fire] in a pit (*kuṇḍa*) that has been dug out and sprinkled like the *gārhapatya* fire, and which reaches the knees. The rule is that this must be done specifically outside the house. *Parisamūhana* is the touching of the four directions with water-sprinkled hands. *Paryukṣaṇa* is the pouring [of water] around. In this way, the spreading of *darbha* grass around the four directions is well-known. Others, however, maintain that the spreading is toward the east, south, and west, based on the observation in the *Vaiśravaṇīya* [text] stating, "he spreads it with three layers."

The melting of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is its liquefaction; the purifying (*utpavana*) is its cleansing by means of a strainer (*pavitram*). Having performed the oblations beginning with the *āghāra* and ending with the *ājyabhāga*, while the bride and the groom stand respectively to the left and right of the fire in its western part, he places a wagon (*anaḥ*), a chariot (*ratha*), or a carriage (*syandana*) with its yoke fastened behind the fire. With the verse beginning "At every yoking" (*yoge-yoge*), he yokes the bride and groom to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by means of a thong (*yoktra*), placing the groom on the southern side and the bride on the northern side.
The meaning is "he joins together. "In every union, in every battle, we, as friends, invoke the most powerful Indra for our protection."

Gāyatrī meter; Maitrī deity; the seer is Kaśyapa. We invoke Indra—we call him. Where? In every *yoga*, that is, in every connection with ritual service between husband and wife who abide together. Likewise, in every *vāja*; the word *vāja* denotes food, strength, and assembly, but here it is understood as meaning "food," since the householder's life is rooted in food, and by the word *vāja*, the means of obtaining food will be expressed—this is an exhortation to offer the first portion of the oblation, whether it be the sacrificial cake or clarified butter. For what purpose do we invoke him?

For protection and for assistance. Of what sort are we? Friends, that is, those of common renown. Of what sort is Indra? *Tavastaram*; the word *tavas* denotes strength or greatness; thus, [we call upon him who is] more powerful or greater. (7)

"Silently unyoking [the horse] at the hole of the chariot, the hole of the wagon, and the hole of the yoke, O Śatakratu—having thrice sprinkled Apālā with water, may Indra make her radiant as the sun. Having tied a piece of gold with a fringed cord and placed it upon her head, he pours water over the right yoke-pin with the mantra: "May the gold be auspicious for you; may the waters be auspicious; may the wedge be auspicious for you; may the pin of the yoke be auspicious. May the hundred-purified waters be auspicious for you; unite yourself with this husband in body. (8)

Just as in the case of the two natural [oxen], here too he prohibits the recitation of the mantra by saying "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*). Having unyoked—that is, having released—the one joined with the whip; and having bound gold with a *darbha*-purifier according to the passage beginning "in the hole of the chariot," he places it into the hole located on the right side of the yoke. How is it bound? The meaning is: "having made it *niṣṭakya*," that is, in such a way that easy release occurs; *niṣṭakya* means easy to unfasten.

Immediately after tying [the garment] with gold, he brings the girl to the bridegroom's place on the right side; then, over the hole in the yoke-pole on the right, he pours water mixed with gold, using the previously mentioned waters. The repetition of *adhi* in *adhyadhi*—according to the rule "the words *upari*, *adhi*, and *adhas* are doubled to express proximity"—indicates proximity. Thus, the meaning is that having placed the girl near the bottom of the hole in the yoke, he pours the golden water upon her head.
At this juncture, an exchange of positions occurs between the girl and the bridegroom; however, they will remain in their respective places once more, as it will be stated: "The man is on the right."
"Khe rathasya... is an Anuṣṭubh verse addressed to Indra; its seer is Brahmā. Even when [the seer] is mentioned elsewhere, the seer is indeed Brahmā.

"And immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths"—thus there is a traditional recollection that all the Vedas were seen by him in general. O Śatakratu (Indra) of infinite action, may the Supreme Lord Āditya (the Sun), among the radiant ones, make this girl possess the splendor of the sun—that is, a luster like that of the sun at the time of its rising. Having done what? Having purified her three times—having made her pure three times. Of what sort is she? Apālā, who before her marriage was a wanderer at will, and therefore fit for purification. Where? [In the waters.]

"In the hole of the chariot," likewise "in the hole"—that is, the aperture—of the cart, the wagon, and the yoke. Alternatively, the explanation contains the sense of the particle *iva*: "May Indra, having purified this maiden like Apālā, make her radiant as the sun."

Just as it is said that Indra, seeing Atri’s daughter named Apālā afflicted with leprosy in a deserted hermitage when the sages had gone out for bathing and other purposes, sprinkled her with golden water through the openings of the sacrificial posts and restored her to a state free from disease and endowed with the splendor of the sun—likewise, may Indra make this woman also free from sin and grant her the brilliance of the sun. Such is the traditional account (itihāsa).

"In former times, Apālā, the daughter of Atri, was a maiden afflicted with skin disease. Seeing her in the solitude of her father’s hermitage, Indra desired her. Having cast her through the opening of his chariot—between the yoke and the cart—he dragged her three times; thereafter she became well. "May gold be auspicious for you," is in the Jagatī meter. O maiden, may gold be *śam*—that is, happiness—for you. "May the waters be *śam*"; here *u* is a particle used in conjunction, meaning "and may the waters also be happiness for you."

May the *methī* (the wooden pin supporting the chariot), the *varūtha* (the fender), and the *śam* (happiness) be for your well-being. May the *tarma* (the hole) of the yoke be a source of happiness for you. May the waters, which possess a hundred purifiers and provide much protection, be bringers of happiness to you. "With this husband, unite with your body"—with this husband, unite and become joined with your body (*tanvā*). In some recensions of the *Śākhā*, however, it is read as *tanvaṃ saṃsṛjaka*, meaning "unite [him] with your body," the sense being that you should join him with yourself. || 8 ||
On the right side, there is a man. || 9 ||

When the consecration rite (*abhiṣeka-saṃskāra*) has been performed for the girl, the man stands facing east on the western side of the fire, while the girl stands to his south; that is, she is understood to be on the northern side. Here, some hold that the girl is the primary agent because she is brought to the southern side and undergoes the consecration; others hold that the man is the primary agent in the marriage ceremony because he remains independent and always stays on the southern side. || 9 ||
Then he offers oblations: "Svāhā to Agni, the knower of the born; svāhā to Soma, the knower of the born; svāhā to Gandharva, the knower of the born. || 10 ||

The word *atha* (now/then) signifies auspiciousness, according to Māṭhara; whereas Ādityadarśana maintains that the word *atha* is used here to indicate the offering of unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata-saktu*) during the interval. For, by the reasoning already stated, those offerings must necessarily be made at the end and the beginning of the [main] oblations; thus, there is no fault in performing them at this very juncture. He states the oblations in their proper sequence, beginning with "To Agni," and so forth.

"It is heard [in scripture]: 'In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni. Therefore, an oblation (homa) is performed for their redemption. And although Soma is the first [among them], the oblation here is offered first to Agni, with the intention expressed in the rule: 'With whatever rite one desires to perform, one should make Agni the mouth [of that rite].
