To Agni, svāhā! May it be well-offered. To what kind of Agni? To the *janivid*, i.e., he who knows (*vid*) or finds (*vindate*) the *janī*—the *janī* being a bride—to him. The rest is explained similarly. || 10 ||
He offers the *saṃtanī* oblations with the formula, "Connecting the breath with life. || 11 ||
The eleven [deities] beginning with Saṃtanya are thus. || 11 ||
The Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt [oblations]. || 12 ||
The word "he offers" (juhoti) is to be supplied [to each clause]. The meaning is that he offers the Jaya oblations, the Abhyātāna oblations, and those Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations. || 12 ||
These are as previously stated. || 13 ||

Those three rites beginning with the *jayā* must be performed without transgressing the prescribed order. Regarding this, Laugākṣi states: "One should offer the *jayā* oblations with [the ladle] filled twelve times. Some maintain that one should recite the mantra exactly as studied and make twelve offerings at the end of each *ṛc* with the utterance of *svāhā*. Others, however, perform the rite by reciting all the mantras for the clarified butter taken in twelve portions; they make only a single offering at the very end with the *svāhā* utterance, while they draw out twelve portions for each individual mantra.

In the *abhyātāna* oblations, however, one offers with four ladlings (*caturgṛhīta*). Therein, the drawing of the *āghāra* [libations] is performed with the verses beginning "bṛhaspatipurohitāḥ" and "devahūtyām. For the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings, there are thirteen oblations using twelve ladlings; having offered with the twelve verses ending in "-vaṭ," one offers the thirteenth with "sa no bhuvanasya pate" while the fire is being placed upon the front of the chariot, as previously described. That triad which is properly established in the *pākayajñas*, we shall explain there itself along with the mantras.
He offers the oblations pertaining to the lordships. || 14 ||

By the word *adhipati* (overlord), the sovereignties (*ādhipatya*) are indicated through their characteristic marks; these, together with their associated elements, constitute twenty-one sacrificial formulas (*yajus*).

Agni is the lord of beings; may he protect me; to him, svāhā! Yama is the lord of the earth; Vāyu is the lord of the intermediate space; Sūrya is the lord of heaven; Candramas is the lord of the stars; Viṣṇu is the lord of the quarters; Pūṣan is the lord of paths; Tvaṣṭṛ is the lord of forms; Savitṛ is the lord of instigations; Indra is the lord of the eldest; Mitra is the lord of truths; Varuṇa is the lord of laws; Rudra is the lord of animals; Bṛhaspati is the lord of sacred formulas; the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of speech; Soma...

May the ocean, the overlord of plants, flow for us; may food, the overlord of invocations (*āmnām*), protect us; to it, *svāhā*! May Gāyatrī, the unerring mistress of meters, protect me; to her, *svāhā*! May the Maruts, the overlords of hosts, protect me; to them, *svāhā*! O fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, may you guard us; may you protect us in this sacred knowledge (*brahman*), in this rite, in this field, in this blessing, in this priestly office, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

Agni is the sovereign lord and controller of all beings, both stationary and moving; may he protect me, may he come to receive the oblation, and may he guard me—*svāhā*! May it be well-offered to him. Yama is the controller of the earth; "may he protect me, *svāhā*" is the syntactical connection. The same applies elsewhere. Viṣṇu is the sovereign lord of the quarters because of his pervasiveness. Pūṣan is [the lord] of paths, that is, of travelers. Tvaṣṭṛ is [the lord] of forms; Tvaṣṭṛ is Prajāpati Viśvakarman, the sovereign lord of all forms and all shapes.

Savitṛ is the lord of *prasavas*; *prasavas* are those things that are brought forth, such as sprouts and the like. Indra is the lord of the *jyeṣṭhas*, that is, of those things that are most excellent. Mitra is the lord of the *satyas*; thus it is heard in scripture: "To Mitra, the lord of truth. Varuṇa is the lord of the *dharmans*; *dharmans* are sustainers, and Varuṇa is their sovereign, as seen in the passage: "You are Varuṇa, whose vow is firm; may Varuṇa purify you. Furthermore, even the Vaiśeṣikas and others have stated that Varuṇa is the sustainer of all sustainers, such as the earth and so forth.

Rudra prays for cattle, thinking, "I alone am the lord of cattle. Bṛhaspati is the lord of the Brahmanas—that is, of the Vedas. The Brāhmaṇa is the lord of speech, for he alone is the instructor of both divine and human speech, according to the Śruti: "Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa speaks both kinds of speech, the divine and the human. Soma, the Moon, is the lord of cultivated and wild plants that perish after the ripening of their fruit.

The ocean is the lord of flowing rivers; the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is the lord of waters, for the intermediate space is the support of water, otherwise how could there be dew? Sovereignty is their power; their food is the solar essence of the earth. The Maruts are the lords of hosts; the Maruts have been explained as the lords of all hosts, including those of the Ādityas and others.

"May those ancestors who are beyond the lower, proximate ones—namely the fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha and Manu, who arose at the beginning of creation—protect us; may they guard us. This is to be understood as required by the context, since the root *ava* here has the sense of "going" (or protecting) in its current application. What [else] should they protect?

In this Veda, in these Brahmins—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—who have been acquired through sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), in this rite called marriage, in this field of protection, and in this blessing being invoked by the priests which results in fruit for the couple: although the specific priests utter the words "May they protect me," nevertheless, because the rite has been purchased by the fee, the fruit belongs to the sacrificer alone; likewise in the office of the domestic priest (*purodhā*), that is, in the work of priesthood, and in the invocation of the gods (*devahūti*), which is the calling or summoning of the deities.
Where there is the giving of the oblation, that is the invocation of the gods; here, it is the ground of marriage.

Having offered oblations with the three verses beginning with "ākūtyā," ending with "tvā," then with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ," verse by verse; with the four Mahāvyāhṛtis beginning with "bhūḥ svāhā"; and with the three Āgnipāvamānī verses beginning with "agna āyūṃṣi," he should, after each offering, pour the remnants (saṃpāta) upon the head [of the child].

Having offered oblations of clarified butter (ājya) repeatedly with the mantras beginning with "ākūtyai tvā," one should pour down or cause to flow the *saṃpātas*—the drops of the remaining butter from the oblations—upon the head of the girl. Regarding the phrase "tvetyantair" (ending with "tvā"), some say that this excludes the ending with the word "svāhā. Others, however, maintain that since the recitation consists solely of mantras ending in "tvā," and because there is no deviation from ending in "tvā," the mention of "tvā" is intended to indicate the presence of other endings as well, such as the ending with "svāhā."

By means of the entire *anuvāka* beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha," let it not be understood that there is only one single oblation; therefore, the phrase "verse by verse" (*pratyṛcam*) is used. "With the *āgnipāvamānī* verses" means with those possessing the characteristic marks of Agni and those possessing the characteristic marks of Pavamāna. "For intention thee, for desire thee, for prosperity thee."

*Ākūti* means intention or purpose; the meaning is: "O *ājya*, for the sake of accomplishing my intended goal, I offer you. The verb *juhoti* ("he offers") is supplied as a component of the explanation of the meaning, but it is not a part of the mantra itself. If that which is supplied were considered a part of the mantra, then because the *ṛc*s would also be incomplete, they would require supplementation, and thus the pause (*yati*) would be lost. Consequently, designations such as "the *gāyatrī* is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*)" or "the *triṣṭubh*" would not be possible. Therefore, they say that the supply is merely a component of the explanation of the meaning, and not a part of the mantra.
I offer you for the sake of desire, for that which is desired and wished for; prosperity is attainment, and for that purpose I offer you.

In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. He supported this earth and yonder sky. To what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (1) This verse belongs to Nārāyaṇa-Puruṣa as its seer. Hiraṇyagarbha, Prajāpati, Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, Prāṇa, Jagatsūtra, Ka, and Samrāj are synonyms. Hiraṇyagarbha arose—that is, he became manifest—in the beginning, at the time of creation.

And he, having been born and manifested, alone was the lord, protector, and master of all that has come into being—the entire collection of elements such as earth, or the manifest derivatives such as the *mahat* and so forth; here the past tense is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*), meaning that at the beginning of the world, Hiraṇyagarbha manifests and becomes the lord of everything. He supports—that is, sustains—me, the perceptible earth, the soil.

And likewise, [he supports] the sky, heaven, and the earth—the word "earth" here refers to the intermediate space (antarikṣa) by proximity. Indeed, everything is strung upon Hiraṇyagarbha alone, like clusters of jewels on a thread. To him—to which Prajāpati, to that deity endowed with qualities such as generosity—we shall offer worship with oblation, namely clarified butter; that is to say, we shall serve him as the recipient of the offering.
He who is the King and Lord of all the moving and breathing world, who rules over its bipeds and quadrupeds—to whom [be this offering]. (2)

He who is the king, the lord, the master, and the protector of gods, humans, and others—who possess inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) as well as the blinking of eyes; by "inhalation" (*prāṇa*), exhalation and the rest are implied, and by "blinking," the capacity for the functions of the sensory and motor organs such as touch and so forth is indicated. One should understand this to include those who breathe, blink, smell, move about, and so on. He has become, or indeed is, the Lord (*vabhūva*) of the entire universe, of all that is moving. For he rules, he has power over the two-footed—gods, humans, and the like—and the four-footed—cows and the like. To him, to what god? As before.
To him who bestows vigor and strength, whose command the entire universe and the gods obey; he whose shadow is immortality and whose shadow is death—to whom [be homage]. (3)

*Ojas* is vigor; *bala* is strength or capacity. He who gives these is the "Giver of Vigor and Strength" (*ojodā baladāḥ*). All people and all gods worship, serve, and follow his command, instruction, and permission. His shadow is his refuge and means of propitiation, which results in immortality—that is, liberation. Conversely, the failure to propitiate him results in death, which causes transmigratory existence. To whom is he? [The answer] is the same as before.
By whom the fierce heaven and the firm earth were made stable, by whom the sun was propped up and the firmament, by whom the wide mid-air was measured out—to whom [be homage]! 4.

By that Prajāpati by whom the sky and the intermediate space were raised up and made formidable, and likewise the earth was pervaded; by whom the *svaḥ* (the celestial realm) was established, pervaded, supported, and stretched across—meaning it was supported even in heaven; by whom the *nāka*, the solar orb, was supported; or rather, *nāka* is an epithet of *svaḥ*: *ka* means happiness, and *na-ka* means suffering; that wherein there is no suffering is *nāka*. And he who measured out—that is, fashioned—the intermediate space, which is *varīyaḥ*, meaning more extensive; the rest is the same as before.
He who supported these two, heaven and earth, which stand firm and hold their bounds though they tremble; he upon whom the sun moves outspread—homage to him! 5.

He who established—that is, sustains—these two, heaven and earth, which are visible to the eye, trembling and shaking; how so? As *rodhasī*, meaning "obstructing" [the boundaries]; and by what means? Having made them *tastabhāne*, that is, "stabilized and free from instability. Upon whom—that is, above whom—the Sun, the Āditya, moves; how is he? *Vitataḥ*, meaning "extended" or "vast."

To him whose greatness these mountains belong, and whom they call the ocean together with the Rasā; he to whom the five divine quarters and intermediate directions belong—to whom [be our offering]! (6)

Of that Hiraṇyagarbha, these well-known mountains such as Meru and others proclaim the greatness—that is, the majesty and magnanimity; likewise, the five directions—east and so forth—together with the zenith, and the five intermediate directions together with the nadir, proclaim his majesty. The phrase "possessing the nature of the goddesses of the directions and so forth" is an epithet of the directions.
When the great waters came encompassing all, bearing the embryo and generating Agni, from that there arose the one life-force (asus) of the gods; for what purpose [was this]? || 7 ||

At the time of creation, when the great waters were first produced, they pervaded—that is, filled—the entire universe. What were they doing? They were "bearing the embryo," meaning they were holding that very Hiraṇyagarbha in the form of an embryo. As it has been said: "In the beginning, he created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed. Of what nature were they? "Generating Agni"—that is, generating Agni in the form of a mass of splendor, as well as the cosmic egg and other things. Alternatively, "Agni" may be an epithet of the embryo, meaning one whose nature is a mass of splendor.

Then, immediately after conception, that single vital breath (asu), which is the life-force of all beings—whether they be radiant deities, sense-faculties, or living creatures such as gods and humans who possess movement and other functions—which emerged and was manifested in the form of the universal thread (sarvasūtra), to that we shall pay worship with an oblation.

May Prajāpati generate offspring for us; may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, bestow it upon us. May the Year, fashioning itself through the seasons, and the Lord of Prosperity, bestow nourishment upon me. (8) May that Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha, who is of the nature of Vyāna, generate offspring for us. Being the Ordainer and the Disposer, may he, with a gracious mind, place the embryo within us.

Being in the form of the year, having been fashioned by the seasons (*ṛtu*)—that is, revolving and undergoing transformation through seasonal phenomena—the term *cāklapānaḥ* is the *kānac* substitute for the perfect tense (*liṭ*). This is an illustration of the primary manifestation (*vivarta*): from water comes Hiraṇyagarbha as a manifestation; from him comes the syllable *Oṃ*; from that, the Vedas; in such a manner, he alone manifests.

Since that Hiraṇyagarbha is the Lord of Nourishment (*puṣṭipati*), may he bestow nourishment upon us. The Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) have been explained. O Agni, purify our lives; speedily bring us strength and food. Drive far away misfortune. (1)

There are three *gāyatrī* verses; they constitute the *ṛṣi*-seership of the *kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns. O Agni, you purify and cleanse our lifespans (*āyūṃṣi*), making them free from disease, old age, and other such impurities. Bestow upon us, O impeller, strength (*ūrjaṃ*), power (*balaṃ*), and nourishment (*iṣaṃ*)—that is, food—and grant it to us. Ward off from afar (*āre*) the ill omens (*duḥśunāṃ*) of wicked beings, which are like dogs (*śunāmiva*). For the word *duḥśunāṃ* is explained in the *Prātiśākhya* as being derived from the root *śvi* preceded by the prefix *dus*. The genitive case in *duḥśunām* is used in the sense of the object, according to the rule that the genitive may be employed with verbs meaning "to harm. || 1 ||
Agni is the seer, the purifying one, the benefactor of all people, the domestic priest; we pray to him for great wealth. || 2 ||

Agni is the seer; as Pavamāna, he purifies the wicked. He is beneficial to the five classes of people—the four social orders (varṇas) and the group born of mixed unions as the fifth. He is the "Purohita" (family priest); for Agni is indeed the Purohita of the gods, placed before them (puraḥ) or for their benefit (hitaḥ) in the next world by means of accomplishing sacred rites. Him we implore, we entreat, for great wealth—that is, a great household. 2.
Flow clear for us, O protector of the dwelling; bestowing upon me splendor, heroic strength, wealth, and nourishment. 3.

O Agni, purify us; cleanse us. *Apaḥ* is a name for ritual action; thus, *svapāḥ* refers to Agni, the one of beautiful deeds, the performer of good works. What doing, do you purify us? Bestowing—granting to us—*varcas*, which is luster, and beautiful *vīrya*, or heroism, as well as *rayi*, wealth, and *poṣam*, nourishment. ||3||15||

With three [mantras]: "That body of yours which is husband-slaying, I make that one husband-protecting for you; svāhā! That body of yours which is childless, I make that one possessed of children for you; svāhā! That body of yours which is cattle-less, I make that one possessed of cattle for you; svāhā! (16)

Having offered oblations with the three mantras beginning with "yā te," one should pour the remnants (saṃpāta) over the head of the girl; this is the completion [of the rite] by way of syntactic connection. As for the meaning of the three mantras: "O girl, that body of yours which is 'patighnī' (fatal to the husband), I make it 'apatighnī' (not fatal to the husband) by means of this pouring of the remnants; likewise, that body of yours which is 'aputriyā' (unfavorable to sons), I make it 'putriyā' (favorable to sons); and that body which is 'apaśavyā' (unfavorable to cattle), I make it 'paśavyā' (favorable to cattle)."
I perform the removal [of obstacles]. At this juncture, one should offer oblations of unbroken barley flour according to the procedure previously indicated. || 16 ||

Regarding the taking of the hand: having placed her to the east of the fire upon *darbha* grass facing eastward, the pure man, standing in front and facing westward as he approaches, takes her hand with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand. He takes her right hand, palm upward, including the thumb, while his own hand is held downward; likewise, he takes her left hand with his left hand. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.7.17)

To the north of the fire, having seated the girl facing east on a spot strewn with *darbha* grass, the teacher causes her relative to take [her] hand by means of the mantra beginning with "Of the god... (*devasya te...*); this must be supplied [in the text] for the sake of establishing a common agent. When the expectation arises as to by whom he causes him to take [the hand], it should be understood from the context that it is by the groom (*vara*) who is approaching (*upayantṛ*). And that groom, having been authorized by the teacher, takes hold of her. What kind of groom takes hold of her?

Pure, authorized to take her hand, with the pure resolve, "This [woman] is for my religious duty," facing westward while standing in front of the girl—[he does so] facing westward as an exception to the rule that "one should perform all rites facing east. With his right hand—the one well-known in the world—he places it palm-upward together with the thumb; "low" (*nyak*) means he reaches down very low with the right hand, being skillful in such movements.

As it is stated in the *Dhanurveda*: "One should first practice with the left hand, for the right is already mastered. The term *nyak* means "bending down" (*nyañcati*); thus, it should be applied by repetition as "low" (*nīcā*) or "having become bent" (*nyagbhūtā*). "Not empty" (*ariktam*) means "adorned with ornaments"; in the absence of such, it means "provided with golden ear-rings and the like," and in extreme poverty, "accompanied by flowers, fruits, and so forth. "With what is not empty" (*ariktena*) refers to that same state. In this way, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the entire mantra and other elements, such that "with the left [hand], [one offers] the left."

O maiden, I take your hand while abiding in the impulse and authorization of the god Savitṛ, the inner self, desiring to perform Vedic rites; or rather, while abiding in the impulse and authorization of the Sun, Savitṛ, I take [your hand] with my own arms made of leather and with the hands of Pūṣan. || 17 ||
Saying "I take," he mutters four verses: two Triṣṭubhs and two Anuṣṭubhs.

I take your hands for the sake of good offspring, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the householdership. (1) This is the seer’s verse of Sūryā; the deity is indicated by the words of the mantra itself.
I take your two hands—why? For what purpose?

For the sake of good progeny and for the attainment of sons who will secure the world, may you, together with me as your husband and lord, reach old age; that is to say, may you become one whose body is worn out by decrepitude, so that your untimely death may not occur. In the alternative interpretation, *jaradaṣṭiḥ* means one whose decay (*daṣṭi*) is brought about by old age (*jarā*). The four gods, Bhaga and the others, gave you (*tvā*) to me for the sake of the household fire (*gārhapatyārtham*).

O Pūṣan, impel that most auspicious [intention] or body of hers, in which men sow the seed; she who, longing for us, spreads her thighs apart, and in whom we, longing, insert the phallus. O Pūṣan, O Āditya, impel—that is, set in motion—this most auspicious intention or body of this beloved woman. In her, being the locus, men sow—that is, cast—the seed, the semen.

She who, being desirous of us and longing for us, spreads her thighs—that is, she makes them wide and brings them together or extends her own thighs—so that we too, being desirous of her and longing for her, may cast our *śepa* (the generative organ) into her; the meaning is: "May there be mutual pleasure between us. For such is the benefit: "Where there is mutual delight between husband and wife, there the three goals of life (*trivarga*) flourish."

"Soma gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni. And Agni has given me wealth and sons, as well as this [maiden]. (3) This maiden was previously related to Soma. That Soma, having enjoyed her, gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva [gave her] to Agni. May Agni now give her to me.

Not only this [maiden], but may Agni also give me wealth (rayi) and sons. The meaning is: "Having given this maiden to me, may Agni make me prosperous with sons and wealth. He elaborates upon this very same point in the fourth verse.

Soma first obtained you; Gandharva obtained you next. Agni was your third husband; I, born of man, am the fourth. (4) O maiden, Soma first obtained you—he became your first husband. After him, the second, Gandharva, obtained you. Agni was your third husband—he became your husband. I, the fourth, born of man—a human being—am [your husband] now. (18)
Then he causes [the student] to recite the verse beginning with "O Sarasvatī, come here," and the section beginning with "Both of you"; some say both if they constitute separate rituals.

"Gāthās" are those very specific ṛks that are sung; for this reason alone, when there is an expectation as to what they are, he recites the section beginning with "sarasvatī preṇā. The meaning is that they are precisely those which are situated in this section. Furthermore, the word *gāthā* is conventionally applied (*rūḍha*) to certain ṛks characterized by two intervals and a particular accent. As it has been said:

"The Chandogas, the Bahvṛcas, and likewise the Vājasaneyins declare that [a recitation] with high and low pitch is called *gāthika*. This is the collective meaning: immediately after that, the bride recites and causes the excellent teacher to recite the *gāthā* as delimited by the *anuvāka* beginning with "Sarasvatī. However, some others maintain that both the girl and the groom cause the teacher to recite the *gāthā*. Is this always the case? No; he says, "if there is separation" (*yadi pṛthaktvam*). Herein lies the intention: for marriage consists of two distinct rites.

The consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the girl is the wedding (*vivāha*); the consecration of the groom is the marriage (*udvāha*). In that regard, if there is a single agent due to the identity of place, time, and agent, then the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is performed by way of a collective ritual (*tantra*); in such a case, the teacher who recites the sacred texts (*svādhyāyika-guru*) pronounces the verses for the groom alone once. However, even if there is identity of place and time, because the bride and groom themselves are the primary subjects and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) have been hired with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), there is a difference of agents; therefore, there is a distinction in the ritual procedure (*tantra-bheda*). Even in the absence of that [distinction], both [the bride and groom] must be made to recite [the formulas]. Thus it is said.

O Sarasvatī, O beloved, O auspicious one, O possessor of plenty, you whom I sing at the forefront of all that has come into being. (1) The seer here is Brahmā; the metre is Anuṣṭubh. It is said that those songs by which the deeds of the Gandharvas, Apsarases, royal sages, and others are sung during the interval between two ages are called *gāthās*. Here, however, *Sarasvatī* is all speech, and the bride is figuratively addressed as being of that nature. Furthermore, Manomegha and others are the Gandharvas.

A corresponding boon is stated for the purpose of praise: "O Sarasvatī. Here, the prefix *pra* is connected with the verb *ava*. O Sarasvatī, do you protect (*prāva*)—that is, guard (*ava* in the sense of protection)—this rite. O Subhage, you who bring about the welfare of all; O Vājinīvati, you who possess the *vājinyah*, the plants that end with the ripening of their fruit. Sarasvatī, whose form is like the sound of thunder, [acts] by means of rain and so forth. I, who am here, sing to you—that is, I call upon you and praise you. Of what sort are you?

"She who existed at the beginning of this entire created universe, prior to its manifestation—since everything is an evolution of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) and Sarasvatī herself is of the nature of sound—I shall today sing that Speech, she who is the supreme mind among women. (2) "And today, on this very day, I shall sing—that is, I shall utter—that speech which is Sarasvatī, she who is the supreme mind among women."

The mind is manifestation; for speech is of the nature of manifestation, and the heart—the consciousness—is of the form of manifestation. And she who came into being first at the beginning of creation, who became the form of all phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*); and upon whom this entire existing universe, the whole world, is dependent. Those people who were here in the past—those earlier than the earliest—the Gandharva Mūrdhanvat protected them from the gods of old. (3)

Those who were the former people here, those who were the first-born in this world, and even those prior to them—before even them, there was a Gandharva named Mūrdhanvat. To speak more broadly, he is one who shone (ātapat) even before the gods; that is to say, he is of the nature of Brahman. He is called *Gandharva* because he holds (*dhārayati*) and chooses (*vṛṇoti*) *Gāṃ*, which is Sarasvatī. Sarasvatī is this maiden consisting of speech as she is being studied, and the Gandharva is the bridegroom in the form of Prajāpati; such is the intended meaning for the sake of encouragement. || 3 ||
He who comes from all directions, purifying himself from the eastern quarters, he, the head-possessor, [is superior] to them. || 4 ||

He who, being of the nature of wind, moves and comes from all sides as the *adhipavamāna*, purifying with excellence; and because of this, the winds coming from the directions such as the east become distinguished by different designations according to the distinctions of regions like the eastern quarter. Even before those divine winds, the Gandharva Mūrdhanvat alone was shining. ||4||
O Blessed One, you shall not die, for I am your medicine; [I am] Mūrdhanvan among them. || 5 ||

O Blessed One, O Lord Jīva, that wind called *prāṇa* which, having arisen previously, exists together with the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—though subject to death, you shall not die as long as I exist, as long as I remain, remaining as the medicine along with the senses. Even from those deities—the senses characterized by luminosity and other qualities—the Gandharva Rāmūrdhan protected me. May Hiraṇyavarṇa Vairampa make your mind [steadfast].

"When the King, possessing great renown, goes to the assembly like unto the ocean—He, the primordial Gandharva, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati)—O bride, may He make you single-minded toward Me. This is what the groom prays for; the meaning is: "May He make you a devoted wife whose heart is focused on Me alone. Of what nature is He? He is golden-hued, His singular form being a radiant light. He is Vairampa: *vīra* refers to the yogi who is capable of deluding the various forms of delusion; his action (*karman*) is *vaira*, and he protects (*pāti*) that, thus he is *vairampa*.

He who is Saubhrava—so called because he is recognized by yogins through the mastery of the beautiful space between his eyebrows—and who shines as a king, goes across, meaning he ferries across, this ocean-like burden of the suffering of saṃsāra, just as one crosses a battle; "ya eti" (he who goes) is from the ablative *prāgbhyaḥ* (from the eastern directions), where the first case ending is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*). Some read *prāgbhyo viśaḥ* (from the eastern people); in that case, there is a metrical alteration of the syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*) according to Vedic license.

The most ancient Vedic scholars, however, read "prāgvādibhyo 'dhipavamānaḥ" and explain the meaning as follows: "prāgvāt" means that which blows, or is blown, or moves first (prāk); [the compound] means "O Pavamāna, you who flow from all directions, from every side."

In the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) mantras whose traditions of transmission have been interrupted but which persist through hundreds of recitations, since there is no possibility of [recovering] their readings through arbitrary fabrication, their presentation exactly as they are observed by the foremost among the virtuous cannot be censured in any way. "Neither is that which is blown away by the wind (*vātasya*) made to blow, nor is that which is held up by the wind made to fall; neither is the burden of that which carries it borne by the wind, nor is that which is measured by the wind made to be otherwise. (7) The wind does not blow—that is, it does not move—along the front of anything else, nor by any other deity whatsoever.

It is not said that [the wind] is blown by anyone, nor is it held against the wind by anyone who intends to come; rather, its greatness is celebrated as being equal to nothing else—neither in bearing the burden of the wind, nor in supporting the earth and other elements, nor in impelling celestial chariots and the like. The particle *ud* is used here in the sense of "together with. The repeated utterance of the word "wind" is for the sake of emphasis, just as one might say, "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful! and so forth.

However, some read it as *ned vātasyādha dhīyate na*, where *na* means "not," *it* means "thus," *vātasya* means "of the wind," *ā* means "then," and *ha* means "indeed" or "in tradition" (*itihāsa*). The syllable *u* is an augment (*varṇāgama*), and the word *ha* refers to traditional narrative. It is recited by another, approached with assistance. || 7 ||

The chariot of the Sun is truly green, belonging to Saubhra, and richly adorned with gold; Vāta indeed impels it with a firm pole from above. (8) The prefix *ā* is connected with the verb *dhajīyati*. "Truly green" (*satyaharita*) refers to the chariot of the Sun, which is primarily characterized by truth and is green in color; or alternatively, it is called *satyaharita* because it possesses horses that are both primarily truthful and green, the suffix *-ta* being used here in the sense of possession.

He is *saubhravaḥ*, one who cannot even be looked upon by those with piercing eyes because of his restraint of the eyebrows. He is *hiraṇyayaḥ*, golden, consisting of light. The upward-moving wind (*udvāta*) carries him aloft; this is a description of the majesty of Vāyu, who is the form of Prajāpati in his manifestation. By what does the upward-moving wind carry him? By a firm yoke—the wind itself, being uplifted and excellent, acting as the *ḍhā* (the bearer) through its shaking power (*dhūtayā*). 8.
O King, yours alone are the drums, yours the dundubhi and the ānaka;
yours are the winds that blow and waft, and yours is the Caitraratha forest.

Mūrdhanvān is called a Gandharva. O King Mūrdhanvān, it is yours alone that the drums—specific musical instruments for proclaiming victory—or excellent sounds and the like, are intent upon making manifest; likewise, the *ānaka*, a specific type of drum known as a *paṭaha*; the wind moving crosswise; the upward-moving wind (*udvāta*) or the wind falling downward; and likewise, the two horses.

Alternatively, the upward-moving breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind that rises, and the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) is the wind that descends; these two winds, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, are like the two horses of the chariot that is the body for all living beings. The forest called Caitraratha, the celestial garden, belongs to you alone; the meaning is that all splendors have you as their master. || 9 ||

They found the seed of Śakra, hidden away in the cave and turned away; from them arose the Gandharva Mūrdhanvān, who covered [it] before the collarbones. These gods, Vāyu and the others, found—that is, they came to know—the seed, the essence of Śakra, the capable one, the Prajāpati who is the cause of all. It was "turned away," meaning it was imperceptible, deposited in the cave within the hearts of the wise; or else, the cave is the expansion of the world of ignorance (*avidyā-bheda-prapañca*).

Alternatively, those gods were the ones who discovered in secret—that is, indirectly—the bright generative seed of Śakra Indra, characterized as water, which was deposited within the cave, namely the mass of rays. Before those gods, the Gandharva Mūrdhanvat discovered it. Up to what limit did he discover it?

From the clavicles, from those that pierce the clavicles, from the joints that bind the clavicles, and from all the foundational supports—Mūrdhanvān obtained by his will alone the entire power of creation, preservation, and dissolution, beginning from the first emission until the final dissolution, which consists of piercing through and destroying. || 10 ||

"O golden-colored one, well-nourished and radiant, having taken the auspicious hand of the maiden, may you, desiring sons, be more submissive to your fortunate husband than a mountain is firm. (11) This verse is currently recited only in Kaśmīra. The groom, having taken the hand of the bride, prays: "May I become more submissive. The form *bhava* is used in the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa*) by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).

Alternatively, the "inner self" (antarātman) is addressed: having taken the hand of the maiden, [the groom says], "O inner self, become more subdued; for the sake of stability, as firm as a mountain. O bride, you too—who are being led by me—become one who desires a son for the sake of her husband. "Desire for a son" (putrakāmā) means she whose desire (*kāma*) is solely for the purpose of a son, not one whose pleasure (*rati*) is the sole fruit. For what purpose? "For good fortune" (*subhagāya*), that is, for the sake of auspiciousness; for it is when she possesses sons that she becomes praiseworthy in the world, and not merely one whose only fruit is sexual pleasure.

Or rather, "subhagāya" is an epithet of the husband. He qualifies the hand: "hiraṇyavarṇam" means having the luster of gold; "subhṛtam" means well-filled with ornaments such as bracelets, and therefore beautiful; and "puṇyam" means pure, because it has been accepted with the recitation of mantras. || 11 ||

"On the mountain Vairampa, on the Muniparvata peak, which resembles the color of green emerald, we two shall wander as gods, possessing auspicious minds, in that place of delight through mere volition (saṃkalpa), where all desired fruits are obtained. The husband said: "O wife, on the mountain named Vairampa, frequented by sages, resembling green [emerald]—that is to say, golden Meru—where the attainment of all desired and excellent fruits occurs through mere volition, we two, having become immortal gods, shall wander with delighted minds for the full span of a human life."

"O bride, may you be as inseparable from me as the axle-pin (*āṇī*) is from the wooden frame (*veṣṭa*) of a chariot; may you be as inseparable from me as a rain-showering lightning-streak (*vārivarṣaṇī*) is from the forest. May you, O Apsaras, radiant as the sun, be self-controlled and devoted to my mind. (13) The term *āṇī* refers to the wooden pin of a chariot. O bride, just as the axle-pin pervades the chariot and is never separate from it, so may you be pure and inseparable from me. The word *va* is used here for comparison. Likewise, just as the rain-showering lightning-streak in the forest is never seen apart from the cloud or the forest, so may you be [inseparable] from me.

"Vārivarṣaṇī" means she who rains down water, falls [from the clouds], and brings it forth; thus she is lightning (taḍit). They also call her an Apsaras. Likewise, "sūryavarcasinī" means radiant with splendor; "vaśinī" means self-controlled; and "īśānā" means sovereign. "Manmanāḥ" means one whose mind is fixed upon me; the sense is that she should become devoted to her husband (pativratā). || 13 ||

"O you who stand above me in the forest, amidst the rain-showering clouds—may you be one who dwells in wealth (*vasugā*), who possesses the luster of the sun (*sūryavarcasī*), and who is self-controlled (*vaśinī*) through your mind (*manmanā*). Or rather, she who stands above as an Apsaras assuming the form of lightning—that very same one has descended here in another form; and I am the cloud, pouring down water. Therefore, may you fix your heart upon me. This is the same as before; the distinction is that she is "one who dwells in wealth" (*vasugā*). 14.
On the Aśvattha tree is the Śyena, named Ramaṇīyatara.

There Rambhā takes her delight, as Śakra does during the night. (15) The Vaṭa tree is praised; upon it dwells the Śyena, a Gandharva named Ramaṇīyatara, who is worthy of praise. There the Apsaras named Rambhā delights and sports. Śakra is the Āditya; he rests during the *paritakmyā*, that is, the night. (15)

O auspicious Sarasvatī, flowing forth from the mountains, distribute wealth to the streams as a mother distributes [inheritance] to her daughters. (16) He prays to the river Sarasvatī, or to Speech, the intermediate power: "O auspicious Sarasvatī, you who have emerged from the mountains and are flowing forth, distribute—divide—the wealth, that is, the water, among the *kulyās*, i.e., other rivers, just as a mother distributes paternal wealth to her daughters."

In the middle view, the mountains are the bodies and the small streams are the openings of the throats. Now, since the Śruti states, "Speech is indeed the Anuṣṭubh; Sarasvatī is speech," and thus establishes that the Anuṣṭubh has the form of Sarasvatī, he speaks in order to praise it in the form of the Anuṣṭubh meter.

"The gods said that the middle of the *chandas* is where they placed the name *pari*. A reddish-brown horse is its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); he who knows this deserves to come here. (17) The word "of the *chandas*" (*chandasaḥ*) is used in the singular by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*). The gods—the officiating priests—say that among the *chandas*, meaning among the gods and the Asuras, that *anuṣṭubh* meter is the middle, that which stands in the center.

In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is said that "Anuṣṭubh" is a name devoid of meaning, which the gods established as something that "goes beyond" (*parā*) and "follows after" (*anu*) among the meters of the gods and the Asuras; thus, the Anuṣṭubh is situated in the middle between them. These [verses] are employed in the *Ṣoḍaśin* cup-offering, and for that *Ṣoḍaśin* cup, a reddish-brown horse is considered its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

It is conceivable that this [Anuṣṭubh], which resembles a king, exists in the midst of other meters; therefore, he who knows—that is, understands—this Anuṣṭubh meter is worthy of coming here to the place of the hand-grasping (the wedding), such as the officiating priests and the bride’s kinsmen, but not one who does not know it. Furthermore, the intermediate position of the Anuṣṭubh among the meters of the gods and the Asuras is thus described: "The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh..."

The *jagatī*—thus should the seven classes of meters (*chandas*) be known. Therein, by the increase of one syllable at a time, there are seven divine (*daiva*) meters beginning with one syllable and ending with seven syllables: the divine *gāyatrī* has one syllable, the *uṣṇik* has two syllables, the *anuṣṭubh* has three syllables, and so on in this sequence until the divine *jagatī*, which has seven syllables; whereas the demonic (*āsura*) *jagatī* has fifteen syllables. Furthermore, by the decrease of one syllable at a time in reverse order, the other demonic meters come into being.

In that regard, there is the nine-syllabled *gāyatrī*. Thus, starting from one syllable up to seven syllables, the divine meters (*daivāni chandāṃsi*) are established in direct order (*ānulomyena*). Starting from fifteen syllables and proceeding in reverse order (*prātilomyena*) down to nine syllables, the asuric meters (*āsurāṇi*) are established. However, the eighth syllable lies between these two groups; therefore, this eight-syllabled *anuṣṭubh* stands in the middle. Enough of this excessive elaboration. || 17 ||

"O you of the color of reeds, O fair one with a beautiful smile! May the Gandharva Mūrdhanvān unite you with me. (18) Some say that *iṣīka* refers to a stalk of reed (*śarakāṇḍa*) or gold. O you of golden hue, or rather, O you whose form is as fair as a stalk of reed; O you addressed as *lekha*, so called because your eyebrows are like lines of collyrium; O fortunate one, lovely to behold; O you of a beautiful smile, charming in your laughter—may the Gandharva Mūrdhanvān unite you with me, making you devoted and solely dependent upon me. For it has been said that he is the master of maidens. (18)

"Both the gods and the Gandharvas, together with the Sadhyas, call upon you. O Sarasvatī, come toward whichever of them you desire. (19) The speech that purchases Soma is called Sarasvatī. O Sarasvatī, both the gods and the Gandharvas, along with the Sadhyas—meaning those who move together or exist together—we call upon you; we offer various invocations to you. From among these two groups, toward whichever you desire—whether the gods or the Gandharvas—come toward them; go facing them.
I turn toward the gods; we desire those who sing.
Women desire one who sings, but not so much one who speaks of Brahman. 20.

"As Sarasvatī sings, I turn toward the gods themselves; I turn facing them, and not toward the gods who merely recite the Vedas. For we desire only him who sings—'I desire,' there is a grammatical transposition [of the verb]. For indeed, women desire only one who sings, and not a mere expounder of Brahman, a reciter of the Vedas. (20)

"O Sarasvatī, who dwells upon the high mountain as if delighting in her own self—verily, I hear that you are indeed soft as fine linen through your power. (21) Sarasvatī stands upon the high mountain, on the peak, or in the cloud, in the form of lightning or as the intermediate voice, as if delighting, as if playing, in her own self, in her own form. O bride, you are she; of this there is no doubt for us. Of what nature? Soft as fine linen (*kṣauma*), tender like silk, by means of the bestowing of rain or by the expression of meaning.

The particles *ha* and *vai* are used here for the purpose of completing the meter. This being so, the groom says to the bride: "Since you are Sarasvatī, therefore, being aided and protected by you, I hear—that is, I listen to and resolve upon as my duty—all that is enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti while there is strength; the meaning is that this is by the power of having obtained you as my partner in dharma. Some, however, read the word as *śṛṇotu*; even in that case, the meaning is "may this self of mine hear. || 21 ||
Thus concludes the commentary on the Sārasvata Anuvāka.

Then he causes [the student] to recite the *Sarasvatī* mantra, followed by the *Preman* section; according to some, this applies to the entire *Anuvāka*. If it were a separate ritual manual (*pṛthaktantre*), it would have been explained by that much; however, if it is a separate manual, it is also connected with the subsequent sūtra. || 19 ||
Having brought the fire around clockwise and seated it right there, one should establish it.

In the alternative view where they are separate, having performed the circumambulation of the fire and brought the bride and groom back, one should settle them—that is, conclude—the *ṛtu-tithyādi-vidhi* (the ritual concerning the lunar day of the season and so forth) as being connected to the marriage at the very place where the taking of hands occurred; then, as being connected to the wedding, one should perform the entire *udvāha-tantra* (marriage ritual) previously shown, beginning with that which is connected to the wedding and proceeding with what is yet to be described. This is the meaning. || 20 ||
In the ritual procedure for a single act, having approached the fire from the north, the marriage ceremony then takes place. || 21 ||

The word *karman* refers to the performance (*prayoga*). In this context, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) constitutes the extension of the injunction (*vidhyanta*). According to the view that the assistance provided by the procedure is rendered once, one returns to the fire from the north, proceeds toward the northern side for a few steps without performing a circumambulation, and then returns; thereafter follows the marriage ceremony, as well as the performance of the rites concerning the lunar mansion, lunar day, and so forth, which will be described as auxiliary to the marriage. The meaning is that there is a single performance of those rites mentioned as assisting the marriage and those yet to be described, through the principle of simultaneous application (*tatreṇa*).
Regarding that single rite, some also offer this interpretation of the words: "characterized by the taking and giving of a wife. || 21 ||
To clarify these very repetitions, he states in a single sūtra for the sake of clarity:

"Those which are the Udvāha-homas beginning with 'These two, Heaven and Earth,' and those beginning with the Jaya-homas, as well as the Sviṣṭakṛt and the Ājyabhāgas, do not belong to a single ritual procedure. (22)

In the *udvāha* (marriage rite), those oblations beginning with the *jaya*, as well as these [mantras] beginning with "dyāvāpṛthivī," likewise the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and likewise the two *ājyabhāgas*—all these are understood by implication not to be performed repeatedly (*āvṛttyā*) within that single ritual procedure. By this, the two-fold meaning of injunctions and prohibitions regarding the literal sense of the sacred texts is illustrated according to their possibility. The word *sviṣṭakṛt* serves as an indicator for the subsequent section of the *tantra*, while the word *ājyabhāga* indicates the preceding section. 22.

To the west of the fire, upon darbha grass, he causes her to recite: "Thou art she; I am he. She is thou; I am he. Come, let us two unite for the sake of producing a male son, for the increase of wealth, for the possession of good offspring, and for heroic vigor. (23)

In that same single ritual action, having approached the fire from the north and led it back, he places the bride and groom with their feet set upon the darbha grass behind [the fire], and then the preceptor addresses the groom with the words, "Sā tvam asi" (You are she). The meaning is that *sā* was the name of the Ṛc and *ama* was the name of the Sāman; thus *sāma* refers to both *sā* and *ama*, meaning the Ṛc and the Gīti (chanting). Such is the etymological derivation of the word *sāma*.

Distinguishing their forms as the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*, the bridegroom declares: "O bride, you are that *Ṛk*; I am this *Amah*, I am the *Sāman*. You are she; I am he. By repeating "you are she" and "I am he," he confirms their nature as the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*. "Come, let us two marry"—O bride, come here, let us two perform the marriage ceremony. For what purpose?

"For a male son" (*puṃse putrāya*)—the suffix *-taven* is used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*) to denote the action to be performed; there is a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), meaning "to produce a male son. Likewise, "for the nourishment of wealth" (*rāyo dhanasya poṣāya*) means for its increase; "for good progeny" (*suprajāstvāya*) means for the attainment of excellent offspring; and "for great heroism" (*suvīryāya*) means for that purpose, namely for the power and vigor of heroic deeds. || 23 ||

Having led [the bride] clockwise around the fire, he makes her step upon a stone with his right foot, saying: "Come, step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm. May all the gods grant you a life of a hundred autumns. And [he says]: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be steadfast. Crush those who seek to harm us; overcome those who attack us. (24)

Having led the bride and groom around the fire clockwise and having placed a stone on the northern side of the fire, the preceptor, acting as the officiant, causes them to step upon it with their right feet; the bride and groom step upon it, each according to the indicative mark of the mantra: first the groom steps upon the stone, and then the bride.

The teacher, however, desires for the two of them this blessing: "O bridegroom, step upon this stone; be firm like a stone. Furthermore, may all the gods grant you a lifespan of a hundred autumns. O bride, step upon this stone and you too be firm like a stone. Likewise, crush—that is, slay—the *duvasyavaḥ*, those enemies who desire to cause harm (*upatāpa*). Likewise, overcome—that is, subdue and conquer—the *pṛtanyataḥ*, those who desire battle, those seeking to fight. The phrase "with the right foot" is to be supplied as a continuation even for the subsequent mantra. || 24 ||

Having spread a base of clarified butter in his joined palms and touched it with the words, "This is the oblation," his brother or a student of sacred knowledge then pours śamī-grain parched rice into her hands.

He spreads clarified butter in his hollowed palms as an under-layer for the four-fold portioning. Then, with the mantra beginning "This oblation," the bridegroom touches the parched grains mixed with *śamī* leaves that are in the winnowing basket. Immediately thereafter, the bride's brother—or, in the absence of the brother, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*)—pours the parched grains mixed with *śamī* leaves into her joined palms.

May this oblation be productive for me—granting ten heroic sons, with all my kinsmen, for my well-being. Bestowing self, bestowing progeny, bestowing cattle, bestowing fearlessness, bestowing the world. May Agni make my progeny abundant; may you bestow upon us food, milk, and seed. This is the seer’s verse of Kokila Rājaputra. The meter is Anuṣṭubh.

May this oblation called *lāja* be for my procreation—that is, the attainment of ten sons—and likewise be for my well-being (*svasti*) and non-destruction (*avināśa*), endowed with all groups (*sarvagaṇa*), that is, joined with the groups of offspring, cattle, and so forth. [The term] *ātmasani*: from the root *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "giving," one who gives or bestows the self—the body—by virtue of its being one's own, is *ātmasani*. Likewise, [may it be] *prajāsani* (bestowing progeny), *paśusani* (bestowing cattle), *abhayasani* (bestowing fearlessness), and *lokasani* (bestowing worlds). In every instance here, the word "oblation" (*havis*) is the object of the other terms.

"May Agni grant me abundant progeny, such as sons, grandsons, and so forth; and may you bestow upon us food and other necessities, making them stable. Because of the plural number, in the latter half [of the mantra], the Aṣṭamaga, Gandharva, and Tryambaka [deities] are likewise entreated while being worshipped. || 25 ||
Interrupting those [offerings], she offers with the verse, "Aryaman, the god... (RV 5.4.1). || 26 ||
Without breaking them—that is, without making a separation—she offers those parched grains with a single pouring, using the mantra beginning with "Aryaman, the god," and so forth.

The maidens have worshipped the divine Aryaman and Agni. May that divine Aryaman release us from the house of that man; *svāhā*. This is the seer’s prayer (*brahmaṇa ārṣam*). The deities are Aryaman, Gandharva, and Tryambaka. These oblation-mantras are in the *upariṣṭād-bṛhatī* meter. "This woman" is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. The maidens have worshipped—the goddess Agni—they have sacrificed. "Aryaman" is an epithet of Agni; he is called Aryaman because he restrains (*yacchati*) his enemies (*arīn*). "Ayakṣata" is a grammatical substitution for the present tense; they sacrifice (*yajante*).

Others, however, explain that the accusative *agnim* is used in place of the locative [in the phrase] *agnāvaryamaṇaṃ kanyā yajante*; in this view, Aryaman alone is the deity. Having recited this, the bride invokes the fruit of the sacrifice: by the word *amuṣya*, the husband’s name is indicated in a general sense. That Aryaman, being worshipped, "let him not release" (*mā pramuñcātu*) this Devadatta from these houses; here, *mā* is a particle used for prohibition. The meaning is: "Let him not cause us distress from these houses, the husband’s home. *Svāhā*: may there be a well-offered oblation.
He makes [the sacrificer] recite: "Agni, who knows all births... and so forth.

The meaning is that the Guru recites the mantra beginning with "Agnir ityādi. "May Agni, who possesses a wife (*janimān*), make me one who possesses a wife. May I become one whose wife is living (*jīvapatnī*). *Janī* means a wife. Since Agni has a wife, may he therefore make me also one whose connection with a wife is uninterrupted. By his grace, may I too become one whose wife is living; that is, may I be one for whom the wife is living (*jīvapatnī*). (27)
The phrase "this woman" is to be supplied everywhere. || 28 ||
The phrase "this woman" (iyaṃ nārī), which is in the anuṣṭubh meter, must be supplied as an anuṣaṅga (supplementary addition) to all three [verses].
This woman speaks thus as she sows the young grain-seeds:
"May my husband be long-lived; may my kinsmen prosper."

This woman speaks. What does she say? "May my husband be long-lived, and may my kinsmen, friends, and others prosper. What is she doing as she speaks? She is sowing young sprouts; that is to say, she is offering parched grains (lājā) into the fire. || 28 ||
In this manner, it is repeated twice more.
"Twice" means two times. In this manner, the subsequent rite should be performed two times. || 29 ||
To demonstrate this clearly, he says:
"At each circumambulation, having offered an oblation of parched grain, he makes the sacrificer and a stone step upon it with the mantra, 'The Gandharva Pativedana... (GS 1.20.30).

The circumambulation of the fire, the joining of the sacrificer, and therein the bridegroom is the agent by implication; then follows the placing of the stone. Having strewn [grass] around it, there is the pouring of parched grains (*lāja*) and the bride's inquiry after her Gandharva husband.

The maiden has worshipped Agni, the Gandharva who procures a husband. May that divine Gandharva release us from the house of that man [we do not desire], svāhā! The meaning is as follows: because other maidens have worshipped Agni—the Gandharva (so called because he "holds" the earth, *gām pṛthvīm dhārayati*)—who is the "procurer of a husband" (*pativedana*), the woman says, "I too sacrifice to him.
And that divine Agni, having been worshipped, being the Gandharva, shall not release us from the houses of that husband [we do not desire]; this is a negation as before. 30.
He makes [the sacrificer] recite: "May Soma be possessed of kinsmen. || 31 ||
The meaning is that the teacher causes [the disciple] to recite the mantra beginning with "Soma. May Soma, who possesses kinsmen, make me possessed of kinsmen; may I have a living wife.
"Since Soma has kinsmen, may he therefore make me too possessed of kinsmen through this woman; may I become one whose wife is living"—thus it is explained. || 31 ||
"We worship Tryambaka... (thus [he says]). || 32 ||

The third oblation is performed with the verse beginning "tryambakam" and so forth: *Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ patipoṣaṇam | urvārukam iva bandhanād mṛtyor mukṣīya māmuṣya gṛhebhyas svāhā.* We worship Tryambaka, the auspicious one (Śaṅkara), honoring him with the offering of oblations (*haviḥ*). He is "sugandhi," meaning of excellent fame; it is well known that the word *gandha* denotes fame. He is the "patipoṣaṇam," the nourisher of the husband. [May I be released from death, like a cucumber from its stalk, but not from the houses of this man. Svāhā!

And may I be released from the presence of Death through the grace of the worshipful Tryambaka. From what? Like what? "Like a cucumber from its bond"—the *urvāruka* is the fruit of the *karkarī* creeper; just as that, when ripe, is released by itself from its bond, the stalk, or is plucked by seekers, so may I be eternally separated from the presence of Death. The prohibition is: "May I never again be released from the houses of this husband."
He causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "May Pūṣan be rich in cattle for me. ||33||
For this [mantra] also, there is only recitation; no oblation is performed with it.

"May Pūṣan, possessing cattle, lead me to possess cattle; may I become one whose offspring live. The distinction is that [the prayer] is: 'May Pūṣan make me, the owner of cattle, [possess cattle] by means of this [cow]. (33)
The performer offers the remaining portions to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the winnowing basket.

The word *lāja* (parched grain) is observed by the author of the Sūtra to be of both genders. From those [grains] which were offered by the girl, he offers as an oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt those parched grains that remain, because of the statement: "He cuts off the remainder for Sviṣṭakṛt. For the primary oblation was performed by the girl with her joined palms; the mention of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) and the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) are intended to exclude her from this [secondary offering]. The agent is whoever performs the rite of marriage. || 34 ||
Then, as to by whom the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is to be given, he says: "The bridegroom [gives] the sacrificial fee. (35)

The bridegroom alone should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the performer of the marriage rite, because he is the owner of the wealth; it is not the woman who gives it—this is the meaning. [The ritual continues] from the lunar day of the *ṛtu* until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. || 35 ||
Having silently released his hands, he loosens the girdle with the mantra, "I loosen for thee... (vi te muñcāmi). || 36 ||

Just as the grasping of the hand was performed with the Sāvitra mantra, so too the releasing [of the hand] should not occur; therefore, the grasping is done silently. Having released both hands, the performer then unties the binding cord (*yoktra*) with the mantra "I unloose thee," because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, and not by himself.
I loosen the girth, I unloose the reins, I unfasten the yokes and the fastenings. Having bestowed upon us here auspicious wealth, O giver of the oblation, announce me to the deities.

Triṣṭubh; the seers are the Yatīs. Because of the statement, "This indeed is its unyoking," this unyoking of Agni is understood through this [verse] elsewhere. Furthermore, the words *raśanā*, *raśmi*, and *yoktra* are said to be designations for a bond. They are called *yoktrāṇi* because things are yoked by means of them. Of what nature are they? They are *parivartanāni*: those whose movement (*cartana*) is on all sides (*samantāt*), characterized by being restrained.

The sacrificer addresses the released fire: "Being released, may Agni grant us wealth—riches useful for sacrifice—and having granted auspiciousness and well-being, may he speak to me. How does he address him? "O giver of the oblation (*havidā*)," meaning the giver of the sacrificial offering; the sacrificer thus prays, "to me who am appointed to the performance of the sacrifice. Here too, although the request is made by the hired officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), because it is for the sake of the sacrificer, it becomes the blessing (*āśis*) of the sacrificer.

The words *raśanā* (girth) and *raśmi* (rein) are synonyms; the use of synonyms is for the sake of emphasis. Alternatively, "the bonds (*yoktrāṇi*) I release" means not only the bonds themselves but also the girth (*raśanā*), which signifies ignorance (*avidyā*); and "the reins (*raśmīn*)" means the reins rooted in ignorance, such as desire and the rest. Furthermore, by the loosening of the bonds of husband and wife, one who was previously confined to the marriage ground becomes liberated through the freedom of movement, thereby avoiding all constraints. Thus, being liberated, he is impelled as before.

To the north of the fire, upon darbha grass, he causes her to step forward toward the east: "One for food (iṣe), two for strength (ūrje), three for the increase of wealth (rāyaspoṣāya), four for happiness (mayobhavāya), five for offspring (prajābhyaḥ), six for the seasons (ṛtubhyaḥ), and seven for long life (dīrghāyutvāya). Be my companion with these seven steps; O Sarasvatī, be gracious to me, let there be no void when we look upon one another. The phrase "May Viṣṇu follow you" is to be supplied [to each]. 37.

To the north of the fire, upon strewn darbha grass, the performer causes the bride to step forward seven steps facing east with seven mantras. The phrase "May Viṣṇu follow you" (*viṣṇus tvānv etu*) is to be supplied everywhere. "One for strength: may Viṣṇu follow you"—place one step for strength, that is, for food, [placing] you...

And as she goes, let Viṣṇu follow her. "Two steps for strength—let Viṣṇu follow you; place these two steps for strength and power," as before. "Three steps for the increase of wealth—let Viṣṇu follow you"—place three steps for the nourishment (*puṣṭi*) of *rāyaḥ*, that is, of wealth. "Four steps for happiness—let Viṣṇu follow you. *Mayas* is happiness; that which brings about this [happiness] is *mayobhū*. For its sake, place four steps; the meaning is: for the prayer that happiness may come to pass.

"May Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of subjects; place five steps for the sake of sons, grandsons, and progeny. May Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of the six seasons; place six steps for the sake of harmony with the seasons—the meaning is that those seasons, being present before you, may be connected to you through their fruits. For the sake of long life, take the seventh step; be my friend in seven steps. O Sarasvatī, be very gracious; let there be no separation while we gaze upon one another. May Viṣṇu follow you—for the sake of long life—place the seventh step."

And by means of these seven steps, become the source of happiness for your husband. O *sumṛḍīkā*—[the word] *mṛḍ* meaning "to give pleasure," thus one who is very pleasant—O Sarasvatī, may no one, even one situated in the sky (*vyoma*), behold your seventh step; nor may anyone see any part of you naked, with your garment blown away by the wind. (37)
"That eye" [the mantra] causes him to worship the sun. || 38 ||
With the words "That eye," and so forth, the officiant causes the girl to worship the sun.
That eye, beneficial to the gods, rises pure in the east;
may we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns.
Beneficial to the gods, ordained by the gods, or beneficial—that is, bringing about welfare—for the gods; bright—that is, white; rising—that is, moving upward, going up—as it ascends. 38.
When the sun has set, [he offers] the fire-oblation. ||39||
If it becomes night while the wedding is being performed, or if the wedding takes place at night, then he should worship the fire with this verse: "That eye... (RV 10.85.20). || 39 ||
He shows Jīvantī, Dhruva, Svastyātreya, and Arundhatī. || 40 ||

"One desiring a living daughter should show her the Pole Star (Dhruva) and so forth. Regarding this, some carry forward the word 'at night' (*rātrau*) from the previous context, on the grounds that the Pole Star and other such stars are not visible by day; others do not carry it forward, because in the subsequent question, 'Do you see [it]? (*paśyasi*), the sense is observed to be that she gives the reply 'I see it' (*paśyāmi*) even though she does not actually see it. For the command 'see' (*paśyeḥ*) is intended merely as a formal act of seeing, and in the response 'I see or not? (*paśyāmi na vā*), the answer given is 'I see' (*paśyema*). || 40 ||
He says: "Do you see each one of these? (41)
The Guru should ask, addressing each one by name, "Do you see?"
"I see," he replies. || 42 ||
When she too is asked, she should reply, "I see it."
"Behold this bride, who is auspicious; having bestowed good fortune upon her, go back to your homes. With these words, he addresses those who have been looking at her. (43)

The preceptor consecrates the objects observed, beginning with the Pole Star (Dhruva), with the Anuṣṭubh verse beginning "Sumaṅgalīr" (May she be auspicious). May this bride be endowed with beautiful auspiciousness through your grace; having come together and assembled, behold her! And having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart thereafter. [Note on grammar: The form "dattvāya" contains the suffix *yak* after the gerund (*ktvā*), which indicates that this rite may be understood as applicable even during the day. For they say that the observation of the Pole Star and other such stars is a sign of longevity.

In this context, it is traditionally taught that even if one does not see anything at this juncture, the response "I see" should be given to ward off untimely death. Therefore, whatever object such as Dhruva one might show, the meaning is that one should show only something auspicious and indestructible. || 43 ||
With the verse "uduttamam," he addresses the woman as she goes toward a dwelling in the northeast, or wherever it may be.

With the four *anuṣṭubh* verses beginning with "uduttamam," he consecrates the house (*āvasatha*) as she goes toward it, facing the northeast—that is, directed toward the north and east—or he should go toward whichever dwelling place it may be.

Ascending the highest [place], as if casting away those who would attack, ascend the head of your husband, O radiant lady of the Aṅga lineage, and shine forth with progeny. (1) O bride, ascending the highest—that is, the most excellent house or virtuous conduct—and as if casting away, that is, driving off, the attackers—those enemies who desire an army—ascend the head of your husband; the meaning is that you should become worthy of honor by his master through the multitude of your own virtues. Likewise, be especially resplendent with progeny, such as sons, grandsons, and so forth.

O Indra, O Bountiful One, make this woman possessed of good sons and endowed with good fortune. Bestow ten sons upon her and make her husband the eleventh. (2) O Indra, "mīḍhvaḥ"—the term *mīḍhvan* is derived from the root *miha*, meaning "to sprinkle"; this address is used because the retention of the seed, known as conception, depends entirely upon the grace of Indra. Make this bride possessed of good sons and endowed with good fortune. Bestow ten sons upon her; ordain them, and provide her with a husband as the eleventh. (2)

Be a sovereign queen over your father-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your mother-in-law. Be a sovereign queen over your sister-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your brothers-in-law. (3) O daughter-in-law, be a sovereign queen—most highly honored and shining with perfect splendor—over your father-in-law; likewise over your mother-in-law, over your sister-in-law, and over your brothers-in-law. Over the daughters-in-law, the fathers-in-law, the offspring, the wealth, the husbands, the brothers-in-law, and the kinsmen, be a radiant light. (4) *Kinsmen* (*sajātāḥ*) refers to relatives, attendants, and so forth.

Regarding the word *devṛṇām*, there is a short vowel according to the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), yet in the Middle Country it is recited with a long vowel as *devarāṇām*. The meaning is: "May everything pertaining to the house be under your control. From this point onward, the section beginning with "Then you, O Agni... continues until the conclusion of the ritual manual (*tantra*). Here, at the occasion of going to the husband's house, the *madhuparka* section is recited; that will be explained in the section on the student who has completed his studies (*snātaka*). || 44 ||
Thus ends the section on marriage in the *Samaṃtrakāṣṭhagṛhabhāṣya*, composed by Devapāla, son of Haripāla, grandson of Bhaṭṭopendra, a resident of Jālandhara and Jayapura.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section (kāṇḍikā). || 25 ||
Now begins the twenty-sixth section. On an auspicious day, he yokes [the horse]. He yokes it with the mantra: "At every union... (RV 1.34.6).

When the bride goes to her husband’s house on an auspicious day, he then yokes a chariot or a palanquin as available. And during that yoking, he yokes the horses and so forth by repeating the mantra explained as "yoke, yoke" (yoga-yoga). || 1 ||

"Those that are curved like hooks on both sides of the chariot, those dark ones that fly toward the front of the wind, those with far-reaching flight, winged and full of vigor—may those fires, being full, carry us across," with these words he consecrates the two wheels.

With the *jagatī* verse beginning "aṅkunyaṅkau," the officiant (*ṛtvij*) consecrates the two chariot wheels during the *agnimāruta* ritual, or [consecrates] the two sides [of the chariot]. The mantra should be recited only once, because of the dual number in its grammatical gender. "Aṅku" means that which bends (*aṅcati*), and "nyaṅku" means that which bends downwards (*nyañcati*). "Aṅkunyaṅkau" refers to the two types of movers (*gantṛ-viśeṣau*) by which the two wheels move—the "bending" and the "downward-bending. May those two "bending and downward-bending" ones, situated on both sides of the chariot, our fires (*agnayaḥ*), carry us across the paths, ferry us over them, or protect us upon the way.

What kinds of fires? Those that are dark and of the nature of gloom, produced from fuel such as wood; those that rush toward the tip of the wind, meaning those of the form of lightning and so forth; and that which has a distant range, meaning that whose radiance extends afar, such as the sun and so forth; and that which possesses birds and possesses horses—meaning "possessing birds" being established in forms such as the wind-god and Garuḍa, and "possessing horses" being dependent on forms such as rice and other grains. Of what sort are these fires?

*Paprayaḥ*: from the root *prī* (in the sense of protecting and filling), they are *paprayaḥ*, meaning protectors or fulfillers of desires; or the word *patri* is derived from the root *prā* (in the sense of filling). || 2 ||

"In the hole for the chariot, in the hole for the pole, in the holes for the yoke-tethers, in the hole for the axle—in these holes of the yoke-tethers, I place the branch of the *śamī* tree," with these words he places the *śamī* branch into the holes for the yoke-tethers.

With the verse beginning "In the hole of the chariot" (*khe rathasya*), he places a branch of the *śamī* tree into the holes of the yoke. He places the branch in the hole of the chariot—that is, in the opening in the sky; likewise in the hole of the cart, that is, of the ox-yoke; similarly in the holes of the yoke; and likewise in the hole of the axle—the specific wooden beam supporting the chariot—and elsewhere as well, in every hole, he places the *śamī* branch for the sake of pacification. || 3 ||

"Ascend the *sukiṃśuka*, the *śalmali*, the one of all forms, golden-hued, well-rolling, with beautiful wheels; O Sūryā, ascend the womb of immortality; make the bridal procession pleasant for your husband"—with these words, she is made to mount [the chariot]. || 4 ||

With the verse beginning "sukiṃśukam," he causes the bride to ascend the chariot: "O bride, ascend the chariot. Of what sort is it? It is *sukiṃśukam*, beautiful with *kiṃśuka* flowers, *śopa* leaves, and other blossoms placed there by the attendants; it is a *śalmali* tree—so called because its nature is to move (*śala hula pallū gatau*), or perhaps because it is constructed from *kiṃśuka* and *śalmali* wood; it is *viśvarūpam*, having various forms; *hiraṇyavarṇam*, of a brilliant appearance; and *suvṛtam*, surrounded by fruits, flowers, and so forth, or perfectly circular.

Easy to turn and easy to maneuver; likewise, with beautiful wheels, you are the source of immortality—the cause of the state of deathlessness and the bringer of non-violence. For the husband, for the supporter, by way of grammatical inversion, provide—make—comfort and happiness for the supporter; [provide] that vehicle which carries him. || 4 ||
"May no waylayers find her," and "She is most auspicious"—thus she is led forth. || 5 ||
With these two verses, "May no waylayers find us" and "The most auspicious," whose meanings have already been explained, he causes the chariot to proceed.

"May Savitṛ make that which is bound around her—multiformed and pleasant for her husbands—manifest through the Veda, with houses, with a non-terrible and friendly eye," [he says] at the union of the bridegroom and bride. 6.

At the union of the bride, one recites this *jagatī* verse beginning with "Make manifest" (*saṃkāśaya*). The two horses are addressed: "With this clearly manifest vision, carry this man forward; together with sacred food (*brahmaṇā*) and with the household (*gṛhaiḥ*)—by the word 'household,' the householder husband is meant—with the non-terrible, auspicious eye, that is, the friendly eye related to Mitra, and not the hostile one. How do you carry him? Fully covered on all sides."

Likewise, whatever manifold form there is here that is pleasant (*syona*) for the husbands of this bride—note the grammatical shift from *patibhyaḥ* (dative plural) to *patye* (dative singular)—let Savitṛ make all that, including happiness and so forth, for the husband. This recitation is performed when there is apprehension of damage or collision between the two chariots.
One recites "ye pathīnām" at crossroads, and also "ime catvāraḥ."
The two mantras have been explained. "ye pathīnām" is an anuṣṭubh; "ime catvāraḥ" is a triṣṭubh. The sūtra is of clear meaning. ||7||
"In the cremation grounds" means in the cremation grounds. || 8 ||
The word "recites" (japati) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis.
May those merit-born spirits who lie among the corpses in the cremation grounds find delight right there; let them not look upon the bride.

Those meritorious beings, the yakṣas, and those who are corpses or hungry ghosts (pretas) who lie upon the beds of the dead in cremation grounds—let them lie and remain in those very cremation grounds; let them take delight there, let them find pleasure there; let them not look after the bride, let them not see the bride. [The word] "bride" (*vadhū*) is used here with a change of case-ending. 8.
"Those who in the forests..."—having seen a great forest and a great tree, one recites this. || 9 ||
This is clear; the mantra has also been explained. || 9 ||
In this context, "raḍi" refers to seeing something cruel. || 10 ||
In this context, the ellipsis is that one recites [the mantra] upon seeing a cruel animal such as a lion, etc., while it is roaring, and so forth.
Here is delight, here is pleasure, here is steadfastness, here is support, here is self-sustenance, here is enjoyment; may they rejoice here at the forefront! Veṭ svāhā! Vaṭ!

"Laḍa vilāse": *laḍana* means play, sport; may it delight us here. Likewise, *ratiḥ* means affection; "may it delight everywhere"—this is supplied to each case. Here, *dhṛtiḥ* means contentment. Here, *vidhṛtiḥ* means sustaining or stability. *Svadhṛtiḥ* means the holding of one's own wealth. Here, *rantiḥ* means sporting; *rantiḥ* [is used] because play (*raḍi*) and so forth—seeing them as harmful—should not be driven away from our presence. Following this, *veṭ svāhā vaṭ* are particles used for the purpose of making an offering (*saṃpradāna*). 10.
"Salutation be to the serpents," [with this he worships] the serpents. ||11||
"Having seen [it], he mutters"—this is the syntactical connection.

Homage be to the serpents, whichever ones are upon the earth; to those in the intermediate space and those in heaven—to those serpents, homage! To those among whom are the sorcerers, or those who dwell in the trees, or those who lie in holes—to those serpents, homage! To those who are there in the luminous realm of heaven, or those who are in the rays of the sun, or those who have made their abodes in the waters—to those serpents, homage!
The meaning has been explained. || 11 ||
Those who [go] to the sacred fords (tīrtha) at the sacred ford, they are called "Mandamānā. || 12 ||

The meaning is that one recites mantras sealed by the *pratīka* at a *tīrtha*. Those which are called "the *tīrthas*" have already been explained. Here, *tīrtha* refers to a watering place, a point of descent into a river. As it has been said:
"Those of perfected intellect desire three things to be designated as *tīrtha*: the sacred scripture, a watering place, and water frequented by seers."

Taking pleasure in the dwelling of man, bestow wealth along with heroic sons upon the eloquent singer. O Lords of Splendor, create a ford with good drinking water; strike down the obstacle standing in the path and destroy evil intent.

Āśvinī; Jagatī meter.
