O Aśvins, being praised (*mandamānau*)—that is, being lauded and filled with joy (as the root *mad* is indicated by meanings such as praise, delight, and exhilaration)—you two have bestowed (*adhattam*; the short vowel is a Vedic [chāndasa] usage) wealth (*rayim*) in the dwelling (*duroṇe*) or house of the human (*manuṣaḥ*). Of what kind is that wealth? It is "possessing heroes" (*sahavīram*), meaning accompanied by sons, or possessing a thousandfold vigor, that is to say, endowed with a succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth.

Furthermore, you two have made a ford (*tīrtha*) and a good drinking place (*suprapāṇa*) that is easy to plunge into; likewise, a pillar (*sthāṇu*), so called because prosperity (*sampad*) stands upon it. For whom? For *vacyasva*, one who desires speech for himself—[derived from] *vacas* with the suffix *kyac* according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ*.

By the rule *kyac-kyāc chandasi*, there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel; thus, [the word] is *vacasyave*. O Lords of Splendor (*śubhaspatī*), you who protect splendor, destroy—meaning, utterly annihilate—the evil thought (*durmatim*) of this man. What kind of evil thought? "Standing on the path" (*patheṣṭhā*); that which stands upon the path, meaning one that is firmly rooted. May this Lord of the Forest (*vanaspati*) lead us safely to the further shore of the great earth. May the furrow (*sīrā*) be easy for us to cross, for the sake of long life and luster.

This is the mantra for crossing a river at a specific sacred ford (*tīrtha*). [The verse is] the Gāyatrī: "This tree-born chariot of the forest-king (*vanaspati*) shall lead us to the further shore of the great river. Having brought about well-being (*svasti*), may the river Sīrā be easy for us to cross. For long life and for splendor, may the Sīrā be ours. In the phrase *dīrghāyutvāya*, the elision of the *s* in *apatyoḥ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

The river flows stony; take hold of one another, arise, let us cross over, O friends! Here we leave behind those who were unfriendly; may we cross over toward auspicious strengths. By this [verse], the river at hand is crossed. "O friends, kinsmen, arise, take hold of one another—be diligent—and let us cross the river. He states the reason for the exhortation to exert special effort: because the river flows with a multitude of stones.

It is crossed. *Śeva* is a name for happiness. And those things which are *aśeva*, meaning unhappy or unpleasant, which exist—those we leave right here in this place; *tyāmaḥ* means we abandon them, the sense being that we go having abandoned them. And may we cross over, having crossed, and reach the auspicious regions (*śivān deśaviśeṣān*), which are directed toward strength (*abhivājān*) and endowed with specific kinds of food (*annaviśeṣayuktān*); such is the aspiration. || 12 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section (kāṇḍikā). 26.
Now begins the twenty-seventh section:
he crosses a river with the verse, "śannaḥ" (May it be auspicious for us).
The meaning, along with the commentary, has been explained. || 1 ||
Regarding the phrase "ya ṛta" when a part of the chariot is shattered:

since no specific part is mentioned, the meaning is that one should mutter the *bṛhatī* verse beginning with "ya ṛta," which is dedicated to Indra, whenever any part of the chariot has become shattered or loose.

Even without a binding, before the breaking of the joints, Maghavā—the possessor of many riches—shall be the restorer; he shall join the joint and repair what was shattered. O chariot, you who were previously destroyed without a binding—that is, without knots, ties, or fastenings—and were lost even before being pierced or harmed, him (you), Maghavā shall restore again; "sandhi" means that which is joined together, and he will make it whole once more.

O friend, he is a reconciler, one whose nature is to bring about reconciliation. Of what kind will he make you who are being reconciled? One fit for a straight and non-crooked gait. Of what kind is Maghavan? One possessing abundant wealth (*purūvasu*). The particle *cit* is a filler used to complete the meter.
In the afternoon, when the sun is over the trees, having approached his house while reciting "Bearing strength," he mutters [the formula] upon beholding his house.

In the afternoon, when the sun is above the trees—meaning when the rays of the sun are seen only over the tops of the trees and not below—it is time to go toward the house. By the mention of "the house," one's own village is indicated; having gone near his own village and seeing his own house there facing him, he mutters the mantra beginning with "ūrjaṃ bibhrati. This recitation belongs to the bride, as is evident from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.

Bearing strength, a winner of wealth, wise, I have come to the house, rejoicing and full of luster. With a non-terrible, friendly eye, looking upon the house, may I prolong my life. May we prolong the life of the house; may the house extend our life. I enter the house with a well-disposed mind, a master of heroes among heroes, most auspicious. Carrying nourishment, sprinkling clarified butter, in them I lie down with a well-disposed mind—those in the midst of which one who dwells abroad returns with great goodwill.

We invoke the houses; may they recognize us who recognize them—those houses that are full of men, possessed of *svadhā*, rich in food, and providing delight. Free from hunger and free from disease, O houses, do not fear us! Cows are invited here; goats and sheep are invited. Furthermore, the sweet essence of food is invited into my houses. Friends with abundant wealth and pleasant gatherings are invited. May all our men be unharmed, and may our houses be secure at all times.

I have come to the houses, bringing strength, holding food, and nourishing; a bestower of wealth (*vasuvani*), distributing riches (*vasūni*); possessed of excellent wisdom (*sumedhāḥ*), rejoicing and gladdened; endowed with beautiful luster (*suvarcāḥ*)—here the genitive case is used by transposition in the sense of the accusative "of the houses"—beholding the houses with a gaze that is non-terrible, gentle, friendly, and well-wishing.

*Vayaḥ* is a name for wealth; I extend—that is, I bestow—wealth upon my dependents. We extend their life (*āyuḥ*) by means of plastering and other such services, thereby securing their stability. May the houses as well—the deities presiding over the houses—extend our life, that is, may they bring it about. I approach, go to, and enter these houses. Of what nature are they? *Sumanasaḥ*: causing mental well-being. *Vīraghnī*: here the root *han* has the sense of "going"; she is the one who brings about or causes the attainment of sons.

She whose husband is a hero is one whose lord is endowed with valor. She is *suśevā*—*śeva* meaning food and wealth; thus, she is one who possesses excellent wealth. What kind of houses? Those that carry—that is, maintain—*irā*, which is food. Likewise, those houses which sprinkle (*ukṣamāṇā*) clarified butter (*ghṛta*), being possessed of many cows and other riches; such houses I enter, being well-disposed in mind. Furthermore, those houses in the midst of which one dwelling attains—that is, reaches—abundant goodwill (*saumanasa*); those houses we invoke, we call upon. May they recognize us as people endowed with knowledge (*jñāna*).

And by the grace of the presiding deity of the house, may we be possessed of *sūnṛtā*—that is, speakers of truthful words—and likewise be *svadhāvantaḥ*, performing the ancestral sacrifices (*pitṛyajña*); may we be *irāvantaḥ*, that is, possessed of food; the particle *ha* is meaningless here; and may we be *sāmadāḥ*, meaning we may be those who win others over through the first of the [four] means, characterized by conciliation (*sāntvana*). As it has been said: "Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force constitute the fourfold [means]; with the addition of illusion, sorcery, and indifference, seven means are proclaimed."

The dative case in *asmabhyam* is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*); thus, the meaning also results that "you should become endowed with truthful speech for our sake. Alternatively, the dative may be applied in the sense of giving (*pradāne*), as in "be gracious to us. O houses, being occupied by us, do not fear us; do not harbor any dread toward us.

And here in these houses, cows, as well as goats and sheep, have been brought and summoned; likewise, the sweet-tasting *kīlāla*, which is related to food, has been summoned into my homes. So too, friends and companions, possessing abundant wealth and great riches—may they, having acted rightly, remain forever filled with perfect joy. Likewise, may our houses and all our people always be free from harm and unassailed. || 3 ||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section (kāṇḍikā). || 27 ||
Now begins the twenty-eighth section (kāṇḍikā).
He spreads a layer of *ulapa* grass from [the foot of] the bed. 1.

*Ulapa* is *vīraṇa*; however, the statement that *prasūnā* refers to long *darbha* grasses is devoid of common usage, because in the Middle Country and other regions, it is only *vīraṇa* grasses that are known as such. The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) spreads—that is, arranges—the row of *vīraṇa* grass from the place where the bridegroom descends from his chariot up to the specific bridal chamber. || 1 ||
He enters by means of that [path]. || 2 ||
Accompanied by that queen, the bridegroom, having descended from his chariot, enters the house together with the bride. || 2 ||
He enters the dwelling where the sacred fire has been established, together with water and medicinal herbs.

He enters—that is, he goes into—the specific dwelling (āvasatha), which is one where the nuptial fire has been established and placed, which is provided with water (sodaka) meaning adorned with a water-pot, and which is furnished with medicinal herbs (sauṣadha) meaning equipped with grains such as rice and other plants; for from this point onward, he is authorized to perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices. And this entry is intended to take place immediately after the *vāstuhoma*. For the Sūtra states: "Having performed the sacrifice of the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Vāstoṣpati with the four verses beginning with 'amīvahā vāstoṣpate', he may then enter the dwelling."
O Vāstoṣpati, dispeller of disease!

The first [verse] is a *gāyatrī*; the [following] three are *triṣṭubhs*. The seer (*ārṣa*) is Brahmā. O Vāstoṣpati—O specific deity of the intermediate region in the form of Vāyu—be free from disease (*anamīva*) for us; that is, be devoid of sickness (*ama* means "disease"), meaning: make us free from illness. You are a destroyer of disease (*amīvahā*), one who brings about the destruction of ailments; and being free from disease (*anamīva*), you are the cause of the stability of the prior non-existence of illness—thus there is no tautology. Furthermore, be very gracious (*suśeva*), meaning easy to dwell with. What while doing so?
Entering all forms while assuming various shapes; or, entering and causing various forms such as horses and so forth to enter [the house], meaning he makes the house prosperous. || 1 ||

O Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge us who are about to enter; look upon us with favor and in a propitious manner. Then, be easy of access, well-received, and free from disease for us. Whatever we entreat or ask of you, accept that with pleasure—meaning, gladden us with what we have requested. Therefore, be a source of well-being (*śambhava*), a form of happiness, for our two-footed humans and our four-footed cattle and the like. 2.

O Vāstoṣpati, be our deliverer; that is to say, deliver us from difficult places. O Indu—because of the commonality of being situated in the middle, O Moon—be swelling (*sphānaḥ*) and prosperous for us in our *gaya*, that is, in our home, with cattle and horses. Through that, remaining in your friendship, may we be ageless (*ajarāsaḥ*), meaning undecaying. And you, favor us and gladden us. Like whom? Like a father his sons. 3.

O Vāstoṣpati, may we be united with your assembly—your assembly characterized by speed and other excellences—which is *śagma*, of the nature of happiness; which is *hiraṇyayā*, consisting of gold and the like; and *gātumatī*, possessing sacrificial acts such as the *yajña* (meaning it is useful for sacrifices and so forth). Having made [this assembly] excellent (*vara*), protect (*pāhi*) us while we abide in *yoga*, which consists in the acquisition of what has not been gained, and in *kṣema*, which consists in the preservation of what has been acquired.

May you [all]—that is, you—protect us at all times with blessings (*svastibhiḥ*) that are indestructible; here there is a grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*) for the singular "you" to take the plural "you [all]. || 4 ||

On the day of Rohiṇī, or Mūla, or on another auspicious day as prescribed, having seated the bride on the hide of a red bull—or even on darbha grass—he offers oblations with the *jaya* formulas and the verse, "May Agni come first."

It should be understood that this occurs when the moon is conjoined with the lunar mansion Rohiṇī or Mūla; or else, it may be on whatever day is declared auspicious in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), being of a meritorious nature and conducive to welfare.

To the west [of the fire], because it is the subject under discussion, [he places] the *āvasathya* fire; there, having seated the bride upon a red bull-hide belonging to a bull (*ānaḍuha*), or having seated her upon mere *darbha* grass, and having himself sat down, the groom—since the clarified butter (*ājya*) is the means of accomplishment—should perform the rites beginning with the *jaya-homa* and ending with the *ājyabhāga*, which by implication include the properties of the clarified butter (*ājyadharma*), preceded by the kindling of the fire (*upasamādhāna*) and so forth, and he should perform the other rituals with the verses beginning "Agni shall come first" (*agniraitu prathamaḥ*). What are those? They are the *pākayajñas*.

May Agni, the first among the deities, come; may he lead her offspring to a full lifespan. May King Varuṇa grant his approval for this, so that this woman may ward off the calamity of losing her grandson. 1.

"May Agni come"—these four *triṣṭubh* verses are addressed to the Viśvedevas. As the gods are arriving, Agni, the first among all the deities, "shall come" (*etu*)—that is, he shall arrive. That Agni, who stands at the forefront of all the gods, shall lead (*nayatu*) the offspring of this bride; that is, he shall cause her offspring to reach [its full measure], and he shall lead that offspring to a full lifespan. This is a verb with two objects, like the expression "he leads the goat to the village."

And may King Varuṇa grant his consent when this life-span is being reached by the fire, saying, "Let there be permission for that; so be it. The mention of the "King" is with the intention that, since he has given his consent, all the gods will likewise consent because they are his followers. And just as this woman, the bride, might ward off this misfortune—the sin—of her son's son (her grandson), so that she does not experience grief for her son, even so may King Varuṇa grant his consent in that manner. || 1 ||

May Agni Gārhapatya protect this woman; may he release her offspring from the noose of death. May she be a mother whose womb is never empty and who lives long; may she fully experience the joy of her grandchildren. Svāhā! || 2 ||

May Agni Āvasathya protect and guard this bride. May this bride have a non-empty lap; that is to say, her lap—her embrace—should be non-empty and not void by means of children and sons born of her in due course. Likewise, may she be the mother of long-lived sons. And may she specifically and fully experience the joy and happiness of these sons and their offspring. (2)

May no terrible thing arise for you in your house at night; let those who weep elsewhere than with you lie down. Having sons living, shine forth in the world of your husband, beholding your offspring healthy and well-disposed. Svāhā! 3.

O bride, may that terrible sound of weeping and the like not arise in your house by night or by day—meaning, O wicked one, may such a sound never occur. Let those who weep, performing their lamentation, settle elsewhere than in your presence; that is to say, let them stay in a place far removed from you.

You, possessing a living son and being long-lived with many children, should shine forth especially in the world of your husband—that is, in his family—and remain joyful, beholding your offspring, such as sons and others, in a state of happiness. || 3 ||

May your suckling child not perish; may you, with disheveled hair, not strike yourself upon the breast. May Savitṛ protect your suckling from being wrapped in [another's] garment; may Bṛhaspati and the Viśvedevas protect it constantly. Svāhā! 4.

May your young infant son, who is still nursing at the breast, not perish; may he not die. And may you, though with disheveled hair and shorn head, not beat your breast—meaning, let there be no striking of your chest caused by separation from your husband. May Savitṛ protect your breast-nourished child, and may Bṛhaspati protect him until the putting on of the garment—that is, until the time of dressing; and may the Viśvedevas protect him constantly. || 4 ||

With these four ṛg-verses, four oblations are to be offered by the bridegroom himself; likewise, the subsequent ones as well. With the yajus-formulas beginning with "agne prāyaścitta," ten other oblations of clarified butter are to be offered in order and out of order.
O Prāyaścitti, you are the expiation of the gods; destroy that body of hers which is most afflicted, svāhā!

Atonement (*prāyaścitta*) is said to be that which wards off evil, generates merit (*dharma*), and brings about well-being. Because it is the cause of that, Agni is called *Prāyaścitti*. O Prāyaścitti, you are the means for the gods to atone for faults, in the removal of defects and the production of auspiciousness; therefore, destroy whatever impure body this bride possesses—whether through her own nature, the influence of her seed, or by the power of wicked deeds committed in childhood—and destroy the inauspiciousness residing within her. For while the defects of the groom arising from the womb and the seed have been destroyed by the *jātakarman* and other rites, those [rites] have generally not been performed for the bride.

"By means of domestic *homa* offerings, the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the tonsure (*cauḍa*), and the tying of the *mauñjī* grass girdle, the taint (*enaḥ*) arising from seed and womb is removed for the twice-born"—so says the *Smṛti*. Here, *enaḥ* refers to sin, impurity, or lack of purification.
O Vāyu, atonement! O Sūrya, atonement! O Candra, atonement! 4. O Viṣṇu, atonement! O Viṣṇu, atonement! O Candra, atonement! O Sūrya, atonement! O Vāyu, atonement! O Agni, atonement!

These five subsequent *yajus* formulas, along with their appendages, are recited in reverse order. Thus, four oblations are completed by means of the four *ṛc*s, and ten by means of the ten *yajus* formulas, making fourteen oblations in total; the fifteenth is performed with the formula "tryāyuṣam"—this is the view of Ādityadarśana. He considers that very oblation which is the pouring of the clarified butter (ājya) remaining from the portion used for this *yajus* formula, as described below, to be the [fifteenth] oblation, or alternatively, he considers it to be a repetition of the mantra itself. || 4 ||

Having poured curd into a portion of the clarified butter while reciting, "The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, that which is the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine," and having consumed the curd three times with the mantra "O Dadhikrāvan... (RV 4.39.6), he places fruits into the lap of the student while reciting, "May food come to me" (RV 10.128.1). || 5 ||

Since these [rites] are to be performed by himself, having offered the previously mentioned oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, he should pour a portion of the clarified butter—taken separately from the vessel—into another vessel, mix curds into that portion of clarified butter, and have the bride eat the curds while reciting the verse beginning with "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam. Then, the groom should give fruits to the young man who has been placed on the bride's lap.

He bestows it with the mantra, "O Agni, [grant] refreshing water. Because it is accomplished by three means—jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs—it is called *tryāyuṣa*. Because it is characterized by the three stages of childhood, youth, and old age; or because it is accomplished through sacrifice, gift-giving, and burnt offerings (*homa*), or because it initiates those [rites], it is called *tryāyuṣa*. The bridegroom invokes this blessing: "May that which is the *tryāyuṣa* of Jamadagni, that which is the *tryāyuṣa* of Kaśyapa, and that which belongs to the gods—all that be mine."
I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the swift horse; may he make our mouths fragrant and prolong our lives.

The meter is Anuṣṭubh; the seer is Indra. Regarding the word *dadhikrāvṇaḥ*: it is derived from *dadhikrām* (the one who takes up the curd), according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*. Here, Agni Vaiśvānara is being spoken of, for he, abiding in the stomach, digests everything consumed, such as curds and other foods. I have performed (*akāriṣam*), that is, I perform, the act of satiating this *dadhikrāvāṇ*, the digestive fire. Of what kind? Of the victorious (*jiṣṇoḥ*), of the nature of conquering; of the horse (*aśvasya*), meaning the eater or the pervasive one; of the vigorous (*vājinaḥ*), the lord of food.

May the fragrant, sweet-smelling [mouth], adorned by the rising of knowledge—that is to say, our mouth—make the curd its object of consumption; this is the sense. The *leṭ* suffix is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*). May it prolong our lives; may it extend them, may it bestow them upon us. As before, this is the fifth tense (*lakāra*). This verse is explained as being identical to the one beginning with "irāvatī. 5.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth kaṇḍikā. || 28 ||
Now begins the twenty-ninth section (kāṇḍikā).

Having silently prepared the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) and having sacrificed to Agni and Prajāpati from it, they both consume the remainder. Food indeed is the means of separation; food is remembered as the means of union. Food is the life-breath of animals; food is remembered as the supreme physician. With a jewel made of food, with the cord of life, the speckled one—with a knot of truth—I bind together your heart and your mind. May your speech and mind be in harmony; may your thought and your vow be in harmony.

"Like the wheel follows the hoofprint of the ox, let your mind follow me alone. Look upon me and the sun, and do not set your heart on others. May this charm of the cakravāka birds be effective for both me and her. (1)

Where the procedure is performed in silence, such as the pouring out [of the oblation] and so forth, one should cook that *caru* with water because its own essence is already established; having offered a portion of it to Agni and Prajāpati, the bride and groom eat the remains of the oblation together from a single vessel. For in other *Gṛhya* texts, this is designated as "eating together" (*samaśana*), and "eating together" is well known to mean eating jointly. Furthermore, there is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "the winning over" (*saṃvanana*). Others, however, do not desire eating together from a single vessel even in this case.

For just as in the case where "the five, including the sacrificer, eat the *irā*" or "they eat together with their wives," even though the number five is heard, the eating of the *ilā* and the *gṛhamedhīya* offerings is distinct; so too must it be here. Furthermore, the mention of "performed silently" (*tūṣṇīm upacarita*) is for the purpose of excluding the *pākayajña* rites. For it has been stated: "In those [rites], the procedure is silent. However, the consumption consists of the four *anuṣṭubh* verses beginning with "annam eva vivinakti," while the recitation of the mantra pertains to the *caru* ritual.

The roots *vana* and *paṇ* mean "to gather" (*saṃbhakta*). Food itself is *vivanana*, meaning "distribution" (*vibhajana*); food itself is known as *saṃvanana*, meaning "that which is eaten together," in the sense of "union" (*saṃśleṣaṇa*). Food is the life-breath (*prāṇa*) of living beings, for by it they live. Food alone is the eldest, the most excellent, and is remembered as the physician’s remedy (*bhiṣag-bheṣaja*), for by it diseases caused by hunger and the like are averted.

The bridegroom says: "O bride, I bind (*sinomi*)—from the root *ṣiñ*, meaning 'to bind'—your heart and your mind. Mind (*manas*) is so called because it is the act of thinking (*mananam*); it is the instrument by which one thinks, namely the five external senses. Heart (*hṛdayam*) refers to the consciousness (*citta*). By what means? By the "knot of truth" (*satyagranthinā*); truth is conduct free from guile, and that itself is the knot. It is "speckled" (*pṛśninā*), meaning white and pure, in the sense of being the form of Dharma. Here, food is like a gem, and the vital breath (*prāṇaḥ*) is like a thread; this constitutes an ornament such as a necklace.

"O bride, let the mind of you and mine be in accord with our words; as is the speech, so let the heart be sincere, and not otherwise in thought or in word through wickedness. Thus, let the minds and consciousnesses of us two be equal, and let the vow and the performed ritual act be fruitful. Let your mind follow me alone, just as the wheel of a cart follows the track of the bull that pulls the cart."

Behold me alone and the sun alone; do not set your mind on other men. May there be a union between me and this bride like that of the cakravāka birds. Just as the pair of cakravāka birds shares and enjoys rain and other blessings according to their lot out of exceeding affection, so may we two; the meaning is: "May there be such great love between us. (1)
Thus ends the section on marriage in the *Samantracārāyaṇīyagṛhyabhāṣya*, composed by Devapāla, son of Haripāla, grandson of Bhaṭṭopendra of the illustrious Jālandhara lineage.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section (kāṇḍikā). || 29 ||
Now begins the thirtieth section:
Next, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).
For one who practices celibacy for a year, twelve nights, six, three, or even one night [is required].

Having practiced celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which is the avoidance of sexual intercourse, one should perform the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is that sexual intercourse must not be performed on the full moon or the new moon day. In this matter, the vow is to be undertaken by each individual practitioner. A year is the primary rule (*prathamaḥ kalpaḥ*). However, due to the excess of youthful passion, there is a secondary rule (*anukalpa*), an alternative (*apatkalpa*), or an optional variation (*vikalpa*): for twelve nights, six, three, or even one night. || 1 ||
The two of them lie down together. || 2 ||

The bride and groom lie together upon one bed; this same procedure, accompanied by the recitation of the four subsequent mantras, applies equally to the first bed after the wedding and to the *ādhāna* (the formal establishment of the sacred fires). || 2 ||

I beheld you with my mind, you who are observant, born of fervor, manifested through fervor. Bestowing upon me offspring here and wealth here, beget offspring through progeny, O you who desire sons! I beheld you with my mind, meditating, striving for success within your own body. As a young woman, come to me from above; beget offspring through progeny, O you who desire sons! O Prajāpati, take pleasure in my body; may Tvaṣṭṛ with the gods and Indra with his power [favor us].

"In harmony with all the gods worthy of sacrifice, may we be mothers of many men. I place the embryo in the plants; I am within all beings. I have generated offspring upon the earth; I [have generated] sons from women. Thus they recite, alternating between the male and female roles. (3)

The bride and groom mutter these *ṛc*s in the *gāyatrī* meter during the first lying down together and at the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite), performing a reversal of the sequence of the verses: the woman recites the first, the man the second, the woman the third, and the man the fourth. "Reversal" (*vyatyāsa*) means inversion. For the man is the primary agent; elsewhere his ritual engagement comes first, but here there is an inversion. "Reversal of the sequence beginning with the woman" (*khyādivyatyāsa*) refers to that inversion in which the woman is the starting point.

The bride says: "O you who desire a son, I have seen you—indeed, I see you, O Cekitāna, shining intensely with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*) and other qualities. With what do I see you? With the mind, and not with the eye. Of what nature are you? Born of austerity (*tapas*). 'Austerity' is the name for both the progenitor (*prajāpati*) and his meritorious deed; you are born from the presence of Prajāpati Brahmā and have emerged and grown through austerity.
Bestow here upon me offspring in the form of a son and wealth (*rayi*); through offspring, procreate—meaning, produce progeny. (1)

O you who desire a son, I see you meditating with your mind, radiant and glowing. Of what sort? One who is *nādhatī*—the root *nādh* (from *nāth*/*nāthū*) meaning "to pray for protection, to suffer, to rule, or to bless"—thus one praying for progeny. Where? In her own body, within her very self. For what purpose? For prosperity, for success, and for the exaltation of both worlds. Abiding near me, may you become great (*uccā*), most venerable through the possession of virtuous sons and the like; being young, may you become exceedingly youthful.
"Be procreated through progeny," because of the statement, "The self is indeed called 'son'," [it means] be procreated in the form of offspring; that is, become possessed of sons. || 2 ||

The bride, superimposing the status of Prajāpati upon her husband, says: "O Prajāpati, enjoy my *tanvaṃ*, that is, my body. O Tvaṣṭṛ, O Prajāpati, being Indra and followed by all the gods (*viśvair devaiḥ*) with power (*sahasā*), being in full agreement with us (*saṃvidānaḥ*), [and] with those worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiyaiḥ*)—this is an epithet for the gods—may we become mothers of many sons. (3)

The Lord said: "In plants, which end with the ripening of their fruit, I alone bestow and have bestowed the power to produce the fruit within the seed. This statement is made because there is no difference between the individual soul and the Supreme Soul. For this very reason, He says: 'I alone abide within all beings as the inner controller (antaryāmin); it is I who have produced and shall produce blameless offspring upon the earth.
It is I who, through the wombs of women—the internal receptacles within the bellies of mothers—beget sons and deposit the seed. (4)
In this very way, those two desiring offspring unite during the proper season. ||4||
The meaning has been explained. || 4 ||
Saying "He shall give," he touches the buttocks.
With the Yajus formula, "karat," the groom touches the vulva, the female organ; the meaning is: "May he produce [karat], may he bring about progeny. || 5 ||
The generation [of the deity] above is with the syllable *bhaṣat*.
With the Yajus mantra "puṃcihnaṃ bhasat," the woman touches [the penis]. The meaning is: "O producer of a male, being radiant (*bhasat*), may you become capable of producing offspring. || 6 ||
"Great," thus it was born. || 7 ||
With the word "bṛhat," he pours forth the generated virility; the meaning is: "May it be vast, extensive, and capable of producing a son. || 7 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth kaṇḍikā. || 30 ||
Now begins the thirty-first section:
Next, the parting of the hair (sīmanta).

In the third month of pregnancy, during the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day or at a festival, having established the fire as prescribed and offered oblations with the *jaya* and following formulas, he unties all the hair of the woman—who is seated facing east on *darbha* grass behind the fire—and combs it.

Beginning from conception, in the third month, on the primary day of the full moon during the bright fortnight, there is a sacramental rite known by the technical term *sīmantonnayana*. The use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) indicates that this rite is to be performed [by another] and not performed by the learned man himself; for it has been shown that even though he is wise, he should not perform it personally. Regarding this, some maintain that it is a sacrament for the vessel alone, arguing that "the benefit to the fetus will come from the sacrament of the vessel itself, just as the benefit to the eye comes from the sacrament of the eyeball. And so says the Smṛti:

"Once the sacramental rites have been performed for the woman, by means of the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony, whatever fetus she gives birth to shall all be considered consecrated. Others, however, consider this to be a sacrament for the fetus itself, because it is only in that context that the phrase "in the third month of the pregnancy" makes sense. For if it were merely a sacrament for the vessel (the woman), what would be the need for reference to the month of the pregnancy? It would simply be prescribed that the *sīmantonnayana* should be performed whenever [it is appropriate], as in the rule: "The *sīmantonnayana* should be performed. This is also supported by the *Smṛti*.

"By means of the purificatory rites for the womb (*gārbha-homa*), the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the tonsure (*cauḍa*), and the tying of the girdle (*mauñjī-nibandhana*), the sin pertaining to the seed (*vaijika*) and the sin pertaining to the womb (*gārbhika*) of the twice-born is destroyed.

Others, however, maintain that both types of purification are required. Among these, the purification of the field (*kṣetra-saṃskāra*) alone is the most widely accepted view among those who know the meaning of the Vedas, because it is well known that its performance is generally sufficient when done once.

As it has been stated: having performed the kindling of the fire and offered oblations beginning with the *jaya* formulas up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, she sits facing east upon darbha grass behind the established domestic fire (*āvasathya*). Having thoroughly and completely loosened all her hair, she combs it—making it distinct—with a *kaṅkata*, which is a wooden comb possessing many teeth on both sides for smoothing the hair—while reciting the three verses that are about to be mentioned. || 1 ||

The parting which your comb has made, or that which the razor has shaved around you—O Aśvins, place that beauty in women; unite this woman with manly vigor and heroic power. Indrāṇī has fashioned the comb; let it glide along the parting. O Agni, give the wife back to her husbands together with offspring. Agni has given back the wife with life and splendor. May the husband of this woman live for a hundred autumns with long life. 2.

The word *iti* here has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Its connection with the preceding is: "By means of these three mantras, one adorns the hair. Regarding the phrase "the parting (*sīmanta*) which your *kaṅkata* (comb) made," or "the parting which the razor (*kṣura*) made"—they explain that the *kaṅkata* is so called because of its sharpness, like a razor; for after marriage, contact with a razor is considered inauspicious for women. And the particle *vā* is seen used in the sense of comparison, as in "or like the ocean, a great being," since particles have multiple meanings.

O Aśvins, that comb of yours which, while shaving the hair, made it distinct—having avoided the hair out of fear of tearing the head—that form, characterized by the ritual mark known as the *sīmanta*, place within women; O Aśvins, likewise endow it with such power through your own vigor. 1.

Indrāṇī, the powerful Śacī, made this *kaṅkata* (comb); therefore, because of its excellence, let this *kaṅkata* glide along the parting of the hair—that is to say, let it arrange and perfect it. O Agni, this wife was given by you at the time of marriage; now, together with her offspring, give this woman back to her husbands—meaning, make her possessed of sons. || 2 ||

Agni has given back this wife, together with long life and luster. May he who is her husband and supporter be long-lived; may he live for a hundred autumns—here the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*); may he live for a hundred autumns, meaning may he live for a hundred years. || 2 ||
Three times he parts her hair with a white porcupine quill and a branch of the Śamī tree bearing leaves, with the verse: "O Rākā, those [teeth] of yours... (RV X. 85.47).

Three times, with three [applications], using a white—that is, a bright—*śalalī*; for *śalalī* means the porcupine (*śvavit*), and its quill is metaphorically called *śalalī*. With that, and with a branch of the *śamī* tree together with its leaves—that is, with its foliage—he parts the hair-parting (*sīmanta*) with the *triṣṭubh* verse beginning, "O Rākā, those [lines] which are yours. As for what some explain—that it is a copper needle, white and not red—that does not accord with what is observed.

O Rākā, daughter of the gods, those auspicious thoughts of yours which are well-formed—well-formedness here meaning that the thoughts are beautiful because they are intent upon bestowing desired fruits—and by means of which you grant riches to the donor, the sacrificer; with those thoughts as your attendants, come to us today, O fortunate one, being well-disposed and bestowing thousandfold prosperity. (This is a ṛṣi-seen prayer. O Rākā, daughter of the gods: those auspicious thoughts of yours which are well-formed—well-formedness here meaning that the thoughts are beautiful because they are intent upon bestowing desired fruits—and by means of which you grant riches to the donor, the sacrificer; with those [thoughts] as your attendants, come to us today, on this very day, being well-disposed.
With a serene mind, O fortunate and beautiful Rākā, bestowing a thousandfold nourishment—that is, wealth numbering in the thousands—[she shines]. ||3||

Then he binds her two separate tresses with a blue-and-red thread; it becomes blue-and-red, for the *kṛtyā*—the magical power—is manifested. "Her kinsmen prosper, while the husband is bound in fetters," so it is said. || 4 ||

Immediately after this, while the pregnant woman’s hair—divided by lines made with a porcupine quill smoothed over a comb—is being parted to create the sections for the *sīmanta* (parting of the hair), he fashions two separate bundles on either side and binds them together with a blue-and-red thread, reciting the mantra beginning with "nīlalohita. "This thread is blue-and-red," he says.

"Kṛtiḥ" means action; by that [action], power is manifested—the meaning is that the masculinity of the fetus is manifested. "Asyāḥ" refers to this pregnant woman; "jñātaya edhante" means her kinsmen prosper—here the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*), meaning "let power be manifested" and "let the kinsmen increase. And "patiśca" (and the husband) should be bound within the bonds of affection and the like. || 4 ||
One should honor that teacher who [is such]. || 5 ||
One should honor with offerings such as the *madhuparka* according to one's ability that Brahmin who is the officiant of the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony. ||5||
This very thing is the removal of the tresses for young maidens; this alone is their anointing here.

At this very time, the rite of *saṭoddharaṇa*—consisting of a specific arrangement of the hair—must be performed for those maidens who have been betrothed. An unguent made from all-herbs, saffron, and other substances is applied, establishing a particular beauty upon the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*). Here, the principal sacrifice is performed with the four-fold portioned oblation (*caturgṛhīta*) while reciting the verse beginning with "ye ke ca jma" directed toward the southeast.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter. || 31 ||
Now begins the thirty-second section:
Next, the rite for the birth of a male child (puṃsavana).

The word "atha" (now) signifies immediate sequence; thus, immediately after the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), the sacramental rite for the embryo known as *puṃsavana* (the male-making ceremony) is to be performed. || 1 ||

When most of the months of pregnancy have passed, he should cook three *sthālīpāka* offerings dedicated to Agni, Indra, and Viṣṇu; he offers them into the fire according to their respective deities with the verses "Agni tuviśravastamam," "Indra kṣattram," and "Pra tad viṣṇuḥ," and he makes an additional oblation with the verse "Pumān. || 2 ||

According to the Vedic revelation, "In the tenth month he is born," and from observation as well, there are ten months of gestation. Among these, five are half-portions, six are more than half, and seven are the majority. When those months of gestation have passed such that the seventh—the majority—is reached, then in the eighth month, according to established custom, one should cook three *sthālīpāka* offerings: for Agni, for Indra, and for Viṣṇu. Taking one or another from among them, he offers it into the fire according to the respective deity.

Where there is a single *sthālīpāka* (cooked offering), even if there is a difference in deities, it constitutes a single ritual action because of the unity of the connection between the substance and the deity. Here, however, because both [substance and deity] differ, there is a multiplicity of rituals due to the difference in their connections. One offers to Agni with the verse beginning "May Agni protect," to Indra with the verse beginning "Indra, the ruling power," and to Viṣṇu with the verse beginning "Praiseworthy is that Viṣṇu"; then, having set aside a portion for each from the [offerings] beginning with "A male," one performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation.
Agni bestows upon the donor a son who possesses most abundant fame, who is a supreme priest of powerful prayers, and who makes his name heard as an invincible lord. 1.

Agni bestows a son upon the sacrificer who has offered the oblation. Of what kind? Most highly renowned—*tuvi* is read among the many names for "much," and *śravaḥ* means either food or fame; thus, it means one who possesses most abundant food or greatest fame. One whose sacred knowledge (*brahman*) is vast—the word *brahman* here signifies the Veda, so the meaning is "one who knows much of the Veda. Likewise, one who is preeminent, surpassing all others; one who is unassailable—meaning free from haste, steady, and expansive—and the lord of those who cause [the truth] to be heard.

The meaning is "the lord of the officiating priests," that is, the sacrificer. "O Indra, you have been born as a protector, as a source of strength, and as a bull among the people. You have driven away the unfriendly folk; you have made wide space for the gods. (2)

O Indra, you were born for *kṣatra*, that is, for the protection of the ruling power; "born" is his [subject], and *ojas* (force) is its qualification. The meaning is: having characterized yourself by the force and strength of the *kṣatra*, you were born. *Vāma* means desirable and worthy of distribution. O *vṛṣabha* (bull), showerer! Of whom? Of the *carṣaṇīs*, that is, of men—here even the gods are considered men. You have driven away (*apānudaḥ*), pushed aside, the people of the Asura world who act like enemies (*amitrayantam*), behaving as if they were foes. What kind of people?

And having pushed aside that [obstruction], you have made wide and expansive for the gods—either for the sake of the gods or belonging to the gods—the world; "sub" is used here by way of metrical transposition. || 2 ||
Thus Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic power, like a terrifying beast that wanders and dwells in the mountains; in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide. 3.
It will be explained. || 3 ||

A male has been born as Agni, a male as Indra, a male as Viṣṇu. May he beget a male son to be brought forth in the tenth month—by whose birth we may live for a hundred autumns and see for a hundred autumns. Grant us such a one, who brings a hundredfold and thousandfold gain, who wins cattle and horses, a heroic son.

By means of these two, the Ṛg and the Yajus, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is performed. May Ayā and the others give birth to a son endowed with excellence of manhood (*pauruṣātiśaya*), for it was from them alone that such men, possessed of excellence of manhood, were born and have arisen throughout the three worlds. "In the tenth month, for the sake of giving birth" (*sūtave*): the suffix *tave* is used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).

O Lord, grant us that son by whose birth we, through him as our sovereign master, may live and see for a hundred autumns; increase him for us—him who possesses wealth amounting to hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands, who is a winner of cattle, a distributor of kine, and likewise a hero who wins horses, a valiant son endowed with prowess. || 2 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter. 32.
Now begins the thirty-third section:
Next, the Soṣyantīsavana rite.

Next, the rite called *soṣyantī-savana* is described; it is a ritual with a visible purpose. This is an etymological designation (*yaugikī saṃjñā*). *Savana* means that by which one is brought forth (*sūyate*), namely, the rite for an easy delivery. The *soṣyantī-savana* is the *savana* for a woman about to give birth (*soṣyamāṇā*), that is, one whose delivery is imminent. || 1 ||
When she is about to give birth, he should place his hand, dripping with water, upon her head and touch her from the heart.

When she is about to give birth and her delivery is imminent, one should place her hand, which is dripping with water, upon her head and touch her down as far as her heart. In this rite, the husband is the performer; in his absence, some trusted person such as a brother-in-law (devara) or similar relative shall act. || 2 ||
He recites the mantra:
"As this wind blows, as the ocean surges, so let your embryo move; together with the afterbirth, let it fall away. Thus, she gives birth quickly. || 3 ||

One should touch [the woman] with this mantra. By doing so, she will give birth quickly and easily; thus he declares the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) of this rite. "Just as this wind blows with great speed, and just as the ocean trembles and shakes, even so let your embryo (*garbha*) move quickly, be born, and fall away—that is, emerge—along with the aged womb. (3)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter. || 33 ||
Now begins the thirty-fourth section:
the naming ceremony (nāmakarma).
When a son is born, a name is bestowed. || 1 ||

When a son is born, having performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), immediately after the cutting of the umbilical cord, a name is assigned or determined with the thought, "I shall give him this name"—so some explain. For the naming ceremony is prescribed by the *Smṛti* for the purification from impurity, stating: "One should perform the naming on the eleventh day or on an auspicious occasion. Others, however, say that this is intended to mean that once the child is born, one should not let the eleventh day or a favorable moment pass by without performing the naming rite. As for us, we shall state the truth shortly. (1)
It consists of four syllables, beginning with a sonant consonant and having a semivowel at its end. (2)

At the beginning of a name, there should be a sonant consonant; in the middle, there should be a letter known as an *antastha*; and it should consist of four syllables. Here, "syllables" (*akṣara*) refers to vowels (*ac*), since there is no restriction regarding the consonants (*hal*). (Verse 2)
Or according to their respective rebirths. || 3 ||
Just as it is appropriate according to the sequence of what has been obtained through the grace of the deity and so forth, so should it be performed. || 3 ||

Having brought fire and offered oblations in it up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* portions, he should pour the remnants (*saṃpāta*) into a bronze vessel together with gold, reciting the two verses: "Hiraṇyagarbha," "The image of the year," and [the mantras] "To Kāya svāhā! To Ka svāhā! To Katama svāhā! To Prajāpati svāhā! and [the verse] "O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you. || 4 ||

In whichever house the birth occurs, one should bring the common (laukika) fire and perform the oblations there up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings. Then, with eight oblations beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," one should pour or let flow the remnants of the offerings (*saṃpāta*)—the drops remaining from what has been offered—into a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) joined with gold. "Hiraṇyagarbha" is the first oblation; "The image of the year" (*saṃvatsarasya pratimām*) is the second; and there are four more: "To Kāya svāhā! To Ka svāhā! To Katama svāhā! To Prajāpati svāhā!"

With the two verses beginning "O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you," there are two [offerings]. Thus, there are eight [in total]. Some say that because it is a primary ritual act (pradhānakarma), the oblation is to be offered with only four ladlings (caturgṛhīta).

In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. He supported this earth and yonder sky. To what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? This verse has been explained in the section on marriage.
O Night, for those who worship you as the image of the year, grant them long-lived progeny and unite them with the abundance of wealth.

O Night, you are the image of the year and its fashioner; for those people who worship you, make their offspring long-lived, and unite them with the increase of wealth—that is, with the abundance of riches.
To the body, svāhā!
May it be well-offered!

To whom, svāhā! To which one, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! "Ka" and the following four are names of Prajāpati. O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you who has encompassed all these created beings; whatever desire we have while offering to you, may that be ours, svāhā!

Virāṭ: O Prajāpati, there is none other than you who has encompassed—meaning who has overcome, brought under control, or pervaded—all these entire born beings that possess birth. These, these very ones; *viśvā* for *viśvāni*, where the suffix *śi* is elided according to the rule *śeś chandasi bahulam*. In the word *paritet*, the syllable *ta* is an augment (*varṇāgama*). May that fruit which we desire as we offer oblations be ours.
He is the son of that one; that one is the son of this one. May we be masters of riches! Svāhā!

"Of such-and-such a person" is the specification of the particular name. "This Viṣṇumitra is the son of that Yajñamitra"—thus there is a double utterance of the names of father and son: the name of the father ending in the genitive case is placed in the middle, while the name of the son occurs at both the beginning and the end. "May we become, may we attain, the lords—masters—of riches, of wealth."

Having made the mouth pure with gold while reciting, "Thou art the life-span of Agni," and having touched the mouth with his hand and washed it, he consecrates the breasts with the three verses beginning, "Honey is the wind for the one who follows the cosmic order," reciting one verse for each breast, and both together with the last verse.

Having made the mouth pure and sanctified with gold using the mantra beginning with *agnirāsy asi*, and having touched the mouth with a hand moistened with water, the father of the child washes his hands and consecrates the breasts of the child’s mother with each verse individually; in his absence, the domestic priest does so. With one verse he consecrates each breast, and with the final verse, both. It is with reference to this plurality that the word "breasts" (*stanān*) is used in the plural. He consecrates the right breast with *madhu vātaḥ*, the left with *madhu naktam*, and both with *madhumān naḥ*.

The word *madhu* (honey) should be understood as the name for the immortal essence that generates the world, which consists of eternal bliss and is well-known through the Madhu-vidyā, occurring within the three mantras.
Honey for the one who follows the cosmic order, honey the rivers flow; may the plants be sweet for us.
May the night and the dawn be honey-sweet; may the earthly realm be honey-sweet; and may our father be sweet for us.
May the tree be full of honey, may the sun be full of honey; may our cows be sweet for us.

*Ṛta* is sacrifice. He who desires sacrifice is expressed by the word *ṛtāyan*, formed with the suffix *kyac* and the present participle suffix *śatṛ*. For that sacrificer who desires sacrifice (*ṛtāyate*), may the wind be honey—may it be the bringer of immortality. May the rivers, the streams, flow with honey—may they pour forth water. May the plants, those which perish at the ripening of their fruit, be *mādhvīḥ*—endowed with sweet flavor.

May the night be honeyed; the word *uta* has the sense of "also"—may the twilight (*naktaṃ sandhyā*) also, together with the dawn and the night, be honey for us. May the earthly realm (*pārthivaṃ rajaḥ*), the world of mortals, be full of honey. May the sky and the intermediate space be honey for us, our father. May the trees (*vanaspatayaḥ*) be full of honey, and may the sun be full of honey for us. And may our cows be sweet, full of sweetness, and rich in honey. || 5 ||

Having rubbed together drops of honey with gold, some say he places it in his mouth and makes him drink it, [saying]: "Suck up life; suck up old age; suck up truth; suck up prosperity; suck up vigor; suck up abundance of wealth; suck up spiritual luster. || 6 ||

Having rubbed together the *saṃpāta* drops with gold and placed them in the child's mouth, he makes him drink them. Some, however, think that one should rub honey together with the *saṃpāta* drops and make him drink them; this is the meaning. Since the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) generally belong to the father, the father says: "O child, drink the *āyuḥ* (longevity)! "Drink the *jarā* (old age)! The meaning is that the *saṃpāta* ghee—or the ghee mixed with honey—and the breast milk being drunk shall be the cause of your longevity and so forth.
*Ūrj* is food and strength; *rāyaspoṣaḥ* is the increase of wealth; *brahmavarcasa* is the abundance of knowledge beginning with the Vedas and spiritual luster. || 6 ||
Having smelled his head while saying, "Live for a hundred autumns; see for a hundred autumns," he causes him to recite a benediction.
The section beginning with "bodhaśca me" is the *anuvāka*. The suffix *ṇic* is used in its own sense [to form the causative] in the word "vācayati. The remainder is clear.

Bodha protect me from the front, and Pratibodha protect me from behind; Atharvan and Mānacadvān protect me from the south; Gopāyamāna and Rakṣamāṇa protect me from there; Jāgṛvi and Arundhatī protect me from the north. Make us free from enemies below; O Indra, make us free from enemies above; make us free from enemies behind; make us free from enemies in front.

May we be free from enemies through these days and nights; O All-Gods, may our dawns be free from enemies, and so too our sunsets. May those six regions and the five intermediate directions protect us; as bestowers of friendship, establish us in friendship, and let there be fearlessness for us. You who attend to the night and you who remain watchful among all beings—you who protect all cattle, be watchful over our very selves.

"O Awakening, O Re-awakening, O Unslumbering, O Unsleeping, O Protecting, O Guarding, O Watchful—those gods who are the protectors of the body, do you protect my body here! "Awakening, Re-awakening"—the sun, indeed, is the Awakening; Agni is the Re-awakening. "Unslumbering"—the moon, indeed, is the unslumbering. "O Unsleeping"—he who blows (the wind) is the unsleeping. "O Protecting, O Guarding"—day is the protecting, night is the guarding. "O Watchful"—the sacrifice, indeed, is the watchful; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is the watcher. These, indeed, are the gods who sustain the kingdom; they [are invoked] for the protection of one's own self.

This is *svastyayana*: *svasti* is non-destruction; its *ayana* is the attainment, the cause for obtaining non-destruction. This is the seer’s [view] regarding the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*. Those who support (*bibhrati*), maintain (*dhārayanti*), and nourish (*puṣṇanti*) the world (*rāṣṭra*) are the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, such as the Ādityas and others; some say they are also the seasons (*ṛtus*). Bodha and the others have been explained previously in this very section: Āditya is *bodha* (awakening), and Agni is *pratībodha* (counter-awakening) because of his illuminating nature.

The moon is *manas* (mind) because it is "sleepless" (*asvapna*) due to its constant wakefulness; or it is the wind (*vāyu*) in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being "unfailing" (*anavadrāṇa*) because its movement is never censured. The day is the "guardian" (*gopāyamāna*) by means of causing the performance of actions that are the cause of life; the night is the "protector" (*rakṣamāṇa*). The sacrifice (*yajña*) is the "wakeful one" (*jāgṛvi*), having the form of Prajāpati, for according to the Vedic scripture, "Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice"; it is "wakeful" because it remains awake within all living beings as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all. *Arundhatī* is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); for she, while warding off enemies (*arīn*), bestows the fruit upon the sacrificer.

May Bodha Āditya protect me from the front, in the eastern direction; and may Pratibodha Agni [protect me]. May Asvapna Candra protect me in the southern direction; and may Anavadrāṇa Vāyu [protect me]. May Gopāyamāna Prāṇa protect me in the western part of the sky; and may Rakṣamāṇa Rātri [protect me]. May Jāgṛvi Prajāpati Yajña protect me in the northern part of the sky; and may Arundhatī Dakṣiṇā [protect me].

*Anamitram no 'dharāk* is a verse addressed to Indra (*aindrī*), in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. "Non-enemy" (*anamitram*) means "friend" (*mitram*); this is because the negative particle (*nañ*) indicates the absence of the original state (enmity). O Indra, make us "non-enemy" (*anamitram*)—that is, create [a state where] there is no enemy—in the lower direction (*adharāk*), meaning in the downward or northern direction (*udak*). The sense is: "Make whoever desires to harm us there favorable to us. The same applies to the subsequent directions: "behind" (*paścāt*) in the western direction, and "in front" (*puraḥ*) in the eastern direction.

*Anamitrair ahobhiḥ*: these two verses consist of *śakvarī* and *uṣṇih* meters. The deity to be addressed is everywhere [the same]. O Viśve Devās, all you gods, may we be accompanied by days that have become friendly; may the dawns, the times of morning, and the *nimrucas*, the nights, be our friends. [The root] *mruc-*, *mluc-* means "to go"; they are called *nimrucas* because the sun goes down (*nitāntaṃ gacchati*) into them. Those six deities who are *urvīḥ*, *urvyaḥ*, meaning great—what are they?

May Heaven, Earth, Day, Night, Dawn, the plants, and likewise the five directions—the four beginning with the East and the upward direction as the fifth—protect us and guard us. O you who have just been mentioned, since you are the ordainers of the work established by Mitra, therefore establish us in Mitra, that is, in auspicious action; and may there be fearlessness for us through your grace.

O gods who have been shown to us—you who abide through the night, who stand having made the night your characteristic mark, and you who remain awake among living beings and protect all cattle—be watchful within our own selves and bodies. "Bodha," "pratibodha," and so forth, are the vocatives for the eight [deities].

O you gods, beginning with Bodha and ending with Arundhatī, who are the protectors of the body (*tanūpāḥ*), that is, the guardians of our bodies (*tanūnām*); do you, as such, protect my body (*tanvam*) here in this dense existence. He explains [the names] by singling out the individual forms of Bodha and the others, starting with "O Bodha, O Pratibodha," and so forth; the meaning of this is already understood. These indeed are the gods—the word *vai* is used for emphasis—these very ones, Bodha and the rest, are the sustainers of the kingdom and of the world, as well as the cosmic seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*); therefore, I praise them. For what purpose?

"For the protection" means for the sake of his own preservation. Other *svastyayana* (auspicious) verses should also be recited here. The root *vac* is listed in the *cur-ādi* class; from that, with the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in its own sense, one says "he causes [him] to recite the *svastyayana*. Therefore, it is appropriate that the speaking is performed by himself before his father. For these acts are generally performed by oneself prior to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*).
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter. 34.
Now begins the thirty-fifth section (kāṇḍikā).
He offers mustard seeds mixed with husks from a ladle, reciting the mantras: "Śaṇḍo marka upavītaḥ," "Ālikhan," "Haryakṣṇaḥ," and "Keśinī. || 1 ||

These oblations during the period of impurity are for the protection of the child and the woman who has recently given birth; therefore, they serve a visible purpose. *Phalīkarana* refers to the husks of grain; one should offer mustard seeds mixed with these husks using a ladle twice daily—morning and evening—for ten days, with the four mantras beginning with "Śaṇḍa. [The first mantra is: "May Śaṇḍa, Marka, Upavīta, Tauṇḍuleya, and Ulūkhalacapala perish from here, Svāhā! (1)

The collective meaning here is: "May Śaṇḍa and the others perish and flee from this place of childbirth. Śaṇḍa and the others are names of Piśācas. Each one is connected with a mantra: "May Śaṇḍa perish from this place; likewise Marka, Upavīta, Tauṇḍuleya, and may the restless Ulūkhala perish from here! Svāhā! May there be a well-offered oblation! || 1 ||
Drawing and scratching, gnashing his teeth, and as restless as a mortar—may he perish from here!
Svāhā! || 2 ||
This is the same as the preceding [section]. || 2 ||
May Kumbha, Śakti, Hantṛ, and the fickle Upaṇīmukha of the tawny-eyed one perish from here—svāhā! || 3 || May Keśinī, Valominī, Kacā, and Kaucāpakāśinī depart and perish from here—svāhā! || 4 ||
Haryakṣṇa and others are names [of demons]. Keśinī is the name of a rākṣasī. Likewise, Śvalominī, Kacā, Kaucā, and Apakāśinī—these too are specific names of rākṣasīs. ||4||
In this manner, one should offer oblations in the evening and in the morning for ten days.
By these four methods, one should offer oblations for ten days; the meaning is that one should offer them until the period of impurity has passed. || 2 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth section. 35.
Now begins the thirty-sixth section:
Next, the naming ceremony.

On the tenth day, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in that same fire with milk, having bathed [the child] including the head with all fragrant substances ending with fruits, and having covered him with a new garment, he offers oblations of the *sthālīpāka* with the two verses beginning "With what [help], O wonderful one... (*kayā naścitra*), and with the two verses "How has he heard this? To Prajāpati, svāhā! (*kayā tacchṛṇve*) and "O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you" (*prajāpate nahi tvat*). 1.

When the tenth day has passed and purification from impurity has been attained, one should perform the naming ceremony on the eleventh or twelfth day; or, if there is an inauspiciousness regarding the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and so forth, on another day. This is because of the traditional rule: "On an auspicious day, at an auspicious moment (*muhūrta*), or under a lunar mansion endowed with good qualities. Furthermore, by the rule based on sunrise, the thirteenth lunar day (*tithi*) is to be taken.

This is because, based on the rule "from an improper rising and an improper lying down, [the impurity lasts] until the current day has passed," and so forth, as well as the observation that even when the night has dawned, the impurity continues until sunrise, according to the rule: "for two [verses] at the end of the night, and for three in the morning."

While the child remains in that very lying-in chamber, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (oblation) in fresh milk and having bathed the child—including the head—with all kinds of herbs and various fragrant substances upon which auspicious items such as *jātī* and *pūgaphala* fruits have been placed, [the father]—excluding a female because of the masculine gender used in the instruction—covers the child with an unused garment and offers five oblations of the *sthālīpāka* with the verses beginning "kayā naścitra," using portions taken alternately from the *sthālīpāka*.
"Thou art the life-span of Agni"—this [formula] is the same up to the touching of the forehead. || 2 ||

The extension [of the ritual] by the statement "Thou art the fiery one" (*āgneyur asi*) and so forth is that it is equal to the *āyuṣeṣṭi* sacrifice. He states the limit: "up to the touching of the forehead. For he will say: "Having touched his forehead, he mutters, 'The breath of the Aśvins'. The meaning is that immediately after that, it is the same as in the *āyuṣeṣṭi*. || 2 ||
That very thing is what is held in mind. || 3 ||
In the *anuvāka*, in place of the word "asau" (so-and-so), that very name which was given at the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) is inserted, and no other. || 3 ||
"Something else," say some. || 4 ||

Others, however, say that something else is prescribed here: for two names must indeed be given to a Brāhmaṇa. Among these, the secret name associated with the birth-rite—as in the rule "when a son is born, a name is bestowed"—is intended so that it is not uttered by others when they perform malevolent magic (abhicāra). The public name, on the other hand, is used for worldly transactions from the eleventh day onwards. Thus says the Śruti: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa has two names. (4)

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having poured purified clarified butter into a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) and placed a piece of gold—which is not to be tied on—with the formula "The life-span of Agni," he makes an offering from it with the five [verses] beginning with "The breath of Indra."

Having poured purified clarified butter (*ājya*) into a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and having placed gold therein with the mantra beginning "Thou art the life of Agni" (*agnerāyurasi*), he offers that gold—which is of such a kind as to be fit for binding around the neck or other parts of a child—into that clarified butter with the five mantras beginning "The breath of Indra" (*indrasya prāṇa*). || 5 ||

The Brahman priest, standing facing east while the Yajus formulas are being recited, places gold into the clarified butter; all the officiating priests do so with the verse, "As thou didst glide away."

Before the sacrifice has been fully established, Brahmā dips gold into the clarified butter and grasps it; all the officiating priests likewise grasp that gold which was placed in the butter for the purpose of binding the *dālagala* and other parts, using mantras beginning with "dasarpa."
Having lifted it up with the verse beginning "By means of the purifying [Soma]," he hands it to the sacrificer with the formula, "The gods are long-lived. || 7 ||
Having extracted gold from the clarified butter with the verse beginning "pāvamānena," he gives it to the sacrificer while reciting the mantras beginning with "devā āyuṣmantaḥ."
He drinks that [nectar] without limit. || 8 ||
The child drinks that clarified butter which flows like gold; he should drink it, swallowing it entirely without leaving any remainder.
Having washed the ghee from the gold with the verse "This [gold], O Agni," he fastens the gold [to the child]. || 9 ||
Having washed the gold vessel with clarified butter, he ties that gold [amulet] around the child's neck and so forth, with the mantra beginning "imamagna" (RV 1.187.10).
Having touched his forehead, he mutters: "The breath of the Aśvins. (10)
Touching the surface of the forehead with the hand, one mutters the mantra beginning with "The breath of the Aśvins," and so forth. || 10 ||

"You arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart. You are indeed the self (ātman) whose name is 'son' (putra); live for a hundred autumns! See for a hundred autumns! Having thus smelled him on the head, he causes him to recite a benediction (*svastyayana*). || 11 ||

Having performed the sprinkling upon the child’s head with the mantra beginning "From limb to limb" (aṅgādaṅgāt) and so forth, he recites the benediction (svastyayana). In some versions, the reading is "nighrāpya"; in that case, the causative suffix (ṇic) is used in its own sense. Some say that the father should employ the mother in his presence; others intend that the officiating priest (ṛtvij) is the one who prompts the father. || 11 ||
In this same manner, after having stayed away from home for a period longer than that. || 12 ||
Therefore, after the naming ceremony, when the father returns from his journey abroad, he should perform the touching of the head in this very same manner. || 12 ||
In this manner, month by month, having performed the sacrifice with a *sthālīpāka*, he should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) with clarified butter.

In this very manner, every month on the birthday, having performed an oblation with clarified butter according to the rite for the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) using a *sthālīpāka* offering, he should perform the smelling of the [butter] upon the head. || 13 ||
In this manner, for one year. || 14 ||
One should perform this monthly duty for the duration of one year. || 14 ||
But they shall not eat meat. || 15 ||
But the mother and father of the child shall not eat its flesh for the duration of one year. || 15 ||
When the year has been completed, having sacrificed with a goat and a sheep to Agni and Dhātṛ, he should feed the Brahmins with food mixed with clarified butter.

When the first year has been completed, having sacrificed to Agni, Aja, and Dhanvantari with a goat—or, according to the word "or" (vā), with clarified butter, or with a *sthālīpāka* offering, or with abundant ghee, along with other purifying substances such as curds and the like—he should feed the Brahmins with food. He should then honor them with their expressions of satisfaction, blessings for well-being, and benedictions. 16.

With what [splendor] has he, the ever-increasing friend, become manifoldly manifest? With what power is he encompassed? (1) Which true exhilaration of the soma-juices, most bountiful, shall intoxicate you so that you may shatter even the firmest wealth? (2)

For the sake of the vow (*vrata*). Indra or Prajāpati is the deity. Citra, whose conduct is wondrous—Prajāpati or Indra—by what aid (*ūti*) does he favor (*ābhuvat*), that is, bring about or generate for us? *Avanam* is *ūti*; according to the rule *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇā*, there is a substitution of the preceding vowel for the third case singular ending, and the elision of the suffix in the word *ūtī*. Of what kind is Prajāpati? A friend (*sakhā*), one who shares the same knowledge, the inner controller (*antaryāmī*). Of what kind are we? *Sadāvṛdhaḥ*: those endowed with increase at all times. By what conduct (*vṛtā*) does he bring about [this state]?

"By what most powerful [means]?"—*śaciṣṭhayā* means "by that which is most capable," whether by an excellence of power (*śakti*) or an excellence of consciousness (*caitanya*). The suffix *tṛc* is elided according to the rule *aturiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*, and the letter *c* is a Vedic metathesis (*varṇavyatyaya*). The meaning is: "By what excellence of power would he act? The intended sense is: "May Prajāpati, who is endowed with an excellence of powers such as being the creator, being worshipped by us in this sacrifice (*ṛtu*) concerning growth, being pleased by this offering (*iṣṭi*), grant the child an endowment of growth and the like."

"O Prajāpati, who is the sacrificer that shall exhilarate you? [He does so] with juice after juice, with the oblation. He breaks open, he shatters—the firm things, the firm ones; he bestows, he distributes riches, treasures, through the door of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth. What kind of sacrificer? One who is true, of supreme being; likewise, among those who are exhilarated, those joined with bliss, he is the most exalted (maṃhiṣṭhaḥ)—the meaning is that he is endowed with supreme bliss, whose nature is Brahman.
The root *mahi* (meaning 'to grow great') serves as the base for the word *maṃhiṣṭha*, which ends in the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*."

By what power is he heard as the most mighty, by which he acts at every moment in some way or other? Most effective in dispersing the distress of the liberal donor, he then bestows wealth upon the singer.

Here too, Prajāpati is the deity. "I hear, I perceive from the Veda. What is that? There is a certain extraordinary power or wisdom belonging to this Prajāpati. Which one? By means of which *śacī*—whether it be power or wisdom—that most exalted (*ṛṣva*) one repeatedly, again and again, cuts away (*kṛntati*), destroys, and removes great sin (*puru aṃhaḥ*). For whom? For the donor, the sacrificer (*dāśuṣe*).

Having destroyed evil, he immediately bestows, grants, or provides abundant wealth and riches to the singer, the praiser, and the donor. Of what nature is Prajāpati? He is the most powerful (*śaciṣṭhaḥ*), meaning most capable or most wise; he is the most discerning (*vicayiṣṭhaḥ*), possessing the greatest collection of various powers. The word *kayā* is used with a grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*), where the third case stands in place of the first.
Svāhā to Prajāpati!
"May it be well-offered to Prajāpati. "O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you"—these two [mantras], "this one" and "that one," have already been explained.

"Thou art the life-span of Agni; of thee, the men are the makers of life-span; therefore, for this [person], for that [deity], [I offer] the Ṛṣi’s portion of the Brahman. With this [formula], he places gold into the clarified butter. "O gold, thou art the life-span of Agni"; *āyuḥ* means that which comes (*āyāti*), thus the meaning is: "thou art produced from Agni. And so says the Śruti:

"The foremost seed was poured out; that became gold. O you who were born in such a manner, those humans—acting as makers of life for you—perform the rites of life for you, the fire, by means of fuel, fanning, churning, and keeping watch, thereby [benefiting] the gold. Because it thus benefits humans, grant life to this sacrificer and to this child, or simply bestow it. "The breath of Indra—that breath of yours grant him; to him whose breath it is, to you, Svāhā!"

Indra is the deity. Indra is the breath; Indra is the master of breath. Therefore, may that Indra grant breath to you. To that Indra whose breath [it is], to you—svāhā! May the breath of the ancestors grant breath to you. To those whose breath [it is], to you all—svāhā!

Since the vital breath (prāṇa) has the ancestors as its deity and the ancestors as its masters, may those ancestors give you life. To those ancestors from whom the breath comes, may this oblation be well-offered for you.

May the breath of the Maruts be yours; may the breath of the Viśvedevas be yours; may the breath of Prajāpati give you life; may the breath of Parameṣṭhin give you life; to those two from whom the breath comes, to you both, Svāhā!

Prajāpati is the lord of breath; may he grant you breath. Parameṣṭhin is the master of breath; may he grant you breath. To both of them, Prajāpati and Parameṣṭhin, from whom breath [proceeds], to you two, svāhā!
When you were a snake, you became clarified butter; when you were curds, you became fresh butter; and when you were whey, you became ghee.

Ghee (*ghṛta*) is thus explained: O Ghee, because you have flowed (*sṛpta*) without ceasing (*asarpa*), you have therefore become *sarpi* (clarified butter). And because, being fresh (*nava*), you have come (*aiḥ*) into existence, you are called *navanīta* (fresh butter). And because you have remained firm (*apriyathāḥ*) having become ghee—derived from the root *dhṛ* (to hold/sustain) with a transposition of letters—the word *ghṛta* is formed.
The stream of clarified butter, the path of immortality, bestowed by Indra and presented by the Maruts—that did Viṣṇu behold; that indeed did Iḷā extend with the products of the cow.

This is a verse of Viṣṇu. In the phrase "dhārāṃ panthām," the accusative case is used in place of the nominative. This stream of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the path—that is, the means—to *amṛta*, the state of immortality. For this clarified butter was given by Indra to the sacrificers through the medium of rain and other such processes; and it was "well-restrained" (*prayata*), meaning it was firmly controlled and established by the Maruts through the medium of their commands and the like. Viṣṇu beheld you as you were being thus bestowed and restrained. Then the deity *Amlā* placed you within the cow (*gavi*).
With the purifying hymn, with the Gāyatrī metre, with the path of the Upāṃśu cup, and with its power, I draw you forth, O [Name].

With the *pāvamāna* hymn, beginning with the *barhiṣpavamāna*, with the splendor of the *gāyatrī*, with the *vartanī*—a constituent part of the Sāman—and with the power and efficacy of the *upāṃśu-yajus*, I draw you forth. One should understand "asau" to be the [person's] name.
With the Bṛhat, with the Rathantara, with the Triṣṭubh, with the path, and with the vigor of the Śukra, I release you, O [Name].
The meaning has already been explained.
By the measure of Agni, by the path of the Jagatī meter, may the god Savitṛ lead you to life—that which belongs to the living.

The phrase "I take up from the fire" (*agner unnayāmi*) is to be supplied as a modification (*vipariṇata*), but the phrase "I lift up" (*uddharāmi*) is not to be supplied, according to the rule: "That which is separated [by another] should not be supplied. They say that the three mantras beginning with "By the purifying one" (*pāvamānena*) are combined, because they constitute separate mantras due to having different verbal roots (*ākhyāta*). Others, however, consider them to be a single mantra.

The six deities beginning with Deva are "possessors of life" (āyuṣmat); they are possessors of life by virtue of the nectar of immortality (amṛta). This [deity] belongs to them by means of that life; thus he is "the possessor of life" (āyuṣmān). || 1 ||
By the lifespan of those gods, by that measure of life, may this sacrificer and this child be long-lived. "Asau" (that one) is as before.

"Brahmāyuṣmat" means: "O venerable one, this [Veda] belongs to you, the venerable one; may you be long-lived through its life. "Brahman" refers to the Veda. And that is "long-lived" (āyuṣmat), meaning indestructible. For it is characterized by the act of non-interruption through the study, retention, and so forth, performed by the Brāhmaṇas—those connected with the Brahman.
