The phrase "this belongs to him," and so on, is as explained previously.
Agni is long-lived; he is that very mind. || 3 ||
Through the trees, O long-lived one, this [fire] is long-lived; the trees are its fuel and the forest is its [abode]. The rest is the same.
The sacrifice is long-lived; it is long-lived by means of its sacrificial fees. By its long life, may this [person], O so-and-so, be long-lived. || 4 ||

Out of desire for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) practice the science of sacrifice and perform the rituals correctly; therefore, through the sacrificial fee, the longevity of the sacrifice is secured.
Soma is long-lived; he is long-lived through the plants; by his life, may this person [Name] here be long-lived. || 5 ||

The plants are rice and so forth; by means of them—having considered that the food and other offerings such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* nourish the moon—one becomes long-lived through the plants, O Soma.
The medicinal herbs are long-lived; they are made long-lived by the waters. By their life-force, may this person, [name], become long-lived. (6)
By rain, the medicinal herbs grow and thrive.

O Agni, bestow long life and splendor upon this child and the sacrificer; O Varuṇa, sharpen his intense vigor. O Aditi, grant him protection like a mother, so that he may reach old age, O All-Gods. O Agni, make this boy and the sacrificer possessed of long life and splendor—*varcas* being the perfection of knowledge—the meaning is: act in such a way that they possess both life and splendor. O Varuṇa, you too, thoroughly cultivate (*saṃśiśādhi*) your own intense (*tigma*) and formidable (*utkaṭa*) vigor (*ojas*), that is, your strength.

O Aditi, Mother of the Gods, grant and bestow upon him protection and happiness, just as a mother, his own progenitor, would. O Viśvedevas, act in such a way that he may reach old age; "jaradaṣṭi" means one who reaches or attains old age—make his body worn out by aging; this is the meaning. The breath of the Aśvins is yours; may they both grant you breath, and by that, live! The breath of Mitra and Varuṇa is yours; may they both grant you breath, and by that, live!

The breath of Bṛhaspati—may that give you breath; live by means of it. The Aśvins are the deities here. The meaning is already explained: "May you live by means of the breath given by the Aśvins and the others."

"You arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart. You are indeed the self (ātman) named 'son' (putra); live for a hundred autumns! See for a hundred autumns! Because you have arisen from the essence and vigor of the sap flowing through all limbs, you come forth perfectly "from limb after limb" (*aṅgādaṅgāt*). And because you have arisen from the heart—the fulfillment of intended desires—you are born "exceedingly from the heart" (*hṛdayādabhijāyase*). The word *vai* is used for emphasis.

Why say more? You are indeed the self named "son. Because you have arisen from my own body, you are truly another form of myself, marked with the name "son" and most beneficial—this is the meaning. Being such as this, may you sustain your life-breaths for a hundred autumns; behold and remain possessed of the five senses for a hundred years. Thus has the ritual sequence from conception (*garbhādhāna*) up to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) been explained. Immediately following this, the author of the Sūtras has described the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*).

For in the *Smṛtis*, after the rites of departure from the house (*niṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*) have been mentioned, it is stated: "The infant's departure from the house should be performed in the third month," and "The first feeding of solid food should be performed in the sixth month," and so forth; therefore, those [rites] are also obligatory. Consequently, he shows here as well, in accordance with other *Gṛhyasūtras*, the rite of showing the moon (*candradarśana*). || 16 ||
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter. || 36 ||
Now begins the thirty-seventh section (Kāṇḍikā).

On the third half-month, on an auspicious day or on a festival day, when the sun has risen, one should smear a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a chariot wheel. Having kindled the fire upon it as prescribed and having offered oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, he offers clarified butter (*ājya*) with the verses: "The crossing one," "The golden ornament of heaven," "Upwards that [sun]," and "The bright face of the gods. || 1 ||

From birth, when two months have passed and the first half of the third month has elapsed, the child should be made to see the sun. Regarding this, the procedure is as follows: on an auspicious day purified according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), or on a festival day (*parvan*) endowed with a favorable constellation (*nakṣatra*) and other such factors, the viewing should be performed. Since one observes that there is an option between a single festival day together with a collection of other lunar days (*tithi*), a superior excellence [of merit] is understood.

Immediately after the sun has risen, having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a chariot wheel in the courtyard of the house—which is adorned by the rays of the sun—he should establish the common fire (*laukikāgni*) there upon that smeared ground. Having performed the kindling as prescribed—consisting of the lifting of the earth, sprinkling with water, sweeping around, pouring water around, spreading grass, preparing the *pavitra* strainers, melting the clarified butter (*ājya*), inspecting the clarified butter, and the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*)—he should then offer oblations with the *jaya* formulas beginning with "taraṇir viśvadarśataḥ," from the *āghāra* offerings up to the *ājyabhāga* portions.
With the four [verses] beginning with "The golden disk of heaven," "Upward that [splendor]," and "The bright [face] of the gods," he offers oblations of clarified butter.
"Mitro janān" and "Pra sa mitre" are [the invitatory and offering verses] for the *sthālīpāka* oblation. || 2 ||

The word "he offers" (*juhoti*) is supplied [from the previous rule]. With the two verses beginning with "Mitra the people... (*mitro janān*) and "And Mitra... (*mitraśca*), he offers the *sthālīpāka* oblation.
With the words "Turn toward us," he brings the boy forward.
Facing the boy with the mantra beginning "abhyāvartasva," the father or the preceptor raises him up and leads him forward.
The worship of the sun is performed with the mantra "Obeisance to the Seer" and also with "They have seen his."
With the words "Obeisance to the Seer, obeisance to the Witness," and so forth, the father performs the worship of the Sun for the child, having placed the child facing him upon his lap. || 4 ||
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas food mixed with clarified butter.
One should feed the Brahmins food accompanied by oblations, consisting of abundant ghee, curd, and other such ingredients.
O Sūrya, you are the deliverer, visible to all, the maker of light; you illuminate the entire radiant realm.

The seer is Prajāpati; the meter is Gāyatrī; the deity is Sūrya. O Sūrya, you are the *taraṇi*—so called because you carry one across the ocean of saṃsāra—and likewise you are *darśata*, the maker of light for all that sees, the dispeller of blinding darkness. You alone, in the form of Prajāpati, illuminate the entire universe; whatever is luminous, whatever is shining—that whole universe, you alone cause to shine.

The golden one, far-seeing, rises from the sky, moving toward distant goals, spreading light and shining brightly. Truly, impelled by the Sun, men go forth to their purposes and perform their works. This Āditya rises in the distance and travels far; he moves. From where? From *div*, that is, from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). "Golden" (*rukma*): from the root *ruc* "to shine," meaning radiant, or gold-colored. "Far-seeing" (*urukṣā*): possessing vast vision. "Goal" (*artha*): that which is reached or sought after by those seeking liberation; thus, *artha* refers to Brahman. "Spreading" (*taraṇi*) has been explained [previously].

Shining and blazing, he is called *janāḥ*—meaning the three worlds—because they are surely (*nūnam*) produced and generated by the Sun, since the Sun is the progenitor of all beings due to his being an emanation of Prajāpati or a transformation of Brahman, and because the Sun is of the nature of Brahman. Indeed, this Sun is seen as manifesting waters—that is, food—by means of rain, and as impelling and setting in motion objects such as sacrifices and gifts that are being sought with speed, by means of making the day. [The verses] "ud u tyaṃ," "citram devānām," and "mitro janān" have already been explained.

O Mitra, O Āditya, let that mortal be foremost who exerts himself for you with sacred observance; he is not slain, he is not overcome—protected by you, neither from near nor from afar does misfortune reach him.

O Mitra Āditya, that mortal who, through his own vow, strives to perform the ritual action according to your law—may he be full of offspring and possessed of food; may he flourish exceedingly. He who is protected by you is not slain by anyone, nor is he overcome or defeated. Nor does distress or sin reach him, whether from near at hand or from afar.
Turn toward us, O Earth, with sacrifice and with milk; Agni, impelled, has ascended your back.

O Earth, turn toward me with the sacrifice and with milk; come into my presence, and being gracious, make me full of milk and successful in the sacrifice. Impelled and sent forth by Agni, may it ascend to your essence upon the sacrificial altar.

Homage to the seer, homage to the overseer, homage to the observer; homage to the proclaimer, homage to the one who makes known, homage to the mother; homage to the hearer, homage to the one who listens closely; homage to the existent, homage to the non-existent, homage to the born, homage to the one yet to be born, homage to the past, homage to the future; homage to the eye, homage to the ear, homage to the mind, homage to speech, homage to Brahman, homage to the weary, homage to austerity.

This is a verse of the Ṛṣis concerning the formidable [deities]. Āditya is praised because, being the Supreme Brahman, he consists of all things. The *draṣṭṛ* is the individual soul (*jīvātman*), and the *upadraṣṭṛ* is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*). Salutation to him who is both. He is the *anudraṣṭṛ*, the soul capable of yoga, who perceives clearly through the practice of yoga that which has been previously seen through the means of valid knowledge such as the Vedas—namely, Dharma and so forth; salutation to him.

It is called *khyātā* because it is manifest; it is the entire world in its nature as the substratum (*dharmin*). The *upakhyātā* is the attribute (*dharma*), such as form and so forth. The *anukhyātā* is that which resides within the attributes, such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and form. The remainder is clear. "Your rays extend along with the people, shining like the sun."

The banners of this Āditya—his horses or rays—are seen following after people as they are born, serving as their distinguishing marks; "rayless" means devoid of cords, that is, free from bonds; they are radiant, shining brightly like fire.
Thus ends the section on the Vision of the Sun in the *Mantragṛhyabhāṣya* of Cārāyaṇīya.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter. 37.
Now begins the thirty-eighth section:
Thus is the observation of the moon.
By the word "thus" (evam), there is an extension [of the procedure] up to the smearing of the sacrificial ground, which is the size of a chariot wheel. He states the specific detail:
with the two verses, "Swiftly Dhātṛ, Mātariśvan" and "Born again," he offers oblations of four-drawn ghee at the conclusion of the Ājyabhāga offerings.
With the two verses, "May you swell" (RV 1.91.16) and "May your milks unite" (RV 1.94.16), [he offers] of the cooked mess of rice.
"Ever new, ever new"—this is the ritual attendance; the light of the moon is the sacrificial fee. || 4 ||
The worship of the moon should be performed with this mantra, "navo nava" (new, new). A bright mirror should be given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Swiftly the Creator, Mātariśvan, and the Moon increase through his words as he is born from the nectar. The Moon extends long life, progeny, immortality, and prosperity; he bestows a long lifespan.

May the Moon extend long life; may he grant it—may he bestow it. Likewise, may he grant progeny, such as sons and so forth, immortality—the state of being free from the nature of death—and good fortune, that is, auspiciousness and being beloved by the world. The repetition of the word "life" (*āyus*) is for the sake of emphasizing excellence. For he, being born from the nectar of the Supreme Brahman at the beginning of each lunar day (*pratipad*), increases day by day. The suffix *asi* is an *auṇādika* (irregular) formation. He becomes the supporter and ordainer of the fourth human goal (*puruṣārtha*), which is honored [as the highest].
Born again from the oblation, the moon is filled from the east with milk and offerings; may the moon—the embryo of milk, swelling for the deities—grant immortality and fearlessness.

And with milks—milk meaning cow's milk—again and again, repeatedly, or many times; and with the embryo—the moon, which is the deity intended for sacrifice—swelling, nourishing through the means of replenishing plants and so forth, may he grant me immortality free from suffering and fear.
Swell up; let virile strength gather from every side unto you, O Soma; be present at the gathering of the prize.

O Soma, swell; cause us to increase. Let your virile power—your capacity for impregnation and your quality of nourishment—come together from every side, from all directions. Furthermore, become the cause of our union with *vāja*, that is, with food.

May thy milks come together, and let thy strengths, thy virile powers that overcome the enemy, unite with thee. Swelling for the sake of immortality, O Soma, bestow upon us the highest glories in heaven. O Soma, may thy milks (*payāṃsi*) come together and meet with thee; may thy strengths (*vājāḥ*), meaning foods (*annāni*), also meet with thee; and may thy virile powers (*vṛṣṇyāni*), which cause increase, likewise meet with thee. Of what sort art thou? Thou art the overcomer of the enemy (*abhimātiṣāhaḥ*), the subduer and conqueror of battles.

O Soma, being nourished by us with this oblation, become immortal for the sake of heaven—that is, for the attainment of the celestial realm—and bestow upon us supreme glories and foods fit for sacrifice.

"Ever new he becomes as he is born; as the banner of the days, he goes to the forefront of the dawns. Bestowing his portion upon the gods, the moon extends long life. This moon, waxing at the beginning of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so forth, becomes ever new. As a banner (*ketu*), he goes to the front of the days—the daylight hours—and of the dawns—the nights—because he serves as the indicator of the time of the first lunar day and subsequent periods.
Furthermore, because he consists of nectar (*amṛta*), he bestows a portion upon the gods and extends long life. This is the contemplation of the moon.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth section (kāṇḍikā). 38.
Now begins the thirty-ninth section:
In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place.
Starting from birth, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) for the child should be performed in the sixth month. || 1 ||

Having combined all the foods and offered oblations with the verses "O God, giver of life" and "O you whose face is ghee," he should have the boy eat the food with the verse "O Lord of food, of the food."

Having mixed all the sacrificial foods together, he should offer oblations with the two verses, "O God, giver of life" (*āyurdā deva*) and "O Agni, whose face is ghee" (*ghṛtapratīka*), and then have the boy eat the food with the mantra, "O Lord of food, [give us] food. "O God, giver of life, choosing old age, clothed in ghee, O Agni whose back is ghee; drinking the ghee and the lovely nectar of the cow, lead this boy to old age, as a father leads his son."

Drinking this cow-born nectar which bestows immortality, and this beautiful, excellent clarified butter (*ghṛta*), lead this child to old age; cause him to reach maturity. Like whom? Like a father leading his son. O radiant one, giver of life, you who choose—that is, increase—old age, clothing yourself in clarified butter (bestowing it), being "butter-backed" (*ghṛtapṛṣṭha*)—that is, endowed with the clarified butter being offered and situated above—lead this child to old age.

*Ghṛtapratīkaḥ, ghṛtapṛṣṭhaḥ, agniḥ, ghṛtāhavanaḥ, ghṛtam asya dhāma. Ghṛtam uṣasaḥ haritaḥ tvā vahantu; ghṛtaṃ piban yajatrā deva devān.* (Triṣṭubh; addressed to Agni. He who calls out to the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is *ghṛtapratīkaḥ*. *Ghṛtapṛṣṭhaḥ* has already been explained. *Ghṛtāhavanaḥ* is that in which the invocation and offering (*āhavana*) of clarified butter take place on all sides. Likewise, clarified butter is the abode (*dhāma*), the home of this Agni. May the golden rays of the dawn carry you, O Agni; drinking the clarified butter, O worshipful God, bring the gods here. (Triṣṭubh; addressed to Agni. He who calls out to the clarified butter is *ghṛtapratīkaḥ*. *Ghṛtapṛṣṭhaḥ* has been explained. *Ghṛtāhavanaḥ* is that where the invocation and oblation of clarified butter occur everywhere. Similarly, clarified butter is the dwelling-place of this Agni.

Since you are such a fire, therefore, O Blessed One, O God Agni, may the drops of clarified butter (*ghṛtapruṣaḥ*), like green horses, carry you—that is, reach you and cause you to swell. And you, drinking the clarified butter, O God, worship the gods; that is, honor and gratify them. For it is through the medium of Agni that the satisfaction of the gods occurs.

O Lord of Food, grant us food that is free from disease and full of vigor. Further the giver; grant us strength for our bipeds and quadrupeds. O Lord of Food, King Soma—for it is heard in the Śruti, "Soma is indeed the king of plants"—grant us food, bestow food upon us that is free from *amīva* (disease) and full of *śuṣma* (vigor), which is happiness and a source of well-being. Further the giver; carry him across, remove the afflictions of the ocean of saṃsāra for him.
"Grant us nourishment, food, and strength for our bipeds and quadrupeds, such as cows, horses, and the like. Thus ends the rite of the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana).
Thus ends the thirty-ninth section (kāṇḍikā). 39.
Now begins the fortieth section:
When the greater part of the third year has passed, one causes the tonsure (cūḍā) to be performed.

When the greater part of the third year from birth has passed, the *cūḍākarma* (tonsure ceremony) must be performed. Taking half [of that year] as the limit, the seventh month is "more," while the eighth is "greater"; when that [eighth part] has passed, it should be performed in the ninth month. It is stated by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) that even a learned man, though capable, should not perform it himself, but rather through another. || 1 ||
To the south, the Kapūjas among the Vasiṣṭhas. ||2||

The *kapūjā* is the *cūḍā*. It should be performed on the right side of the head for those born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage. [The word] "dakṣiṇe" [is used here]; the suffix *-tasi* is applied after words such as "dakṣiṇa" in the sense of "on the right. || 2 ||
In this case, the rule applies to both sides of the descendants of Kaśyapa.
On the southern and northern parts of the heads of both, the topknot (śikhā) should be made for those born of the Atri lineage and the Kaśyapa lineage respectively. || 3 ||
The Bhṛgus are shaven-headed. || 4 ||
Those born of the Bhṛgu lineage should be made shaven-headed and devoid of topknots. ||4||
The five-crested ones are the Aṅgirasas. || 5 ||
Those born in the Āṅgirasa lineage are to be made five-crested. || 5 ||
Some [say] "vājine. || 6 ||
Some desire the Vājis for the Āṅgirasas; the Vāji is the row of hair. 6.
Others [hold that] the crest-lock is for the sake of auspiciousness.

Those who are other than those mentioned—namely Agastya, Viśvāmitra, and the rest—are born with tufts of hair (*śikhin*). For what purpose? For the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). Indeed, the state of being devoid of a tuft (*niḥśikhatva*) is an inauspicious quality and a cause of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*). Thus they recite:
"This head is impure which is without a tuft."
And the traditional injunction regarding the practice of wearing a topknot (*śikhā-karma*) is based on the disparaging statement: "Where arrows fly together like the featherless shafts of youths. (7)
Or according to the family custom. || 8 ||

Or, one should perform the single-crest (ekashikha) and other rites without transgressing the family customs, for even family practices are remembered as being dharma: "By that path which his fathers have gone, by that which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that, he shall not come to harm.

On an auspicious day of the bright fortnight or on a festival day, having kindled the fire as prescribed and offered oblations with the *jaya* and other formulas, he consecrates the warm water with the mantra: "This Savitṛ has come with the razor; O Vāyu, come with warm water! The Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, being of one mind, shave [the hair] of King Soma, they who are wise. || 9 ||

The portion beginning with *puṇyāha* and ending with *hutvā* has already been explained. With the verse beginning *āyam agāt*, he consecrates the warm water with the *brahman* [formula]. The meter is *jagatī*; the deities are the Viśvedevas; [the seer is] Brahmā.

The *ārṣa* [mantra] continues up to the conclusion of the initiation (*upanayana*). This Savitṛ has come with the razor and warm water; therefore, O Vāyu, you too come along with these two. O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, being of one mind and single intent, you too shave this boy—meaning, you should tonsure him—just as one would for King Soma. According to the Vedic text, "Soma is indeed the king of plants," the sense is that you should tonsure him, regarding him as a vessel of honor like a king.

"May all the warm and cold [waters], having come together—Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ of true law—grant their approval to that. "You are givers of moisture; you are givers of life. O flowing waters, flow here, moisten him for living, for long life, and for splendor"—with these words, he should pour water over him. 10.

With the words beginning with "uṣṇāśca" and ending with "varcase," he sprinkles [the boy]; the meaning is that he should wash the boy's head with consecrated waters using the root *undī* in the sense of "cleansing."

O Waters, protect and guard this young boy right here in this very place—both you who are warm and those who are cool, all of you having come together and united. And may Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ grant their consent and favor to that protection. Of what nature [are they]? They are "possessors of true dharma" (*satyadharmāṇaḥ*), for truth alone is their dharma; and for this very reason, he is one whose resolve is true (*satyasaṃkalpaḥ*). O Waters, you are "givers of moisture" (*ārdradānavaḥ*), bestowers of the state of moistness. [The word] *dānu* is derived from the root *dā* (to give) with the suffix *anu*, according to the rules of the Uṇādi-sūtras.

Thus, you are givers of life; you are those who bestow life. Moistening, that is, causing to be wet, may the waters moisten [you] for living—that is, for the sake of life—and for long-livedness, and for vitality (*āyus*). [The form] *tvapate* is a contraction of *tvapatyoḥ*. For splendor—that is, for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and for excellence of form. || 10 ||

On the right side of the hair-parting, having placed a blade of *darbha* grass between with the mantra, "O herb, protect [him]," and having applied the razor with the mantra, "O razor," he shaves with the mantras: "With that razor wherewith Savitṛ, the knower, shaved the hair of King Soma and Varuṇa, with that, O Brahmins, shave this [boy] today, so that he may be long-lived, reaching old age, and established in this world, [N.N.]. "With that wherewith Dhātṛ shaved for the sake of the life of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra, with that shave his hair for the sake of life, for renown, and for well-being. "With that wherewith Pūṣan shaved for the sake of the life of Prajāpati, Agni, and Sūrya..."

"By that [means], bestow upon him life, renown, and well-being; by which he may live long and behold the sun again and again. "By that [means], bestow upon him life, renown, and well-being. With these mantras, he performs the darbha-sickle rite, moving clockwise toward each direction.

On the right side of the head, having placed a blade of *darbha* grass between [the hair and the razor] with the mantra "O herb, protect him," and having applied and pressed down the razor with the mantra "O razor, do not harm him," the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should perform the ritual action of shaving with the *darbha*-grass and razor using the four *anuṣṭubh* verses beginning with "With that wherewith he shaved... starting from the right side and proceeding clockwise, one mantra for each direction: with the first verse on the right side, and with the second verse on the western side.

With the third [verse], on the subsequent day; with the fourth, on the sky. "O herb, protect this boy; guard him. O razor, svadhiti, do not harm this boy. With that razor with which Savitṛ shaved the head of King Soma and Varuṇa, with that, O Brahmins, shave—i.e., tonsure—the head of this child today, on this day. Of what sort is Savitṛ? Knowing—that is, aware. Shave in such a way that this child becomes long-lived.

He reaches old age and becomes one whose life has reached its full span. By the word "this" (*asau*), a specific name is indicated. With that very razor with which Dhātṛ, Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra shaved their heads for the sake of long life—with that same razor, shave the head of this child for the sake of long life, for good renown, for fame, and likewise for well-being and non-destruction. The mantra beginning with "with which Pūṣan... has its meaning already explained by the preceding commentary.

"By which [razor] the night may see the sun again and for a long time; by which razor the night shaved the sun again and again. "Again" (*bhūyas*) means repeatedly. "For a long time" (*jyok*) means for a duration. "Paśyā" means that which sees; thus *jyokpaśyā* is the night that sees much. The rest, beginning with "by which," is the same as before. || 11 ||

"O barber, as you shave the hair with a well-fashioned razor, may you shave the hair; cleanse the head, do not rob him of his life"—with these words, he hands over the iron razor for the shaving of the hair. || 12 ||

With the *yajus* beginning with "yatkṣureṇa," he gives the razor to the barber; "lohāyasam" is a name for a specific type of blade well-known among barbers. Others, however, say that since the fact that it is made of metal (*loha*) is already established by the mention of "razor" (*kṣura*), the mention of "metal" (*loha*) is for the purpose of praise.

"O barber, with that razor—which, being possessed of the quality of extreme sharpness and so forth, is most excellent—the meaning being 'with that which is most praised'—the word *yat* here ending in the elided third case singular; O shaver, O barber, with that razor by which you shave the hair, with that well-fashioned one, with that revolving and turning [tool], do not steal away his life, i.e., do not kill him; rather, cleanse his head, purify his head. || 12 ||

"May this splendor not depart following after your hair; likewise may Dhātṛ grant it to you. May Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ bestow radiance (*varcas*) upon you"—with these words he consecrates [the child] as it falls.

(13) With this preceding *bṛhatī* verse, he consecrates the falling hair: "May this well-known splendor, such as form and so forth, not go away following after your hair—that is, behind the hair. Likewise, may Dhātṛ Prajāpati grant splendor to you. Likewise, may Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ bestow—may they grant—radiance, such as excellence of form and so forth, upon you. (13)
She gathers the unripe fruits, which are to be accepted by her friends, upon green cow-dung.
The rule is that the hair should be caught by a friend as it falls;

she gathers those falling hairs while they are being rubbed and shaved upon green cow-dung—she gathers them thoroughly, receives them, and having mixed them with the green cow-dung, forms them into balls; such is a certain custom. || 14 ||

"Having plucked out the hair of King Varuṇa, Soma, Dhātṛ, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and Agni—seeking help, they have found for them a manifold place of deposit between heaven and earth. With this verse he consecrates the [stalks] as they are being carried toward the north-eastern direction.

With this *triṣṭubh* verse addressed to Viśvedevas, the performer recites over the hair as it is being led toward the north-eastern direction by Mitra: "Having shaved you, having shorn you, they found in many ways that receptacle—that place—belonging to King Varuṇa, for the sake of those [hair]. Where? In the midst, between heaven and earth. Who are they? Soma (the Moon), Dhātṛ (Prajāpati), Savitṛ (the Sun), and Viṣṇu (Agni)."
The term *avasyuḥ* is connected with each [of the preceding words]. *Avaḥ* means protection (*avana*). One who desires protection is *avasyuḥ*;
by the rules "supa ātmanaḥ kyac" and "kyāc chandasi," the suffix *u* is added, meaning "one who desires protection. || 15 ||
"Embrace her when she is not empty," so says the Śruti. ||16||

In a cool place provided with non-empty durvā grass, creepers, trees, and so forth, one should have the hair bound together as if it were a friend; this is established by the Vedic scripture, demonstrating that this rite is rooted in the Śruti, as shown in the passage beginning: "Where the arrows fly forth like boys with feathered shafts. (16)
He grants a boon to the performer. || 17 ||
The sacrificer gives a boon as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priest according to his ability; they say that a four-year-old cow is the sacrificial fee in this case. (17)
He offers a tuft of eyelashes as soft as sesame seeds for the purpose of shaving his hair. || 18 ||
One gives a sesame vessel wrapped with fine woolen threads to a barber. || 18 ||
One should feed the Brahmins food accompanied by clarified butter. ||19||

The meaning has been explained. Because the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) are specified in the *cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure ceremony) while the primary element (*pradhāna*) is not explicitly mentioned, they say that the primary rite should be performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) using either a verse addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*) or one addressed to the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevī*). Alternatively, by the phrase "having kindled [the fire]" (*upasamādhāya*), another portion of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) is indicated, and that itself is the primary rite. However, for those for whom the "kindling" is merely a consecration of the fire, the former [the kindling] is the primary rite. || 19 ||
Thus ends the commentary on the tonsure ceremony.
And the fortieth section (kāṇḍikā) is completed. || 40 ||
Now follow the Laugākṣi Gṛhyasūtras belonging to the Caraka recension of the Kaṭha school.
Accompanied by the commentary composed by Devapāla.
The forty-first section (kāṇḍikā).
The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa occurs in the seventh year. 1.

From birth, in the seventh year from conception, the *upāyana*—the approaching of the teacher and the sacrament of binding the girdle (*mekhalā-bandhana*)—is the primary rite for a Brāhmaṇa. For when that has occurred, one gains the right to study the Śruti and Smṛti. Therefore, it is recorded as a second birth: "The first birth is from the mother; the second is from the binding of the girdle. Here, Sāvitrī is called the mother, and the teacher is called the father. (1)
In the ninth [month], for the Kṣatriya. || 2 ||

According to the principle of the *aveṣṭi* section, a king is a Kṣatriya; his offspring is a Rājanya, that is, a Kṣatriya boy. For him, the initiation (*upanayana*) takes place from the ninth year after birth, that is, in the tenth year. || 2 ||
In the eleventh year, for a Vaiśya. || 3 ||
It is the same as the preceding.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the time for initiation does not expire until the sixteenth year; for a Rājanya, until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, until the twenty-fourth.

The prefix *ā* is used here in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). For a Brāhmaṇa, the time for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is not exceeded until the end of the sixteenth year; likewise, for a Kṣatriya until the end of the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya until the end of the twenty-fourth. || 4 ||

When he has bathed and his hair is combed, having established the fire as prescribed and offered oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, he addresses an unwashed garment with the mantra: "The Revatīs anointed you; the Kṛttikās fashioned you; the waters stretched you out; the prayers wove you; the goddesses cleansed you; a thousand approached you from all sides; eighty wove the middle; the women [wove] you. (5)

Having bathed, with his hair grown and his head shaved, when that young student has arrived, the officiant—having performed the ritual kindling of the fire according to rule, its establishment upon a specially prepared spot of earth that has been swept, sprinkled, and cleared of grass, followed by the fanning, the sprinkling around, and the strewing of grass—and having placed the clarified butter nearby, melted it, and inspected it; then, having brought the staff, girdle, and other implements as required, the initiator (upanetā) offers oblations with the *jaya* verses and others ending with the names of the seasons and constellations, and with the *śakvarī* verse beginning "revatīstva... and so forth.

Placing a new, unwashed, and unused garment in his hand, he consecrates it with the following mantra. Indeed, this is the sequence of the garment’s production: first, the cotton is beaten and winnowed by divine women with clods of earth; then it is spun, meaning it is wound and brought to the state of thread; thereafter, it is stretched out by a weaver; then it is smoothed with a brush. After that, the weaver weaves the cloth; and once the cloth is finished, he joins the fringes to both ends like two sprouts.

In this mantra, the sequence is praised by superimposing the agency of specific deities upon the destruction and other processes of cotton and similar materials. O cloth, the Revatī deities "wove" (vyakṣṇan) you—that is, they specifically spun you; while in the state of cotton, they struck you with clods of earth and other tools. The Kṛttikās—derived from the root *kṛt* in the sense of "encircling"—made "weavings" (*kartayaḥ*), that is, they performed the encircling; they fashioned the thread and, through that means, brought you into being.

The active and sinless Maruts stretched you out—that is to say, they specifically stretched you out, having brought you to the state of being woven. For the weaving of a specific cloth is accomplished through a specific application of the intellect; thus, "the Gnas purified [you]. According to the rule *avyavahitāśca*, the word *ava* is connected with *mṛjinā*. The Gnas—the deities—purified [you]; that is to say, they performed the cleansing of the thread already stretched out by means of a brush (*kūrca*), as the root *mṛj* signifies purification.

"Stretching out a thousand ends on both sides"—the word *abhitaḥ* means "on both sides," that is, at the two ends; the particle *uditi* has the sense of *tathā* ("so"); the word *sahasra* signifies "a great number. They stretched out—that is, they bound—a thousand ends of ten [folds]. Of what? It should be construed with "the *gnās* (women/divine powers). "Eighty women spun the middle quickly"—the word *nu* expresses speed; the eighty *nārīs*, who are the goddesses Nāgas, spun (*avayan*) the middle of the cloth, meaning they wove it. || 5 ||
"O divine waters, clothe the god Savitṛ with splendor for the sake of Savitṛ; lead him to a life of a hundred years so that he may live"—with these words, he causes him to put on the garment.

With this *yajus* (sacrificial formula), he causes him to put on the garment: "O goddesses, Revatī and the others, put on this garment; cause it to be put on. For whom? For the radiant youth (*māṇavaka*). You too, O youth, put it on; cause it to be put on. Savitṛ—by way of transposition, 'O Savitṛ'—cause this garment to be put on for the youth, the progenitor of the knowledge of the deity. You too, O youth, put it on; cause it to be put on, having become Savitṛ."

Lead him, bring him; lead this young boy to Brahman—that is, cause him to attain the state of a Brāhmaṇa, meaning make him endowed with the abundance of the Vedas—and make him one who lives for a hundred years.

This [set of] three mantras is for the putting on of the lower garment (*adhovāsas*) among the various garments; the upper garment (*uttarīya*) is said to be an antelope skin (*ajina*). According to Ādityadarśana, one consecrates the person who has put on the garment with the verses beginning "Go to old age" (*jarāṃ gaccha*). However, such is not the practice of the teachers (*ācāryas*), nor does the indicative mark of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*) support this; therefore, the application must be construed otherwise: that each mantra is specific to a single garment, meaning the triad of mantras is used for the putting on of each individual garment.

In that regard, "tatra devīr devāya" is the first mantra common to all three castes; "jarāṃ gaccha" is the second, common to all in the rite of donning the garment; and for the three beginning with "paramam," each one is respectively specific to each caste—thus there are three mantras for the donning of the garment for each individual. || 6 ||
Go to old age; put on the garment. You have become full-bodied, a protector against imprecation. Live for a hundred autumns, many in number, and clothe yourself in the nourishment of wealth. 7.

By the indicative mark of the mantra, this [garment] is also for the purpose of wearing. The initiator says: "O boy, put on the garment. He pronounces a blessing: "Go to old age"—that is, become one whose body is worn out by old age. "Become swollen" (*āpīvān bhūḥ*): from the root *sphāyī*, *opyāyī*, meaning "to grow," with the prefix *ā-*. By the rule "*āto maninkanibvanipaśca*," the suffix *vanip* is applied; thus, the meaning is "become fully grown."

The phrase "you have become a purifier from reproach" (*anabhiśastipāvā abhūḥ*) is to be supplied [from the preceding verse]. "Reproach" (*abhiśas*) is censure; it is the connection with evil. "Non-reproach" (*anabhiśasti*) is the warding off of that, which is the absence of evil. Having established this as a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), there is a connection with the ritual duty (*dharma*) through exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Thus, "one who protects against reproach" is *anabhiśastipāvā*. Live for a hundred autumns, and may you maintain your vital breaths for a hundred autumns.

"Purucīḥ" is an epithet for "autumns" (*śaradaḥ*); the word *puru* signifies abundance. [They are called] *purūcyaḥ* because they lead to or accomplish many purposes for men. "Of the *purucīnām*—that is, of abundant—wealth (*rāyaḥ*) and prosperity (*poṣam*), provide nourishment; maintain it on all sides. (7)

"We place this Soma for great splendor and for great hearing, so that it may lead him to old age, that he may long remain awake for hearing, and that he may ever be alert regarding his hearing"—this is for a Brāhmaṇa. (8)

This is the mantra for the investiture of the Brahmin, because it contains the term "Soma"; since the other two [castes] lack a connection with Soma, the Śruti states: "If he should officiate at a sacrifice for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, having brought branches of the Nyagrodha tree, having crushed them and mixed them with curd, he should give that to him as his portion, but not Soma."

"O young student, we clothe you with this garment, saying 'We clothe you (idantaḥ)'; we clothe you, we cause you to be clothed; indeed, we cause Soma himself to be clothed. For by means of you, through this rite of initiation (*upanayana*), Soma himself will be clothed and maintained; for the Veda shall belong to you through the medium of the study of its meaning. For what purpose do we clothe you? 'For great splendor' (*tejase mahe*); that is, for great [splendor], or for honor—for *maha* is a form derived from the root *maha*, meaning 'to honor.'"

The *śrotra* is that which is heard; it refers to the Veda. For the sake of that means for the purpose of attaining the Veda and its meaning—or alternatively, for the sake of the *śrotriya*, i.e., the disciple endowed with hearing—the purport is: "O Teacher, may you become one who has mastered the Vedas and is beneficial to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*)."

Just as this particular garment brings you to old age—that is, the youth leads you to old age—so do we cause you to put it on by means of dressing you; that is to say, I dress you in such a way that many garments will be worn out through use. "Be watchful for a long time for the ear"—that is, for the Veda; the meaning is: may you remain vigilant for a long duration regarding the Veda and its meaning, consisting of study, comprehension, and practice.
May he remain ever vigilant in his hearing; may he stay awake for a long time to instruct his disciples, for he is preeminent in the supreme dharma of altruism. || 8 ||

"We place this Indra for great power and for great dominion, so that he may lead him to old age, that he may long remain watchful for dominion, and that he may long keep watch over his dominion"—this is for the Rājanya. 9.

"O student (brahmacārin), we clothe you; we cause you to put on the garment. Together with Indra, by our two arms—we who are born as Indra, the Kṣatriya, that supreme lord himself, through his capacity for protecting the subjects—for what purpose? For vigor (ojas), that is, for strength; for greatness (maha), that is, for being honored; and for dominion (kṣatra), that is, for the protection of the virtuous and for enthusiasm. The rest has already been explained. (9)

"We place this man about for long life and for great prosperity, so that they may lead him to old age, that he may long remain awake for prosperity, and that he may ever be vigilant for prosperity"—this is for the Vaiśya. (10)
He is called Manu because he belongs to the human race (*mānuṣatva*). "Poṣa" means the nourishment of wealth; it is for that purpose. The rest is the same [as before]. || 10 ||

"Put on this garment for well-being; be stout, a protector against curses. Live a hundred autumns as a hero of great prowess; being powerful and living well, distribute riches. With these words, he consecrates the garment that has been put on. || 11 ||

The initiator (upanetā) performs this consecration with the formula for all three castes who have put on the garment. Here too, as before, the word *pari* has a non-adjacent connection (vyavahitānvaya). "O boy, you have put on (*pari-adhidhāḥ*), that is, you have clothed yourself in (*paryaṣyadhāḥ*) this garment with excellence and distinction; for the sake of well-being (*svastaye*), that is, for the sake of non-destruction (*avināśāya*), may you become full (*āpīvā*), that is, swollen (*āpīnaḥ*) and increased. Being a protector against reproach (*anabhiśastipāvā*)—one who protects (*pāti*) or guards (*rakṣati*) against being reproached (*anabhiśasta*)—may you live for a hundred autumns, and may you be possessed of good heroes (*suvīraḥ*)."

Be joined with excellent sons; likewise, being noble, distribute your riches and wealth—especially bestow them or give them to your attendants, kinsmen, and others. Living well means living a good life through happiness and such. 11.

With the two verses, "At every junction" (*yoge yoge*) and "The youth, well-clothed" (*yuvā suvāsaḥ*), he leads Agni toward the south; then, with the verse, "Come, mount the stone; like a stone, may you be firm. May all the gods grant you a life of a hundred autumns," he makes him step upon the stone with his right foot. || 12 ||

Having taken aim at the fire with the mantra "yoge yoge" and the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," and having brought the young student around so that he remains to the right [of the fire], the teacher causes him to step upon a stone with his right foot while reciting the mantra "āśmānamātiṣṭha. Thus, the teacher makes him stand firmly upon the stone.
In every endeavor, in every contest, we invoke the most powerful Indra as our friend for protection.

This has been explained. Here, in the circumambulation of the fire (*vahni-pradakṣiṇa*), the connection (*yoga*)—that is, the relationship—is specified. In every instance of the connection (*yoge yoge*) that must be performed in relation to the duties of a religious student (*brahmacāri-kriyā*), and at every offering of oblation (*vāje vāje*, i.e., *haviṣi haviṣi*), we invoke (*havāmahe*) Indra for protection (*ūtaye*, i.e., *avanāya*), the most powerful (*tavastaraṃ*, i.e., *balavattaraṃ*) friend (*sakhāyaṃ*, i.e., *sahāyam*).
The youth, well-attired and girt with the sacrificial cord, has come; he becomes more excellent as he is born. Wise poets, devout in mind and seeking the gods, uplift him.

This mantra is employed elsewhere for the raising of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). In that context, the meaning of the mantra is as follows: the sacrificial post itself—youthful, new, and recently cut—has arrived, completely encircled by a beautiful cloth and a girdle. Wise ones—the learned officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), desiring the gods and wishing to perform the animal sacrifice—raise it up with their minds.

The subject under discussion here is this: the youthful celibate student (*brahmacārī*), well-dressed in beautiful garments, fully veiled and covered—the celibate self (*brahmacāry-ātmā*)—for he is eternally young and clothed in hempen raiment, has come; he has arrived at this body by the power of karma. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) connected with the celibate student must be explained; for he too, like a garment, is veiled by the body and has entered the body of the celibate student.

And that youth, eternally youthful and a celibate student (brahmacārī), being born, rises and becomes exalted; like the wind in the sky, his self (ātman) increases through hunger and other such states.

The wise—the steadfast, the learned, the poets who possess far-reaching vision—elevate it; they lead it upward, cause the self to attain liberation, cause the vital breath to ascend, and lead it to the aperture of Brahman (brahmadvara). They also elevate the body of the celibate student (brahmacārin) and bring it to excellence through the performance of the sections on ritual action and knowledge. Being of noble intellect and virtuous deeds, they elevate it with one-pointed mind.
"Come hither," [it says]. O young boy, come, approach; mount upon the stone, the rock; be firm like a stone. May all the gods grant you life for a hundred autumns, for a hundred years. || 12 ||

"I give my vow to your heart; let your mind be in accordance with my mind. Delight in my word with single-minded devotion; may Bṛhaspati unite you to me. With these words, he strokes [the student] upward from the region of the navel with his hand.

With the mantra beginning "mama vrata" (my vow), the preceptor strokes the student, who is a *brahmacārin*, starting from the navel up to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). "Vrata" is a name for the ritual act. "O *brahmacārin*, I place your heart within my vow"—that is, I give your heart to my ritual act; the meaning is that your heart should be an assistant to the act I intend to perform. "May my mind be your following mind"—the meaning is that your mind should follow after my mind.

"Be single-minded toward my words—my speech—and take pleasure in them; that is to say, being one-pointed in mind, study what I teach. Speech indeed is the *Bṛhatī*, and its lord is Bṛhaspati, the Self. May He enjoin you—that is, through the means of right resolve, may He set you to work in service to me and so forth—for my sake; for if that is so, there will be the fulfillment of my role as teacher and it will be a benefit to me as well. (13)
Having consumed the curd three times with the mantra "O Dadhikrāvan," he causes [the student] to recite: "I have come to the state of celibacy; lead me to it! Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. || 14 ||

The student (*brahmacārī*) speaks; the teacher (*ācārya*) causes him to recite the formula beginning with *brahmacaryam* and ending with *svar*. Having done what? Having caused the student to consume curd three times with the mantra beginning *dadhikrāvṇaḥ*, and having employed the student in that consumption. The intended meaning is that after eating and rinsing his mouth (*ācānta*), the student recites "brahmacaryam" and so forth, being prompted by the teacher.

"I have praised Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the swift horse. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives. This [verse] has been explained. Regarding the words "brahmacaryam" and so forth, the student (*brahmacārī*) speaks: "O Teacher, I have come to *brahmacarya*; I have arrived at, I have attained, the practice (*caraṇa*) of *brahman*, that is, the Veda. *Brahmacarya* has been resolved upon by me as something necessarily to be performed. Therefore, initiate me (*upanayakha*), meaning 'purify me'. The verb form is the imperative (*loṭ*) used for a request.

He [the teacher] makes this known through the use of the *ātmanepada* ending: "The fruit of your success as a teacher will be that you sanctify me. However, Ādityadarśana has explained it thus: the Guru said, "Brahmā is Prajāpati; his 'foot' (caraṇa) is the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*). I have gone to—that is, reached—that state. Therefore, initiate me; lead me into the presence of Brahman, O student (*brahmacārin*), and so forth. This should be reflected upon. "Om" is the designation of Brahman, according to the Vedic scripture: "Om is Brahman; Kha is Brahman."

"Bhūḥ" refers to the deity residing in the earthly realm (bhūrloka), who is said to be Agni by virtue of his form; "bhuvaḥ" refers to the deity of the intermediate space (antarikṣa), who, as before, is so called because of his location therein, and he is Vāyu; "svaḥ" refers to the deity residing in the heavenly realm (svarloka), who is said to consist of Āditya. || 14 ||

Driving away ill-spoken words, purifying my pure color, this goddess has come to me; bestowing strength through out-breath and in-breath, may this auspicious, fortunate goddess, the girdle, be my friend. Guardian of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), overcomer of heat, slaying the demon and conquering the enemy—encompass us on every side with your blessing! O girdle, may we not come to harm while you are our supporter. Born from faith and arisen from ascetic fervor (*tapas*), she became the sister of the seers who composed the mantras.
While making him recite, "O girdle, embrace me; bestow upon me fervor and sensory power," he ties the girdle around him. || 15 ||

The teacher brings the girdle while having the student recite these *triṣṭubh* verses beginning with "This [girdle] from ill-spoken words. The student speaks; the teacher causes him to recite: "This girdle, warding off—that is, preventing—ill-spoken words such as evil or untruthful speech, purifying the *varṇa* (caste), namely the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, by means of restraining the fickleness of speech, hands, and feet through the injunction of discipline, and thereby producing fitness for study and so forth; or else, purifying the *varṇa* (complexion) such as beauty, etc., when it is bound upon him."

"Pure by nature," or "fit for purification. She has come—that is, she has arrived—to me, bestowing or granting strength through the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) by means of Vedic study and so forth. Regarding the root *bhaj* in the sense of "crushing" (*āmardane*), she "crushes" or destroys that which consists of [mere] phonemes; for when she is present, study is performed. And since that study is performed by restraining the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, her strength—that of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—is taken away by her. She is a "companion" (*sakhā*) because she shares the same name. She is a "goddess" (*devī*) because she is endowed with qualities such as luminosity.

She is auspicious and heart-pleasing, joined with fresh and tender *muñja* grass. She is the lineage of *ṛta* (the cosmic order) and truth, and its protectress; for when she is present, the speaking of what is desired [but false] is prevented. Or, she is the guardian of *ṛta*, that is, of the sacrifice (*yajña*), because one proceeds to the sacred sites of the Vedas and so forth while wearing the girdle. She is the savior of austerity—that is, of Vedic study accompanied by vows and observances—leading it across and bringing it to its completion. She is the destroyer of *rakṣases* and *yātudhānas*; for the Śruti declares, "The girdle is indeed a thunderbolt."

Overpowering the enemy, or rather, overcoming and subduing the one who gives to the foe—meaning she wards off both wretchedness and enemies—may she come to us from every side with auspicious conduct. O girdle, may we, being your supporters and sustainers, not suffer harm; for "riṣ" is a verb meaning injury, let there be no injury to us who wear you. She is the daughter of Faith (Śraddhā), that is, the daughter of the quality of trustworthiness, and Faith is her mother.

Born from austerity, austerity is her father; she became the sister—the very sibling—of the seers who are composers of mantras and possessors of perfect knowledge. O girdle, you who are such as this, lick me thoroughly (the root *lih* meaning "to taste" undergoes a phonetic change in the Vedic form *rerihava*); embrace me, bestow upon me austerity—that study joined with self-restraint—and grant me the keenness of the senses. 15.
He gives a triple-stranded girdle made of muñja grass to the Brāhmaṇa, a bowstring made of murvā fiber to the Rājanya, and one made of hempen threads to the Vaiśya.

[It should be] made of seven muñja grasses, triple-stranded—that is, wound three times. "Trivṛt-vajra" means a ninefold [braid]. In such passages as "one should encircle the sacrificial post with a triple-stranded [rope]," the word *trivṛt* refers to the rope; in such passages as "the *trivṛt* stoma," the word *trivṛt* refers to a group of nine. Here too, the word *trivṛt* refers to the rope when it is threefold, according to established usage (*sadācāra*). Therefore, some explain the girdle (*mekhalā*) as being ninefold out of error.

*Murva* is a specific kind of grass; its derivative form is *maurvī*, which refers to the bowstring—the cord to be stretched upon the bow. He gives this to the Kṣatriya. To the Vaiśya, he gives a *sautrī* string; although the term is used generically, according to the Smṛtis, it should be understood as being made of cotton thread. One should understand that the sequence is such that he first gives [the string] and subsequently ties it on.

"Thou art the equal of the mind; thou art the divine knot; do not come loose"—having thus made a knot, he causes [the student] to recite: "The eye of Mitra, the supporting, for strength, lustrous, glorious, firm, and prosperous; this unwearied, moving garment, the skin of the antelope—this may I put on as a prize-winning skin. He gives the skin of the black antelope to a Brāhmaṇa, that of the tiger to a Rājanya, and that of the ruru deer to a Vaiśya. (17)
Having tied the knot of the girdle with the mantra, "Thou art equal to the mind," the initiator, as prescribed by family tradition—according to the traditional rule:

"With a triple-knotted [girdle], or with one, three, or five knots"—reciting the mantra beginning with "Of Mitra," gives the skin of a black antelope (*aiṇeya*) to a Brāhmaṇa, a tiger skin to a Rājanya, and the skin of a *ruru* deer to a Vaiśya. For both the tying of the girdle and the giving of the skins, the two mantras are common to all three castes.

"Of the mind": O Knot, you are equal to the mind; just as the mind of a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) does not waver from his vow and remains pure through his study and other duties, so too you do not waver, because you remain steadfast for as long as the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*). "Divine" means related to the gods; this is praise for you, the Knot. Therefore, do not loosen—that is, do not become released.

The verse beginning with "mitrasya" is a Triṣṭubh. The religious student (brahmacārī) says: "I put on this antelope skin; I put this on. Of what kind is it? It is like the renowned vision (*cakṣus*) of Mitra—the non-injurious one—and of the Hariṇa and Ruru deer. Even in the case of the tiger-skin [option], the tiger is indeed a friend, because of the king's appreciation for the gift of its hide and the remembrance of its courage. It is a "support" (*dharuṇa*), meaning it sustains the practice of celibacy and other virtues.

I entrust this garment for the sake of strength—that is, for the power of celibacy—because it is the instrumental cause of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and brilliance. It is glorious and brings glory. It is "ancient" (*sthavira*), meaning venerable like an elder or exceedingly firm. It is "prosperous" (*samṛddha*), meaning it causes prosperity. It is "not subject to injury" (*anāhanasya*): from the root *āhan* (to strike), the suffix *asun* is applied according to the rule *sarvadhātubhyo'sun*; that which is good for striking is *āhanasya*, and its negation is *anāhanasya*. It is a garment, a covering.

It was "cariṣṇu," meaning it had the habit of moving about during its state as a deer. It was "vājin"; that which possesses "vāja"—meaning food—is a *vājin*. Since they devotedly offered food to it when it was invested with the sacred thread during its state as a student (*brahmacarya*), its status as "food" (*vāja*) is used here figuratively. || 17 ||
"That eye" [the formula] causes one to worship the sun. ||18||

With the words "That eye," and so forth, he causes the worship of the Sun to be performed: "That eye, established by the gods, the bright one rising in the east—may we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns."

That very eye of the three worlds rises, emerges, in the east, in front; it is "devahita," established, impelled, or created by the gods, or beneficial for the gods—that is, for the sense organs. "May we see for a hundred autumns, and seeing, may we live for a hundred years"—thus the student recites while worshipping the sun.
When asked "Who are you? upon the greeting being uttered, he replies, "I am so-and-so, sir. (19)

The teacher asks, "Who are you by name? The word *ka* is a name for Prajāpati; thus, the Brāhmaṇa states: "Who are you by name? Prajāpati indeed is 'Ka' by name. Because he is intent on receiving the Veda, this is a direct question in the form of a riddle, as evidenced by the manner in which the answer is provided. Being questioned by the teacher, the student offers his salutation.

When it is said "this one" by means of uttering his own name, the name is understood; for example, "I am Viṣṇumitra, sir, I salute you. When addressed with such a salutation by a student (*brahmacārin*), the teacher utters a return greeting (*pratyabhivādana*) ending in the nominative case, according to the Smṛti rule: "In a return greeting, [the name] is used [in the nominative], except in the case of a Śūdra," saying, "May you be long-lived, gentle Viṣṇumitra! According to the Smṛti as well: "One should say, 'May you be long-lived, gentle one,' with the final syllable protracted (*pluta*). (19)
At the impulse of God Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand; I initiate you, O [Name]! 20.

The teacher, with his right hand, takes the right hand of the student observing the vow of celibacy (*brahmacārin*) according to the rite prescribed for marriage, beginning with the mantra "Of the god... (*devasya te*). Addressing the disciple by his own name, saying, "O *brahmacārin* Viṣṇumitra, I, the teacher named Hariśarman, initiate you," the Guru, having grasped the hand, speaks while pronouncing his own name. The first word "one" (*ekaḥ*) is for the purpose of addressing the disciple; the second is for the purpose of indicating the teacher’s name. [He says: "I take your hand. Of what kind [of you]?

Of the God, whose nature consists of luminosity and other such qualities, the Impeller (Savitṛ), the generator of knowledge regarding objects and so forth—for what purpose? For the sake of "impulsion" (prasave), that is, for the production of superior knowledge and the like. To offer praise, he says: "One should not wander with the thought, 'I am grasping the hand with my own two arms made of skin,' that is, with my own two hands. What then? [It is done] by the arms of the Aśvins, the divine physicians, and by the hands of Pūṣan. (20)
Savitṛ has taken your hand; Agni is your teacher. Who initiates you into whom? To whom do I entrust you? || 21 ||

The teacher, having taken his hand, says: "Savitṛ—the progenitor of what is desired—Āditya, has taken your hand. The teacher figuratively addresses himself as Savitṛ. "Agni is your teacher, not I; for I am Agni, your teacher, because I blaze forth through my knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, their performance, austerity, and so forth. Being Prajāpati, I, the teacher, initiate you—who are yourself Prajāpati—in your true form, O Viṣṇumitra by name."

He alone is the one who stands within all; and he alone is refined through the removal of defects caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) via various forms of ritual arrangements (*saṃsthāna*). The meaning is: "I entrust you to Prajāpati for the sake of protection; I hand you over to Brahman. (21)
"Whose student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) are you? "I am the student of sacred knowledge of Prāṇa," he replies. || 22 ||

When the teacher asks the indirect question, "Whose brahmacārī are you?", the disciple replies with an indirect answer of acceptance: "I am the brahmacārī of Prāṇa. For Prāṇa is indeed Prajāpati himself, the thread of the universe. Thus says the Śruti: "O Indra, you are Hiraṇyagarbha, the Puruṣa, the Great One; you are Prāṇa, the beginningless thread of the universe; you are Consciousness, the Pure One, the inner Self more radiant than heat; such, O God, are you, the Ordainer of this world. (22)
I entrust you to Prajāpati; I entrust you to the god Savitṛ; I entrust you to Bṛhaspati, O [Name]! O god Savitṛ, this is your student; protect him, that he may be long-lived and not die. 23.

"O Brahmachārin, I give you to Prajāpati for the sake of protection; I give you to the god Savitṛ, the Inner Self, and to Bṛhaspati—for *bṛhatī* is Speech, and its Lord is the Self—to Him I give you. This is the same [as before]. The word "asau" (so-and-so) is for the purpose of indicating the teacher’s name. "O Deva," shining by virtue of self-luminosity; "O Savitṛ," O progenitor of desired vows and the like; "this Brahmachārin is yours"—belonging to you—"protect him, guard him. May he be long-lived; may there be no death for him, may death not happen to him. Even though it is directly perceived...
The Vedic usage is an indirect indication; it is a transposition. || 23 ||
O son of Agni, son of Vāyu, son of Sūrya, son of Viṣṇu, son of Brahmā—this is your brahmacārī; protect him, that he may be long-lived and not die.

The *Ṛgveda* is the son of Agni; the *Yajurveda* is the son of Vāyu; the *Sāmaveda* is the son of Sūrya. O *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*, this religious student (*brahmacārī*) has been given to you for the purpose of protection; thus, he belongs to each of you individually, so guard him. Accordingly, the Brāhmaṇas demonstrate that the *Ṛgveda* and the others possess the status of being sons of Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, respectively.

"Prajāpati alone existed in the beginning; he performed austerity. From him, performing austerity, the three gods were created: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya. They performed austerity, and from them, performing austerity, the three Vedas were created: the Ṛgveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vāyu, and the Sāmaveda from Āditya."

Thus, the aggregate of beings consists of the son of Viṣṇu and the son of Brahmā. Alternatively, the earthly world (bhūloka) is the son of Agni, and its presiding deity is Agni; likewise, the intermediate space (antarikṣaloka) is the son of Vāyu, and the heavenly world (dyuloka) is the son of Sūrya. Or else, "son" (putra) means that which protects much (puru trāyate); thus, he who is both Agni and a son is Agniputra. The same construction applies elsewhere as well. 24.
"You are a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī). Drink water; perform your duties; do not sleep during the day; restrain your speech. ||25||

The Guru said: "O celibate student, since you have now become a *brahmacārin*, understand that these five duties must be performed. Drink water when it is occasioned by the need for sipping (*ācamana*) and so forth; likewise, perform service to the Guru and such acts as the study of the Vedas. Avoid sleeping during the day, yet by my grace, permit yourself to sleep during the day in cases of physical weakness or incapacity, for there is no prohibition against the voluntary desire [for rest].
Furthermore, exercise restraint over your speech; the meaning is that you must not speak untruths, harsh words, or the like."
"So be it," is the acceptance. || 26 ||

The Aṅgirasas have granted me intelligence; the Seven Seers have granted me intelligence. May Agni and Vāyu grant me intelligence; may Dhātṛ grant me intelligence. May King Varuṇa grant me intelligence; may Agni grant me intelligence. May Indra and Sūrya grant me intelligence; may the goddess Sarasvatī grant me intelligence. That intelligence which is among the Apsarases, that mind which is among the Gandharvas, and that divine intelligence which is in man—may it enter into me here. May my body be discerning; may my speech yield honey-sweetness.

"Whatever has been observed, let me observe; whatever has been heard by me, let it be heard. May that which has been recited to me delight me, and may I be able to recite it after. May we be dear to what is heard, and may we be endowed with wisdom. I have grown strong, you have grown strong, O gentle one; you are my vital breath. Protect my sacred knowledge. You two are the poles of the chariot; may what I have heard not be lost to me. Thus he causes [the student] to recite. (27)

The student recites the five *ṛc*s beginning with "medhāṃ mahyam" and the sixth *yajus*; the teacher causes [the student] to recite them. *Medhā* is an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass. May the *Aṅgirases*—the vital airs (*vāyu*) consisting of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna—grant that to me. Because they cause the limbs to flourish (*rasayanti*), they are called *Aṅgirases*; likewise, may the seven seers (*saptarṣayaḥ*), Vasiṣṭha and the others, grant me *medhā*. This is the same for the two following *ṛc*s.

That wisdom which exists among the Apsarases, that internal organ—the mind—which exists among the Gandharvas, and that goddess who directly perceives the meaning of the Vedas and so forth, which resides as wisdom among humans in this world—she [is she].

May everything enter me; may it penetrate me. May my body be discerning and wise through the mediation of its presiding deity. And may speech—in the form of the Vedas and other scriptures—milk forth for me honeyed, sweet fruit. Whatever has been heard by me, established within me, and thoroughly observed, may I contemplate that correctly. Whatever has been spoken to me by my teacher, may that delight me. And whatever I repeat after my teacher, may I be able to do so.

"May we be dear to what has been heard, and may what has been heard reach its fulfillment for us. May we be endowed with wisdom; may we be united. Addressing himself by means of the *yajus*, the disciple says this: "O inner self, Prāṇa, and so forth, I, Viṣṇumitra, have grown; may I grow further. You too have grown—O Prāṇa and so forth—for in you also there will be excellence through the study of the Vedas and other such means. O gentle one, you are the thread of the world; therefore, protect me."

"You are the leader of Brahman; you are the essence. "May what has been heard not desert me" means: "may that which has been heard, pertaining to me, not abandon me. Here, the fourth [verse] is in the *uṣṇih* meter; the remaining ones are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. "I have grown strong," etc., is the sixth *yajus*. 27.
With these same four [verses], he should offer the *anupravacanīya* oblations, reciting the last one with a *yajus* formula.

The term *anupravacanīya* is an etymological designation for those oblations (*homāḥ*) whose purpose is subsequent recitation (*anupravacanam*). For after [the initiation], the teacher will cause the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* to be performed at a later time (*anu-uttarakālam*). Alternatively, they are called *anupravacanīya* because they merit subsequent recitation; for in this context, the teacher speaks first, and the student subsequently recites (*anupravakti*).

One should offer these oblations known as *anupravacanīya* with these very four verses already mentioned—beginning with "medhāṃ mahyam" and so forth—according to the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*. Thus, there are four oblations. Regarding the fifth, some say: "With a *yajus*, the last"—meaning one should offer the fifth oblation with the *yajus* beginning with "avṛdham. Others, however, say: "In this view, it would follow that there is no application for the fifth verse."

The feminine designation "the highest" (*uttamām*) is not appropriate, because the *anupravacanīya* under discussion is masculine; for in relation to that, it would follow that one should say "the highest" (*uttamam*). Furthermore, the word "oblation" (*āhuti*) has not been introduced in the context. Therefore, the meaning is that one should offer the fifth *anupravacanīya* by joining the highest *ṛc* with the *yajus*. || 28 ||

He states the sixth, the *anupravacanīya* oblation: "To the meters, svāhā! Just as a ritual (*kratu*) becomes what it is by means of its specific name, so too do all the [rituals] declared in the Vedas. || 29 ||

The *ṛtu* here refers to the ritual action (*karman*). One should offer the oblation by means of the name of that action. This is the seventh *anupravacanīya* oblation. How is it to be offered by means of the name of the *ṛtu*? It should be offered in such a way that the *ṛtu* becomes as it has been introduced—that is, in whatever manner the ritual action under discussion has been introduced and intended, so should it be offered. By means of the name of the action, which possesses the power of designation through its connection with the dative case and the utterance of *svāhā*, [one offers] either "for the sake of receiving, *svāhā*" or "for the sake of initiation, *svāhā*."

In this manner, all the rites declared in the Vedas are to be offered by means of this very method; having invoked them with "Svāhā to the meters by their own names," they are to be sacrificed according to the formula "Svāhā to the Traividyaka," and so forth. || 29 ||

To the west of the fire, seated on darbha grass and facing east, he recites the Sāvitrī verse three times to one who is seated facing west—first quarter by quarter, then hemistich by hemistich, and finally the whole verse; this is also for anyone who desires wisdom.

Afterwards, seated on *darbha* grass to the west of the fire, facing east, the Guru recites the *Sāvitrī*—the *Gāyatrī* verse dedicated to the deity Savitṛ beginning with "tatsavitur..."—three times to the disciple who is seated facing west, directly opposite the Guru. This should be understood as applying to a Brāhmaṇa; however, this is merely an illustration, for according to the Smṛtis and established custom, different *Sāvitrīs* are to be known for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya: "adabdhebhiḥ savitaḥ" for the Kṣatriya, and "viśvā rūpāṇi" for the Vaiśya. How does he recite it?

In the first recitation, one should recite verse by foot, that is, foot by foot (*pādaśas*). In the second recitation, one should recite half-verse by half-verse (*ardharcaśas*), meaning each half-verse (*ardharca*) individually. At the end, finally, one should recite the entire verse; or in the third recitation, one may recite the entire verse according to one's ability. Furthermore, whoever desires wisdom for a disciple should also recite it verse by foot, half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse. This [verse] beginning with "tat savituḥ" has thus been explained.

With your unfailing and auspicious protections, O Savitar, guard our household today. O golden-tongued one, protect us for new-found prosperity; let no malevolent speaker have power over us. The Seer puts on all forms; he has sent forth what is auspicious for bipeds and quadrupeds. Savitar, the most excellent, has looked out upon the vault of heaven; unassailable, he shines forth resplendently.

One should recite these [verses] respectively for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. O Savitṛ, O Āditya, on this day protect—guard—our *gaya*, that is, our home, with your *pāyus*, meaning protectors, namely your rays, which are *adabdhebhiḥ* (unassailable), *śivebhiḥ* (auspicious and cause-givers of happiness), and because you are *hiraṇyajihvaḥ* (golden-tongued) with radiant rays. For the sake of *suvitāya* (well-being) and for the one who offers oblations and performs hymns, you act like a boat—you will carry us across, as it were, from the ocean of calamity. Therefore, protect us.
May no one whatsoever—be it a thief or another—who speaks evil or sin against us, have power over us.

Savitṛ releases—that is, illuminates—all forms, all existents; he is the seer, the wise one of far-reaching vision. He has impelled, he brings forth, he generates auspiciousness and happiness for both bipeds and quadrupeds. He has illuminated, he makes manifest the *nāka*, the heaven (as previously explained). Worthy of choice, worthy of being sought after, and worthy of prayer, he shines forth, having made the departure of the dawns his mark or having caused them to pass; he radiates because the darkness of night has been dispelled. 30.

Having anointed a single-jointed palāśa leaf with fresh butter, he causes [the student] to recite over its shadow: "O you of good fame, you are of good fame; as you are of good fame, so make me of good fame and possessed of good renown. As you are of good fame among the gods, the guardian of the treasure of the Veda, so may I become the guardian of the treasure of the Brahman among the Brāhmaṇas. (31)

This is a *pālāśa* staff, made from the *palāśa* tree. Having anointed it with fresh butter—making it single-stemmed (without intermediate branches), straight, with its bark intact, and free of wounds—the teacher, grasping it with his own hand, establishes the student in the shadow cast by that staff and causes him to recite "O you of auspicious hearing," and so forth.

The *pālāśa* is thus described: "O *suśravaḥ*, you are *suśravas*"—one whose hearing (*śravaṇa*) is auspicious (*su*) is *suśravas*. For when that [wood] is employed as a constituent part of the ritual, there is no hearing of the wicked sound consisting of ill-repute. This is a restatement [of the fact]: "He for whom the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood hears no evil report. This is also stated in the Brāhmaṇa. *Śravas*.

"O Brahman, the gods indeed conversed; then that Brahman heard it from the Parṇa tree: 'He is indeed named Suśravas (the Well-heard),' so it is said. The meaning is that when the gods conversed regarding the Veda, which is Brahman, that Brahman resided in the Parṇa—that is, in the Palāśa tree. For this very reason, the Palāśa is well-known by the name Suśravas; such is the purport of the Brāhmaṇa. O Suśravas, bestow *sauśravasa* (glory of being well-heard); for one who is well-heard (*suśravas*) is indeed *sauśravas*, and [bestow] that *sauśravasa*.

Just as you, O Suśravas, are the guardian of the treasure of the Vedas—the protector of the collection of the treasures of the Vedas for the contending gods—so may I become the guardian of the treasure of the Brahman, the Veda, belonging to the Brāhmaṇas. || 31 ||
He gives a staff made of *pālāśa* wood to the Brāhmaṇa. || 32 ||
In this manner, at the conclusion of the recitation, the teacher hands over the prescribed staff made of *pālāśa* wood to the Brāhmaṇa student who is observing the vow of celibacy. || 32 ||
The *āśvattha* tree for a member of the royal caste. || 33 ||
The aśvattha tree is the vaṭa tree. || 33 ||
For a Vaiśya, [the tooth-stick] should be from the Nyagrodha tree. || 34 ||
He imposes a fine related to the banyan tree upon a Vaiśya. || 34 ||

Having caused him to recite the *Pūrvatantra* in its shadow and having given him the staff, he asks, "What does the teacher cause you to do? and makes him recite: "Remembered by me and not remembered by me—that is my twofold vow (*ubhayavrata*). Censure by me and non-censure by me—that is my twofold vow. Knowledge by me and ignorance by me—that is my twofold vow. Faith by me and lack of faith by me—that is my twofold vow. Truth by me and untruth by me—that is my twofold vow. Mortality by me and immortality by me—that is my twofold vow."

What has been heard by me and what has not been heard by me—that is my vow of both. What is the vow for me and what is the non-vow for me—that is my vow of both. That which is the vow of the Brāhmaṇa in the Brahman; that which is the vow of Agni, together with Indra, Prajāpati, the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, and men; together with the kingly men; together with the Gandharvas and Apsarases; together with the crawling creatures and other beings; together with the plants and trees; together with domestic and wild animals; together with the sky and the light.
Of that which has its appearance and its manifestation—whatever vow is mine within my own self—that is my all-encompassing vow. 35.

That which was remembered by Manu and others, and that which was not remembered, should both be observed respectively as a vow (*vrata*)—that which is to be practiced and that which is to be avoided. Likewise, "this is my censure" and "this is my non-censure": what is censured is to be avoided, and what is not censured is to be adopted. Alternatively, the censure of others is to be avoided, while non-censure—that is, praise—is to be employed on appropriate occasions.

It should be performed so as to culminate in benefiting others. In this way, knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are to be understood for the purpose of relinquishing the latter and adopting the former. Faith (*śraddhā*) is the state of being a believer; lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) is atheism or disbelief. Likewise, there are truth (*satya*) and untruth (*anṛta*). "Immortal" (*amṛta*) refers to that which causes immortality, because it is enjoined as the combination of knowledge and action; this is to be known as my vow (*vrata*).
