"Mortal" (*mṛta*) refers to that which causes death—the desire-driven (*kāmya*) rites which are the cause of *saṃsāra*. That too must be known by one seeking the supreme human goal for the sake of its abandonment, whereas by one seeking heaven and such, it is to be adopted.

*Śruta* refers to the study of the Mīmāṃsā and other such sciences; *aśruta* refers to "bad learning," namely the domain of pseudo-scriptures such as the Lokāyata. *Vrata* is a virtuous vow; *avrata* is a mere semblance of a vow, meaning a semblance of what ought to be done. That vow which belongs to a Brāhmaṇa regarding the Veda—that is, for the purpose of study and so forth—is my necessary duty, preceded by knowledge. Whatever vow or ritual act belongs to Agni together with Prajāpati and the others, that must be known and performed by me in due order.
"O Guru, bestow your grace everywhere"—this is what is being requested. The addition of the letter *s* in "janakasya" is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). || 35 ||

"Here I place this fuel upon the fire; O Agni, may I become one who observes all vows. "I have studied one, two, two, three, or indeed all of these Vedas"—thus says the Śruti regarding him whom one initiates while knowing this. (36)

With the mantra-linga "this I [place]," one throws the fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire. The change of gender in "this" (*idam*) is for metrical reasons; it means "this fuel-stick I place into the fire. The word *abhi* has the sense of "towards" or "in front of. O Agni, by your grace, may I become one who observes all vows—may I be so. The passage beginning with "he studies" (*adhīte ha*) is for the purpose of praising the initiator (*upanetṛ*). Only he who is learned, knowing both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, is authorized to perform the initiation, and no other.

For he who initiates [a student] studies, according to his desire, one, two, or three of these well-known Vedas consisting of infinite branches—or indeed all of them, adorned with every branch. The word "ha" indicates this is from the Itihāsa. Therefore, because it is praised in this way, the initiation (*upanayana*) is known from Śruti; it is not merely Smārta like other sacraments (*saṃskāra*). For this very reason, some say that even those incapable of performing the initiation must certainly perform it. That is incorrect, because even the Smārta rite is rooted in an inferred Śruti.

If it is argued that there is no injunction (*vidhi*) therein because it is not directly perceived (*apratyakṣa*), that same logic applies equally to the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, as for the claim that because the verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*) contained in a mantra is not injunctive, one should not perform the insertion of fuel sticks (*samit-prakṣepa*) with the words "I am this," that too is the talk of one who has not studied Mīmāṃsā; for even if the verbal form were not injunctive, the insertion is established through the indicative power (*liṅga*) [of the mantra itself]. || 36 ||
He grants a boon to the performer. || 37 ||
At the conclusion of the Upanayana, the father is the master who gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the student; in his absence, it is the eldest brother or another such relative. || 37 ||
One should remain [in that state] for the remainder of the day. ||38||
One should not cause [him] to sit down, nor should one cause [him] to move about. || 38 ||
The practice of celibacy has been explained. || 39 ||

Since the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has already been explained at the outset by such statements as "from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) onwards, he shall be a performer of vows," it is not stated again here.
Thus ends the initiation ceremony.
Thus ends the forty-first section (kāṇḍikā). || 41 ||
Now begins the forty-second section:
[The Traividyaka]. || 1 ||

The *traividyaka* vow is that which has its origin, its acquisition, or its purpose in the three branches of knowledge (*tisṛṣu vidyāsu*), consisting of the three Vedas. The word "we shall explain" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 1 ||
Regarding the one to whom this is spoken—that unawakened religious student (brahmacārī)—it might be suspected that the instruction is therefore useless; anticipating this, he says:
"The rule for the teacher. (2)
The meaning is that this must be performed by the teacher. || 2 ||
He who studies this Veda should place fuel sticks on the fire with the *aṃhomuk* verses both before and after [the recitation]. || 3 ||

At the beginning and at the conclusion of Vedic study, one should place three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire with the *aṃhomuk* verses; the meaning is that one should perform the mere act of throwing them in, devoid of even the utterance of *svāhā*. Otherwise, he would have said "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*). The *aṃhomuk* mantras are those which liberate from *aṃhas*, i.e., from sin. They are as follows: *yad devā devahelanaṃ devāsaś cakṛma vayam | agnir mā tasmād enaso viśvān muñcatv aṃhasaḥ ||* "O Gods, whatever offense against the gods we, O gods, have committed—may Agni release me from that sin and from all distress."

Whether by day or by night we have committed sins, may Vāyu release me from that sin, from all distress. Whether while awake or while asleep we have committed sins, may Sūrya release me from that sin, from all distress.

"O gods, indeed, O gods"—the repetition of "gods" (*devāsaḥ*) is for the sake of emphasis according to the rule *ājaserasuk*. O gods, whatever offense we have committed against you through lack of respect—that is, through arrogance or disrespect—may Agni release me from that entire sin, from that total distress (*aṃhas*). The mention of both *aṃhas* and *enas* is a restatement regarding one who is afflicted by suffering; or rather, the word *enas* refers to the excess of suffering caused by the commission of sin.
By this very [explanation], the second and third [cases] are also understood; by the words "day" (divā) and "night" (nakta), the two twilights occurring between them are also included. || 3 ||
The undertaking and release of the vow have been explained. || 4 ||

The "undertaking" (upāyana) of a vow is its formal acceptance, and "release" (vimocana) is its relinquishment. Both of these are prescribed for the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Accordingly, the relevant sūtra states: "Having washed his hands, standing to the south of the fire, he should say: 'O Agni, lord of vows; O Vāyu, lord of vows; O Sūrya, lord of vows.'"

O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have undertaken a vow; I declare it to you. May I be able to fulfill it; may I prosper through it. O Vāyu, Lord of Vows... O Sūrya, Lord of Vows... O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; I declare it to you. Protect it for us. O Vāyu, Lord of Vows... O Sūrya, Lord of Vows...

These six have been explained in the section on the rules for penance (*kṛcchra*). Here, they are to be applied equally both at the undertaking of the vow and at its release. However, there is this distinction: at the release, one should throw the staff into the fire, or into the water, as well as the girdle and the garment, until the completion of the oblation. From that point on, the staff and the other items are subject to the repetition of the mantra. And so Manu says: "Whatever skin, whatever sacred thread, whatever girdle, whatever staff, and whatever garment is prescribed for each, all of those [are used] during the vows as well.
Thus concludes the section on the three Vedas, together with liberation.
Thus ends the forty-second section (kāṇḍikā). 42.
Now begins the forty-third section (kāṇḍikā).
Now, therefore, regarding the office of the four Hotṛ priests: he undertakes the vow according to the rule for Vedic studentship.

The mantras beginning with *cittiḥ sruc* are called the Caturhotṛs; one should undertake the vow pertaining to them (*cāturhotṛka-vrata*), as enjoined by the section of the Veda that teaches the duties of a student (*brahmacāri-dharma*) according to the ritual manual for students (*brahmacāri-kalpa*). || 1 ||
For a year, or for eight months, or for four months. ||2||

"One should undertake this vow for a year"—this is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*). "Or for eight [or] four months"—this is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*). On an auspicious day of the bright fortnight, or on a festival day (*parvan*), having established the fire as prescribed and having offered oblations with the *jaya* and other formulas, he should drive a bunch of *darbha* grass into the ground to the east of the fire, seat a Brāhmaṇa to the south, and place fuel sticks upon the fire while reciting the four verses beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ."

Having fixed a bundle of *darbha* grass at the eastern part of the fire, and having seated another student who has studied the Veda on the southern side of the fire, one standing behind the western half of the fire should offer four fuel-sticks into the fire as before with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. These four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" have been explained in the section on cleansing (*saṃmārjana*). || 3 ||
In the offering for the perpetual vow, "O Brāhmaṇas, lords of vows! is the fourth [formula].

Regarding this initiation (*vratagrahaṇa*) which has been introduced as the constant and obligatory duty of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), he should perform the fourth part with the mantra: "O Brāhmaṇas, lords of vows, I undertake the vow; I declare it to you; may I be able to do it; may I prosper through it. But the three [parts] previously explained—"O Agni, lord of vows... O Vāyu, lord of vows... O Sūrya, lord of vows..."—remain here as well. || 4 ||
Now, the oblations for the vows.
The word "we shall explain" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 5 ||

One desiring splendor [should sacrifice] with clarified butter using the fourfold portions and the Caturhotṛ formulas; one desiring cattle, with barley-gruel (yāvaka); one desiring vigor, with food; and one desiring spiritual luster, having cooked a mess of rice in milk, mentally consecrates each oblation as it is offered.
Whatever vow belongs to Vedic study is the vow here.

There are seven *caturhotṛ* mantras here. The portion ending with "having cooked" (*śrapayitvā*) is clear. One should mentally recite (*anumantrayate*) each *caturhotṛ* mantra as it is offered; that is to say, one should follow the sequence of the mantras by means of the mantras themselves. He should cause [the sacrificer] to recite: "Whatever vow is prescribed in the Veda, may my vow here be fulfilled. || 6 ||
We shall enumerate the transgressions: one should not sit with four people, nor eat in the presence of four, nor eat together with four, or even as the fifth among them.
The same applies in the case of liberation. || 8 ||
Apavarga means the completion of a vow; in that regard... || 8 ||
He gives the garment to the teacher as a choice gift while he is seated to the south. || 9 ||
He should give a garment as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher who is seated to the south.

We shall explain the Caturhotṛ mantras, which—whether based on the theory of Brahman as illusory transformation (vivarta) or as actual transformation (pariṇāma)—have as their sole purpose the inner self (ādhyātmika). I bow to these Caturhotṛ mantras.

Intelligence is the sacrificial ladle, thought is the clarified butter, speech is the altar, what has been studied is the sacred grass, intention is the fire, discernment is the fire-kindler, the Lord of Speech is the Hotṛ priest, the mind is the Upavaktṛ, breath is the oblation, and the Sāman-chant is the Adhvaryu; go to Indra, Svāhā!

The seer (ṛṣi) of the Caturhotṛ hymns is [the same]; Indra is the deity. Regarding the root *hu*, "to give" or "to eat": those who offer (*juhvati*) or bestow (*dadati*) are the Hotṛs. The Caturhotṛs are the givers of the four—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; they are Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Vāsudeva, and Saṅkarṣaṇa, the first manifestations (*vivarta*) of Brahman. Thus, the Brāhmaṇa states: "The Caturhotṛs are indeed Brahman," and also, "Prajāpati desired, 'May I become many,'" and so forth. In this way, the Supreme Self alone is praised in the form of the sacrifice.

"Yajña is indeed Prajāpati," and "Viṣṇu is yajña"—such are the scriptural texts. Therefore, he describes the nature of the internal sacrifice (adhyātmayajña) through a metaphor: consciousness (*cetana*), which is the act of thinking (*citti*) or knowledge (*jñāna*), is the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*). Mind (*citta*), *manas*, *svānta*, *antaḥkaraṇa*, *cetas*, and *mānasa* are synonyms; the mind is the clarified butter (*ājya*). Just as clarified butter is poured into the fire with a ladle, so too is the mind cast into the fire of meditation on supreme bliss by means of discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*).

For just as clarified butter thrown into a fire is consumed, so too the mind, when cast into the meditation upon the inner self (*adhyātma-dhyāna*), dissolves of its own accord and causes all varieties of ignorance to dissolve, like the powder of the *kataka* fruit. Speech is the altar (*vedi*) because it is the support for sacrifice; for just as sacrificial vessels depend upon the altar, [so do the other faculties].

Just as the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and other implements are employed in their respective functions, so too, depending upon the Vedic word in the form of the Upaniṣads, the mind and the rest produce their own respective effects up to the point of supreme knowledge. "Recited *barhis* grass" refers to the mental recitation (*ādhyāna*), which is the act of reciting (*ādhīti*); this is the *barhis* for those who meditate with the mind, because the ladles of consciousness (*citti-sruk*) and the rest depend upon it, according to the Śruti: "He prepares the *juhū* on the *prastara*, and all the *sruva* ladles."

*Keto-agni* [is explained as follows]: the suffix *asun* is applied to the root *ci*, meaning "to perceive" (*saṃjñāne*), with a phonetic change (*varṇavyatyaya*) according to Vedic usage. *Keta* is a specific kind of wisdom (*prajñāviśeṣa*). That itself is the fire (*agni*), because by means of that very [wisdom], the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) such as the limbs of yoga are ignited. *Vijñāta-agni*: distinguished knowledge (*viśiṣṭaṃ jñānam*) which grasps the meaning of the Vedas; the shortening of the vowel to *agni* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Just as a sacrificial fire is kindled by a particular officiating priest (*ṛtvigviśeṣa*), so too is the internal fire of the mind (*adhyātma-cittāgni*) kindled further and further by the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.

Vācaspati is the Hotṛ priest; Vācaspati is the inner self (*antarātman*). He is the Hotṛ because he impels the mind, speech, and so forth; or alternatively, he is the Adhvaryu, the summoner who directs the officiating priests beginning with the mind. The mind is the Upavaktṛ; the mind is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) because it thinks and assents. It is the Upavaktṛ, that is, the Brahmā priest. For whatever the individual soul (*jīvātman*) knows or does, all that is assented to by him in the form of verbalizing, observing, and so on. Vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the oblation (*havis*), for that Supreme Self is offered as an oblation into the fire at the time of departure (*utkrānti*).

It is cast into the Supreme Brahman through the door of Brahman. Regarding the term *sāmādhvaryu*: the word *sāman* denotes the *vyāna* breath. Just as the Adhvaryu priest directs all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in their respective duties by means of injunctions (*praiṣa*), so too the vital air called *vyāna*, situated ten finger-breadths above the navel at the locus of the Person (*puruṣasthāna*), keeps the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—which possess mutually opposing movements—within their own respective limits. This has been determined by us in the *Yogasāra*.

Whatever is the station of Puruṣa, that indeed is the station of Vyāna, the controller of Prāṇa and Apāna. When the Adhvaryu is called by the term "Hotṛ," the purpose of demonstrating two Adhvaryus is the perception of the distinction between the sacrifice to the elements (bhūtayajña) and the sacrifice to the self (ādhyātmayajña). Thus, Prajāpati—designated by the words Indra and others, and manifested as the fourfold states of Pradyumna and so forth—having made himself tenfold through the four Hotṛs, performed the offering unto the Supreme Self.

Regarding this, it is said: "Go to Indra, svāhā! O Prāṇa, go to Indra, the Supreme Self; may there be a good offering, or a well-invoked one. And the excellence of the invocation culminates in its execution. In this way, people like us—who are either transformations (*vivarta*) or evolutes (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman and who desire the cessation of transmigratory existence—perform [this rite]. Furthermore, we have stated in the *Sāṃkhyasāra* and the *Śārīraka* that even the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) culminates in the attainment of non-duality (*advaita*). Thus, the first *caturhotṛ* has been explained. Now, the second.

The Earth is the Hotṛ, the Sky is the Adhvaryu, Tvaṣṭṛ is the Agnīdh, and Mitra is the Upavaktṛ. O Lord of Speech, with the most powerful vigor of speech you shall sacrifice; may Vācaspati, performing what is beneficial for the lord of the sacrifice, drink the Soma and generate Indra for the sake of sensory power—Svāhā!

By this, the divine means of sacrifice belonging to the Prajāpati-sacrifice are described. The earth is the *hotṛ*, for she nourishes the Prajāpati of the physical sacrifice by providing oblations such as food. The sky is the *adhvaryu*, because of its sending forth rain and so on. Tvaṣṭṛ, the sun, is the *agnīt*, because of his quality as a cooker. Mitra is indeed the *upavaktṛ* (the Brahmā), because he is adorned by the stainless realization of the meaning of the three Vedas.

O Vācaspati, O Prajāpati, you who possess the form of the Caturhotṛ—by me, through the power of speech consisting of mantra and brāhmaṇa, which has been accumulated with excellence by the force of awakening to the true nature of reality, you shall be worshipped. Being thus honored, you, for the sake of the lord of the sacrifice (yajñapati), the sacrificer, bring forth heaven (svaḥ); that is, make it manifest before him. What kind of heaven? That which is worthy of being chosen (vārya). May Vācaspati and Prajāpati drink the Soma; here, by the word "Soma," the sacrificial oblation in general is indicated, and by the verb "to drink" (pibati), its consumption is meant. By this [rite] of the Caturhotṛ, he caused Indra to be born.
By means of ritual action (*karman*), Prajāpati generated Indra, who is a transformation of Indra.
And so says the Śruti:

"Those Cāturhotṛs sat down for Soma as the householder, [thinking] 'Let us generate Indra. " Those [elements], Earth and the others, having made Soma the householder, sat down upon the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) with the Cāturhotṛ mantra, [thinking] "Let us generate Indra. "For the sake of the senses" (*indriyāya*) means for the sake of the perfection of the power of the vow (*vrata-vīrya*). "Svāhā" has been explained. Now, the third [offering].
For what purpose? The four hotṛ-priests are for Soma; the leader of Soma is the bright one; the leader of the bright one is the cooked [oblation].
O Indra, these Somas of yours have been prepared, O Vātāpi, you who hear the invocation! Svāhā!

Soma is in the form of a creeper; Soma is the leader, the precursor, of the Moon (candra). Or, Soma is the manifest Śukra; he is the leader of Śukra, the planet, or of Śukra, the preceptor of the Asuras. The *somāḥ* are cooked, ripened, or dependent [upon him]. The word *soma* is used figuratively for sacrificial offerings (*havis*) in general. The basis for this figurative usage is that through the perfection of one’s vows, one gradually attains fitness for the Soma sacrifice. O Vātāpi, you who subsist on wind, O you who hear the invocation, let there be a well-offered oblation (*suhuta*) or a well-invoked call (*svāhūta*) for you.
These four Hotṛ-priests, who partake in the employment of many rituals, should be applied according to their suitability for various purposes.

Agni is the Hotṛ, the Aśvins are the Adhvaryus, Rudra is the Agnīdh, Bṛhaspati is the Upavaktṛ. O Lord of Speech—O you who know the heart by name—the Lord of Speech has drunk the Soma; bestow manly vigor upon us! Svāhā!

This is the Pañcahotṛ; for its Brāhmaṇa states: "Those Pañcahotṛs—Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and the others—sat down [thinking], 'Let us generate Indra. And here, in the mantra, the identity of those pertaining to the sacrifice with those pertaining to the deities is expressed: Agni is the Hotṛ, and thus the Śruti says, "Agni indeed is the Hotṛ of the gods," and there is also the indicative mark of the mantra: "I praise Agni, the Purohita. The Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, are the Adhvaryus—the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ. Rudra is the Agnidh; the Agnidhra is Rudra.

Bṛhaspati is the upavaktṛ (the invoker). O Vācaspati, O Hṛdvidhe (O you who are known by the heart)—Hṛdvidhi means the inner controller (antaryāmī); the address is "O Hṛdvidhe," O Inner Controller known by that name! You are the Lord of Speech (vācaspati), the drinker of Soma; therefore, drink the Soma here among us, and bestow upon us manly strength (nṛmṇa) and power.

Speech is the Hotṛ, Vāta is the Adhvaryu, Dīkṣā is the wife, and the Waters are the Abhigara. In the heat (tapas), I offer the mind as the oblation. O Lord of Speech, with unimpaired speech and an unimpaired tongue, do thou, who hast increased the gods in heaven, impel the Hotṛ-offerings; Svāhā!

This is the *ṣaḍhotṛ* (the sixfold offerer). In the context of the inner self (*adhyātman*), that which is speech (*vāk*) is itself the *hotṛ*. The wind (*vāta*) is the *adhvaryu*, as is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose movement is in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Consecration (*dīkṣā*) is the wife (*patnī*), consisting of the fulfillment of vows. Water is the *abhigara* (the reciter); "recitation" is the *abhigara*, and in this regard, water alone is the agent by means of providing food and other necessities. The mind (*manas*) is the oblation (*havis*), because it is offered into the fire of the Self; "I sacrifice in the Brahman through austerity"—I cast the mind and the rest into the Brahman.

O Vācaspati, with unbroken—that is, imperishable—speech, which is of the nature of internal illumination, and with an unbroken tongue, O Divine One in heaven, impel and accomplish my work for me. With what kind of speech? With "increasing sacrificial invocation" (avṛdhaddhotrā), meaning that which effects the performance of unseen oblations and other rites.

Mahāhavis is the Hotṛ; Satyahavis is the Adhvaryu; Acittapājas is the Agnīdh; Acittamanas is the Upavaktṛ; Anādhṛṣya and Apratidhṛṣya are the Abhigara; Ayāsya is the Udgātṛ. O Vācaspati, Vidhe, we worship your name; you, Vidhe, protect our name. May the thread of the gods not be severed, nor that of men. Svāhā!

This is the Saptahotṛ mantra: "Those Saptahotṛs, with Aryaman as their householder, sat down for the crossing. For its Brāhmaṇa states: "The crossing is the attainment of Brahman. The Mahāhavis is the moon, because it is the sustenance of all; for this very reason, its waning occurs during the dark fortnight. He is the Hotṛ, because he nourishes the gods through the offering of oblations. The Satyahavis is the sun, because of its constant impelling; he is the Adhvaryu.

The Agnīdhra is one whose mind is not an object of thought (*acittapājā*); the meaning is that he is the Agnīdhra who is empty of mental cognition (*cittaprajñāśūnya*), like fire. Thus, being without mind or thought (*acittamanāḥ*) and devoid of the mental faculty (*jñānamanovihīnaḥ*), he is a forest-dweller subsisting on fruits, vegetables, and the like. Of what nature is he? He is "unassailable" (*anādhṛṣya*) and "unconquerable" (*apratidhṛṣya*), meaning he cannot be overcome; the repetition is for the sake of emphasis. He is the "Abhigara," where the root *gṛ* signifies praise. The Udgātṛ is "Ayāsya"; from the root *yasu* meaning "effort," he is the Udgātṛ who has achieved his state without effort—the Udgātṛ whose form is the Vedas and Upaniṣads—and he sings forth the Reality (*tattva*).

O Vācaspati, O Vidhi, we worship your name; the meaning is that we perform this sacrifice for the sake of your name. And since you alone are our name—that is, our very essence—therefore, let not our thread be severed; do not cut off the continuity of us gods and humans. May [this offering] be well-sacrificed unto you.
Thus end the mantras for the four officiating priests (cāturhotṛka).
Having praised the infallible Supreme Self, who consists of knowledge and bliss,
the commentary on the mantras of the Pravargya vow is now commenced.

In this context, the binding of peace (*śāntibandhana*) is performed with the *anuvāka* beginning with "Namo vāce," excluding the four *yajus* beginning with "Prācyā tvā," and with the two *anuvākas* beginning with "Divyo gandharvo bhuvanasya" and "Āhus te bhaga. Furthermore, its placement within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) after consecrating it with these aforementioned *anuvākas* is prescribed. Thereafter, the release of peace (*śāntivimoka*) must necessarily be performed. These mantras, though experts in the purification (*saṃmārjana*) found in the *Mantrarahasya* and other texts, are here employed for the purpose of binding peace.

Homage to Speech! Homage to the Lord of Speech! To that speech which is uttered and that which is unuttered—to that very Speech, homage! Homage to the Seers, the makers of mantras, the knowers of mantras! May the Seers, the makers of mantras, the knowers of mantras, not abandon me. May I utter divine speech—auspicious, eternal, beloved by the gods, accompanied by *svadhā* for the ancestors, and worthy of being heard by men. May the gods protect me for my glory; may the ancestors rejoice after me. May I be clear-sighted with my eyes, radiant of countenance with my mouth, and well-hearing with my ears. Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ.

For the sake of Rudra. The "object" (*artha*) is that which is denoted, namely the deity. To that speech which consists of the *ma* syllable, let there be salutation (*namaḥ*). To Vācaspati—the Lord of Speech, the master of words in the form of utterances—to him, the one who articulates, [let there be] salutation. To that speech which teaches and is subtle, to that speech, salutation after salutation (*namo namaḥ*). The repetition of the word *namaḥ* is for the sake of intensification; for by these two, people consider the meaning to be greater, just as in the expression, "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful! (*aho ramaṇīyā aho ramaṇīyā*).

And to those seers who are knowers of the mantras and makers of the mantras, salutations again and again. Among them, the "knowers of mantras" are Sanaka and others who grasp, all at once, both the words and the meaning of the mantras that issued forth from the four mouths of Brahmā. Thus it is said in the Āraṇyaka:
"Just as when firewood is split and lit, various smokes issue forth, even so, my dear, this Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda are the breath of this Great Being.
It is also stated elsewhere:
"Those seers who had directly realized the Dharma imparted the mantras to others who had not directly realized the Dharma," and so forth.

[The mantra says: "May the seers, the makers of mantras and knowers of mantras, not cast me away from divine speech. The seers who are the makers and knowers of mantras—may they not cast me away; here the accusative case is used in the sense of the ablative, meaning "from my presence. May they not turn their faces away from me, from the speech in the form of mantras. What then? "I shall utter divine speech"—the root *yā* is used in the sense of "attaining"; thus, the meaning is that I shall attain it with excellence.

Auspicious (*śivām*), meaning conducive to welfare; eternal (*ajastrām*), meaning constant; cherished by the gods (*juṣṭām devebhyaḥ*), meaning generating delight for the gods—[the root] *juṣ* meaning "to delight in" or "to serve"; possessed of the *svadhā* offering for the ancestors (*svadhāvatīm pitṛbhyaḥ*), meaning rich in food for the ancestors; for indeed, the gods are delighted by mantras and the ancestors partake of the *svadhā*; worthy of being heard from humans (*śuśrūṣeṇyām manuṣyebhyaḥ*), meaning [a speech] that is to be listened to with eagerness.

May the gods protect me, who am such as I have become, while I am praising; and may the ancestors protect—that is, rejoice in—me while I am characterized by splendor (*śobhā*). For the sake of splendor, may the gods and the ancestors be delighted. Furthermore, by the grace of the gods and the ancestors, may I be "well-eyed" (*sucakṣas*) with my eyes—the meaning being that I may possess good vision—and may I be "radiant" (*suvarcas*) with my face, possessing great luster. By the words *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, the plenitude of speech is expressed in brief, since the three worlds are an evolution (*vivarta*) of the plenitude of speech.

Through the eastern direction, with Agni as the deity, and with the Gāyatrī metre, I enter the spring season. Through the southern direction, with Indra as the deity, and with the Triṣṭubh metre, I enter the summer season. Through the western direction, with Savitṛ as the deity, and with the Jagatī metre, I enter the rainy season. Through the northern direction, with Mitra and Varuṇa as the deities, and with the Anuṣṭubh metre, I enter the autumn season.

Through the upward direction, with Bṛhaspati as the deity, and with the *pāṅkta* metre, I enter the winter season. Through this direction, with Prajāpati as the deity, and with the *anāpta* metre, I enter the cool season (*śiśira*). I enter the *gāyatrī* metre; I enter the *triṣṭubh* metre; I enter the *jagatī* metre; I enter the *anuṣṭubh* metre; I enter the *paṅkti* metre; I enter the *aticchandas* metres; I enter the metres.

May they carry us across; may they protect us; may he who hates us and whom we hate encounter them. May the waters enter us; may the waters watch over us. May I attain full life, universal life, all-encompassing life; may I attain complete life.

But at the very moment one begins the immersion in water, having superimposed the non-difference of the *chandas* (metres) and the rest from the water, he addresses the water: "O Water, I enter you, who have become the spring season; having propitiated you through this rite currently performed, may I obtain fruits consisting of you. With what do I enter? With the eastern direction, with Agni as the deity, and with the *gāyatrī* metre. In this manner, the sentences for entering the five seasons are to be joined accordingly, such as "I enter the *gāyatrī* metre," and so forth.

The statement regarding the entry into the *chandas* (Vedic meters) should be applied with the intent of entering a state of fearlessness for the sake of protecting oneself and others. May those *chandas* carry us across—that is, may they bring the present undertaking to completion. May they protect us, guard us, and satisfy us. May he reach those [meters] who hates us and whom we hate; may he whom we hate and who hates us reach those *chandas*. The meaning is that having encountered those meters and so forth, he shall dissolve into them.

"May the waters enter into us"—the meaning is that the presiding deity [of the waters] may preside over me as a protector. "O waters, be wakeful among us"—O waters, be watchful within us. "Long life, all-encompassing life, the entirety of life, may I attain; may I attain the full span of life"—by the grace of the waters, may I especially pervade [attain] long life; the repetition of "all-encompassing life, the entirety of life," and so forth, is for the sake of intensification, as explained previously.

The divine Gandharva, the lord of the world, alone worthy of praise by the mind among all beings—O God, I approach you with a sacred prayer; homage be to you! Your dwelling is in heaven. Seated upon heaven, the worshipful one with the skin of the sun, the one who has descended from the celestial heat, the peerless friend of humanity, most gracious—the Gandharva, the lord of the world, has united with the blameless Apsarases in their own abodes.

The ocean was their dwelling place, they say; from there, O cloud-born ones, you move forth, you who belong to the day and the night. To those who have joined with Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva—to them let there be homage! May they be gracious to us, may they grant us protection. Him whom we hate and him who hates us, we place within their jaws.

That which exists in heaven is divine (*divya*); he who holds the rays (*gāḥ*) is the *gandharva*; he is indeed intended as Rudra. He alone is the Lord of the world (*bhuvanasya patiḥ*). For it is heard [in scripture]:

"These worlds are indeed the *bhuvana*; of them, he who is Rudra is the sovereign lord. He alone protects (*avati*) and guards everything, thus he is called *Ekāvya*. "Worthy of praise among the people" (*vikṣvīḍyaḥ*): among the people—that is, within the divine armies—he alone is worthy of praise and laudation; the meaning is that he is to be propitiated by the mind through reflection, meditation, and so forth. Alternatively, there is a transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*): he is to be worshipped (*ījyaḥ*) by the minds of the people, that is, of human beings; he is that Puruṣa mentioned in the Upaniṣads who dwells within the sun.

O God, whose functions consist of illuminating and so forth—to you who are such, because you have become the sovereign lord of the world, I go; that is, I reach you by means of the *brahman*, the Veda consisting of mantras, praising you with hymns. Or, "I approach" (*āyāmi*) means "I desire to attain" you. Therefore, let there be salutation to you, whose dwelling place (*sadhastha*) is in heaven. "Seated in heaven" (*divi pṛṣṭaḥ*): this is said with reference to the officiating priests for the purpose of commencing the *pravargya* rite and the oblation.

O priests, this Āditya—who is situated upon the heavenly sky (divi svarge pṛṣṭhabhūtaḥ), meaning he is the supreme among all gods—is Sūryatvag-avayāḥ; that is, his skin (tvak) is like the sun (sūryasya tvag iva), and thus he is Sūryatvag-avayāḥ, being devoid of states such as childhood and so forth, because Brahman is without beginning or end.

Therefore, O priests, worship this divine *hara*, whose form is splendor (*tejas*). Among men—that is, among those humans who desire liberation—there is a virtuous man who is *suśeva*. *Śeva* is a name for happiness; the meaning is that he is of the nature of eternal bliss. Or, *suśeva* may mean "easily served," with a metrical change of letters (*varṇavyatyaya*) according to Vedic usage. Some read *suśevāḥ*. He is *mṛḍāt*: *mṛḍa* is happiness, and he eats (possesses) happiness, thus he is *mṛḍāt*, the enjoyer of eternal bliss. *Gandharva* has already been explained. With what [offerings] do you worship?

With blameless oblations, having made them equal and striving together; because there are multiple performers, the simultaneity is figurative. Regarding the statement "the Gandharva was in the waters," the Gandharva is the Sun (Āditya), and he exists even in those [waters]. This is the distinction here: if someone should suspect how the oblations of the student’s vows can be offered in the Āhavanīya fires given the absence of the *tretā* (three-fold fire-set), this is said in response: even though the oblations are in the waters, the Sun exists therein, for he is omnipresent.

Therefore, O priests, they say that the ocean—the Veda in the form of mantras—is the *sadana*, the abode or home, of these oblations belonging to you; the meaning is that it is the Person dwelling within the sun.

Therefore, let the worldly fires be offered with that power. What are they? Those which, once offered, proceed together with the sacrificer by the very force of the mantra—to where? To the fire that is in the blinding darkness covered by clouds; that is to say, obscured by ignorance. To the light of the stars; that is to say, in the illumination of knowledge. "Didyut" means shining intensely, driving away the veil of the clouds of ignorance.

He who causes all—the universe—to dwell is Viśvāvasu; that Gandharva, the Āditya, you too, O officiating priests (ṛtvijas), go toward him—this is an exhortation. Let there be homage to those Vrata-oblations of great power. May they be gracious to us, may they bring us happiness, and likewise grant us refuge and bliss. The repetition is for the sake of unsurpassed bliss of liberation.
Whomever we hate, and whoever hates us—that one we place and cast into the fire, which is the "jaw" (jambha) of these oblations.

Bhaga dwells in the two eyes; look upon me with them. With this essence of honey, I anoint your form; with that, may you anoint my form. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, and with the rites and ointments of the gods, I anoint you. You are the name Bhaga; for you, the Ṛcs, the Yajus, and the Sāmans are in Agni, one eye is in the Sun, and another eye is in the Moon. May I become Bhaga.

"You are the breath, you are the eye, you are the ear; you are speech named *Puraṃdhi*. By that [power] through which Śatakratu partakes of his portion, by that do you bestow fortune upon yourself. "O Heroes (Aśvins), I disclose for you that fierce deed for the sake of gain, as thunder discloses rain, since Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, with the head of a horse, declared the honeyed secret to you both. "Agni is the lord of wealth; Agni is the lord of great fortune. May he grant these things to us. In this passage as well, the Supreme Self alone is praised in the form of Rudra, while the Sun and the Aśvins are praised in the form of Agni.

"Bhaga" is one who is to be worshipped and served; it is Rudra, the Supreme Self. This is his address: "O Bhaga, the knowers of the Veda say that your two eyes are [the sun and moon]; the knowers of the Veda call you the possessor of eyes. According to the Śruti, "The sun and the moon are indeed his two eyes.

With those two eyes, look upon me specifically, facing me and with favor. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. "Saraghā" means honey-bees. That which belongs to them is "sāragha," the well-known honey. Some say: "With that, I anoint your form, which consists of splendor."

That which destroys the firm essence of *saṃsāra* is *sāragha*; because it yields sweet fruit, it is "honey"—namely, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). With that, I anoint your two eyes, which are in the form of the moon and the sun; that is to say, I refine them when they have been prepared, bringing them into the range of the knowledge of reality. Through that, you shall perceive my form, and you too, with your eyes purified by me through the actions of knowledge, [shall perceive it].

That form which consists of the ultimate reality of Brahman—that you should refine through non-apprehension; the meaning is: make it free from the affliction of dissolved ignorance. Regarding the word *devasya*: "O Rudra, I anoint you with the ointments belonging to the gods—those characterized by the qualities of the divine abode and so forth—and with the sages who are skilled in the study of the Vedic meaning, by whom you were anointed with the oblations of knowledge and the like. Being under the impulse (*prasave*) or command of the god Savitṛ, [I anoint you] with the two arms of the Aśvins, the physicians of the gods.

But [he is carried] by his own two leather ones; the Aśvins are the sun and moon because they move in horse-chariots, and by the hands of Pūṣan, that is, Āditya, and of the gods. By the *ṛtus*—that is, by the oblations connected with the *pravargya*, the vows, and the *homa* sacrifices. The common explanation is that the *ṛtus* are the movements, meaning the constant ritual actions and knowledges. O Rudra, O Blessed One, you are the name; the meaning is that you are the sovereign lord of all.

For you who are thus constituted, the *ṛcas* are the Ṛgveda, the *yajūṃṣi* are the Yajurveda, and the *sāmāni* are the Sāmaveda; "speech" (*vāk*) means that which speaks, namely the triple Veda (*trayī*), the sense being that it is expressive of you. Or rather, because you remember [it] at the beginning of each creation through the analogy of one who has awakened from sleep, the triple Veda belongs to you, as does speech. Furthermore, there is another eye in Agni and another in the Sun: that vision of yours which is satisfied by the oblations of optional rites (*kāmyakarma*) in the fire is distinct, as it is the bestower of fruits such as heaven.

When the Sun, whose sole nature is luminosity, is realized through meditation and other means, there is another [form of] vision—distinct from that previously mentioned—which consists of seeing Your own essential nature within the Fire that is gratified by the oblations of obligatory and occasional rites (nitya-naimittika-karma), free from those acts performed for desire or prohibited acts; this is the means by which You grant liberation. The meaning is that You bring about liberation for householders even through the combination of knowledge and action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya). However, in comparison to lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya), liberation produced by knowledge alone has been described as being more manifest.

Therefore, by means of this vow, the meaning is: "May I become the Blessed One; may I attain the state of Brahman. "Thou art *aira*"; *ira* is food, so the meaning is: "Thou art the lord of food (*aira*). "Thou art sight. "Thou art hearing. "Thou art *Puraṃdhri*"; she who sustains the *puras*, which are the collections of the three worlds, is named *Puraṃdhri*; the meaning is that thou art Speech consisting of the triple Veda (*trayī*), or as many things as there are that are illuminating.

"O Bhaga, O Rudra, with that mantra I invoke you; I call upon you by which Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, invoked—that is, gave or consumed—the offering of the portion of Soma and other oblations (the roots *hu* and *dā* signify both giving and eating). Therefore, O two heroes—whether the Aśvins or the Sun and Moon conceived as distinct entities—I manifest this portion of the oblation for the sake of distribution (*sanaye*). It is formidable, possessing great strength. Like what? Like the thunderbolt (*tanyatu*), which [produces] rain or sound."

In the state of distraction (*pamāyām*), the wind (*tanyatu*)—so called because it is a differentiation within the continuity of clouds and the like—manifests rain, just as the wind manifests rain by agitating the lightning-fire (*vaidyuta-tejas*). Regarding the verse, "Dadhyaṅ, indeed, [spoke] the honey to Atharvaṇ" (*dadhyaṅ ha yanmadhvātharvaṇe*): Dadhyaṅ is the name of one who is the offspring of Atharvan; he, being endowed with good intelligence (*sumati-yukta*), invoked you two with the head of a horse—that is, having become possessed of a horse's head. For what purpose?

For the sake of *madhu*, meaning for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*), since liberation consists of the nature of honey that is beautiful with eternal bliss (*nityānanda-sundara-madhu-mayatva*). Similarly, I too, being of good intelligence, have spoken thus: I invoke you two.

"Agni is the Lord": Agni is the lord (*īśa*) of wealth (*vasavya*); "wealth" (*vasavya*) means that which is conducive to riches, such as gold and so forth; the meaning is that Agni is its master and owner. "Agni is greatness": the connection is that he is the lord of good fortune (*saubhaga*); the meaning is that Agni is the sovereign of great auspiciousness. "May he grant us those riches and fortunes"—Agni bestows them upon us.

"O Agni, Lord of Vows, you are the sovereign; you are the protector of vows; you are the bearer of vows; you are the lord of vows. I undertake the vow; I declare it unto you. May I be able to perform it; may I prosper through it. With these three [verses]—"O Vāyu, Lord of Vows... "O Sūrya, Lord of Vows... and "O Agni, Lord of Vows"—while standing near the fire, he undertakes the vow. O Agni, Lord of Vows, of the vow that has been undertaken...

You have been protected; you are the sovereign (*samrāṭ*), for you shine perfectly; you are the guardian of the vow (*vratapā*), the protector of the vow. You are the bearer of the vow (*vratabhṛt*), you are the nourisher of the vow. You are the lord of the vow (*vratapati*), you are the master of the vow. Since you are such, it is said: "I undertake the vow"—that is, I begin it. Therefore, I declare this to you: may I be able to perform that vow through your grace, and by that action, may I attain its fulfillment characterized by its fruit. The [formulas] "O Vāyu, lord of the vow... and "O Sūrya, lord of the vow... have their meaning already explained by this very [passage].

The earth is kindled by fire; I kindle it. May it, being kindled and well-kindled, kindle me with splendor, luster, fame, and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). The atmosphere is kindled by wind; I kindle it... The sky is kindled by the sun; I kindle it...

With these three [verses], he places three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire in their respective order; because of the association with the vow (*vrata*), he stands while doing so, not sitting. This is the first: "The fuel-stick is the earth, because of its earthly nature. Agni kindles that fuel-stick—using the *uttama-puruṣa* (first person) by way of grammatical transposition—he kindles it. "I kindle it," that is, I make it blaze. Being well-kindled, having been thoroughly ignited, may it kindle me with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and other such qualities; may it so kindle me. The second is like the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and the third is like heaven (*dyu*); the rest is the same.

O Lord of the solar vow, you are the sovereign; you are the guardian of the vow; you are the upholder of the vow; you are the lord of the vow. I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; we declare that to you; protect us. O Vāyu, Lord of the vow... O Agni, Lord of the vow...

By these three [formulas] purified by the sequence of the *bhikṣūlikā*, the vow (*vrata*) is released. The meaning is indeed already stated; only the sequence differs in the common words. However, the distinction lies in the phrases "I have performed that" and "I was capable of that. That vow has been performed by me through your grace; and since it has been accomplished according to my capacity, it requires only protection. Therefore, O Sūrya, Vāyu, and Agni, protect—that is, guard—our extended [vow]. At the release of the vow, the gift of a sacrificial fee (*samiṣṭayajus-dāna*) must be made.

There too, the mantras are desired according to the sequence of the *cūlikā* beginning with *samit*, and the taking of the fuel-sticks (*samid-ādāna*) occurs while standing, due to its association with the vow (*vrata*). The oblation (*homa*) is performed with the ten-verse section (*anuvāka*) beginning with *ud u tyam*: "His rays bear up that god Jātavedas, the Sun, so that all may behold him."
This [verse] has been explained in the context of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). "O Agni, among the gods, proclaim for us this newest Gāyatra gift."

In the word *pravocat*, the suffix is the *loṭ* (imperative) in the sense of "addressing" (*ākhyāpane*), which here functions as *leṭ*; by the rule "there is elision [of the *i*] after *it* in the *parasmaipada*," the *i* is elided; and by the rule "in *leṭ*, there are the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ*," the augment *aṭ* is added. The syllable *ū* is meaningless, while *ṣu* is the root.

The prefix *su-* is connected with the word *sani*. O Agni, proclaim this oblation (*homa*) among the gods—this oblation belonging to us, performed by means of this *gāyatrī* verse; that is to say, announce that "this is our oblation, which is pleasing to you. [He should offer] a *susanim*—the root *van* in the sense of "to share" (*saṃbhakti*)—meaning one characterized by a beautiful distribution, and *navīyasam*, meaning exceedingly new.

O Indra, Lord of the Bay Steeds, lead us together with our minds, with cattle, with wise patrons, and with well-being; lead us together with the sacred prayer that is fashioned by the gods, and with the benevolent favor of the deities worthy of sacrifice.

O Indra, O Lord of the bay horses (*harivān*), you who are yoked with horses of golden hue (*haritavarṇa*), you lead us together, you distribute to us, and you bestow upon us a beautiful mind, meditation, and so forth; such is the meaning.

Thus you lead us together with cattle; you lead us together with wise patrons (*sūri*)—learned priests who are companions in sacrifice; you lead us together with well-being (*svasti*), characterized by non-destruction and the attainment of liberation; likewise, you lead us together with the *brahman*—both the Veda and the Supreme Self—leading us to the state of becoming Brahman (*brahmabhūya*); you lead us together with whatever else is excellent and created by the gods; and you lead us together with the auspicious wisdom (*sumati*) belonging to the gods, such as Bṛhaspati and others. Of what kind [of gods]?
Of those worthy of sacrifice, that is, of those deserving of sacrifice; or rather, the connection is: "by the good-will of the gods who are worthy of sacrifice, you lead [us] together."

Together with splendor, together with nourishment, together with our bodies, and with a gracious mind, we have come. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the skillful shaper, bestow wealth upon us; may he mend whatever in our bodies is injured.

O Indra, through your grace, may we be united with splendor and radiance; may we be united with nourishment and our bodies—our children and those related to us—and may we be united with a mind that is auspicious and peaceful. Likewise, may Tvaṣṭṛ bestow wealth (*rāyaḥ*) upon us; he who is a noble giver (*sudatraḥ*), a beautiful or excellent donor. May that Tvaṣṭṛ subsequently (*anu*) cleanse (*mārṣṭu*) us, or rather, may he polish us thoroughly (*anumāṣṭṛ*). What is it that he polishes?

That which is fit for wiping away is, by implication, sin. Of what nature is it? Some say it means "worn away" (*viliṣṭa*), that is, "stuck fast" (*vilagna*). However, this is the meaning here: since the root *liś* signifies "becoming small," that which has been specifically diminished through the performance of obligatory and occasional rites—that alone Tvaṣṭṛ wipes away with ease.

Agni, the first Jātavedas, has looked along the beginning of the dawns; day after day he has looked along the days. He has extended himself along the many rays of the sun, and along heaven and earth. Agni, the first Jātavedas—born at the beginning of creation, possessing wealth (or fuel) and possessing wisdom even without that [external] form—has looked along, that is, he has illuminated and brought about, the beginning, the commencement, of the dawns, i.e., of the nights. Thereafter, he looked along the days, the daylight hours. Then he looked along the rays of the sun; he has made them manifest.

What kind of fire is it? It is the protector (*trātṛ*) of many (*purūṇām*), that is, of many people; or rather, *purutrā* is simply *puru*, with the secondary derivative suffix *tra* in the sense "one who protects from men" (*purubhyo manuṣyebhyas trāti*). And you have extended across both heaven and earth.
O Aśvins, with that whip of yours which is honey-sweet and full of truth, sprinkle the sacrifice.

O Aśvins, that whip of yours which is speech—indeed, like a whip, it is the restrainer of the horses of the mind; being honey-sweet (*madhumatī*), meaning having honey as its transformation, and full of pleasant truth (*sūnṛtāvatī*) and truth (*satyavatī*), with such [speech] "mimikṣataṃ," i.e., mix together or prepare the sacrifice as a constituent part of the vow—so say some. But this is the meaning: from the root *miha* "to sprinkle," it means "you two sprinkle," that is, "you two cause to swell."
May Dhātṛ, the lord of the moving world, bestow wealth upon us; may he favor us with abundance.

May Dhātṛ, Prajāpati, bestow or sustain wealth (rayi) upon us; for he is the sovereign lord (īśāna) of the world—that is, of the moving creation or of the three worlds—and he is the protector of the worlds (jagatāmpati). May that Dhātṛ favor us with a full and undiminished distribution; for the root *van* (in *avana*) signifies "to share," may he therefore distribute [wealth] to us in abundance.
As Dhātṛ, you rule over progeny and wealth; as Dhātṛ, you have generated this entire world. You bestow abundant riches upon the donor. May we be masters of riches.

The Ordainer (Dhātṛ) rules over all creatures; he exercises sovereign power. Or rather, what need is there for others? The Ordainer alone has generated, produced, and sustained this entire universe—the three worlds—along with their boundaries. It is the Ordainer alone who bestows and grants to the donor, the sacrificer, that which is to be shared: abundant, vast, and desirable water, as well as the fruits of sacrifice and other such rewards. Therefore, by the grace of the Ordainer, may we become masters of riches and wealth.

The thirty-three threads with which they have woven this sacrifice, those who bestow it with *svadhā*—may we mend whatever breach there is therein; may this sacrifice, accompanied by *svāhā*, ascend to the gods. Those who extend the sacrifice are the threads, beginning with the sacrificer and the officiating priests. "Thirty-three" is used as a designation for the total number, since it serves as an indicative mark according to the circumstances. The word "yān" (whom) is an instance of grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

Those who extend this sacrifice with *svadhā*—that is, with food—or those who offer the sacrifice itself, or alternatively, those who offer *svadhā*, that is, food, to the gods: for them, we mend (*pratidadhmaḥ*) their deficiency—the obstruction of their vows, the failure of their performance, and so forth—and by means of this [sacrifice], we remedy and ward it off.

By means of this oblation—meaning that whatever obstacle exists here in this vow, we ward it off by this oblation—may there be a well-offered *svāhā*. May this sacrifice also go to and reach the gods. Viṣṇu strode across this; he established his foot in three places; his footprint is gathered in the dust.

Viṣṇu, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), strode across this triple world (*trailokya*) in the form of the sacrifice and so forth; he placed his foot in three ways, meaning he manifested or evolved into the form of the three worlds by means of three steps. His fourth step—the true form of Brahman which is neither manifested nor evolved—was submerged in the dust (*pāṃsure*); that is to say, it is completely submerged in the dust of ignorance and is not accessible to those who lack yoga.
And here, upon the conclusion of the vow (*vratāpavarga*), twenty-nine oblations are to be offered, one for each verse, with the *anuvāka* beginning "Mā no dharma" (*Do not distress us, O Gharma*).

"Mā no gharma vyathito vivyatho no mā naḥ paramadhāmāhuto naiḥ | moṣvamāṃstamasyantarādhā mā rudriyāso abhikurvato naḥ ||" O Gharma, even though you are distressed by our negligence and have been rendered defective through our transgression, do not cause us further pain. Do not cast us into the darkness of the highest realm; may the followers of Rudra not strike us down as we perform this rite. The meaning is: O Gharma, even though you are agitated by us and have reached a state of deficiency due to our error born of heedlessness, do not inflict suffering upon us.

"Do not lead us, O Unbent One (*ahuta*), to the supreme abode. [The root] *hṛ* means "crookedness"; thus, being unbent (*ahuta*)—that is, not crooked—do not lead us to the supreme abode, the highest place, the house of death. "Do not place us within the darkness": here, *mā-u-su*—the word *mā* is for prohibition, the word *u* has the sense of "and," and the word *su* is connected with the word *tamaḥ*. And do not place us, *su*, within (*antaḥ*) the darkness—the blinding darkness of hell. Do not cast us into it.
May the Rudriyas—the fierce powers belonging to Rudra—not act against us as we advance; may they not direct their assaults toward us, but let there be a state of non-cruelty.

May our own desires be honored by our sacred rites; O Good Guide, do not let our enemies prevail over us. Let not Agni, nor Destruction, nor the Foe overcome us; O Heaven and Earth, do not be angry with us, do not show contempt for us.

Rudra is being entreated: "May those enemies who are hostile toward us—not, while engaged in performing sacrifices, offer praise to me; lest the delighted Rudra, because of their enmity toward us, should inflict some deformity or some undesirable thing upon us. The meaning is: "May those who hate us not become performers of sacrifice. What then? May they perish by their own evil deeds. Do not fail us in our good guidance.

"O Sunīti," [is a vocative] formed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "O you who possess a beautiful method (of guidance). The sense is: "O you endowed with an excellent way, do not cause us to become offenders—that is, do not make us guilty of transgression. In the passage beginning with "mā no agniḥ," the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative; thus, "mā no agniḥ helate" means "may Agni not show contempt toward us"—the root *heḍ* meaning "to disregard"—that is, may he not direct anger or disdain toward us. In this same manner, the construction should be applied to "may Nirṛti and Arāti not show contempt," and likewise, "may Heaven and Earth not show contempt. Such is the syntactical connection to be made.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect us here; looking upon us with favor, you two friends, come toward us. May the powerful, auspicious, and well-guiding extension of the Ādityas—the protector of our oblation—choose us for protection.

Mitra is so called because he benefits all living beings; Varuṇa is the time of night, so named from *varaṇa*, meaning "enveloping" due to his envelopment with darkness. In this rite of concluding the vow (*vratasamāptikarman*), may Mitra and Varuṇa favor us and protect us. Of what nature are they? They are shining brightly with splendor, facing toward us, and are our friends.

Likewise, may the *prasṛti*—the spreading or the mass of rays belonging to the Ādityas—avoid (*parivṛṇaktu*) our oblation; that is to say, may it spare the sacrificial food and grain so that, due to its extreme brilliance, it does not burn the crops and other offerings. Since it is *hṛti*—so called because it carries away (*harati*) strength through its intensity—may it become *śivā*, auspicious and peaceful. Because it is *praṣṭhā*, meaning preeminent or foremost (according to the grammatical rule: *praṣṭho ’gragāmini*), the sense is that although it is fierce (*ugrā*), by virtue of this prayer it shall become tranquil.

The gray-haired one has swallowed the young moon as it fled in the assembly of many. Behold the poetic power of the god through his greatness: he who is equal [to all] has suddenly died in heaven. Rudra himself is praised here in the form of the Āditya (the Sun). Therefore, the ellipsis is "we offer oblations to these two.

Behold the poetic power (*kāvya*)—the act of traversing—of the shining god Āditya through his greatness (*mahitvā*); for by his stride, that which is capable of enduring (*sahyaḥ*), or the state of endurance (*sahanāhaḥ*) or co-existence (*sahabhāvaḥ*), the moon, being equal in its nature as vital energy (*ojas*), has died in heaven—that is, in the sky—at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), having relinquished its life-force.

Likewise, Yama Āditya—the gray-haired old man, or rather, the one who has swallowed from all sides—swallowed even the youth, the full-orbed and capable moon (*vidhu*), which was engaged in the act of moving (*vidhāvanakriyāyukta*) and therefore constantly fleeing (*dadrāṇa*). This occurred at the *samana*, the gathering of many, namely the rays of the sun or his own digits, on the full-moon day. The construction is: "even the youth."
Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā | Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā | Oṃ svaḥ svāhā | Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā.
His rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas, the Sun, so that everyone may behold him.
This has been explained.

"Beholding the light higher than darkness, we have gone to the god Sūrya among the gods, the highest light. This too has been explained. "Arise from our sacrifice, O divine one, with your gracious form, so that we may behold you with your splendor. Come, O Agni, with great and most brilliant rays, accompanied by excellent praises."

O you of the beautiful sacrifice (*svadhvara*), performer of the *pravargya* vow, arise, arise! The word *ud-* is for the purpose of completing the meter; rise up! Protect us with divine grace—that is, with the power belonging to the gods—and with great radiance, so that we may see [you].
O Agni, you too go forth, characterized by beautiful flames of valor and the like, and by excellent praises—meaning, distinguished by auspicious signs of praise.
Stand up erect for our protection like the god Savitṛ; standing erect as the winner of booty when we call upon you with ointments and shouts of "vāṣat."

We invoke you manifoldly; by what? By *añjibhiḥ*—by manifest words. Of what kind? By *vāghadbhiḥ*—meaning those that are uttered by the officiating priests (*voddhṛtamaiḥ*) and are capable of purification and so forth. The word *yat* is used in the sense of "because. Therefore, stand up; become upright. The particle *ū* is meaningless (anarthaka). [The word] *su*... [is used as an exclamation].

The prefix *upa-* is connected with the word *ūtaye*. For what purpose? So that you may stand upright for our beautiful protection (*sūtaye*). Like the divine Savitṛ—the particle *na* being used in the sense of comparison—just as the god Savitṛ, so do you stand upright as the winner (*sanitā*) of *vāja*, that is, food; [the root] *avan* (from *ava-ṣaṇa*) means "to bestow," thus you are the distributor.

"Return again with vigor; return again with food and with life-force. O Agni, being gratified by *ūrj*—that is, by the sacrificial butter characterized as food—return again; being gratified once more by *iṣ*, that is, by food characterized as boiled rice, and being endowed with life-force—that is, having increased through the oblation—return again. And furthermore, protect us, guard us from sin (*aṃhas*)."
Return with wealth, O Agni; swell with a stream that provides for all, on every side.

O Agni, turn back; even though our vows have been completed, do not go away, but remain with us along with prosperity and wealth. Furthermore, overflow [with abundance] and gladden us. By what? By a sustaining stream, by a supporting power. Of what kind? All-pervading (*viśvapnyā*), flourishing in the origin of all things, and situated above everything (*viśvatas pari*).
May Dhātṛ, the sovereign lord of the moving world, bestow wealth upon us; may he favor us with abundance.

You, O Dhātṛ, rule over progeny and also over wealth; you have created this entire world. You bestow abundant riches upon the donor. May we be masters of riches. *O Agni, [grant] long lives...* *O Agni, spread forth...* *Thou, O Agni, art ours...* *As such, do thou, O Agni, be ours...* *Vāyu was first among the cows...* These seven mantras have been explained.

With those teams by which you go toward the donor for the sake of sacrifice in his dwelling, O Vāyu—harness our chariot that brings excellent nourishment, and bestow upon us a hero and wealth consisting of cattle and horses! O Vāyu, with those teams of horses by which you go forth—you travel—to the donor, the sacrificer who offers the oblation; for what purpose? For the sake of sacrifice (*iṣṭaye*). The particle *accha* functions here in the sense of the word *abhi*; thus, "you go toward" (*abhigacchasi*).

With those teams (*niyudbhiḥ*), draw us toward you in our home (*duroṇe gṛhe*); [the root *yu* means "to mix," so] yoke us [to yourself]. Bestow upon our house wealth (*rayim*) consisting of excellent food (*subhojasam*), and bestow upon us a heroic son (*vīram*). Of what kind? One that is "cattle-like" (*gavyam*), excellent for cows, as well as "horse-like" (*aśvyam*) wealth and gain (*rādhaḥ*). The repetition is for the sake of emphasis; for in the case of repetition, people consider the meaning to be more intense, just as one says, "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful! (*aho ramaṇīyāho ramaṇīyā*).
Hiraṇyagarbha... He who [gave] breath... He who gave vigor... By whom [the worlds were measured]... He who [made] these two, heaven and earth... Of whom all this...
These six have been explained.

To whom both the crying worlds, supported by his work and trembling in spirit, looked up; whereon the risen sun shines forth—to which god shall we offer worship with oblation? The meaning of this verse beginning with "To whom both the crying worlds" (*yaṃ krandasī*) is as follows:

This [pair] is well known among ritualists as a designation for Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). Whereon the sun, the Āditya, has risen and shines forth—to that *Ka*, Prajāpati, the Self of All, let us offer worship with oblation; that is to say, let us present the oblation and serve him with the oblation.

The intended meaning is: we offer the oblation, characterized by clarified butter, to that Prajāpati, upon whom both Heaven and Earth—the two "kandasi," meaning those joined with crying and possessing the sound of deep thunder and Vedic recitation—beheld [all things] as free from evil (apasa) through their support; who, being established in truth, determine all effects; who, through the mind (manas), are supported by reflection and are unshaken (arejamāne), meaning motionless and stable; and upon whom everything is established.

From this point forward, the ritual release (*vimoka*) for peace (*śānti*) in the *pravargya* vow is established; it must also be performed here. We shall explain it: "O giver of life, give me life; O giver of breath, give me breath; O giver of out-breath, give me out-breath; O giver of in-breath, give me in-breath; O giver of sight, give me sight; O giver of hearing, give me hearing; O giver of luster, give me luster; restore life to us."

These are seven sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*). For all seven, there is a common syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*): "Give us back our life. [The subject] is either the Pravargya rite or Prajāpati, who is the performer of all rites. O Pravargya rite, or O Prajāpati, you are indeed the giver of life; therefore, grant me long life.

"Grant us life again"—by the word *āyuṣe*, which ends in the dative case denoting purpose (*tādarthya*), the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) characterized by longevity are indicated; the meaning is: "Grant me life again for the sake of performing the obligatory and occasional rites (*nityanaimittikakarman*). The direction [of application] is the same for all six of these Yajus formulas.
Homage to Rudra, who dwells in heaven, whose arrows are the rain; homage to you, homage in battle—do not harm me!

The Sun (Āditya) here is Rudra. "Salutation to Āditya. He who sits in heaven is *diviṣat*; salutations be repeatedly offered to him. To him whose raindrops are arrows—that is, to him whose shafts are the rain, the downpour, and the torrent—let there be repeated homage. And being propitiated by that salutation, may you, O Rudra, not harm me; do not kill me. The use of the second person pronoun *mā* (as an enclitic for *mām*) is intended to include those belonging to us; the meaning is: "do not harm my children and others as well. *Samare* means in battle or conflict.

Homage to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space, whose arrows are the winds; to him, [homage]. Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth, whose arrows are food; to him, [homage]. The same as before.

They mutter the section beginning with "Thou art the under-layer for the Brahman. While muttering, they gaze at the sun with the first verse addressed to Mitra, "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people," and they touch water with verses containing the word *ap* (water).

[The formulas are: "Thou art the under-layer for the Brahman; I spread thee as an under-layer for the Brahman. Thou art the dwelling-place (*vāstu*) of Iḷā; mayest thou be possessed of a dwelling-place; may he who hates us and whom we hate become devoid of a dwelling-place."

O water, you are the under-layer for the Brahman; having spread you as an under-layer, the Brahman creates the worlds from you, who have become the seed. As it has been said: "In the beginning, he created only water; then he cast his virility into them. This virility is the power (*śakti*) of water itself, which serves as the instrumental cause for all effects. I spread you as an under-layer for the Brahman; I touch you for the attainment of the state of Brahman. And I touch you for *ilā*; *ilā* is food, and that is to be sought even by one desiring the state of Brahman, because liberation (*apavarga*) is achieved through the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and other duties which are caused by that [food].

You are the dwelling-place (*vāstu*), you are the house, because you are the refuge of all; for Brahman, the possessor of the dwelling-place, indeed exists as your house and support. May I become possessed of a dwelling-place—here there is a change of person (from second to first)—meaning: by your grace may I become possessed of a dwelling-place, may I dwell in a home, and may I attain the state of Brahman (*brahmabhūya*). May he who hates us and whom we hate become homeless; may he be without a firm foundation.
You are the foundation; may you be my foundation; may he who hates us and whom we hate be without a foundation.
In you, O Water, upon whom the worlds are established, you are our support; therefore, may you be my support. But he who hates us and whom we hate, may he be without support.
O Vāta, blow hither the medicine; O Vāta, blow away whatever is harmful. For you, as the physician of all, move as the messenger of the gods.

O Vāta, bring hither—that is, cause us to attain—the medicine which is the fruit of good deeds, characterized by the attainment of Brahman; drive away that form of evil which is characterized by ignorance. Since you are the medicine for all, an antidote because you counteract the disease of *saṃsāra*, and since you move as the messenger of the gods, uniting them with the fruits consisting of the performance of ritual actions—for you are such—you are therefore so called. Since the treasure is deposited in your house, O Vāta, bestow it upon us so that we may live; grant us freedom from fear.

O Vāta, that treasure of yours which is deposited in the house of the possessor of treasure—from which the origin of the fruit of all actions arises—deposit for us from that [treasure] whatever portion belongs to our action. In the word *yatadaḥ*, the substitution of *t* for *d* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage; some, however, read it as *yadataḥ*. Those who study the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa also read it as *nidhir hi saḥ*.

The meaning here is that Prajāpati, who is the ordainer of all fruits, resides in your house as one who provides no refuge for you. For what purpose, then, do you not grant us our portion? "For the sake of living" (*jīvase*) means for the sake of life, that is, for the enjoyment of fruits such as heaven to be experienced for a very long time. Therefore, "grant us fearlessness" (*abhayaṃ kṛdhi*); grant us fearlessness regarding the action we perform—that is, effect the removal of the fear of the afflictions characterized by ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live, which constitute the darkness of saṃsāra.

They explain it thus: "O Vāta, from that fruit which is established in the house of you who strive, who exert yourself—bestow a portion thereof for our livelihood and for fearlessness. "O Aśvins, protect us with your auspicious blessings, day and night, through unharmed means. May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this."

O Aśvins, protect us on all sides; guard us with days—by what kind of days? By nights that are manifest, cloudless, and therefore auspicious, and by those that are *ariṣṭa*, meaning free from *riṣṭa* or harm. And whatever we do, may they honor it exceedingly (*māmahantām*). Who are they? Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu—the river and the ocean—and Earth as well as Heaven.

The earth is peace, the atmosphere is peace, the sky is peace, the quarters are peace, the waters are peace, the herbs are peace, the trees are peace. By this peace of yours, by all-encompassing peace, I bring peace for my two-footed and four-footed beings. May there be peace for us! You are peace; peace, peace, peace, peace!

"May the earth be peace for us"—this phrase "may [it] be" is to be supplied everywhere. And this supplied word "may it be" undergoes grammatical modification to agree with the plural endings of the subjects beginning with "the trees."

O Water, through you who are peace by nature and the nature of all peace, may I be endowed with peace—this is the ellipsis. Therefore, for my own sake (*svārtham*), for the sake of bipeds such as sons and others, and for the sake of quadrupeds such as cows and others, I bring about peace. Since you are peace, may there be peace for us; the meaning is that our afflictions, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), may be stilled. For one desiring liberation, the repetition "peace, peace, peace" is for the sake of emphasizing excellence and for the purpose of demonstrating that [the world] consists solely of the afflictions of *saṃsāra*.
Whether thou art sounded or unsounded, O Sarasvatī, be auspicious and most peaceful unto us; be very gracious, and let not thy sky be seen by us.

O Vāk Sarasvatī, you who are uttered aloud in the form of *vaikharī*, and you who are unuttered within in the forms of internal discourse and so forth—whether as *madhyamā*, *paśyantī*, or *sūkṣmā*—may you be auspicious (*śivā*) to us, bringing security; most peaceful (*śaṃtamā*), most blissful (*sukhatamā*), and most gracious (*sumṛlīkā*). The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of intensification.

"May I not see your void" (*mā te vyoma saṃdṛśi*): "void" (*vyoma*) means a gap or separation; the meaning is, "may I never, even for a moment, be deprived of you," and the further meaning is that I may know you in your uninterrupted state through divine vision.

I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra; I look closely at you with the eye of Mitra. I gaze upon you with the eye of Sūrya; I look closely at you with the eye of Sūrya. O Speech, I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra; I look closely at you with the eye of Mitra—meaning that I perceive you through the vision of Mitra. The same should be explained for Sūrya. Here, the prefix *abhi* denotes directness or facing toward.
Reciting the verse "Of Mitra, the supporter of people," he gazes at the sun while muttering the *maitrī* [formula]:
"The fame of the god Mitra, the supporter of people, is winning; his splendor possesses the most wonderful renown."

"I behold" (the remainder of the sentence)—the *śravaḥ* (glory), which is wealth characterized by rays, because it is the cause of food and so forth, belonging to Mitra, the Sun who causes universal delight. Of what sort is Mitra? "The supporter of men" (*carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*), meaning the sustainer of *carṣaṇis*, i.e., human beings; and "the god" (*devasya*), whose nature consists of luminosity and other divine qualities. Of what sort is this *śravaḥ*? "Winning" (*sānasi*), causing affection—the word *sānasi* is specifically prescribed in the *Uṇādi* list in the sense of affection. It is "resplendent" (*dyumnam*), meaning endowed with brilliance or possessed of glory, or else endowed with food.

And thus says the author of the Nirukta: "Dyumna is derived from the root *dyut* (to shine); it means glory or food. The term *citraśravastama* means "possessing most wonderful wealth. "The glory of the god Mitra, the sustainer of the people, is winning; it is true and possesses most wonderful renown."
He recites this by himself; here, the distinction is merely this much: that it is the truth.
The three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" have already been explained in the context of the ritual sprinkling.
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body, so that I may long behold the sun.

O Waters, you are my medicine; fulfill—complete—the beneficial work, such as the study of the Vedas and other duties. You alone are the protection, the home, and the refuge for my body. And through your grace, may I long behold the sun for a great length of time.
"May the goddesses be auspicious for our desire"—
this has already been explained.

May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us. May Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us, and may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. The meaning is: may Mitra and the others be of the nature of happiness and bestowers of happiness upon us. "Viṣṇu of the wide stride" means one whose stride is extended for the traversing of the three worlds.

May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us. May Indra and Agni be auspicious to us, and may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Herein lies the distinction regarding the verb "be" (*astu*) and the distinction regarding the deities. We invoke here for our well-being that Tārkṣya—the swift, the one impelled by the gods, the powerful, the overcomer of chariots, whose rim is uninjured, the conqueror of armies. We invoke that very Tārkṣya, Garuḍa, here into our presence; we call him hither. The particle *ū* is meaningless (used as an expletive).

*Ṣu* is the word *su* (well/excellent). We invoke the one with excellent speed (*suvājinam*), meaning beautiful motion; the one impelled by the gods (*devajūtam*), which is to say, the beloved cause of delight for the gods; the one possessing power (*sahovānam*)—*saha* being a name for strength—meaning the powerful one who overcomes even chariots, the deliverer (*tarutāram*); the one with unassailable rims (*ariṣṭanemim*), meaning whose course is unhurt; the conqueror of armies (*pṛtanājam*), meaning the victor over hostile forces; the swift one (*āśum*), meaning of rapid movement. For what purpose do we invoke him? For well-being (*svastaye*), that is, for non-destruction.
The three-verse hymn to Vāmadeva, beginning with "kayā naś citra," is recited solely for the purpose of pacification:
"By what aid will he come to us—he who is wondrous, our ever-increasing friend? By what most powerful assembly?"

O Indra, by what turn of action does your protection—the warding off of the afflictions of saṃsāra—become manifest on all sides? Wondrous; that is, wonderful and consisting of the supreme human goal (purushārtha). By what turn do the prosperities of all times become ever-increasing? "Friend" (*sakha*) is an epithet of this protection. "By the most powerful" (*śaciṣṭhayā*) is an epithet of "turn" (*vṛtā*), meaning by the most capable one. "Who among the true exhilarations is the most generous to intoxicate you, so that you may shatter even the darkness and bestow wealth?"

"O Indra," [the word] "you" (*tvām*) is to be supplied [after "indratvā"]; excluding you, who else is true—that is, whose resolve is infallible?
