Among those most exalted (*maṃhiṣṭhaḥ*)—that is, among those who are joyful by virtue of being worthy of the joy that consists of eternal bliss—who is most exalted, meaning most preeminently worthy of worship?

Therefore, who other than you is truly real—who, with a mind that is exceedingly firm (*dṛḍhā cit*), meaning with consciousness (*cit*) in the form of knowledge (*vidyā*), can "break apart" (*āruje*), that is, destroy, the "wealth" (*vasu*)—the power consisting of the impressions of beginningless ignorance—which belongs to "sin" (*aṃhasaḥ*), i.e., the intoxicating evil that causes the afflictions of saṃsāra? And who else is the "intoxicator" (*matsat*) of that sin? No one but you.

"Be truly our protector with your hundreds of aids, O friend of our singers. O Indra, be the protector of us who are good friends—those of excellent common renown—and the direct guardian (*abhya-vitā*) of those who praise you; "be" (*bhavāsi*) means "become" (*bhava*). The word "hundred" (*śata*) signifies great abundance; the meaning is: "be a protector with very many aids," that is, with acts of protection. *Bhavāsi* is the imperative form of the root *bhū*.

May the wise Sūrya, the bull with ruddy eyes, who rose from the great ocean in the eastern direction, shining resplendently in the midst of the moving expanse (the atmosphere), purify me with his mind through contemplation. May that wise Sūrya, consisting of knowledge, purify and cleanse me with his mind—that is, through reflection and meditation—who rose in the east from the vast ocean, shining intensely and blazing in the midst of the *sarira*, the path of movement, namely the intermediate space.

He is the showerer of desires, or rather, the bull, the most excellent among all lights. He has ruddy eyes, that is, red eyes or golden eyes. "May that which we have spoken as the Brahman not abandon me; salutations, salutations to the resplendent Sūrya!"

That Brahman which we have proclaimed and recited—may it not abandon me, may it not forsake me. Let there be repeated salutation to Sūrya, the one who shines with special brilliance. Peace and liberation.
From every single place, from here and there, all the waters have been pressed out; Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya together have fashioned them with their creative wisdom.

These supreme Upaniṣadic mantras are the ultimate secrets, supremely purifying, and generally effective everywhere as means for crossing the terrible ocean of saṃsāra; furthermore, even within the Pravargya rite, mantras such as "āpam āpam" are useful in the context of the peace-chant (śānti). Therefore, they must necessarily be explained here. Having placed water in a vessel, he praises it: "I have obtained all waters; I have obtained [them] repeatedly. The repetition is for the sake of emphasizing intensity.

"From this and that—from here and from there": "from this" is a reference to perceptible reservoirs of water such as rivers; "from there" is a designation for imperceptible sources. The repetition [of "from"] is for the sake of totality. All these waters, having been consolidated and stabilized by wisdom (*dhi*), were gathered together by means of intelligence (*prajñā*).
With wind-horses, lords of rays, whose nature is light and who are free from malice—these divine ones, wide-ranging through the world, have brought you forth with sons.

The horses are all-pervading like the wind. Who are they? They are the lords of the rays (*raśmipatayaḥ*), meaning the rays themselves are the lords or protectors. Furthermore, being embryos, the rays become clouds; therefore, they are of the nature of *marīci* (light-rays), meaning the waters exist within the *marīci*. They are "non-malicious" (*adruhaḥ*), meaning that although they reside within the midst of the light-rays in a subtle form, they are devoid of malice and non-injurious. They are the divine waters (*devīr āpaḥ*). They are the "producers" (*sūvarīḥ*) of the world, meaning they have the nature of giving birth to the worlds. They have given birth to these worlds (*asuvaḥ*).
For the protection of his sons—meaning for the protection of their individual souls—and for the sake of their refuge, that is, for the pacification of the afflictions of saṃsāra.
The Mahānāmnīs, the Mahāmānās, the Mahāyāmās, and the Mahāsomās—
these goddesses, born of Parjanya, grant this [child] to me so that I may possess sons.

Water is addressed with the *mahānāmnī* verses. These verses are called *mahānāmnī* because water is designated by that name; the meaning is that their name is "great" (*maha*), implying they possess great power. For this very reason, they are "of great honor" (*mahāmānā*), being endowed with vast reverence. They are "of great extent" (*mahāyāmā*), meaning they are of great dimension. Likewise, they are "the great Soma-pressings" (*mahāsomāsaḥ*), for it is by means of these very verses that the Soma becomes fit for sacrifice once it has been pressed. And being such as these, they are "producers of Parjanya," the rain-cloud.
Having made this one possessed of a son, impel this celibate student toward possessing a son; bring him to perfection so that he is fit for the procreation of sons.
Without attainment, without limit, without attainment, without end; without support, moving among men—without these, O Goddess, my blessings are of no avail.

The form *apaḥ* is the substitution for the genitive plural ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). *Snaṣṭiḥ* means "a part. The word *spṛśāmi* ("I touch") is to be supplied. Thus, the meaning is: "I touch a portion of the waters. For it has been stated that a portion of the water is drawn out and consecrated here. In this way, I touch the extracted protective portion of the waters; [I touch] the essence and strength of the waters. *Apāgham* refers to that which dwells within the waters; I touch—that is, I drive away—the *agham*, the evil, of the waters.

Regarding the existence of sin within the waters, he states the proof: "following after" (*anujāvarti*). The "followers" (*anujāḥ*) of the waters are the individual souls (*jīvātman*), because they are produced from them; the presence of sin—that is, impurity—within them indicates its persistence in the cause as well, just as fragrance and other qualities residing in a jar and such are present in the lump of clay. Therefore, having removed the existing sin from these [waters] by means of purificatory mantras, one should perform purification for rites such as propitiation (*śānti*). "Maidens dear to me, dear to my *ṛta*, and dear to my sacrifice and truth. Alternatively: "The maidens, the waters, are dear to me; just as the sacrifice (*yajña*) is dear to me, so is *ṛta*—or the word 'truth' (*satya*)—dear to me."
O goddesses, you have risen as the Vajra; O divine mothers, you have risen as Varuṇa; O goddesses, you have risen as the Ādityas. Rise up from the womb!
May you arise like a thunderbolt for the warding off of evil;

for you are the suns of Varuṇa, the god who removes defects. O goddesses, rise upward—meaning, accomplish that which is most excellent—for him who performs the rites, vows, and other desired acts of the Ādityas. This is by means of the womb, that is, by the power of the Supreme Brahman which is the cause of your own birth.
Mantras such as these possess great power and are useful for pacification and liberation.

"O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With steady limbs and bodies, may we, offering praise, attain that lifespan ordained by the gods. Such are the *japa* mantras useful for pacification (*śānti*). O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious—that which is praiseworthy and beneficial, such as the Vedānta and other scriptures culminating in the attainment of Brahman. O Holy Ones, protectors of those who sacrifice, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.

Likewise, being characterized by firm and indestructible limbs such as hands and feet, and offering praise—praising that life which is beneficial to the gods and established among the gods—we may attain it specifically with our bodies, our physical forms.

May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being. Indra of far-reaching fame—one whose wealth is increased, whose riches are manifold—may he grant us well-being, that is, security from destruction; he shall give or maintain it for us. Likewise, may Pūṣan, the son of Aditi, the omniscient knower of all, grant us well-being.

May Tārkṣya, Garuḍa, and Ariṣṭanemi—"*Ariṣṭi*" being the act of harming—[he whose] *nemi*, or rim/abode/place, is *ariṣṭa*, meaning unhurt; thus, one whose station is unharmed. Alternatively, *nemi* means the edge or limit; [thus, one] whose boundary is unharmed, meaning he has not been transgressed by anyone. And may Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, bestow or maintain *svasti* (well-being) upon us.
The ruddy rays, accompanied by the people, girdled by the wind, have established themselves in a hundredfold manner; yea, in a thousandfold manner.

Those known as the *ketus*, who are of a reddish (aruṇa) color and are knowers, are established in the *vātamekhalā* [the wind-girdle] in a hundred ways (*śatadhā*) and are well-composed; having experienced stability in meditative absorption (*samādhi-sthairya*) and other qualities within their bodies, they have thereafter attained liberation—this is the meaning. The syllable *ya* in the word *śatadhāya* is meaningless. Alternatively, it is *sahasradhāya*; that is, "in a thousand ways" (*sahasradhā*), meaning that liberation is obtained after a very long time. And thus says the Smṛti: "By means of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and the ritual sacrifices (*yajña*), this body is made fit for Brahman (*brāhmī kriyate tanuḥ*)."
May the divine waters, the plants, and the trees be auspicious and most peaceful for us.
May you be auspicious to us—blessing us with security—and most peaceful, bringing us the greatest happiness.

"O Sarasvatī, be very gracious; may I not behold your void in my sight. With this [verse], one touches the ground. O Sarasvatī, possessor of water, be very gracious—that is, a bestower of great happiness—and may I not behold your void, a rupture or calamity caused by robbers and the like. Thus ends the commentary on the Aruṇa-mantra.

The vow of the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin) has been declared; now the meaning of the mantra is being explained. Among the fifteen sections (anuvākas) renowned as Upaniṣads in the *Śatādhyayana*, the first, eleventh, and twelfth have application here. Of these, the first is for the pacification of obstacles, the eleventh for the instruction of the disciple, and the twelfth also for pacification. Therein, first, regarding the first and the twelfth:

May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us. May Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us, and may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutations to Brahman; salutations to Vāyu. Homage to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the manifest Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the manifest Brahman; I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Peace, peace, peace.

In this context, Mitra and the others are the internal deities (*adhyātmika-devatā*). Thus says the Śruti: "The world, the *sūtra*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, are either the manifestations (*vivarta*) or the transformations (*pariṇāma*) of the Supreme Self; the deities presiding over them are Mitra and the rest. Likewise, the specific deity who presides over the eye is Amā. Aryamā is he who restrains (*niyacchati*) our enemies—those who oppose our Vedic study and other such duties. May Mitra be our friend (*mitra*); may he bring us peace (*śam*), that is, may he produce happiness for us. This same logic should be applied to Varuṇa and the others as well. Viṣṇu is the all-pervading inner controller (*antaryāmī*), whose stride is wide—that is, whose step is vast.

Salutation to Brahman; let there be homage to the Supreme Self. Likewise, let there be homage to Vāyu, who is of the nature of wind and who serves as the thread of the universe. O Vāyu, salutations to you! Having praised him indirectly, he now praises him directly: O Vāyu, you alone are the manifest Brahman; rising from the navel, you alone evolve or transform yourself in the form of the Vedas—this is the meaning. Therefore, I shall speak of you alone as the manifest Brahman, since you alone are the manifest Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as *ṛta* and as truth.

In this context, knowledge and action—which constitute the means to liberation—are expressed by the word *ṛta*, while their procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is expressed by the word *satya*. Alternatively, since the words *ṛta* and *satya* have the same meaning, the repetition is for the sake of emphasis. May that *ṛta* and that *satya* protect me; may they protect the speaker. The repetition is as before. Alternatively, "may they protect me" refers to the speaker, and the "teacher" refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). "Peace, peace, peace"—the ellipsis is "let there be [the cessation] of obstacles."
The triple recitation is for the sake of excellence, because of the great abundance of obstacles in saṃsāra. This is the first section (anuvāka).

May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious, may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Agni be auspicious to us, and may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Homage to Brahman! Homage to Vāyu! Salutations to you, O Vāyu; you alone are the perceptible Brahman. To you alone as the perceptible Brahman have I spoken; I have spoken the eternal; I have spoken the truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. It has protected me; it has protected the speaker. Peace! Peace! Peace! In this [section], from the first [verse] onwards, only the deity is specified, and the action is in the past tense.
May he protect us both; may he nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be powerful; may we not hate each other. Peace! Peace! Peace!

This [is said] when the disciple and the preceptor speak together; otherwise, it may also be between a husband and wife. May the host of deities beginning with Mitra protect (*avatu*) us two—the disciple and the preceptor—who are the objects of the action, as we stand together; likewise, may they nourish (*bhunaktu*), that is, preserve or feed us, with the fruit of liberation (*apavarga*) whose nature is eternal bliss. And while standing together, may they grant us vigor (*vīrya*) characterized by extreme purity, which arises from the study of the Vedas.

"Let us both recite; let us perform [this rite]. May we two be resplendent, such that neither can be overcome by anyone. Whatever has been studied, may that remain firm for us both. Let us not hate one another; may there be no mutual enmity between us. Thus "peace" (*śānti*) is explained. Having thus performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) at the point of insertion, the teacher should cause the student—who desires both intelligence and non-forgetfulness—to recite this *dvaya*.

May Indra, the bull of the meters (*chandas*), who possesses all knowledge and has arisen from the immortal meters, endow me with wisdom. May I become a bearer of the Veda of the immortal. May my body be discerning, and may my speech yield honey. With my two ears, may I hear much that is auspicious. I am the treasury of the sacred word (*brahman*), covered by wisdom; protect what I have heard. From the mere recitation of these mantra-verses, one obtains the fruit of wisdom and other benefits: the power of retention and the quality of not forgetting. One attains that very capacity.

He who is the bull—the showerer or the preeminent one—of the *chandasaḥ*, the Vedas; who is *oṃkāra*; who is *viśvavedāḥ*, the all-knowing or the possessor of all wealth; he has emerged as the immortal form from the *chandasaḥ*, that is, from the Upanishads (*vedānta*). The meaning is that one who has fallen into duality through the power of ignorance becomes, by means of the practice of the meaning of the Upanishads—or by the practice of the meaning of all the Vedas, or by the combination of knowledge and action—the supreme immortal form, the nature of eternal bliss and non-duality. That Indra, Prajāpati, [endows] me with wisdom (*medhā*).

May it satisfy and gladden me. For the sake of immortality—that is, for liberation—may I be endowed with the power to retain the Vedas; even the quality of not forgetting is mentioned here. Likewise, may my body be *vicakṣaṇa*, skillful in the performance of the means to liberation. And may my speech, joined with the Veda, milk—that is, yield—the sweet-flavored fruit of action. With both ears, may I hear for a long time much (*bhūri*) and well-heard (*suśrava*), that which is the form of the Vedānta.

"May I be the treasury of Brahman—that is, the storehouse for the collection of jewels consisting of the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda. And since a storehouse is covered by a lid, he says: "It is closed, that is, covered and protected, by *medhā*—by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by wisdom—so that, through the power of firm impressions, the meaning of the Veda is not forgotten. 'Protect what has been heard by me' means: guard my learning and act so as to employ it for the benefit of others."
One desiring prosperity (*śrī*) should offer oblations with the verses beginning with "āvahantī vitanvānā":
"Bringing [wealth], spreading [it out], and securing for herself what is most excellent—O Vāc, increase my garments, my cows, and my food and drink."
Bring prosperity to me, together with woolly livestock; svāhā!
One should offer two oblations with these two, the *Ṛc* and the *Yajus*; according to some, only one, because there is a single utterance of "svāhā" at the end of both the *Ṛc* and the *Yajus*.

Other oblations here are to be performed with feminine forms as explained previously. O Śrī, increase my garments, my cows, and my food and drink. What is she doing? Bringing them forth—conveying and presenting them. Spreading them out—extending them variously and specifically. And making for herself a choice—making excellent and desirable things such as jewels, gold, and so forth her own.

Therefore, bring prosperity to me, since I am one who has properly studied the Veda, or one who is a distinguished supplicant arrived at a time when the teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must necessarily be paid. For that reason, [bring] *lomaśām*—[the cow] adorned with hairy goats, sheep, and so forth, along with livestock such as horses and the like. They say this is stated for the *upakurvāṇaka* (the student still under training). One desiring glory should offer oblations with the eight verses beginning with "May they come to me.
Whether the teacher performs the sacrifice or the student himself, in both cases the fruit belongs to the student, because the rite is performed for his sake.

May the students of sacred knowledge come to me; svāhā! May the students of sacred knowledge gather together with me; svāhā! The glory of ascetic heat, the glories of glory; svāhā! The glory of people, the glories of glory; svāhā! O Bhaga, I enter into you; svāhā! O Bhaga, enter into me; svāhā! O Vasu, being superior, the glory of glory; svāhā! In you, who have a thousand branches, may I be distributed; I cleanse myself in you; svāhā!
"May those qualities and accomplishments belonging to celibates come to me. Thus is Prajāpati entreated; and for that purpose:

May it be well-offered! May those who are my spiritual companions (*brahmacārin*), as well as my kinsmen, restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, thus come to me in the right manner. Regarding the term *tapo-yaśo-yaśāni*: austerities themselves are the various forms of glory; thus, "the glories that are austerities" (*tapo-yaśo-yaśāni*). May these glories of austerity come together—the reduplication being according to the rule "in the sense of variety, [there is] doubling of a word denoting a quality. And for that purpose, may there be a well-offering. Or, the meaning is: may those various forms of glory that exist in the world of austerity (*tapas-loka*) or in a particular heaven come together. In this same way, *jano-yaśo-yaśāni svāhā* is to be explained.

"Enter thee as Bhaga"—O Bhaga, O adorable Brahman, I enter into thee. "Enter me as Bhaga"—O Bhaga, do thou enter into me. "More excellent, O Vasu, fame upon fame, Svāhā!"—O Vasu, O bestower of wealth, thou art more excellent and highly praiseworthy; therefore, by thy grace, may glories enter into me, and for that purpose, may this be well-offered.

"In this [text] consisting of a thousand [verses], in this Yajurveda with its many branches, or in the path of the *Brahmavibhava Upaniṣad*, divide it; make me one who possesses the yoga of division. O Brahman, when you have become the object [of my devotion], I cleanse myself within you—I purify myself, making myself free from all impurity and dissolved in Brahman. For that purpose, may this be well-offered. This task is to be performed at the conclusion of the ritual procedure (*paddhati*)."

Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil with this eleventh section of the Upaniṣads: "This must be done; this must not be done. The eleventh section is as follows: "Speak the truth. Practice virtue. Do not neglect your private study of the Veda. Having brought wealth that is pleasing to your teacher, do not let the thread of progeny be broken. One must not swerve from the truth. One must not swerve from virtue. One must not swerve from effort. One must not swerve from what is beneficial."

One must not neglect the private recitation of the Vedas and their exposition. One must not neglect sacrifices and the rites performed for the gods and ancestors. Be one to whom the mother is a god; be one to whom the father is a god; be one to whom the teacher is a god; be one to whom the guest is a god. Whatever actions are blameless, those alone should be performed by you, and not others. Furthermore, whatever good conduct has been practiced by us, that should be performed by you, and not others.

Now, whatever Brahmins who are superior to us might come, you should honor them with a seat. One should give with faith or give without faith; one should give with deliberation or give without deliberation; one should give out of shame or give out of fear; one should give for the sake of prosperity or give for the sake of non-prosperity.

Now, if you should have any doubt regarding ritual action or doubt regarding livelihood, then as those Brahmins there who are reflective, disciplined, diligent, free from blemish, free from greed, and lovers of dharma conduct themselves in that matter, so should you conduct yourself toward them. Furthermore, regarding those who are falsely accused, as those Brahmins there who are reflective, disciplined, diligent, free from blemish, free from greed, and lovers of dharma conduct themselves in that matter, so should you conduct yourself therein.
This is the instruction, this is the teaching, this is the secret doctrine of the Veda, this is the admonition; this is to be meditated upon.

This is stated precisely after one has studied the *Upaniṣat-saṃhitā*. At the conclusion of the study of the Upaniṣads, the teacher causes the student to grasp the principles set forth in the eleven sections (*anuvākas*). For this very reason, the sage Jaimini declared: "Immediately after the study of the Veda, the inquiry into Dharma must be undertaken. Indeed, at the very commencement of the eleventh section, there exists the scriptural authority (*śruti*) stating, "Having taught the Veda," which serves as the foundational source. For it is only the logic arising from the Veda that constitutes valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding this, it is said: "He who investigates the instruction on Dharma with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows Dharma, and no one else. However, fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*) that is not rooted in the Vedas and is conceived merely by human intellect is not an authority concerning Dharma and Adharma, such as the systems of the Buddhists and the followers of Bṛhaspati. Concerning this, it is stated:

"The Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstra of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs, and medical science—these four are established by authority and must not be undermined by mere reasoning. "Reasoning is unstable, the Smṛtis are diverse, and there is no sage whose opinion is not divided.
The true nature of Dharma is hidden in a cave; the path is that which has been trodden by great men."
"Like a blind man by means of the touch of his hand," it is said.

O student (*brahmacārin*), speak the truth; yet truth culminates in the benefit of others. Even untruth may sometimes be spoken which has the fruit of truth, by which the killing of a Brahmin and so forth is prevented. As it has been stated:

"One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant; and one should speak an untruth that is pleasant—this is the eternal dharma. Practice dharma; perform the prescribed duties, conduct, and observances. Do not neglect your private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*); do not commit the negligence regarding *svādhyāya*, such as failing to study due to laziness or other causes.

Having brought the desired wealth for the purpose of the teacher’s fee (*ācāryadakṣiṇā*), one should not cause the severance of the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth; the meaning is that one should perform the marriage after giving the fee to the guru. Neglect (*pramāda*) regarding truth is the speaking of untruth. Neglect regarding duty (*dharma*)—characterized as obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)—is its non-performance. Regarding optional (*kāmya*) rites, however, it is both their defective performance and their non-performance. Likewise, neglect regarding effort is being impaired by laziness and the like.

Virtue consists of protecting the body and so forth; negligence in this regard occurs when one fails to maintain health even when free from fear, or fails to perform rites for its pacification. *Svastya-ayana* (the rite for well-being) is the daily form of pacification prescribed for the *vaiśvadeva* and other such ceremonies. One must not be negligent regarding *svādhyāya* (Vedic study); even if one has mastered the Veda through teaching and recitation, it must be further refined and continued to be taught. Likewise, one must not be negligent—characterized by non-performance—regarding sacrifices, such as the *pākayajña* and others. He for whom his mother is like a god...

"Be one for whom the mother is a deity. You must perform only those actions that are blameless and beyond reproach, never others. Even those acts prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* which are censured by the world—such as entering a *purāṇa*, seeking liberation [through improper means], or residing [in forbidden places]—must be avoided. Furthermore, you should practice only the virtuous conduct and deeds of our gurus, their wives, children, and so forth, and not others.

Even those actions performed and practiced by virtuous gurus which cause delusion must not be followed with faith, such as Viśvāmitra’s eating of dog-meat—the lowest of foods—and his officiating at sacrifices for Caṇḍālas. Likewise, whatever Brahmins may come who are significantly superior to me in age, learning, and other qualities, they should be honored by offering them one's own seat; "honoring" consists of providing a seat, massaging their feet, and relieving their fatigue by removing their exhaustion.

The meaning is that one should perform [the act] according to the prescribed characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), but one must not, out of pride, undertake such things as public displays of ostentation; it should be given with *śraddhā*—that is, with a mind of faith and conviction. However, sometimes it may even be given without faith for the sake of avoiding public reproach. When a large number of people have gathered together and a collective gift is proposed regarding matters such as singing and the like, it means that one may give even without faith in order to avoid being known as unacquainted with established custom. 1. By reason of possessing much wealth, etc.

Alternatively, there is an elision of the vowel *a* in the word *aśraddhayā*, meaning "without faith. *Saṃvit* refers to a promise made for the sake of supporting dependents and others, such as: "This shall be given by me. The meaning is that it should be given according to that promise. Even without such a promise (*asaṃvidā*), one should give upon seeing the skill of the recipient's work. Furthermore, even in times of poverty, one should give—according to one's capacity and out of a sense of shame—to relatives, kinsmen, petitioners, or guests, such as speech, land, grass, water, and so forth.

The offerings of oblations (*bali*) and other gifts previously intended for the fierce deities such as the Nāgas, Vināyakas, and Durgā should be given out of fear that they might otherwise invade [the house]. They should be given for the sake of *vitti*—where there is wealth (*vitta*), there is purpose (*prayojana*). And sometimes they should be given even for the sake of *avitti*. Sometimes they should also be given for the sake of *bhūti*, meaning prosperity or power. Or rather, this entire passage is a restatement of the injunction "it should be given with faith" (*śraddhayā deyam*), intended for the purpose of praise.

Thus, for one who abides by the meaning of the Vedas, if at any time a doubt should arise regarding certain Vedic rituals, or regarding one's conduct (*vṛtti*)—that is, the means of livelihood and the acquisition of wealth—as to what should be accepted from this [person] and what should not, then that doubt must be dispelled by those Brāhmaṇas who reside in that same region where you live. What kind of Brāhmaṇas?

They are skilled in right reflection, disciplined, and possessed of unimpaired faculties; they are dedicated, intent on performance, gentle, and not of cruel mind—this same meaning applies even if the reading is *arūkṣāḥ* (not harsh); they are not greedy, not covetous, and free from greed. Or they may be seekers of dharma—if they are indeed seekers of dharma, you should proceed in that very manner as they do in their professional conduct and so forth, and from that alone you should make your decision. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, when questioned by another teacher, you must provide instruction according to the truth as the facts require. However, do not cause confusion or contradiction in the minds of those who are there accused—meaning those whose intellects are directly opposed [to the truth]. Rather, you should conduct yourself with propriety (*saṃvṛtti*) in such a way that those Brāhmaṇas possessing the aforementioned qualities may proceed as they should. "Accused" (*abhyākhyātāḥ*) means those who are openly proclaimed, such as ministers and others.

That which is this my teaching is an injunction (*ādeśa*), the command of a righteous king or similar authority; it is an instruction (*upadeśa*) based on the Vedas that culminates in welfare, or specifically the secret essence (*rahasya*) of the Upaniṣads—meaning it must be practiced as such through the absence of transgression, by force, by greed, and by the proclamation of its secrecy. Thus end the forest observances (*āraṇyaka-vratas*).
Thus ends the forty-third chapter. 43.
